That is why their lifetime is short. **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)** lets supporting resources (Graph, Exchange, SharePoint, and others) reject tokens almost immediately after events such as a disabled account or password change, which is why CAE-aware clients can safely receive longer-lived tokens.
- **Refresh tokens are revoked** by password changes, admin revocation (`revokeSignInSessions`), or inactivity, and they are bound to the client that received them.
- **Never log or store tokens in plain text.** Treat refresh tokens like passwords.

**Example: the token response, and using a refresh token**

```json
// Response from POST /oauth2/v2.0/token (authorization_code grant)
{
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "scope": "api://9f2c.../Orders.Read",
  "expires_in": 4473,                                  // seconds until the access token expires
  "ext_expires_in": 4473,
  "access_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...",   // for the orders API
  "refresh_token": "1.AXEAv4j5cvGGr0GRqy180BHbR...",        // opaque; store securely
  "id_token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs..."       // for the client
}
```

```python
import requests

def refresh(tenant: str, client_id: str, refresh_token: str, scope: str) -> dict:
    """Exchange a refresh token for a new access token (and usually a new refresh token)."""
    resp = requests.post(
        f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token",
        data={
            "client_id": client_id,
            "grant_type": "refresh_token",
            "refresh_token": refresh_token,
            "scope": scope,                  # may be a DIFFERENT resource than the original token
        },
        timeout=10,
    )
    body = resp.json()
    if "error" in body:
        # invalid_grant: expired/revoked refresh token, so the user must sign in interactively again
        raise RuntimeError(f"{body['error']}: {body.get('error_description')}")
    return body   # always persist the NEW refresh_token: refresh tokens rotate

# Same refresh token, two different APIs
orders_token = refresh("contoso.onmicrosoft.com", "1111-...", rt, "api://9f2c.../Orders.Read")
graph_token = refresh("contoso.onmicrosoft.com", "1111-...", rt, "https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read")
```

In real applications MSAL performs these refreshes automatically from its token cache (see 2.3). The raw call is shown so you can recognize it in network traces.

**Key takeaways**

- ID token: for the client, proves sign-in. Access token: for one API, sent as a bearer token. Refresh token: for the authorization server, used to get new access tokens.
- Clients must treat access tokens as opaque. Only the target API validates them.
- Access tokens are short-lived because they cannot normally be revoked. CAE allows near-real-time revocation for supporting services.
- Refresh tokens rotate and are long-lived credentials: store them securely and always save the newest one.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Paste an ID token and an access token from the same sign-in into a local JWT decoder (for example, `jwt.ms` or a short script) and compare their `aud`, `exp`, and claims.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use a refresh token to obtain tokens for two different resources. Then revoke your sessions (`az rest --method POST --uri https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/me/revokeSignInSessions`) and try the refresh again. Record the error.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A developer wants to send the ID token to their backend API because it already contains the user's name. What is wrong with that?" *Hint:* audience validation, scopes, and what the API is actually authorizing.

#### JWT Structure and Validation

When an API receives `Authorization: Bearer eyJ...`, it has to decide whether to trust it without calling Entra ID on every request. That works because Entra ID tokens are **JSON Web Tokens (JWTs)**: self-contained, digitally signed documents. Anyone can read a JWT, but only the holder of the private key can produce a valid signature, so the API can verify the token locally using Entra ID's public keys.

Analogy: a banknote. Anyone can read what is printed on it, but its security features (the signature) prove it was issued by the central bank. A shop checks the features rather than calling the bank for each note.

A JWT has three base64url-encoded parts separated by dots: `header.payload.signature`.

```text
 eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1Qi...  .  eyJhdWQiOiI5ZjJj...  .  NHVaYe26MbtOYhSKkoKY...
 +------------------+    +-----------------+    +-------------------------+
 | Header           |    | Payload (claims)|    | Signature               |
 | typ: JWT         |    | aud, iss, exp,  |    | RS256(                  |
 | alg: RS256       |    | oid, tid, scp,  |    |   base64url(header) +   |
 | kid: key id ---------> picks the public key from jwks_uri to verify     |
 +------------------+    | roles, ...      |    |   "." + base64url(body))|
                         +-----------------+    +-------------------------+
```

Common claims in Entra ID access tokens:

| Claim | Meaning | Validate? |
|---|---|---|
| `aud` | Audience: the API this token is for (client ID GUID in v2 tokens, often App ID URI in v1 tokens) | Yes, must be your API |
| `iss` | Issuer: `https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tid>/v2.0` (v2) or `https://sts.windows.net/<tid>/` (v1) | Yes |
| `exp`, `nbf`, `iat` | Expiry, not-before, issued-at (Unix seconds) | Yes, with small clock skew |
| `tid` | Tenant that issued the token | Yes for multi-tenant APIs |
| `oid` | Object ID of the user or service principal | Use as the identity key |
| `sub` | Pairwise subject, unique per user and app | Optional identity key |
| `azp` / `appid` | Client ID of the calling app (v2 / v1) | Optional: allow-list calling apps |
| `scp` | Delegated scopes granted (space-separated) | Yes, for user tokens |
| `roles` | App roles granted to the user or app | Yes, for app-only tokens or role-based checks |
| `ver` | Token version: `1.0` or `2.0` | Informational |

The token version your API receives is set by the API's own registration (`api.requestedAccessTokenVersion`), not by the client. Set it to `2` for new APIs so that `iss` and `aud` are predictable.

**Validation checklist** for an API:

1. Parse the header. Accept only expected algorithms (`RS256`). Never accept `alg: none`.
2. Fetch signing keys from the tenant's `jwks_uri` and cache them. Select the key by `kid`. Entra ID rotates keys regularly, so refresh the cache when an unknown `kid` appears instead of hardcoding keys.
3. Verify the signature.
4. Check `iss` (and `tid` for multi-tenant), `aud`, `exp`, and `nbf`.
5. Authorize: check `scp` or `roles` for the operation being performed.

Do not try to validate tokens that are not addressed to you. For example, access tokens for Microsoft Graph contain extra processing in the header that makes signature validation fail outside Graph. That is expected: only Graph needs to validate them.

**Example: decode (inspection only) versus validate (trust)**

```python
import base64, json

def peek(token: str) -> dict:
    """Decode the payload WITHOUT verifying it. For debugging only. Never trust the result."""
    payload_b64 = token.split(".")[1]
    payload_b64 += "=" * (-len(payload_b64) % 4)          # restore base64 padding
    return json.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(payload_b64))
```

```python
# pip install "pyjwt[crypto]"
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient

TENANT_ID = "72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47"
API_CLIENT_ID = "9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001"   # aud for v2 tokens

# One client per process: it caches the signing keys and refetches on unknown kid
jwks_client = PyJWKClient(
    f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}/discovery/v2.0/keys",
    cache_keys=True,
)

def validate_access_token(token: str, required_scope: str) -> dict:
    signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)   # matches the header's kid
    claims = jwt.decode(
        token,
        signing_key.key,
        algorithms=["RS256"],                                    # pin the algorithm
        audience=API_CLIENT_ID,                                  # aud check
        issuer=f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}/v2.0",  # iss check
        leeway=60,                                               # tolerate 60 s clock skew
        options={"require": ["exp", "iat", "nbf", "iss", "aud"]},
    )
    scopes = claims.get("scp", "").split()
    if required_scope not in scopes:                             # authorization, not just authentication
        raise PermissionError(f"Missing scope {required_scope}")
    return claims
```

In production web frameworks, prefer the platform's middleware (`Microsoft.Identity.Web` in ASP.NET Core, `jose` or `jwks-rsa` with `jsonwebtoken` in Node.js, or App Service Easy Auth) over hand-written validation. The code above shows what that middleware does.

**Key takeaways**

- A JWT is `header.payload.signature`. Anyone can decode it, but only the signature makes it trustworthy.
- Validate signature (key from `jwks_uri` selected by `kid`), algorithm, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`/`nbf`, and then authorize with `scp` or `roles`.
- Cache signing keys and handle key rotation. Never hardcode keys.
- Set `requestedAccessTokenVersion` to 2 on your API registration, and do not attempt to validate tokens meant for other APIs such as Graph.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Decode a token with the `peek` function and identify which claims tell you the user, the tenant, the calling app, and the expiry time in local time.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write tests for `validate_access_token` that confirm it rejects an expired token, a token for a different audience, and a token signed with an unknown key (generate your own RSA key pair to forge one).
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your API validates tokens correctly for weeks, then suddenly rejects all of them with 'signature verification failed'. What happened?" *Hint:* key rotation and how the API obtains its keys.

#### Scopes, Permissions, and Consent

An access token should grant only what the app needs. If a calendar app only needs to read your calendar, it should not get a token that can also delete your mail. **Permissions** describe these fine-grained capabilities, **scopes** are how a client asks for them, and **consent** is the record that someone with authority approved them.

There are two types of permission:

| | Delegated permissions | Application permissions |
|---|---|---|
| Acts as | The signed-in user, through the app | The app itself; no user |
| Token claim | `scp` (space-separated) | `roles` (array) |
| Effective access | The intersection of what the app was granted and what the user can do | Everything the permission allows, across the whole tenant |
| Who can consent | The user (if tenant policy allows), or an admin | Always an admin |
| Flows | Auth code, OBO, device code | Client credentials |
| Example | Graph `Mail.Read`: read *the signed-in user's* mail | Graph `Mail.Read` (application): read *every mailbox* in the tenant |

**Scope strings** combine a resource identifier and a permission:

- `api://9f2c.../Orders.Read`: the `Orders.Read` scope of your API.
- `User.Read`: shorthand for `https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read`. Graph is the default resource.
- `https://storage.azure.com/user_impersonation`: delegated access to Azure Storage.
- `<resource>/.default`: "all permissions that have already been configured and consented for this app on this resource". It is required for client credentials and is common for OBO and managed identities.

**Consent** models:

- **Static consent**: permissions listed in the app registration's API permissions are consented up front (with `.default`).
- **Dynamic and incremental consent**: the app requests additional scopes at runtime, when the user first uses a feature that needs them. For example, request `Calendars.Read` only when the user opens the calendar page.
- **User consent**: the user approves delegated, low-risk permissions for themselves. Many tenants restrict this to verified publishers and low-impact permissions, or disable it entirely.
- **Admin consent**: an administrator approves for the whole tenant. This is required for application permissions and for high-privilege delegated permissions (for example, `User.Read.All`).

```text
 Client requests scope=api://orders/Orders.Read Calendars.Read
            |
            v
 Already consented? --yes--> issue token with scp="Orders.Read Calendars.Read"
            | no
            v
 Permission requires admin? --yes--> "Need admin approval" (or admin consent workflow)
            | no
            v
 Tenant allows user consent for this app/permission? --no--> blocked
            | yes
            v
 Show consent prompt --> user accepts --> grant stored on the service principal
```

**Example: configure, consent, and enforce permissions**

```bash
GRAPH_API=00000003-0000-0000-c000-000000000000          # Microsoft Graph's well-known app ID

# Delegated permission User.Read (=Scope) for a web app
az ad app permission add --id "$WEB_APP_ID" --api "$GRAPH_API" \
  --api-permissions e1fe6dd8-ba31-4d61-89e7-88639da4683d=Scope

# Application permission User.Read.All (=Role) for a daemon
az ad app permission add --id "$DAEMON_APP_ID" --api "$GRAPH_API" \
  --api-permissions df021288-bdef-4463-88db-98f22de89214=Role

# Admin consent for everything configured on the daemon (requires an admin role)
az ad app permission admin-consent --id "$DAEMON_APP_ID"

# See what has actually been granted
az ad app permission list-grants --id "$WEB_APP_ID" -o table
```

```python
from functools import wraps

def require(scope: str | None = None, role: str | None = None):
    """Authorize based on the validated token: delegated scope OR application role."""
    def decorator(handler):
        @wraps(handler)
        def wrapper(claims: dict, *args, **kwargs):
            scopes = claims.get("scp", "").split()   # present on delegated (user) tokens
            roles = claims.get("roles", [])          # present on app-only tokens and for user app roles
            if (scope and scope in scopes) or (role and role in roles):
                return handler(claims, *args, **kwargs)
            raise PermissionError("403: insufficient permissions")
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@require(scope="Orders.Read", role="Orders.ReadWrite.All")
def list_orders(claims: dict):
    if "scp" in claims:
        return f"orders owned by user {claims['oid']}"   # delegated: limit to the user's data
    return "all orders"                                   # app-only: tenant-wide access
```

**Key takeaways**

- Delegated permissions (`scp`) act as the user and are limited by the user's own rights. Application permissions (`roles`) act as the app across the tenant and always need admin consent.
- Scope strings are `<resource>/<permission>`. `/.default` means "everything already configured for this resource" and is mandatory for client credentials.
- Use incremental consent to request permissions only when a feature needs them.
- An API must check `scp` or `roles` for each operation. A valid token alone is not authorization.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For each Graph permission, say whether it is delegated or application and whether it needs admin consent: `User.Read`, `User.Read.All` (delegated), `Mail.Send` (application).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a test app that requests `User.Read` at sign-in and `Calendars.Read` only when a "Show calendar" button is clicked. Observe the second consent prompt and the change in the `scp` claim.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why might an app work in your development tenant but fail with `AADSTS65001` in a customer's tenant?" *Hint:* who consented in each tenant, and what the customer's user consent settings allow.

<a id="23-microsoft-authentication-library-msal"></a>
### 2.3 Microsoft Authentication Library (MSAL)

Implementing OAuth and OIDC by hand means handling PKCE, state, nonce, caching, refresh, key rotation, and dozens of error codes. MSAL is Microsoft's family of libraries that does all of this for you, with the same concepts in every language.

#### Public vs Confidential Clients

Some applications can keep a secret and some cannot. A web API running on a server can hold a certificate in Key Vault that no user ever sees. A desktop app, mobile app, or SPA runs on the user's device: anything shipped inside it (a "secret" in a config file, a JavaScript bundle, or an APK) can be extracted. OAuth therefore distinguishes two kinds of client, and MSAL mirrors that distinction in its main classes.

Analogy: a confidential client is a bank teller who can keep the vault key in a locked drawer. A public client is a kiosk in a shopping mall: anything stored inside it could be extracted by whoever walks up to it, so it must not hold a key at all.

| | Public client | Confidential client |
|---|---|---|
| Can hold a credential? | No | Yes: secret, certificate, or federated assertion |
| Runs on | User's device: desktop, mobile, SPA, CLI | Server you control: web app, web API, daemon, function |
| MSAL class | `PublicClientApplication` | `ConfidentialClientApplication` |
| Flows | Auth code + PKCE (interactive), device code, refresh | Auth code (web apps), client credentials, OBO, refresh |
| Can use application permissions? | No | Yes |
| Redirect URI platform | Mobile and desktop, or SPA | Web |

MSAL libraries by platform:

| Platform | Package | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| .NET | `Microsoft.Identity.Client` | Core library. `Microsoft.Identity.Web` adds ASP.NET Core integration. |
| Python | `msal` | `msal-extensions` adds a persistent, encrypted token cache. |
| JavaScript (browser) | `@azure/msal-browser` | Wrappers: `@azure/msal-react`, `@azure/msal-angular`. |
| JavaScript (Node.js) | `@azure/msal-node` | Public and confidential clients for server and desktop apps. |
| Java | `msal4j` | |
| Go | `github.com/AzureAD/microsoft-authentication-library-for-go` | |
| Android / iOS | MSAL Android, MSAL for iOS and macOS | Support brokers such as Microsoft Authenticator. |

MSAL is for apps that need **user tokens or app registration credentials** for arbitrary APIs. When your code only needs to call Azure services (Storage, Key Vault, Service Bus), use the **Azure Identity** library instead (see 2.4). It wraps MSAL and adds managed identity and developer-tool credentials.

**Example: creating each client type**

```python
import msal

TENANT_ID = "72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47"
AUTHORITY = f"https://login.microsoftonline.com/{TENANT_ID}"

# Public client: a desktop/CLI tool. Only a client ID, no credential.
public_app = msal.PublicClientApplication(
    client_id="11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
    authority=AUTHORITY,
)

# Confidential client: a backend service. Proves its identity with a certificate.
with open("orders-api.pem") as f:
    private_key = f.read()

confidential_app = msal.ConfidentialClientApplication(
    client_id="9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
    authority=AUTHORITY,
    client_credential={
        "private_key": private_key,
        "thumbprint": "A1B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F9012345678",  # SHA-1 thumbprint of the uploaded cert
    },
)
```

```csharp
using Microsoft.Identity.Client;

IPublicClientApplication publicApp = PublicClientApplicationBuilder
    .Create("11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555")
    .WithAuthority(AzureCloudInstance.AzurePublic, "72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47")
    .WithRedirectUri("http://localhost")                     // loopback redirect for desktop apps
    .Build();

IConfidentialClientApplication confidentialApp = ConfidentialClientApplicationBuilder
    .Create("9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001")
    .WithAuthority("https://login.microsoftonline.com/72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47")
    .WithCertificate(LoadCertificateFromKeyVault())         // X509Certificate2 with private key
    .Build();
```

**Key takeaways**

- Public clients run on user devices and cannot keep secrets. Confidential clients run on servers and authenticate themselves with a credential.
- Only confidential clients can use client credentials, OBO, and application permissions.
- MSAL exposes `PublicClientApplication` and `ConfidentialClientApplication` with the same concepts across languages.
- For calling Azure services, prefer the Azure Identity library, which builds on MSAL.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Classify as public or confidential: an Electron app, an Azure Functions timer job, a React SPA, an ASP.NET Core MVC app, a Python CLI.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** A team embedded a client secret in their mobile app "to make the token call easier". List what an attacker could do with it and how to redesign the app.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why can a SPA use the authorization code flow without a client secret, and what keeps it safe?" *Hint:* PKCE, the SPA redirect URI platform, CORS on the token endpoint, and refresh token lifetime limits for SPAs.

#### Acquiring Tokens Interactively

When a user is present, the app eventually has to show a sign-in screen, but it should do that as *rarely* as possible. MSAL's core pattern is **silent first, interactive only when required**: try to get a token from the cache (refreshing it in the background if needed), and only if that fails show UI.

```text
 acquire token for scopes
          |
          v
   account in cache? --no--------------------------------+
          | yes                                          |
          v                                              v
   acquire_token_silent ---- valid access token ---> return it
          |
          +-- expired -> use refresh token -> new token --> return it
          |
          +-- fails (no RT, RT revoked, MFA/consent/CA needed)
                         |
                         v
              acquire_token_interactive (browser, broker, or popup)
```

Interactive options:

- **System browser with loopback redirect** (desktop and CLI): MSAL opens the default browser and listens on `http://localhost:<port>`. Register `http://localhost` under the **Mobile and desktop applications** platform. The port is not part of the match for loopback URIs.
- **Authentication broker** (Windows Web Account Manager, Microsoft Authenticator, Company Portal): gives single sign-on with the OS account and supports device-based Conditional Access. Enable it explicitly in MSAL.
- **Popup or redirect** (SPAs with MSAL.js): `acquireTokenPopup` or `acquireTokenRedirect`.
- **Device code** (no browser on the device): the app shows a code, and the user enters it at `https://microsoft.com/devicelogin` on another device.

Prompts you can control: `prompt=select_account` (choose an account), `prompt=login` (force credentials), `prompt=consent` (force the consent screen), and `login_hint` to prefill the username.

**Example: silent-then-interactive in a Python desktop tool**

```python
import msal

app = msal.PublicClientApplication(
    "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
    authority="https://login.microsoftonline.com/organizations",   # any work/school account
)
SCOPES = ["api://9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001/Orders.Read"]

def get_token() -> str:
    result = None
    accounts = app.get_accounts()                      # accounts already in the token cache
    if accounts:
        result = app.acquire_token_silent(SCOPES, account=accounts[0])
    if not result:
        result = app.acquire_token_interactive(        # opens the system browser
            SCOPES,
            prompt="select_account",
        )
    if "access_token" not in result:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{result.get('error')}: {result.get('error_description')}")
    return result["access_token"]

def get_token_headless() -> str:
    """Device code flow, for SSH sessions and containers without a browser."""
    flow = app.initiate_device_flow(scopes=SCOPES)
    print(flow["message"])                             # "To sign in, use a web browser to open ..."
    result = app.acquire_token_by_device_flow(flow)    # blocks until the user finishes or it times out
    return result["access_token"]
```

**Example: the same pattern in a browser SPA (MSAL.js)**

```javascript
import { PublicClientApplication, InteractionRequiredAuthError } from "@azure/msal-browser";

const msal = new PublicClientApplication({
  auth: {
    clientId: "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
    authority: "https://login.microsoftonline.com/72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47",
    redirectUri: "https://orders.contoso.com/",        // registered under the SPA platform
  },
  cache: { cacheLocation: "sessionStorage" },           // tokens cleared when the tab closes
});

await msal.initialize();
await msal.handleRedirectPromise();                     // completes a redirect sign-in, if any

const request = { scopes: ["api://9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001/Orders.Read"] };

export async function callOrdersApi() {
  let account = msal.getAllAccounts()[0];
  if (!account) {
    await msal.loginRedirect(request);                  // navigates away; resumes on return
    return;
  }
  let token;
  try {
    token = (await msal.acquireTokenSilent({ ...request, account })).accessToken;
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof InteractionRequiredAuthError) {  // consent, MFA, or expired session
      token = (await msal.acquireTokenPopup(request)).accessToken;
    } else {
      throw err;
    }
  }
  return fetch("https://api.contoso.com/orders", {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
  });
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Always try `acquire_token_silent` first, and fall back to interactive only on an "interaction required" error.
- Desktop apps use the system browser with a loopback redirect, or an OS broker for SSO and device-based Conditional Access.
- SPAs use MSAL.js with redirect or popup, and register their URI under the SPA platform.
- Device code flow covers devices and sessions without a browser.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the Python sample twice. Confirm that the second call in the same process does not open a browser, and explain why the next *process* run does.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a second scope that requires extra consent (for example Graph `Calendars.Read`) and observe how `acquire_token_silent` behaves for it. Handle the case cleanly.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why does Microsoft recommend the system browser or a broker over an embedded webview for desktop sign-in?" *Hint:* SSO with existing sessions, phishing resistance, password managers, FIDO2 keys, and device compliance signals.

#### Client Credentials Flow

Many workloads have no user at all: a nightly job synchronizing HR data, a queue processor writing to a database, a service exporting reports to SharePoint. These apps authenticate *as themselves* using the **client credentials flow**, and their tokens carry **application permissions** in the `roles` claim.

Analogy: a company car with a fleet badge. No individual driver's identity is involved; the badge itself grants access to the parking garage, and the garage controls which floors fleet cars may use.

How it works:

1. The app sends its client ID and a credential (secret, certificate-signed assertion, or federated token) to the token endpoint, with `scope=<resource>/.default`.
2. Entra ID checks the credential and looks up which application permissions an admin has granted to the app's service principal on that resource.
3. The access token contains those permissions in `roles`, and `oid` and `sub` refer to the service principal.

You cannot request individual scopes in this flow, only `/.default`, because there is no user to consent interactively. All application permissions must be granted in advance by an admin (Graph and other APIs), or through app role assignment (your own APIs).

Credential options, from least to most preferred:

| Credential | Risk | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| Client secret | A string that can leak in logs or repos. Maximum lifetime of 2 years. | Avoid in production. If used, keep it in Key Vault and rotate it. |
| Certificate | Private key can be kept non-exportable in Key Vault or an HSM | Good for workloads outside Azure without OIDC support |
| Federated credential (workload identity federation) | No long-lived secret at all | Best for GitHub Actions, Kubernetes, other clouds (see 2.4) |
| Managed identity | No credential to manage; Azure handles it | Best when the code runs on Azure (see 2.4) |

**Example: a Python daemon calling Microsoft Graph**

```python
import msal, requests

app = msal.ConfidentialClientApplication(
    client_id="2222aaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000002",
    authority="https://login.microsoftonline.com/72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47",
    client_credential={"private_key": open("daemon.pem").read(),
                       "thumbprint": "A1B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F9012345678"},
)
# Create the app ONCE per process: its in-memory cache stores the app token.

def graph_get(path: str) -> dict:
    # Recent MSAL Python versions check the cache before calling Entra ID
    result = app.acquire_token_for_client(scopes=["https://graph.microsoft.com/.default"])
    if "access_token" not in result:
        # e.g. AADSTS7000215 (invalid secret) or AADSTS700027 (certificate not registered)
        raise RuntimeError(f"{result.get('error')}: {result.get('error_description')}")
    resp = requests.get(
        f"https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0{path}",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {result['access_token']}"},
        timeout=30,
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()   # 403 here usually means the application permission was not admin-consented
    return resp.json()

print([u["displayName"] for u in graph_get("/users?$select=displayName&$top=5")["value"]])
```

```csharp
// .NET: same flow; MSAL.NET caches app tokens in the application instance
var app = ConfidentialClientApplicationBuilder
    .Create("2222aaaa-0000-4000-8000-000000000002")
    .WithTenantId("72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47")
    .WithCertificate(certificate)
    .Build();

AuthenticationResult result = await app
    .AcquireTokenForClient(new[] { "api://9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001/.default" })
    .ExecuteAsync();

Console.WriteLine($"Token from {result.AuthenticationResultMetadata.TokenSource}, " +   // Cache or IdentityProvider
                  $"expires {result.ExpiresOn:u}");
```

For your *own* API to accept app-only callers, define an app role with `allowedMemberTypes: ["Application"]` (see App Registrations in 2.1), assign it to the calling app's service principal, and check `roles` in the API.

**Key takeaways**

- Client credentials is for app-only access. The token carries application permissions in `roles`.
- Always request `<resource>/.default`. Permissions must be granted in advance by an admin or by app role assignment.
- Prefer managed identity (on Azure) or federated credentials (elsewhere), then certificates. Avoid client secrets.
- Create the confidential client once and reuse it so the app token cache works.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Register a daemon app, grant it Graph `User.Read.All` (application) with admin consent, and list five users with the Python sample.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Make your own API accept app-only calls: define an application app role, assign it to the daemon's service principal with `az rest` (`POST /servicePrincipals/{id}/appRoleAssignedTo`), and enforce it in the API.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why can't a client credentials request ask for `User.Read` instead of `.default`?" *Hint:* who would consent, and where application permissions are recorded.

#### On-Behalf-Of Flow

In a layered architecture, a client calls API A, and API A needs to call API B (for example Microsoft Graph) *as the same user*. API A cannot just forward the incoming token, because its audience is API A, so API B would reject it. Using API A's own app permissions would also be wrong, because it would grant access to *all* users' data instead of only the caller's. The **on-behalf-of (OBO) flow** solves this: API A exchanges the user's token for a new token for API B, preserving the user's identity and delegated permissions.

Analogy: a travel agent booking a hotel for you. The agent cannot use your passport at the hotel desk, but can present a booking voucher that says "on behalf of this guest", issued by a trusted authority.

```text
  User + SPA                  API A (middle tier)            Entra ID               API B (Graph)
      |  token T1 (aud=API A)      |                            |                        |
      |--------------------------->| validate T1                |                        |
      |                            | POST /token                |                        |
      |                            |  grant_type=jwt-bearer     |                        |
      |                            |  assertion=T1              |                        |
      |                            |  requested_token_use=      |                        |
      |                            |    on_behalf_of            |                        |
      |                            |  scope=User.Read           |                        |
      |                            |  + API A's own credential  |                        |
      |                            |--------------------------->|                        |
      |                            |   token T2 (aud=Graph,     |                        |
      |                            |   same user, scp=User.Read)|                        |
      |                            |<---------------------------|                        |
      |                            | GET /me  Bearer T2                                  |
      |                            |---------------------------------------------------->|
```

Requirements and rules:

- API A must be a **confidential client** with its own credential, and must have *delegated* permissions on API B.
- T1 must be a **user token** whose audience is API A. App-only tokens cannot be exchanged with OBO.
- **Consent** must cover both hops. Common approaches: grant admin consent for API A's downstream permissions, or list the client in API A's `knownClientApplications` so that a single consent prompt covers both.
- If API B needs more (MFA step-up, extra consent, Conditional Access), the OBO call fails with `interaction_required` and a `claims` challenge. API A cannot show UI, so it must return a 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header that tells the client to re-authenticate with those claims.
- Cache OBO results per incoming token, so repeated requests from the same user do not hit Entra ID each time.

**Example: Python middle-tier API exchanging the token**

```python
import msal

obo_app = msal.ConfidentialClientApplication(
    client_id="9f2c1a7e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",          # API A's own registration
    authority="https://login.microsoftonline.com/72f988bf-86f1-41af-91ab-2d7cd011db47",
    client_credential={"private_key": open("api-a.pem").read(),
                       "thumbprint": "A1B2C3D4E5F60718293A4B5C6D7E8F9012345678"},
)

def get_my_profile(incoming_token: str) -> dict:
    # incoming_token has already been validated (aud = API A, scp contains Orders.Read)
    result = obo_app.acquire_token_on_behalf_of(
        user_assertion=incoming_token,                       # T1
        scopes=["https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read"],    # what we need from API B
    )
    if "access_token" in result:
        return call_graph("/me", result["access_token"])     # T2: same user, audience Graph
    if result.get("error") == "interaction_required":
        # Pass the claims challenge back so the CLIENT can prompt the user (MFA, consent)
        raise ChallengeRequired(claims=result.get("claims"))
    raise RuntimeError(result.get("error_description"))
```

**Example: ASP.NET Core with Microsoft.Identity.Web**

```csharp
// Program.cs
builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApi(builder.Configuration.GetSection("AzureAd"))   // validates T1
    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi()                               // enables OBO
    .AddInMemoryTokenCaches();                                                 // caches T2 per user

// ProfileController.cs
[Authorize]
[RequiredScope("Orders.Read")]
public class ProfileController(ITokenAcquisition tokens) : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet("/me")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Get()
    {
        // OBO under the hood; on interaction_required, the library produces the 401 challenge
        string graphToken = await tokens.GetAccessTokenForUserAsync(
            new[] { "https://graph.microsoft.com/User.Read" });
        // ... call Graph with graphToken
        return Ok();
    }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- OBO lets a middle-tier API call a downstream API as the original user with delegated permissions.
- Never forward the incoming token downstream, and do not substitute app permissions for user context.
- The middle tier must be a confidential client. Only user tokens addressed to it can be exchanged.
- Propagate `interaction_required` claims challenges back to the client, which is the only party that can show UI.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Explain why forwarding T1 directly to Graph fails, in terms of a specific token claim.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a SPA, a middle-tier API, and a Graph call using OBO. Configure `knownClientApplications` so the user sees one consent prompt, and verify the scopes in T2.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A downstream API now requires MFA. How does your middle-tier API handle it, given it cannot show a sign-in page?" *Hint:* `interaction_required`, claims challenges, `WWW-Authenticate`, and the client's role.

#### Token Caching

Requesting a new token for every API call would add latency (a network round trip to Entra ID each time), make your app depend on Entra ID's availability for every request, and quickly trigger throttling. MSAL keeps a **token cache**, and its "silent" methods read from it first. The cache stores access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens, and account metadata.

By default, MSAL's cache is **in memory and lives as long as the application object**. That default is right for some apps and wrong for others:

| App type | Cache contents | Recommended storage |
|---|---|---|
| Daemon (client credentials) | One app token per resource | In memory, with a single long-lived app object |
| Desktop / CLI | User tokens for one user | Persisted to disk, encrypted with OS protection (DPAPI, Keychain, libsecret) |
| Web app / web API (many users) | User tokens for *many* users, partitioned by user (or by incoming token for OBO) | Distributed cache (Redis, SQL) so it survives restarts and works across instances |
| SPA | User tokens in the browser | `sessionStorage` (default) or `localStorage`, managed by MSAL.js |

Common caching mistakes:

1. **Creating a new MSAL client per request.** The new instance has an empty cache, so every request goes to Entra ID. Create the client once, or share a cache between instances.
2. **In-memory caches on a scaled-out web app.** Each instance has its own cache, and a restart logs everyone out of downstream APIs. Use a distributed cache.
3. **Unencrypted persistent caches.** Refresh tokens are credentials. Encrypt them at rest.
4. **Unbounded memory growth** for multi-user caches. Set eviction and size limits.

**Example: persistent, encrypted cache for a Python CLI**

```python
# pip install msal msal-extensions
import msal
from msal_extensions import build_encrypted_persistence, PersistedTokenCache

# Encrypted with DPAPI on Windows, Keychain on macOS, libsecret on Linux
persistence = build_encrypted_persistence("/home/ada/.orders-cli/token_cache.bin")
cache = PersistedTokenCache(persistence)          # reads/writes the file with locking

app = msal.PublicClientApplication(
    "11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555",
    authority="https://login.microsoftonline.com/organizations",
    token_cache=cache,                            # silent calls now survive process restarts
)
```

```python
# Manual serialization, useful to understand the mechanism or plug in your own store
import msal, os

CACHE_FILE = "cache.json"
cache = msal.SerializableTokenCache()
if os.path.exists(CACHE_FILE):
    cache.deserialize(open(CACHE_FILE).read())

app = msal.PublicClientApplication("1111-...", token_cache=cache)
# ... acquire tokens ...
if cache.has_state_changed:                       # only write when something changed
    with open(CACHE_FILE, "w") as f:
        f.write(cache.serialize())                # WARNING: plain text; encrypt in real apps
```

**Example: distributed cache for a scaled-out ASP.NET Core app**

```csharp
builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(OpenIdConnectDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddMicrosoftIdentityWebApp(builder.Configuration.GetSection("AzureAd"))
    .EnableTokenAcquisitionToCallDownstreamApi(new[] { "User.Read" })
    .AddDistributedTokenCaches();                         // use IDistributedCache for MSAL

builder.Services.AddStackExchangeRedisCache(options =>
{
    options.Configuration = builder.Configuration["Redis:ConnectionString"];
    options.InstanceName = "msal:";                       // key prefix
});

builder.Services.Configure<MsalDistributedTokenCacheAdapterOptions>(options =>
{
    options.Encrypt = true;                               // encrypt cache entries (Data Protection API)
    options.SlidingExpiration = TimeSpan.FromHours(12);   // evict inactive users
});
```

**Key takeaways**

- The token cache is what makes silent acquisition fast and keeps you from being throttled.
- The default cache is in memory and tied to the client instance: reuse the instance.
- Desktop apps need encrypted persistent caches. Multi-instance web apps need distributed caches partitioned per user.
- Treat cached refresh tokens as credentials: encrypt them and set eviction policies.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add `msal-extensions` to a Python CLI and confirm that the browser opens only on the first run.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a load test against a daemon that creates a new `ConfidentialClientApplication` per request, then fix it with a singleton. Compare the number of calls to `login.microsoftonline.com` (use `token_source` in the result or network logs).
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your web app runs on three App Service instances, and users randomly get 'consent required' errors after deployments. What is the likely cause?" *Hint:* where the token cache lives and what happens to it on restart or when requests reach a different instance.

<a id="24-managed-identities-and-azure-identity-library"></a>
### 2.4 Managed Identities and Azure Identity Library

Every credential your app holds can leak, expire, or be forgotten during rotation. This section covers how Azure removes credentials from your code entirely, and how the Azure Identity library lets the same code authenticate on a laptop, in a pipeline, and in production.

#### System-Assigned Managed Identity

Even with Key Vault, there is a bootstrapping problem: to read secrets from Key Vault, your app needs a credential for Key Vault. Where do you store *that*? Any answer ("in an app setting", "in an environment variable") leaves a secret that can leak and must be rotated. **Managed identities** break the cycle. Azure gives the resource itself an identity in Entra ID and manages its credentials internally. Your code asks a local endpoint for a token and never sees a secret.

Analogy: instead of giving a delivery van a key to the warehouse, the warehouse recognizes the van's registered license plate. No key can be copied or lost, and the van's identity is tied to the van itself.

A **system-assigned** managed identity is created *as part of* a specific Azure resource (an App Service app, Function app, VM, Container App, Logic App, and so on):

- It is enabled with a switch on the resource and creates a service principal of type `ManagedIdentity` with the same name as the resource.
- Its lifecycle is tied to the resource: deleting the resource deletes the identity and all of its role assignments.
- It cannot be shared: one resource, one system-assigned identity.
- The identity's credentials (certificates) are rotated automatically by Azure.

How code gets a token:

```text
  +----------------------- Azure host (VM, App Service, Functions, ...) -------------------+
  |                                                                                         |
  |   Your code --(1) GET token for https://vault.azure.net--> local identity endpoint      |
  |                                                            IMDS 169.254.169.254 (VMs)   |
  |                                                            or IDENTITY_ENDPOINT (PaaS)  |
  |                                                                 |                       |
  +-----------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------+
                                                                    | (2) platform authenticates
                                                                    v     the resource to Entra ID
                                                               Microsoft Entra ID
                                                                    | (3) access token (aud=Key Vault)
  Your code <-------------------------------------------------------+
  Your code --(4) GET secret, Authorization: Bearer <token>--> Key Vault (checks RBAC on the SP)
```

The local endpoint is only reachable from inside the resource, so the token request does not need a secret. A managed identity only proves *who* the app is: you still have to grant it RBAC roles on the target resources.

**Example: enable, authorize, and use a system-assigned identity**

```bash
# Enable the identity on a web app; principalId is the service principal's object ID
PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az webapp identity assign -g rg-orders -n app-orders-prod --query principalId -o tsv)

# Grant it read access to secrets in one Key Vault (RBAC-mode vault)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope "$(az keyvault show -n kv-orders-prod --query id -o tsv)"
```

```bicep
// The same in Bicep: identity on the resource, role assignment scoped to the vault
resource app 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'app-orders-prod'
  location: location
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' }
  properties: { serverFarmId: plan.id }
}

resource kv 'Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults@2023-07-01' existing = { name: 'kv-orders-prod' }

var keyVaultSecretsUser = '4633458b-17de-408a-b874-0445c86b69e6'   // built-in role definition ID

resource kvAccess 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments@2022-04-01' = {
  name: guid(kv.id, app.id, keyVaultSecretsUser)       // deterministic name: redeploys are idempotent
  scope: kv
  properties: {
    roleDefinitionId: subscriptionResourceId('Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions', keyVaultSecretsUser)
    principalId: app.identity.principalId
    principalType: 'ServicePrincipal'
  }
}
```

```python
# Application code: no secrets, no connection strings
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient

credential = ManagedIdentityCredential()   # system-assigned: no arguments needed
client = SecretClient("https://kv-orders-prod.vault.azure.net", credential)
db_password = client.get_secret("orders-db-password").value
```

```bash
# What the library does under the hood on App Service / Functions (run from the Kudu/SSH console)
curl -s "$IDENTITY_ENDPOINT?resource=https://vault.azure.net&api-version=2019-08-01" \
  -H "X-IDENTITY-HEADER: $IDENTITY_HEADER" | jq '{expires_on, resource, token_type}'

# On a VM, the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) plays the same role
curl -s -H "Metadata: true" \
  "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://vault.azure.net"
```

Managed identity tokens are cached by the Azure infrastructure, typically for up to 24 hours. Changes to the identity's **group memberships** can therefore take that long to take effect. Direct role assignments are evaluated by the resource provider and usually take effect within minutes.

**Key takeaways**

- Managed identities remove credentials from code. The resource requests tokens from a local endpoint that only it can reach.
- A system-assigned identity is created with, tied to, and deleted with one resource. It cannot be shared.
- An identity only authenticates the app. You must grant it RBAC roles on target resources.
- Use the SDK (`ManagedIdentityCredential` or `DefaultAzureCredential`) rather than calling IMDS or `IDENTITY_ENDPOINT` directly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Enable a system-assigned identity on a Function app, find its service principal under Enterprise applications (filter by Managed Identities), and note its object ID.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the Bicep above, then delete and recreate the web app with the same name. Explain why the app can no longer read Key Vault, and how to make the deployment self-healing.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How does a managed identity get a token without any secret, and why can't an attacker on the internet do the same?" *Hint:* where the identity endpoint is reachable from, and what the platform knows about the caller.

#### User-Assigned Managed Identity

System-assigned identities have practical limits. If ten Function apps all need the same access, you create ten identities and thirty role assignments. If you deploy with blue-green swaps or recreate resources often, each new resource gets a new identity, and its permissions must be granted again after it exists. This can race with the app's startup. Some scenarios (for example encrypting a storage account with a customer-managed key at creation time) need the identity to exist *before* the resource. A **user-assigned managed identity** is a standalone Azure resource (`Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities`) that you create first and then attach to one or more resources.

Analogy: a system-assigned identity is a staff badge printed for one specific employee and shredded when they leave. A user-assigned identity is a role badge ("night shift supervisor") that exists independently and can be handed to whoever fills the role.

| | System-assigned | User-assigned |
|---|---|---|
| Created | With the resource, by enabling it | Separately, as its own resource |
| Lifecycle | Deleted with the resource | Independent; deleted explicitly |
| Sharing | One resource only | Many resources can use it |
| Per resource | At most one | Several can be attached |
| Pre-provision permissions | No: the resource must exist first | Yes: assign roles before deploying the app |
| Selecting it in code | Automatic | Must specify its client ID (or resource ID) when more than one is attached |
| Good for | Simple apps with a 1:1 identity | Shared access, frequently recreated resources, scale sets, AKS workload identity, deployments needing the identity up front |

Trade-off: sharing one identity across many apps widens the blast radius if any of them is compromised, and makes audit logs less precise. Share identities only among components that genuinely need identical access.

**Example: create once, grant once, attach anywhere**

```bash
# 1) Create the identity and capture its IDs
az identity create -g rg-orders -n id-orders-prod
CLIENT_ID=$(az identity show -g rg-orders -n id-orders-prod --query clientId -o tsv)       # used in code
PRINCIPAL_ID=$(az identity show -g rg-orders -n id-orders-prod --query principalId -o tsv) # used in RBAC
IDENTITY_ID=$(az identity show -g rg-orders -n id-orders-prod --query id -o tsv)           # ARM resource ID

# 2) Grant access BEFORE any app exists
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Contributor" \
  --scope "$(az storage account show -n storders001 --query id -o tsv)"

# 3) Attach it to two different apps
az webapp identity assign -g rg-orders -n app-orders-api --identities "$IDENTITY_ID"
az functionapp identity assign -g rg-orders -n func-orders-worker --identities "$IDENTITY_ID"

# 4) Tell the code which identity to use
az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-orders -n app-orders-api --settings AZURE_CLIENT_ID="$CLIENT_ID"
```

```bicep
resource uami 'Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities@2023-01-31' = {
  name: 'id-orders-prod'
  location: location
}

resource app 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'app-orders-api'
  location: location
  identity: {
    type: 'UserAssigned'                         // or 'SystemAssigned, UserAssigned' for both
    userAssignedIdentities: { '${uami.id}': {} }
  }
  properties: {
    serverFarmId: plan.id
    siteConfig: {
      appSettings: [
        { name: 'AZURE_CLIENT_ID', value: uami.properties.clientId }   // read by DefaultAzureCredential
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

```python
import os
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

# Explicitly select the user-assigned identity by client ID
credential = ManagedIdentityCredential(client_id=os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_ID"])
blobs = BlobServiceClient("https://storders001.blob.core.windows.net", credential=credential)
```

Attaching a user-assigned identity to a resource requires the **Managed Identity Operator** role on the identity (or a role that includes its `assign/action` permission). This lets you control who may "borrow" a powerful identity.

**Key takeaways**

- A user-assigned identity is a standalone resource that can be shared and outlives the resources using it.
- Grant its roles before deploying apps, which avoids races and repeated role assignments when resources are recreated.
- When more than one identity is attached, select one in code by client ID (commonly via `AZURE_CLIENT_ID`).
- Sharing an identity widens blast radius. Group only components that need identical access.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a user-assigned identity and list its three identifiers (`clientId`, `principalId`, `id`). State where each is used.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Attach both a system-assigned and a user-assigned identity to one app. Write code that uses each explicitly and verify which one accessed storage by checking the storage account's diagnostic logs.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you choose a user-assigned managed identity over a system-assigned one?" *Hint:* resource churn, shared access, pre-provisioned permissions, and dependencies at resource creation time.

#### DefaultAzureCredential

Your code runs in several places: on your laptop (where you are signed in to the Azure CLI or Visual Studio), in a CI pipeline (with a service principal or federated credential), and in production (with a managed identity). Writing `if environment == "local": ... elif ...` logic everywhere is error-prone. **`DefaultAzureCredential`**, from the Azure Identity library, is a ready-made chain of credentials that tries each source in a fixed order and uses the first one that works, so the same line of code authenticates correctly in every environment.

Analogy: a universal key ring. You try each key in a fixed order until one opens the door, and the ring remembers which key worked so it goes straight to it next time.

```text
 DefaultAzureCredential.get_token(scope)
   |
   |-- 1. EnvironmentCredential        AZURE_TENANT_ID + AZURE_CLIENT_ID + secret/certificate env vars
   |-- 2. WorkloadIdentityCredential   AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE (AKS workload identity)
   |-- 3. ManagedIdentityCredential    IMDS / IDENTITY_ENDPOINT (Azure-hosted code)
   |-- 4. Developer tool credentials   IDE sign-in (Visual Studio / VS Code), shared token cache,
   |                                    Azure CLI (az login), Azure PowerShell, Azure Developer CLI (azd)
   |-- 5. InteractiveBrowserCredential excluded by default
   v
 first credential that returns a token wins, and is reused for later calls
```

The exact membership and order differ slightly between languages and library versions (for example, .NET includes a Visual Studio credential, and some developer-tool credentials are opt-in in some versions), so check the reference documentation for your package version. The overall shape is constant: **deployed-service credentials first, developer-tool credentials after**.

| Where code runs | Credential that typically succeeds | What you configure |
|---|---|---|
| Laptop | Azure CLI / IDE / azd | `az login` (in the right tenant) and RBAC for your user |
| GitHub Actions | Environment or Azure CLI (after `azure/login`) | Federated credential, then RBAC for the app |
| AKS pod with workload identity | WorkloadIdentityCredential | Service account annotation and pod label |
| App Service, Functions, Container Apps, VM | ManagedIdentityCredential | Enable identity, `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` for user-assigned, RBAC |

**Example: one credential for every environment**

```python
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()        # create once; share across all clients
blobs = BlobServiceClient("https://storders001.blob.core.windows.net", credential=credential)

for c in blobs.list_containers():            # works with `az login` locally and with MI in Azure
    print(c.name)
```

```csharp
// .NET: same idea; options let you narrow or tune the chain
var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential(new DefaultAzureCredentialOptions
{
    ManagedIdentityClientId = Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable("AZURE_CLIENT_ID"), // user-assigned MI
    ExcludeInteractiveBrowserCredential = true,
});
var secrets = new SecretClient(new Uri("https://kv-orders-prod.vault.azure.net/"), credential);
```

```javascript
// JavaScript / TypeScript
import { DefaultAzureCredential } from "@azure/identity";
import { ServiceBusClient } from "@azure/service-bus";

const credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();
const sb = new ServiceBusClient("sb-orders-prod.servicebus.windows.net", credential);
```

**Production guidance.** Trying several credentials has costs: slower startup when early credentials time out, harder debugging, and the risk of silently picking up the wrong identity (for example a stray `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` environment variable). Common approaches:

- Use `DefaultAzureCredential` in development, and a specific credential (such as `ManagedIdentityCredential`) or a narrow `ChainedTokenCredential` in production (see next topic).
- In recent library versions, set the `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS` environment variable to `prod` (only deployed-service credentials) or `dev` (only developer-tool credentials) to restrict the chain without code changes.

**Debugging.** When every credential fails, the exception lists each attempt and its reason. Turn on library logging for details:

```python
import logging, sys
logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout)
logging.getLogger("azure.identity").setLevel(logging.DEBUG)   # shows which credential was tried and why it failed
```

Typical local problems: `az login` signed in to the wrong tenant (use `az login --tenant <id>`), your user lacking a *data-plane* role (see 2.5), or a leftover `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` pointing to another app.

**Key takeaways**

- `DefaultAzureCredential` tries environment variables, workload identity, managed identity, and then developer tools, and uses the first that succeeds.
- The same code then works locally, in CI, and in Azure. Only configuration and RBAC differ.
- Create one credential instance and share it across clients, because it caches tokens and remembers the successful credential.
- In production, narrow the chain (specific credential, `ChainedTokenCredential`, or `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS=prod`) for speed and predictability.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the Python sample locally after `az login`. Then set `AZURE_CLIENT_ID` to a random GUID, run it again, and explain the outcome using debug logs.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the same code to App Service with a user-assigned identity. Verify from logs that `ManagedIdentityCredential` was used, and measure startup time with and without `AZURE_TOKEN_CREDENTIALS=prod`.
> 3. **(Interview)** "What are the risks of using `DefaultAzureCredential` in production, and how would you mitigate them?" *Hint:* unexpected credential selection, environment variable leakage, timeouts, and how to pin the chain.

#### Credential Chains

`DefaultAzureCredential` is one predefined chain. Sometimes you need a different one: production should use only a managed identity, CI should use only a federated credential, and developers should use the Azure CLI. Or a team wants a test credential in unit tests. The Azure Identity library is built from small, composable pieces: every credential implements the same **`TokenCredential`** interface, and **`ChainedTokenCredential`** combines any of them in any order.

The interface is small. In Python a credential is any object with `get_token(*scopes, **kwargs) -> AccessToken`. In .NET it is the abstract class `TokenCredential` with `GetToken` and `GetTokenAsync`. Every Azure SDK client accepts any `TokenCredential`, which is why credentials and clients can be combined freely.

How a chain decides what to do next:

| Outcome of a credential | Meaning | Chain behavior |
|---|---|---|
| Returns a token | Success | Stop and use it. Later calls go straight to this credential. |
| `CredentialUnavailableError` | This source is not configured here (no env vars, no IMDS, not logged in to CLI) | Try the next credential |
| Other authentication error | The source exists but authentication failed (wrong secret, missing consent) | Stop and raise, so misconfigurations are not hidden |

That last rule is deliberate: if a managed identity exists but is misconfigured, silently falling back to a developer's CLI login would hide the problem.

Commonly used credentials:

| Credential | Source |
|---|---|
| `ManagedIdentityCredential` | System- or user-assigned managed identity |
| `WorkloadIdentityCredential` | Federated token file (AKS) |
| `ClientSecretCredential`, `ClientCertificateCredential` | App registration with secret or certificate |
| `ClientAssertionCredential` | App registration with an external token supplied by your callback |
| `EnvironmentCredential` | Secret, certificate, or user settings in `AZURE_*` env vars |
| `AzureCliCredential`, `AzurePowerShellCredential`, `AzureDeveloperCliCredential` | Developer tool sign-ins |
| `InteractiveBrowserCredential`, `DeviceCodeCredential` | Interactive user sign-in |

**Example: explicit chains for each environment**

```python
import os
from azure.identity import (
    AzureCliCredential, ChainedTokenCredential, DefaultAzureCredential,
    ManagedIdentityCredential, WorkloadIdentityCredential,
)

def build_credential():
    env = os.getenv("APP_ENV", "local")
    if env == "prod":
        # Only the managed identity: fast, predictable, nothing else can be picked up
        return ManagedIdentityCredential(client_id=os.environ["AZURE_CLIENT_ID"])
    if env == "aks":
        return WorkloadIdentityCredential()           # reads AZURE_* env vars injected by the webhook
    # Local: prefer the CLI, then fall back to a managed identity on a dev VM
    return ChainedTokenCredential(AzureCliCredential(), ManagedIdentityCredential())

# Alternatively, trim DefaultAzureCredential with exclusion flags
credential = DefaultAzureCredential(
    exclude_environment_credential=True,
    exclude_shared_token_cache_credential=True,
    exclude_powershell_credential=True,
)
```

```csharp
// .NET equivalent: managed identity in Azure, Visual Studio or CLI on developer machines
TokenCredential credential = new ChainedTokenCredential(
    new ManagedIdentityCredential(ManagedIdentityId.FromUserAssignedClientId(clientId)),
    new VisualStudioCredential(),
    new AzureCliCredential());
```

**Example: a custom credential for tests**

```python
import time
from azure.core.credentials import AccessToken

class StaticTokenCredential:
    """Implements the TokenCredential protocol. Useful against emulators or mocked endpoints."""
    def __init__(self, token: str = "fake-token"):
        self._token = token

    def get_token(self, *scopes, **kwargs) -> AccessToken:
        return AccessToken(self._token, int(time.time()) + 3600)   # (token, expires_on)

# Any SDK client accepts it, for example in tests against a local mock server
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient
client = BlobServiceClient("https://localhost:8443/devstoreaccount1", credential=StaticTokenCredential())
```

**Key takeaways**

- Every credential implements `TokenCredential`, so any credential works with any Azure SDK client.
- `ChainedTokenCredential` tries credentials in order. "Unavailable" moves to the next; a real authentication failure stops the chain.
- Build explicit, minimal chains per environment, or trim `DefaultAzureCredential` with exclusion options.
- Custom credentials are simple to write, which makes them handy for tests and special token sources.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a `ChainedTokenCredential` that uses a managed identity first and the Azure CLI second. Run it locally and explain why the first one is skipped.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a credential wrapper that logs (without the token itself) which scopes were requested and when the token expires, then wrap `DefaultAzureCredential` with it.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why does a chain stop on an authentication failure instead of trying the next credential?" *Hint:* think about what a silent fallback to a developer's personal identity would hide in production.

#### Workload Identity Federation

Managed identities only work for code running *on Azure*. A GitHub Actions workflow deploying to Azure, a pod in a Kubernetes cluster, or a job running in Google Cloud traditionally needed a client secret or certificate stored in that external system, which had to be rotated and could leak. **Workload identity federation** removes those secrets: Entra ID is configured to *trust tokens issued by another identity provider* for a specific workload, and exchanges them for Entra ID access tokens.

Analogy: a visa waiver agreement between countries. Instead of issuing you its own document, the destination country accepts your home country's passport, but only if the passport comes from a trusted issuer and matches what was agreed.

Most CI systems and Kubernetes clusters already issue short-lived **OIDC tokens** to their workloads. You add a **federated identity credential (FIC)** to an app registration or a user-assigned managed identity that says which external tokens to accept:

| FIC field | Meaning | Example (GitHub Actions) |
|---|---|---|
| `issuer` | The external IdP's OIDC issuer URL | `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` |
| `subject` | The exact workload identity inside that IdP | `repo:contoso/orders:environment:production` |
| `audiences` | Expected `aud` of the external token | `api://AzureADTokenExchange` |

```text
  External workload (GitHub job / K8s pod)          Microsoft Entra ID                Azure resource
         |                                                 |                                |
  (1) gets OIDC token from its own IdP                     |                                |
      iss=token.actions.githubusercontent.com              |                                |
      sub=repo:contoso/orders:environment:production       |                                |
         |                                                 |                                |
  (2) POST /token  grant_type=client_credentials           |                                |
      client_id=<app or UAMI client ID>                    |                                |
      client_assertion_type=...jwt-bearer                  |                                |
      client_assertion=<external OIDC token> ------------->|                                |
         |                       (3) fetch issuer's keys, verify signature,                 |
         |                           match iss + sub + aud against a FIC                    |
         |<----------------------- (4) Entra access token -|                                |
  (5) call Azure with Bearer token ---------------------------------------------------------->|
```

Rules to know:

- `issuer`, `subject`, and `audience` must match **exactly**. A workflow on a different branch or environment produces a different `sub` and is rejected. That precision is the main security property.
- An app registration or user-assigned identity can have up to 20 FICs.
- The issuer's discovery document and keys must be reachable by Entra ID over the public internet.
- The Entra token is still subject to RBAC: federation authenticates the workload, and role assignments decide what it can do.

**Example: GitHub Actions deploying without secrets**

```bash
# Trust tokens from the 'production' environment of one repository
az ad app federated-credential create --id "$APP_ID" --parameters '{
  "name": "github-orders-production",
  "issuer": "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com",
  "subject": "repo:contoso/orders:environment:production",
  "audiences": ["api://AzureADTokenExchange"]
}'
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  id-token: write       # allow the job to request a GitHub OIDC token
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # determines the token's 'sub' claim
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v2         # exchanges the GitHub token for an Entra token
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}           # IDs are not secrets
          tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - run: az webapp deploy -g rg-orders -n app-orders-api --src-path app.zip
```

**Example: AKS pod using a user-assigned identity**

```bash
# Cluster must expose an OIDC issuer and run the workload identity webhook
az aks update -g rg-aks -n aks-prod --enable-oidc-issuer --enable-workload-identity
ISSUER=$(az aks show -g rg-aks -n aks-prod --query oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl -o tsv)

# Trust the Kubernetes service account 'orders-sa' in namespace 'orders'
az identity federated-credential create -g rg-orders --identity-name id-orders-prod \
  --name aks-orders-sa --issuer "$ISSUER" \
  --subject "system:serviceaccount:orders:orders-sa" \
  --audiences api://AzureADTokenExchange
```

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: orders-sa
  namespace: orders
  annotations:
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "<client-id-of-id-orders-prod>"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-worker
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-worker }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: orders-worker
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"   # webhook injects AZURE_CLIENT_ID, AZURE_TENANT_ID,
                                              # AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE, AZURE_AUTHORITY_HOST
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: orders-sa
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: crorders.azurecr.io/orders-worker:1.4.2   # code uses DefaultAzureCredential
```

**Key takeaways**

- Workload identity federation lets workloads outside Azure authenticate without any stored secret, by exchanging their own OIDC token.
- A federated identity credential trusts an exact `issuer` + `subject` + `audience` combination.
- Use it for GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, AKS, other clouds, and any OIDC-capable platform.
- The SDK handles the exchange (`WorkloadIdentityCredential`, `DefaultAzureCredential`, `azure/login`). RBAC still decides permissions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write the FIC `subject` for: GitHub pushes to branch `main` of `contoso/web`; GitHub pull requests in the same repo; Kubernetes service account `api` in namespace `shop`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Convert an existing GitHub workflow that uses an `AZURE_CREDENTIALS` secret to OIDC. Delete the old secret and confirm the deployment still works.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why is workload identity federation more secure than storing a certificate in your CI system?" *Hint:* token lifetime, where the credential lives, and what an attacker would need to replay it.

<a id="25-authorization-with-azure-rbac"></a>
### 2.5 Authorization with Azure RBAC

Authentication tells Azure who is calling. Azure role-based access control (RBAC) decides what that caller may do on which resources. Every "AuthorizationFailed" or 403 you see in Azure comes from this system.

#### Role Definitions and Assignments

Azure has thousands of operations (create a VM, read a secret, delete a blob) and many principals (people, groups, apps, managed identities). Granting operations one by one to each principal would be unmanageable. RBAC introduces two indirections: operations are grouped into **role definitions**, and a **role assignment** binds a role to a principal at a particular scope.

Analogy: a building's access system. A role definition is a badge *type* ("Cleaner: lobby, offices, storage rooms"). A role assignment is "give Bob a Cleaner badge valid on floors 3 to 5". The badge type is defined once and handed out many times.

A role assignment answers three questions:

```text
        WHO                     WHAT                         WHERE
  +----------------+     +---------------------+     +-----------------------------+
  | Security       |     | Role definition     |     | Scope                       |
  | principal      |  +  | (set of allowed     |  +  | /subscriptions/<id>/        |
  | user, group,   |     |  operations)        |     |  resourceGroups/rg-orders   |
  | SP, managed ID |     | e.g. Reader         |     |                             |
  +----------------+     +---------------------+     +-----------------------------+
                                     = role assignment
```

A **role definition** is a JSON document with four permission lists:

| Field | Applies to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Actions` | Control plane (ARM) | Management operations allowed, such as `Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/read` |
| `NotActions` | Control plane | Operations subtracted from `Actions` (not a deny) |
| `DataActions` | Data plane | Operations on data, such as `.../blobs/read` |
| `NotDataActions` | Data plane | Data operations subtracted from `DataActions` |
| `AssignableScopes` | Where the role may be assigned | Management groups, subscriptions, resource groups |

Operation strings follow the pattern `{Provider}/{resourceType}/{action}`, and `*` is a wildcard. For example, the built-in Contributor role is `Actions: ["*"]` with `NotActions` covering authorization writes and a few others, which is why Contributors can manage resources but cannot grant access.

How Azure evaluates a request:

1. Collect every role assignment for the caller (directly, and through groups) at the target scope and all parent scopes.
2. RBAC is **additive**: the effective permission is the union of all matching roles.
3. Check **deny assignments** (created by the platform, for example by deployment stacks or managed applications). A deny wins over any allow.
4. If an assignment has a **condition** (attribute-based access control, ABAC), evaluate it against the request's attributes.

Role assignment changes can take several minutes to propagate. Plan for this in deployment scripts (retry the first data access) instead of assuming immediate effect.

**Example: inspect a role and create assignments**

```bash
# What does a built-in role allow?
az role definition list --name "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --query "[0].{actions:permissions[0].actions, dataActions:permissions[0].dataActions}" -o json
# {
#   "actions": [ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/read",
#                "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/generateUserDelegationKey/action" ],
#   "dataActions": [ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/blobServices/containers/blobs/read" ]
# }

# Assign it: WHO (object ID + type), WHAT (role), WHERE (scope)
az role assignment create \
  --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/rg-orders/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/storders001"

# Everything a principal can do, including inherited and group-based assignments
az role assignment list --assignee "$PRINCIPAL_ID" --all --include-inherited --include-groups -o table
```

```bicep
// Role assignment as code; the name must be a GUID, so derive it deterministically
param principalId string
var storageBlobDataReader = '2a2b9908-6ea1-4ae2-8e65-a410df84e7d1'

resource sa 'Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts@2023-05-01' existing = { name: 'storders001' }

resource readerAssignment 'Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments@2022-04-01' = {
  name: guid(sa.id, principalId, storageBlobDataReader)
  scope: sa
  properties: {
    roleDefinitionId: subscriptionResourceId('Microsoft.Authorization/roleDefinitions', storageBlobDataReader)
    principalId: principalId
    principalType: 'ServicePrincipal'   // avoids failures when a new principal has not replicated yet
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- A role definition groups operations. A role assignment binds a principal + role + scope.
- `Actions` cover management operations and `DataActions` cover data operations. `NotActions` subtract from what is granted; they are not denies.
- Permissions are additive across all assignments. Only deny assignments override them.
- Propagation takes minutes. Use deterministic GUID names for assignments in IaC and specify `principalType`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use `az role definition list` to compare the `Actions` and `NotActions` of Owner, Contributor, and Reader, and explain why a Contributor cannot create role assignments.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a Bicep module that takes a principal ID and a list of role names and creates assignments on a storage account, with idempotent names. Deploy it twice and confirm nothing changes.
> 3. **(Interview)** "If a user has Reader on a subscription and Contributor on one resource group, what can they do in that resource group, and can you take away delete permissions on one resource inside it?" *Hint:* additive model, inheritance, and the difference between `NotActions` and deny assignments.

#### Built-In vs Custom Roles

Azure ships hundreds of **built-in roles**, maintained by Microsoft and updated automatically when services add new operations. Most of the time one of them fits. When none does, typically because the closest built-in role grants too much, you can define a **custom role** with exactly the operations you need.

Built-in roles every developer should recognize:

| Role | Grants | Typical holder |
|---|---|---|
| Owner | Full management access, including granting access to others | Subscription owners (few, ideally via PIM) |
| Contributor | Full management access, but cannot grant access or manage some governance features | Platform engineers, deployment pipelines on non-production scopes |
| Reader | View all resources, no changes, no data access | Auditors, support staff |
