```python
    "network_profile": {"network_interfaces": [{"id": nic.id, "delete_option": "Delete"}]},
    "tags": {"env": "dev", "owner": "team-api"},
})
vm = poller.result()
print(vm.name, vm.provisioning_state, vm.identity.principal_id)
```

Setting `delete_option` on the disk and NIC matters more than it looks. Without it, deleting the VM leaves orphaned disks and NICs that keep costing money and block subnet changes.

**Key takeaways**

- A VM is a graph: VM, disks, NIC, subnet/VNet, NSG, and optionally a public IP. Errors and costs often come from the dependencies.
- The CLI creates missing dependencies with permissive defaults. Override them (no public IP, no open SSH) for anything beyond a throwaway box.
- The management SDK makes you create each dependency explicitly, and every create is a long-running `begin_*` operation (see 1.5).
- Set delete options so disks and NICs are removed with the VM, and deallocate (not just stop) idle VMs to stop compute billing.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a VM with `az vm create` using only the required parameters, then list every resource that appeared in the resource group. Which of them did you not ask for?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a Python script that lists all VMs in a subscription with their power state (hint: `instance_view`) and deallocates any VM tagged `env=dev` that is running after 20:00.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your team's dev subscription bill keeps growing although developers say they delete their VMs. What do you check?" *Hint:* orphaned disks, NICs, public IPs, snapshots, stopped-but-not-deallocated VMs, and missing delete options.

#### Custom Script Extension

A freshly provisioned VM is an empty OS. Your app still needs a runtime, configuration files, a service definition, and perhaps a monitoring agent. You could SSH in and type the commands, but that is slow, error-prone, and impossible to repeat across fifty VMs. **VM extensions** are small agents that Azure installs and runs on a VM through the Azure control plane, and the **Custom Script Extension (CSE)** is the general-purpose one: it downloads scripts and runs them on the VM for you.

Analogy: instead of driving to each branch office to install software, you put the installer in a shared folder and send each office manager the same instruction: "download this and run it." The Azure VM Agent (preinstalled on Marketplace images) is that office manager.

How it works:

```text
  You / pipeline                Azure Resource Manager             VM
  az vm extension set  ------>  stores extension settings  ----->  VM Agent (waagent / WindowsAzureGuestAgent)
                                                                     | 1. downloads fileUris (Storage, GitHub, ...)
                                                                     | 2. runs commandToExecute as root/SYSTEM
                                                                     | 3. reports exit code + stdout/stderr
  az vm extension show  <-----  provisioning state  <-------------+
```

Important details:

| Aspect | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|
| Publisher / type | `Microsoft.Azure.Extensions` / `CustomScript` (v2.1) | `Microsoft.Compute` / `CustomScriptExtension` (v1.10) |
| Runs as | root | Local System |
| Logs on the VM | `/var/log/azure/custom-script/handler.log`, output under `/var/lib/waagent/custom-script/download/<n>/` | `C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\Plugins\Microsoft.Compute.CustomScriptExtension\` |

- **Settings vs protected settings.** `settings` are stored in plain text and visible to anyone who can read the VM resource. `protectedSettings` are encrypted and only decrypted on the VM. Put commands that contain secrets, and storage keys, in protected settings, or better, use `managedIdentity` to download from a private storage account with no key at all.
- **Runs once per configuration.** The extension runs when it is added or when its configuration changes. Re-applying identical settings does nothing. To force a re-run, change a value such as `timestamp` (Linux) or bump `forceUpdateTag`.
- **One CSE per VM.** A VM can have only one Custom Script Extension instance. Put several steps into one script, or orchestrate them from one entry point.
- **Time limit.** The script has 90 minutes. Long or reboot-requiring installs should be split or moved into a custom image.
- **Idempotency.** Scripts can be re-run (after a configuration change, reimage, or retry), so write them to be safe to run twice.

For one-off administrative commands, prefer **Run Command** (`az vm run-command invoke`), which runs a script without registering an extension in the VM's configuration.

**Example: install and configure a web server with CSE**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# install-api.sh: stored in a private blob container
set -euo pipefail                         # stop on the first error so CSE reports failure
apt-get update -y
apt-get install -y nginx python3-venv
mkdir -p /opt/api
if [ ! -d /opt/api/.venv ]; then          # idempotent: only create the venv once
  python3 -m venv /opt/api/.venv
fi
systemctl enable --now nginx
```

```bash
# Give the VM's managed identity read access to the scripts container
PRINCIPAL=$(az vm show -g rg-vmdemo -n vm-api-01 --query identity.principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Storage Blob Data Reader" \
  --scope "$(az storage account show -n stscripts001 --query id -o tsv)/blobServices/default/containers/scripts"

# Run the script; the URI and the command go in protected settings
az vm extension set -g rg-vmdemo --vm-name vm-api-01 \
  --publisher Microsoft.Azure.Extensions --name CustomScript --version 2.1 \
  --protected-settings '{
    "fileUris": ["https://stscripts001.blob.core.windows.net/scripts/install-api.sh"],
    "commandToExecute": "bash install-api.sh",
    "managedIdentity": {}
  }'                                            # {} = use the system-assigned identity

# Check the result; on failure the message contains the script's stderr
az vm extension show -g rg-vmdemo --vm-name vm-api-01 --name CustomScript \
  --query "{state:provisioningState, msg:instanceView.statuses[0].message}"

# Ad-hoc alternative: Run Command (no extension state left behind)
az vm run-command invoke -g rg-vmdemo -n vm-api-01 --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "systemctl status nginx --no-pager"
```

**Key takeaways**

- CSE downloads and runs scripts on a VM through the VM Agent. No SSH or RDP access is needed.
- Put secrets and download credentials in `protectedSettings`, or use `managedIdentity` to fetch scripts from private storage without keys.
- It runs once per configuration change, one CSE per VM, with a 90-minute limit. Make scripts idempotent and fail fast (`set -euo pipefail`).
- Use Run Command for ad-hoc troubleshooting, and custom images for slow, heavy installs.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use CSE to install `nginx` on a Linux VM from an inline command, then find the extension's stdout on the VM.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Change your script and re-apply the extension with identical settings. Observe that nothing happens, then make it re-run without removing the extension.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why would you choose a custom image over a Custom Script Extension for configuring scale set instances?" *Hint:* compare time to a ready instance during scale-out, dependency on external downloads at boot, and reproducibility.

#### Cloud-init

Custom Script Extension runs *after* the VM is up and the Azure agent is ready. Linux has a native, cross-cloud tool that configures the machine *during its very first boot*: **cloud-init**. Most Linux images on Azure (Ubuntu, RHEL, Debian, Azure Linux, and others) include it, and the same cloud-init file works on Azure, AWS, GCP, and OpenStack.

Analogy: CSE is an installer you run after moving into a new house. Cloud-init is the checklist the builders follow before handing you the keys: create these users, install these packages, put these files in place, start these services.

You pass a cloud-init configuration as **custom data** when you create the VM. Azure places it on the VM, and cloud-init processes it on first boot:

```text
 az vm create --custom-data cloud-init.yaml
        |
        v
 First boot: cloud-init stages
   init      -> network, disks, SSH keys, users
   config    -> write_files, packages, apt/yum repositories
   final     -> runcmd (your commands), service start
        |
        v
 VM reported as ready; /var/log/cloud-init-output.log has the full output
```

A cloud-init file starts with `#cloud-config` and uses declarative modules. Declarative modules are preferable to shell commands because they are idempotent and readable:

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `package_update`, `package_upgrade`, `packages` | Refresh repositories, upgrade, install packages |
| `users`, `groups` | Create accounts and SSH keys |
| `write_files` | Write files with content, owner, and permissions |
| `runcmd` | Run shell commands at the end of first boot |
| `mounts`, `disk_setup`, `fs_setup` | Format and mount data disks |

Constraints to keep in mind:

- Custom data is limited to **64 KB** (before base64 encoding). Keep large assets elsewhere and download them.
- It runs **once**, on first boot. Changing custom data on an existing VM does not re-run it. (Azure also offers **user data**, which can be updated and read through the Instance Metadata Service, but cloud-init does not re-process it automatically.)
- Custom data is **not a secret store**. Anyone with read access to the VM configuration, or code on the VM, can read it. Fetch secrets at runtime with a managed identity instead.
- Azure reports the VM as created before cloud-init has finished. Scripts that SSH in immediately should wait with `cloud-init status --wait`.

| | Cloud-init | Custom Script Extension | Custom image |
|---|---|---|---|
| When it runs | First boot only | Whenever added or reconfigured | Already baked in |
| OS | Linux | Linux and Windows | Any |
| Portability | Cross-cloud standard | Azure-specific | Azure (Compute Gallery) |
| Boot-to-ready time | Depends on installs | Depends on installs | Fastest |
| Best for | Base configuration of new Linux VMs and scale set instances | Post-deployment configuration, Windows | Heavy, slow-changing software stacks |

**Example: a Python API server configured entirely by cloud-init**

```yaml
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - nginx
  - python3-venv

write_files:
  - path: /etc/systemd/system/api.service          # systemd unit for the app
    permissions: "0644"
    content: |
      [Unit]
      Description=Orders API
      After=network-online.target
      [Service]
      User=www-data
      WorkingDirectory=/opt/api
      ExecStart=/opt/api/.venv/bin/gunicorn -b 127.0.0.1:8000 app:app
      Restart=always
      [Install]
      WantedBy=multi-user.target
  - path: /etc/nginx/sites-available/default       # reverse proxy to gunicorn
    content: |
      server {
        listen 80;
        location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000; }
      }

runcmd:
  - mkdir -p /opt/api && cd /opt/api
  - python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install flask gunicorn
  - printf 'from flask import Flask\napp = Flask(__name__)\n@app.get("/")\ndef hi(): return "ok"\n' > app.py
  - chown -R www-data:www-data /opt/api
  - systemctl daemon-reload
  - systemctl enable --now api
  - systemctl restart nginx
```

```bash
az vm create -g rg-vmdemo -n vm-api-03 --image Ubuntu2404 --size Standard_B2s \
  --vnet-name vnet-app --subnet snet-app --public-ip-address "" --nsg-rule NONE \
  --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys \
  --custom-data cloud-init.yaml                   # processed by cloud-init on first boot

# Wait for cloud-init and show its result (Run Command works without SSH)
az vm run-command invoke -g rg-vmdemo -n vm-api-03 --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "cloud-init status --wait --long; tail -n 20 /var/log/cloud-init-output.log"
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cloud-init configures Linux VMs on first boot from a declarative `#cloud-config` file passed as custom data.
- It is portable across clouds, idempotent when you use modules, and runs only once.
- Custom data is limited to 64 KB and is not secret. Fetch secrets at runtime instead.
- The VM can report "succeeded" before cloud-init finishes. Use `cloud-init status --wait` and the logs under `/var/log`.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a cloud-init file that creates a user `deploy` with your SSH key and installs `git` and `htop`. Deploy a VM with it and verify both.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Introduce a typo in a `runcmd` line. Find where the error appears, and explain why `az vm create` still reported success.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A colleague put a database password into cloud-init custom data. What are the risks, and what would you do instead?" *Hint:* who can read the VM model and IMDS, where custom data persists, and how managed identities with Key Vault avoid storing the secret.

#### Virtual Machine Scale Sets

A single VM is a single point of failure and has a fixed capacity. To serve more traffic or survive a host failure you need several identical VMs, plus a way to add or remove them automatically. Managing that fleet by hand (creating, configuring, patching, and load-balancing each VM) does not scale. A **Virtual Machine Scale Set (VMSS)** manages a group of VMs as one resource: you describe the VM once, then say how many you want and when the count should change.

Analogy: instead of hiring each delivery driver individually, you contract a staffing agency with a template ("licensed driver, own van, available 8 to 18"). You tell the agency how many you need today, and it sends identical drivers and replaces any who call in sick.

Scale sets have two **orchestration modes**:

| | Flexible (recommended for new workloads) | Uniform |
|---|---|---|
| Instances | Standard VM resources you can manage with normal VM APIs | Special "VMSS VM" instances, managed through the scale set |
| Mixing | Can mix sizes, and even add existing VMs | All instances identical |
| Fault domains / zones | Spreads across zones and fault domains, up to 1,000 instances | Same, built for large homogeneous fleets |
| Typical use | General-purpose and stateful-ish workloads, HA | Large stateless fleets, legacy integrations |

Key capabilities:

- **Autoscale** with Azure Monitor rules (CPU, memory via the guest agent, queue length, schedules), as introduced in 1.1. Stateless app design is the prerequisite.
- **Load balancing** with Azure Load Balancer (layer 4) or Application Gateway (layer 7).
- **Zone spreading** (`--zones 1 2 3`) so a datacenter failure removes only part of the capacity.
- **Health monitoring** with the Application Health extension or a load balancer probe, and **automatic instance repairs** that replace unhealthy instances.
- **Upgrade policy** for changes to the model (new image, new extension settings): *Manual* (you upgrade instances), *Automatic* (all at once, risky), or *Rolling* (in batches, with health checks between batches).
- **Spot priority mix**, to run part of the capacity on discounted Spot VMs.

```text
                         Azure Load Balancer (public or internal)
                          health probe: GET /healthz
                     +-------------+-------------+-------------+
                     |             |             |             |
                Zone 1         Zone 2         Zone 3        (scale out adds
             +---------+    +---------+    +---------+      instances here,
             | vm  #0  |    | vm  #1  |    | vm  #2  |      spread across zones)
             +---------+    +---------+    +---------+
                 ^ every instance built from the same model:
                   image + size + cloud-init/extensions + identity
                                   |
                   Autoscale: min 3 / max 12; +2 when CPU > 70%, -1 when CPU < 30%
```

**Example: a zone-redundant, self-healing, autoscaling scale set**

```bash
RG=rg-vmss; LOC=westeurope
az group create -n $RG -l $LOC

# Every new instance configures itself from cloud-init, sits behind a Standard
# Load Balancer, and receives model changes in health-checked batches (Rolling)
az vmss create -g $RG -n vmss-api \
  --orchestration-mode Flexible \
  --image Ubuntu2404 --vm-sku Standard_D2s_v5 \
  --instance-count 3 --zones 1 2 3 \
  --custom-data cloud-init.yaml \
  --lb lb-api --lb-sku Standard \
  --upgrade-policy-mode Rolling \
  --admin-username azureuser --generate-ssh-keys

# Health signal from inside the instance: the app's /healthz endpoint
az vmss extension set -g $RG --vmss-name vmss-api \
  --publisher Microsoft.ManagedServices --name ApplicationHealthLinux --version 1.0 \
  --settings '{"protocol": "http", "port": 80, "requestPath": "/healthz"}'

# Replace instances that stay unhealthy for 30 minutes
az vmss update -g $RG -n vmss-api \
  --enable-automatic-repairs true --automatic-repairs-grace-period 30

# Autoscale between 3 and 12 instances on CPU
az monitor autoscale create -g $RG -n as-vmss-api \
  --resource vmss-api --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets \
  --min-count 3 --max-count 12 --count 3
az monitor autoscale rule create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-vmss-api \
  --condition "Percentage CPU > 70 avg 5m" --scale out 2
az monitor autoscale rule create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-vmss-api \
  --condition "Percentage CPU < 30 avg 15m" --scale in 1
```

**Key takeaways**

- A scale set manages many identical VMs from one model, with autoscale, zone spreading, load balancing, and self-healing.
- Use Flexible orchestration for new workloads. Uniform remains for large homogeneous fleets and older integrations.
- Instances are created and destroyed automatically, so they must be stateless and self-configuring (custom image, cloud-init, or extensions).
- Combine a health signal, automatic repairs, and a Rolling upgrade policy so that bad updates are caught before they reach every instance.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a Flexible scale set with two instances and scale it manually to four with `az vmss scale`. Where do the new instances appear in `az vm list`?
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Generate CPU load on the instances (for example with `stress-ng` through Run Command) and watch the autoscale rules add instances. Record how long it takes from the spike to a new instance serving traffic, and which part of that time is boot and configuration.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you run a web API on a VM scale set instead of App Service?" *Hint:* OS-level control, custom agents or drivers, GPU sizes, licensing, network appliances, and the operational cost you take on in exchange.

<a id="32-azure-app-service"></a>
### 3.2 Azure App Service

App Service is Azure's PaaS for web apps and APIs. You bring code or a container, and the platform provides the OS, runtime, load balancing, TLS, scaling, and deployment tooling. This section covers what you need to run a production web app on it.

#### App Service Plans and Tiers

A web app needs CPU and memory somewhere. In App Service, that "somewhere" is the **App Service plan**: a set of VMs (called *instances* or *workers*) of a given size, in a given region and OS. Web apps don't get compute of their own. They are **placed into a plan** and share its instances. Understanding this separation explains most App Service cost and performance surprises: the bill is for the plan, not the apps, and a noisy app slows down every other app in the same plan.

Analogy: the plan is an apartment you rent (size, number of rooms, monthly rent). Apps are the roommates. Adding a roommate costs nothing extra, but everyone shares the kitchen. Scaling out means renting identical apartments next door, and *every* roommate moves into each one.

```text
  App Service plan "plan-shop-prod" (Linux, P1v3, 3 instances)    <- you pay for this
  +------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
  | instance 1       |   | instance 2       |   | instance 3       |
  |  app-shop-web    |   |  app-shop-web    |   |  app-shop-web    |
  |  app-shop-api    |   |  app-shop-api    |   |  app-shop-api    |
  +------------------+   +------------------+   +------------------+
         ^ every app in the plan runs on every instance (unless per-app scaling is enabled)
```

The plan's **pricing tier** decides the hardware and which features are available:

| Tier | Compute | Max instances | Deployment slots | Autoscale | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Free (F1) | Shared with other customers, CPU minutes per day capped | 1 | No | No | Experiments |
| Shared (D1, Windows only) | Shared, higher CPU quota | 1 | No | No | Hobby sites with a custom domain |
| Basic (B1–B3) | Dedicated VMs | 3 (manual) | No | No | Dev/test, low-traffic production |
| Standard (S1–S3) | Dedicated VMs | 10 | 5 | Yes (rules) | Production baseline |
| Premium v3 (P0v3–P5mv3) | Dedicated, newer hardware, memory-optimized variants | 30 | 20 | Yes, plus automatic scaling | Most production workloads, zone redundancy |
| Isolated v2 (I1v2–I6v2) | Dedicated, inside an App Service Environment in your VNet | 100 | 20 | Yes | Strict network isolation, very large scale |

A newer Premium v4 generation is also rolling out by region. Exact limits change over time, so check the current documentation before you depend on a number.

Other facts that shape design decisions:

- **OS is fixed per plan.** A Linux plan hosts Linux apps (code or containers), and a Windows plan hosts Windows apps.
- **Shared tiers (F1, D1) have no SLA** and run your app on VMs shared with other customers.
- **Always On** (Basic and above) keeps the app loaded. Without it, an idle app is unloaded after about 20 minutes and the next request pays a cold start.
- **Scale up** changes the tier/size for all instances. **Scale out** changes the instance count. Both apply to the whole plan.
- **Per-app scaling** (`--per-site-scaling`) lets a lightweight app run on fewer instances than the plan has, which is useful for high-density plans.
- **Zone redundancy** (Premium v3+, minimum instance count set) spreads instances across availability zones.

**Example: create plans and choose tiers**

```bash
# Linux Premium v3 plan, zone redundant (needs an instance count of at least 2 or 3, depending on region rules)
az appservice plan create -g rg-shop -n plan-shop-prod --is-linux \
  --sku P1v3 --number-of-workers 3 --zone-redundant

# A cheap dev plan
az appservice plan create -g rg-shop-dev -n plan-shop-dev --is-linux --sku B1

# Scale up (bigger instances) and scale out (more instances)
az appservice plan update -g rg-shop -n plan-shop-prod --sku P2v3
az appservice plan update -g rg-shop -n plan-shop-prod --number-of-workers 4

# Which apps share this plan (and therefore its CPU and memory)?
az webapp list -g rg-shop --query "[?appServicePlanId.contains(@, 'plan-shop-prod')].name" -o tsv
```

**Key takeaways**

- The plan is the unit of compute and billing. Apps in it share its instances, and scaling applies to all of them.
- Tiers gate features: slots and autoscale need Standard or above, and network isolation needs Isolated.
- Use Free and Shared only for experiments. They have no SLA and share hardware with other customers.
- Group apps by load and lifecycle. Put a busy or critical app in its own plan so it cannot slow down others.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a B1 plan and two web apps in it. Delete one app and confirm that the cost of the plan does not change.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Five small internal apps each need about 300 MB of memory and little CPU, and one public API needs to scale between 2 and 10 instances. Propose a plan layout and tier for each, and justify it.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why did adding a new app to an existing plan make our checkout API slower?" *Hint:* shared CPU, memory, and connections per instance; scale-out multiplies every app in the plan; consider per-app scaling or a separate plan.

#### Creating and Deploying Web Apps

Once a plan exists, a **web app** (a `Microsoft.Web/sites` resource) is the container for one application: its code, configuration, host name, and deployment history. The hard part in practice is not creating the app but getting code onto it reliably. Copying files over FTP may work once, but it leaves half-updated sites, no history, and no way to roll back.

App Service supports several **deployment methods**:

| Method | How it works | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ZIP deploy (`az webapp deploy`) | Upload a ZIP of your app; optionally build it on the server | Simple, scriptable |
| Run from package | App mounts the ZIP read-only (`WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1`) | Atomic updates, faster cold start; app cannot write to its own folder |
| GitHub Actions / Azure Pipelines | CI builds the artifact, then deploys with OIDC credentials | Recommended for teams |
| Container image | App pulls an image from a registry (chapter 4) | Full control of the runtime environment |
| Local Git / external Git | Push to a Git remote hosted by App Service | Quick demos |
| FTP/FTPS | Copy files directly | Avoid; disable it (see 1.1) |

For **code** deployments, the platform runs a build engine (Oryx on Linux) when you set `SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true`: it detects the language, installs dependencies (`pip install -r requirements.txt`, `npm install`), and generates a startup command. Every app also has a companion **Kudu (SCM) site** at `https://<app>.scm.azurewebsites.net` that handles deployments and offers a console, process explorer, and log streaming.

On Linux, each app runs in a container built from a platform image for your runtime (for example Python 3.12). If your framework needs a specific start command, set it as the **startup command**. New apps get a default host name of the form `<app>-<hash>.<region>.azurewebsites.net` when unique default host names are enabled, which prevents someone else from claiming your old name after you delete an app.

```text
  Developer / CI                    Kudu (SCM) site                   Worker instances
  zip (code + requirements.txt) --> /api/publish --> Oryx build -->   /home/site/wwwroot
                                    (pip install, detect app)         container starts:
                                                                      gunicorn app:app
```

**Example: create, configure, and ZIP-deploy a Flask app**

```bash
az webapp create -g rg-shop -p plan-shop-prod -n app-shop-api --runtime "PYTHON:3.12"

# Build on the server during deployment, and set an explicit start command
az webapp config appsettings set -g rg-shop -n app-shop-api \
  --settings SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true
az webapp config set -g rg-shop -n app-shop-api \
  --startup-file "gunicorn --bind=0.0.0.0:8000 --workers=4 --timeout 120 app:app"

# Package and deploy (app.py + requirements.txt at the root of the ZIP)
zip -r app.zip app.py requirements.txt
az webapp deploy -g rg-shop -n app-shop-api --src-path app.zip --type zip

az webapp browse -g rg-shop -n app-shop-api
```

**Example: CI deployment from GitHub Actions with OIDC (no stored password)**

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy-api.yml
name: deploy-api
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  id-token: write          # needed to request the OIDC token for azure/login
  contents: read
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest -q   # test before shipping
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with:
          client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}             # federated credential, see 2.4
          tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
          subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
      - uses: azure/webapps-deploy@v3
        with:
          app-name: app-shop-api
          package: .
```

**Key takeaways**

- A web app lives in a plan and holds one application's code, configuration, and host names.
- Prefer ZIP or package-based deployments from CI over FTP or manual copies. Run from package makes updates atomic.
- Oryx builds code on Linux when `SCM_DO_BUILD_DURING_DEPLOYMENT=true`. Set a startup command when the default detection is not enough.
- The Kudu/SCM site is your deployment and diagnostics back door. Protect it like production.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Deploy a "hello world" app in your language of choice with `az webapp up`, then find the generated startup command in the app's configuration.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Switch the app to run from package and try to write a file into `/home/site/wwwroot` from code. Explain the error and where the app should write files instead.
> 3. **(Interview)** "What are the trade-offs between building on the server (Oryx) and building in CI and deploying an artifact?" *Hint:* reproducibility, build-time dependencies, test coverage of the exact artifact, deployment speed, and native packages.

#### App Settings and Connection Strings

The same code should run in dev, test, and production with different databases, keys, and feature flags. Hardcoding those values (or committing a `.env` file) mixes configuration with code and leaks secrets into source control. App Service provides **app settings** and **connection strings**: name/value pairs stored with the app, encrypted at rest, and injected into the process as **environment variables** at startup.

Analogy: the app is a rental car, and app settings are the driver profile loaded when you start it. Same car, different seat position and radio stations for each driver.

How values reach your code:

| Configured as | Exposed as environment variable | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App setting `FEATURE_X=on` | `FEATURE_X` | All languages |
| App setting `Logging__LogLevel__Default` | `Logging__LogLevel__Default` | .NET maps `__` to `:` for hierarchical keys. Use `__` because `:` is not allowed on Linux |
| Connection string `Orders` of type SQLAzure | `SQLAZURECONNSTR_Orders` | Prefix depends on type: `SQLCONNSTR_`, `MYSQLCONNSTR_`, `POSTGRESQLCONNSTR_`, `CUSTOMCONNSTR_`, ... |
| Connection string, .NET apps | Also available through `ConnectionStrings:Orders` | Overrides `appsettings.json` |

Behavior to know:

- **Changing settings restarts the app.** Plan changes outside peak hours, or use slots.
- **App settings override** values in files such as `appsettings.json` or `web.config`.
- **Slot settings** ("deployment slot setting") stay with a slot during swaps (see the next topic).
- **Key Vault references** let a setting point to a secret instead of containing it: `@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-shop.vault.azure.net/secrets/DbPassword/)`. The app's managed identity needs read access to the secret. Omitting the version makes the platform pick up rotated values (typically within 24 hours, or on restart).
- **Prefer no secret at all.** With managed identity (2.4) the setting can be just an endpoint, such as `STORAGE_URL=https://stshop.blob.core.windows.net`.
- Anyone with Contributor rights on the app can read its settings. Settings are not a substitute for Key Vault.

**Example: settings, connection strings, and Key Vault references**

```bash
APP=app-shop-api; RG=rg-shop

# Plain settings
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP --settings \
  APP_ENV=production FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT=false \
  STORAGE_URL=https://stshop.blob.core.windows.net

# A connection string of type PostgreSQL
az webapp config connection-string set -g $RG -n $APP --connection-string-type PostgreSQL \
  --settings Orders="host=pg-shop.postgres.database.azure.com dbname=orders sslmode=require"

# Key Vault reference: enable the identity, grant it access, then point the setting at the secret
PRINCIPAL=$(az webapp identity assign -g $RG -n $APP --query principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id "$PRINCIPAL" --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" --scope "$(az keyvault show -n kv-shop --query id -o tsv)"
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP --settings \
  PAYMENT_API_KEY="@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://kv-shop.vault.azure.net/secrets/PaymentApiKey/)"

# Verify the reference resolved (status should be "Resolved")
az rest --method get \
  --url "$(az webapp show -g $RG -n $APP --query id -o tsv)/config/configreferences/appsettings?api-version=2023-12-01" \
  --query "value[].{name:name, status:properties.status}"
```

```python
# app.py: code reads plain environment variables, whatever their source
import os

APP_ENV = os.environ.get("APP_ENV", "development")
NEW_CHECKOUT = os.environ.get("FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT", "false").lower() == "true"
ORDERS_DSN = os.environ["POSTGRESQLCONNSTR_Orders"]      # prefix added by connection string type
PAYMENT_API_KEY = os.environ["PAYMENT_API_KEY"]          # already resolved from Key Vault by the platform
```

**Key takeaways**

- App settings and connection strings are injected as environment variables. Connection strings get a type-specific prefix.
- Use `__` for hierarchical keys. Changing settings restarts the app.
- Keep secrets in Key Vault and reference them with `@Microsoft.KeyVault(...)` through the app's managed identity, or avoid secrets entirely with identity-based connections.
- Settings are readable by anyone with write access to the app, so manage access to the app accordingly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add an app setting and a connection string of type `Custom`, then print all environment variables from the Kudu/SSH console and find both.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Configure a Key Vault reference, remove the app's role assignment, restart, and observe the setting's resolution status and the value your code receives.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why is a version-less Key Vault reference usually preferable, and when might you pin a version?" *Hint:* rotation without redeploy versus controlled, auditable changes and the refresh delay.

#### Deployment Slots and Swaps

Deploying directly to production means users hit the new version while it is still starting: they get cold caches, failed requests during restart, and no quick way back if something is wrong. **Deployment slots** (Standard tier and above) are live, separately addressable copies of your app, such as `app-shop-api-staging.azurewebsites.net`, that run on the same plan. You deploy to a non-production slot, warm it up and test it, then **swap** it with production.

Analogy: a theater with a revolving stage. The next scene is built and lit on the hidden half while the audience watches the current one. When it is ready, the stage rotates, and if something goes wrong, it rotates back.

What a swap does (staging into production):

```text
 1. Apply production's slot-specific settings to the staging instances  -> staging restarts
 2. Warm up: send requests to each staging instance (default "/"; custom path optional)
    and wait until they respond
 3. Switch routing: production host name now points at the warmed instances
 4. The old production code is now in the staging slot (ready for an instant rollback)
```

Because routing switches only after warm-up, users see no downtime and no cold start. **Rolling back** is just swapping again.

Not everything moves with a swap. Code and most configuration move, but some settings belong to the slot:

| Swapped (moves with the code) | Not swapped (stays with the slot) |
|---|---|
| App settings and connection strings, unless marked as slot settings | Settings marked as **slot settings** ("sticky") |
| Runtime stack and general settings | Custom domains and TLS bindings |
| Handler mappings, WebJobs content | Scale settings, Always On |
| Public certificates | IP restrictions, CORS, VNet integration |
| | Managed identities, diagnostic settings, publishing endpoints |

Mark environment-specific values (the database a slot talks to, `APP_ENV`) as slot settings. Otherwise staging's test database moves into production on the first swap.

Related features:

- **Swap with preview** pauses after step 1, so you can validate staging with production's settings before completing or cancelling.
- **Auto swap** swaps automatically after every successful deployment to a slot (Windows apps).
- **Warm-up control**: `WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH` and `WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES` let you warm up a specific health endpoint and accept only certain status codes.
- **Testing in production**: route a percentage of production traffic to a slot. Clients stick to it with an `x-ms-routing-name` cookie, and you can opt in manually with `?x-ms-routing-name=staging`.

**Example: blue-green deployment with a staging slot**

```bash
APP=app-shop-api; RG=rg-shop

# Create the slot, cloning production's configuration
az webapp deployment slot create -g $RG -n $APP --slot staging --configuration-source $APP

# Sticky settings: each slot keeps its own environment name and database
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP --slot staging \
  --slot-settings APP_ENV=staging DB_NAME=orders_staging
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP \
  --slot-settings APP_ENV=production DB_NAME=orders

# Warm up a dedicated health endpoint and require HTTP 200 before switching (set on both slots)
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP --slot staging \
  --settings WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH=/healthz WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES=200
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP \
  --settings WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH=/healthz WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES=200

# Deploy the new version to staging and smoke-test it
az webapp deploy -g $RG -n $APP --slot staging --src-path app.zip --type zip
curl -fsS https://$APP-staging.azurewebsites.net/healthz

# Optional canary: send 10% of production traffic to staging for a while
az webapp traffic-routing set -g $RG -n $APP --distribution staging=10
az webapp traffic-routing clear -g $RG -n $APP

# Swap; run the same command again to roll back
az webapp deployment slot swap -g $RG -n $APP --slot staging --target-slot production
```

**Key takeaways**

- Slots are live copies of the app on the same plan. Deploy to a slot, warm it up, then swap for zero-downtime releases.
- A swap applies target settings, warms up instances, and then switches routing. Rollback is another swap.
- Mark environment-specific settings as slot settings so they don't travel with the code.
- Slots share the plan's capacity, so a heavy test in staging can affect production.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a staging slot, deploy a version that returns "v2" to it, swap, and verify that production returns "v2" and staging returns "v1".
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add one sticky and one non-sticky setting to each slot, swap twice, and record where each value ends up after each swap.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A swap completed, but users saw errors for a minute afterwards. What could be wrong?" *Hint:* the warm-up path does not exercise real dependencies, settings that changed during swap trigger extra restarts, database schema changes that are not backward compatible, and in-memory session state.

#### Autoscaling Rules

Traffic is rarely flat: a shop is busy at lunchtime and quiet at 3 a.m., and a campaign can multiply load in minutes. A fixed instance count either wastes money at night or fails at peak. **Autoscale** (Standard tier and above) adjusts the **plan's** instance count automatically. The general concepts (metrics, rules, cool-downs, scale-in rules) were introduced in 1.1. This topic covers what is specific to App Service.

App Service offers two autoscaling mechanisms. You use one or the other on a plan, not both:

| | Rule-based autoscale (Azure Monitor) | Automatic scaling (platform-managed) |
|---|---|---|
| Tiers | Standard, Premium, Isolated | Premium v2/v3 (and newer) |
| How it decides | Your rules on metrics (CPU, memory, HTTP queue, custom) and schedules | Platform watches HTTP load and scales per app |
| Pre-warmed capacity | No | Yes (pre-warmed instances, minimum "always ready" instances per app) |
| Control | Full: thresholds, steps, cool-downs, schedules | Max burst for the plan, minimum instances per app |
| Best for | Predictable patterns, non-HTTP load (background jobs), fine control | Spiky HTTP traffic, teams that don't want to tune rules |

Useful App Service metrics for rule-based autoscale (all measured at the plan level):

| Metric | What it indicates |
|---|---|
| `CpuPercentage` | CPU pressure across instances |
| `MemoryPercentage` | Memory pressure, important for Python/Node workers and caches |
| `HttpQueueLength` | Requests waiting for a worker; a direct sign of saturation |
| `DiskQueueLength` | Storage bottlenecks |

Good practices:

- Always pair a **scale-out** rule with a **scale-in** rule, and leave a gap between their thresholds (for example out above 70%, in below 40%) to avoid **flapping**.
- Set the **minimum to at least 2** (3 with zone redundancy) for production, so one instance failure or platform update does not take the app down.
- Use **schedule profiles** for known peaks, so capacity is already there instead of being added after users notice.
- Make apps stateless and **disable ARR affinity** (sticky sessions), or new instances will receive little traffic.
- Configure **Health check** (`/healthz`): unhealthy instances are removed from the load balancer and eventually replaced.

**Example: rules plus a business-hours profile for a plan**

```bash
RG=rg-shop; PLAN=plan-shop-prod
PLAN_ID=$(az appservice plan show -g $RG -n $PLAN --query id -o tsv)

# Default profile: 2 to 10 instances
az monitor autoscale create -g $RG -n as-shop --resource "$PLAN_ID" \
  --min-count 2 --max-count 10 --count 2

# Saturation signals: requests queuing or CPU high -> add instances
az monitor autoscale rule create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-shop \
  --condition "HttpQueueLength > 20 avg 5m" --scale out 2 --cooldown 5
az monitor autoscale rule create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-shop \
  --condition "CpuPercentage > 70 avg 10m" --scale out 1 --cooldown 10
az monitor autoscale rule create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-shop \
  --condition "CpuPercentage < 40 avg 20m" --scale in 1 --cooldown 15

# Business-hours profile: at least 4 instances on weekdays from 08:00 to 19:00
az monitor autoscale profile create -g $RG --autoscale-name as-shop -n business-hours \
  --min-count 4 --max-count 10 --count 4 \
  --recurrence week mon tue wed thu fri --start 08:00 --end 19:00 \
  --timezone "W. Europe Standard Time"

# Stateless app: turn off sticky sessions and add a health check
az webapp update -g $RG -n app-shop-api --client-affinity-enabled false
az webapp config set -g $RG -n app-shop-api --generic-configurations '{"healthCheckPath": "/healthz"}'
```

```bash
# Alternative on Premium v3: platform-managed automatic scaling instead of rules
az appservice plan update -g $RG -n $PLAN --elastic-scale true --max-elastic-worker-count 20
az webapp update -g $RG -n app-shop-api --minimum-elastic-instance-count 2 --prewarmed-instance-count 1
```

Note that a schedule profile replaces the default profile while it is active, so it needs its own metric rules.

**Key takeaways**

- Autoscale works on the plan, so every app in it scales together.
- Choose rule-based autoscale for fine control and non-HTTP signals, or automatic scaling (Premium) for hands-off HTTP scaling with pre-warmed instances.
- `HttpQueueLength` and CPU are the usual saturation signals. Always add scale-in rules and leave a gap between thresholds.
- Production minimum of 2 or more, schedule profiles for known peaks, no sticky sessions, and a health check path.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Configure autoscale for a Standard plan between 1 and 3 instances on CPU, then view the autoscale history in the Activity log or the autoscale run history.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Load-test the app (for example with Azure Load Testing or `hey`) and compare how fast `CpuPercentage` and `HttpQueueLength` rules react. Which one would you rely on for a Python app with few workers?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Autoscale added instances, but response times did not improve. Why?" *Hint:* downstream bottleneck (database, external API), sticky sessions, slow startup without warm-up, connection limits, or the plan already at its maximum.

#### Custom Domains and TLS Certificates

Users should reach `shop.contoso.com`, not `app-shop-api-a1b2.westeurope-01.azurewebsites.net`, and browsers refuse or warn about anything without valid HTTPS. App Service handles both: you prove that you own a domain, map it to the app, and bind a TLS certificate that matches it.

Analogy: mapping a custom domain is like registering a trading name for your business. The registry (DNS) says "Contoso Shop" is operated from this address. The TLS certificate is the notarized certificate on the wall that proves to customers that the sign on the door is genuine.

Steps for a custom domain:

```text
 1. Ownership:  TXT  asuid.shop.contoso.com  = <app's customDomainVerificationId>
 2. Routing:    CNAME shop.contoso.com       -> app-shop-api.azurewebsites.net     (subdomain)
          or    A     contoso.com            -> <app's inbound IP>                 (apex/root domain)
                TXT   asuid.contoso.com      = <verification ID>
 3. Add the host name to the app
 4. Bind a certificate (SNI SSL) for that host name
 5. Enforce HTTPS only and a minimum TLS version
```

The `asuid` TXT record proves ownership even before traffic moves. This lets you migrate a live domain without downtime and prevents another Azure customer from claiming a domain whose CNAME still points at a deleted app (**subdomain takeover**).

Certificate options:

| Option | Cost | Wildcard | Renewal | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| App Service managed certificate | Free | No | Automatic | Basic tier and above; cannot be exported; apex domains need an A record |
| App Service certificate (purchased) | Paid yearly | Yes (wildcard SKU) | Automatic, stored in Key Vault | Can be used by other services |
| Import from Key Vault | Your CA's price | Yes | Rotation in Key Vault syncs to the app | Best for enterprise CAs and central certificate management |
| Upload PFX | Your CA's price | Yes | Manual re-upload | Simplest, but easy to forget to renew |

**SNI SSL** is the normal binding type: many certificates share one IP, and the client sends the host name during the TLS handshake. **IP-based SSL** dedicates an IP address to the binding and is needed only for very old clients.

**Example: map a domain and secure it with a free managed certificate**

```bash
APP=app-shop-api; RG=rg-shop; HOST=shop.contoso.com

# 1) Values to put in DNS
az webapp show -g $RG -n $APP --query "{verificationId:customDomainVerificationId, defaultHost:defaultHostName}"

# 2) Create the DNS records (here with Azure DNS; any DNS provider works)
az network dns record-set txt add-record -g rg-dns -z contoso.com -n asuid.shop --value "<verificationId>"
az network dns record-set cname set-record -g rg-dns -z contoso.com -n shop --cname "<defaultHost>"

# 3) Add the host name, 4) create and bind the free managed certificate
az webapp config hostname add -g $RG --webapp-name $APP --hostname $HOST
THUMB=$(az webapp config ssl create -g $RG -n $APP --hostname $HOST --query thumbprint -o tsv)
az webapp config ssl bind -g $RG -n $APP --certificate-thumbprint $THUMB --ssl-type SNI

# 5) Enforce HTTPS and modern TLS
az webapp update -g $RG -n $APP --https-only true
az webapp config set -g $RG -n $APP --min-tls-version 1.2
```

```bash
# Alternative: certificate managed centrally in Key Vault (rotations in Key Vault sync to the app)
az webapp config ssl import -g $RG -n $APP --key-vault kv-certs --key-vault-certificate-name wildcard-contoso
```

**Key takeaways**

- Prove ownership with an `asuid` TXT record, then route with CNAME (subdomains) or A (apex domains).
- Delete DNS records when you delete an app. Dangling CNAMEs invite subdomain takeover.
- Use the free managed certificate for simple cases, and Key Vault-backed certificates for wildcards, central management, and enterprise CAs.
- Bind with SNI, then enforce HTTPS only and TLS 1.2 or later.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** List the DNS records you need to map `api.example.com` and `example.com` to the same app, and explain why they differ.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Migrate a live domain from another host to App Service without downtime. Describe the order in which you create the TXT record, add the host name, bind the certificate, and switch the CNAME.
> 3. **(Interview)** "What is a subdomain takeover, and how does App Service's domain verification help prevent it?" *Hint:* a CNAME pointing at a deleted resource's name, someone else creating a resource with that name, and the role of the `asuid` record.

#### Diagnostic Logging

When an app returns 500 errors at 2 a.m., you cannot attach a debugger to production. You need **logs**: what the app printed, what requests arrived, and what the platform did (restarts, deployments, crashes). App Service collects several kinds of logs. Most are off by default, because collecting them costs storage and performance, so turn on the ones you need *before* the incident.

Log types:

| Log | Contents | Linux | Windows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Application logging | What your code writes to stdout/stderr or the logging framework | Yes (container stdout) | Yes (filesystem: auto-disables after 12 hours; Blob for longer) |
| Web server logging | Raw HTTP request log (W3C format) | Via diagnostic settings | Yes |
| Detailed error messages | Error pages for HTTP 400+ responses | No | Yes |
| Failed request tracing | Detailed IIS traces for failing requests | No | Yes |
| Deployment logs | Output of deployments and builds | Yes (Kudu) | Yes (Kudu) |

There are two ways to use them:

1. **App Service logs** (`az webapp log config`): written to the app's file system or Blob Storage. Good for live tailing and quick downloads.
2. **Diagnostic settings**: stream platform log categories to a **Log Analytics workspace**, Storage, or Event Hubs. This is the production option: logs are retained, queryable with KQL, and can trigger alerts.

| Diagnostic settings category | Contents |
|---|---|
| `AppServiceHTTPLogs` | Every request: path, status, duration, client IP |
| `AppServiceConsoleLogs` | stdout/stderr of the app container |
| `AppServiceAppLogs` | Logs from the app's logging framework (supported stacks) |
| `AppServicePlatformLogs` | Container start/stop, platform events |
| `AppServiceAuditLogs` | Publishing logins (FTP, Kudu) |

For distributed tracing, dependency calls, and exceptions with stack traces, add **Application Insights** (chapter 11). The portal's **Diagnose and solve problems** blade runs built-in detectors for common issues such as crashes, high CPU, SNAT port exhaustion, and failed swaps.

**Example: enable logs, tail them live, and query them with KQL**

```bash
APP=app-shop-api; RG=rg-shop

# Container stdout/stderr to the file system, then stream it
az webapp log config -g $RG -n $APP --docker-container-logging filesystem
az webapp log tail -g $RG -n $APP

# Download everything as a ZIP for offline analysis
az webapp log download -g $RG -n $APP --log-file app-logs.zip

# Production: send platform logs to Log Analytics
LAW_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g rg-monitor -n law-shop --query id -o tsv)
az monitor diagnostic-settings create -n to-law \
  --resource "$(az webapp show -g $RG -n $APP --query id -o tsv)" --workspace "$LAW_ID" \
  --logs '[{"category":"AppServiceHTTPLogs","enabled":true},
           {"category":"AppServiceConsoleLogs","enabled":true},
           {"category":"AppServicePlatformLogs","enabled":true}]'
```

```kusto
// 5xx errors per path in 5-minute buckets over the last day
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) and ScStatus >= 500
| summarize errors = count(), p95_ms = percentile(TimeTaken, 95) by CsUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| order by errors desc
```

```python
# Python: log to stdout with levels; App Service collects stdout as console logs
import logging, sys

logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO,
                    format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("orders")
log.info("order created", extra={"order_id": 42})   # structured fields help with KQL filtering later
```

**Key takeaways**

- Most App Service logs are off by default. Enable them before you need them.
- On Linux, write logs to stdout/stderr. They become console logs that you can tail or ship.
- Use diagnostic settings to Log Analytics for retention, KQL queries, and alerts. File system logs are for quick, short-term troubleshooting.
- Combine platform logs with Application Insights for end-to-end tracing, and use "Diagnose and solve problems" for common failure patterns.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Enable container logging, add a log line to a request handler, and see it appear in `az webapp log tail`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Send `AppServiceHTTPLogs` to a workspace and write a KQL query that shows the 10 slowest endpoints by 95th-percentile duration for the last hour.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Users report intermittent 502 errors, but your application logs show nothing. Where do you look next?" *Hint:* platform logs (container restarts, out-of-memory), HTTP logs, health check removals, the 230-second request timeout, and outbound SNAT exhaustion.

#### Built-In Authentication (Easy Auth)

Adding sign-in to an app normally means choosing a library, handling redirects, validating tokens, managing cookies, and keeping all of it patched. For many apps (internal tools, admin dashboards, APIs called by known clients), App Service's **built-in authentication**, nicknamed **Easy Auth**, does this *outside* your code. You turn it on, pick identity providers, and the platform intercepts every request before it reaches your app.

Analogy: a receptionist at the building entrance checks ID and gives visitors a badge. Your office (the app) only needs to read the badge, not verify passports.

```text
 Browser / client
      |  GET /orders
      v
 +----------------- App Service front end / instance -------------------+
 |  Easy Auth module (separate from your code)                         |
 |   - no session?  -> redirect to provider (/.auth/login/aad)         |
 |   - callback     -> validates tokens, creates session cookie,       |
 |                     stores tokens in the token store                |
 |   - valid session or bearer token?                                  |
 |        -> strips any incoming X-MS-* headers (anti-spoofing)        |
 |        -> injects identity headers                                  |
 |   +-------------------------------------------------------------+   |
 |   | Your app: reads X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-NAME, X-MS-CLIENT-... |   |
 |   +-------------------------------------------------------------+   |
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Supported providers include Microsoft Entra ID (workforce and external tenants), Google, Facebook, X, GitHub, Apple, and any **OpenID Connect** provider. Useful built-in endpoints:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/.auth/login/<provider>` | Start sign-in (for example `/.auth/login/aad`) |
| `/.auth/me` | Return the current user's claims and tokens as JSON |
| `/.auth/refresh` | Refresh provider tokens in the token store |
| `/.auth/logout` | Sign out and clear the session |

Headers your code receives:

| Header | Contents |
|---|---|
| `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-NAME` | User's name (for example UPN or email) |
| `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-ID` | User's ID at the provider (for Entra ID, the object ID) |
| `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-IDP` | Provider name (`aad`, `google`, ...) |
| `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL` | Base64-encoded JSON with all claims |
| `X-MS-TOKEN-AAD-ACCESS-TOKEN`, `X-MS-TOKEN-AAD-ID-TOKEN` | Provider tokens (when the token store is enabled) |

What to do with **unauthenticated requests** is a key setting: redirect to login (web apps), return 401 or 403 (APIs), or **allow anonymous** and let the code decide per route (mixed public/private apps).

Limitations: Easy Auth authenticates, but authorization beyond "signed in or not" (roles, per-resource checks) is still your code's job, using the claims it receives. The headers are trustworthy only because the platform strips spoofed versions. Never trust them in code paths that can be reached without passing through App Service (for example, local runs or other hosting). For complex scenarios, such as fine-grained token handling or calling many downstream APIs with on-behalf-of flows, a library like MSAL or Microsoft.Identity.Web (2.3) gives more control.

**Example: protect an app with Microsoft Entra ID**

```bash
APP=app-shop-admin; RG=rg-shop; TENANT_ID=$(az account show --query tenantId -o tsv)

# Register an app for sign-in (redirect URI is the Easy Auth callback)
CLIENT_ID=$(az ad app create --display-name app-shop-admin --sign-in-audience AzureADMyOrg \
  --web-redirect-uris "https://$APP.azurewebsites.net/.auth/login/aad/callback" \
  --enable-id-token-issuance true --query appId -o tsv)
SECRET=$(az ad app credential reset --id $CLIENT_ID --append --query password -o tsv)

# Store the secret in an app setting and point the provider at it
az webapp config appsettings set -g $RG -n $APP --settings MICROSOFT_PROVIDER_AUTHENTICATION_SECRET="$SECRET"
az webapp auth microsoft update -g $RG -n $APP --client-id $CLIENT_ID \
  --client-secret-setting-name MICROSOFT_PROVIDER_AUTHENTICATION_SECRET \
  --issuer "https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT_ID/v2.0"

# Require sign-in for every request; enable the token store
az webapp auth update -g $RG -n $APP --enabled true \
  --unauthenticated-client-action RedirectToLoginPage --redirect-provider AzureActiveDirectory \
  --enable-token-store true
```

```python
# Flask: read the identity that Easy Auth injected
import base64, json
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)

def current_principal():
    raw = request.headers.get("X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL")
    if not raw:
        return None                                    # anonymous (only if anonymous is allowed)
    data = json.loads(base64.b64decode(raw))
    claims = {}
    for c in data.get("claims", []):                   # [{"typ": "...", "val": "..."}, ...]
        claims.setdefault(c["typ"], []).append(c["val"])
    return claims

@app.get("/admin")
def admin():
    claims = current_principal() or abort(401)
    if "Shop.Admin" not in claims.get("roles", []):   # authorization is still your job
        abort(403)
    return {"user": request.headers["X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL-NAME"]}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Easy Auth handles sign-in, token validation, and sessions outside your code, for Entra ID, social providers, and any OpenID Connect provider.
- Your code reads identity from `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL*` headers. The platform strips spoofed copies, so trust them only behind App Service.
- Choose the unauthenticated action per app type: redirect for web UIs, 401 for APIs, allow anonymous for mixed apps.
- Authorization (roles, ownership checks) remains your responsibility. Use MSAL-based libraries when you need fine-grained control.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Enable Easy Auth with Microsoft Entra ID on a test app, sign in, and open `/.auth/me` to inspect your claims.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Configure the app to allow anonymous requests, then return different content on `/` for signed-in and anonymous users, and protect `/admin` with an app role.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you choose Easy Auth over implementing authentication with MSAL in the app?" *Hint:* speed and security of a platform feature versus portability, local development, testing, fine-grained token control, and calling downstream APIs.

<a id="33-azure-functions-fundamentals"></a>
### 3.3 Azure Functions Fundamentals

Azure Functions is Azure's serverless compute service: you write small pieces of code that run in response to events, and the platform handles hosting, scaling, and billing per execution. This section explains how the model works, how to choose a hosting plan, and how to build, configure, and run functions locally.

#### Serverless Execution Model

Many workloads are not "a server waiting for requests" but "do something when X happens": resize an image when it is uploaded, process an order when a message arrives, send a report every morning. Running a VM or App Service plan 24/7 for these tasks pays for idle time and still needs capacity planning for bursts. **Azure Functions** turns the model around: you write a **function** bound to a **trigger** (the event), and the platform runs it, as many copies in parallel as needed, only while there is work.

Analogy: instead of employing a full-time receptionist who mostly waits, you use an on-call service. Nobody is paid while the phone is silent. When calls arrive, the service sends as many operators as there are callers, and you pay per call handled.

Building blocks:

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Function | One piece of code with exactly one trigger |
| Trigger | The event that starts an execution: HTTP request, queue message, timer, blob, event, ... |
| Bindings | Declarative connections to data (read input, write output) without client boilerplate |
| Function app | Deployment and scaling unit: a group of functions sharing configuration, runtime version, and plan |
| Functions host (runtime) | The process that listens to triggers and invokes your code (runtime version 4.x) |
| Scale controller | Platform component that watches event sources and adds or removes instances |

```text
   Event sources                    Scale controller
   (HTTP, queue, timer, ...)  ----> "queue has 5,000 messages, 2 instances busy -> add 8"
          |                                      |
          v                                      v
   +---------------+   +---------------+   +---------------+
   | Instance 1    |   | Instance 2    |   | Instance N    |   <- created on demand,
   |  Functions    |   |  Functions    |   |  Functions    |      removed when idle
   |  host +       |   |  host +       |   |  host +       |      (scale to zero on
   |  your code    |   |  your code    |   |  your code    |       serverless plans)
   +---------------+   +---------------+   +---------------+
```

Design consequences of the serverless model:

- **Stateless and short-lived.** Any instance may run any execution, and instances disappear without warning. Keep state in storage, queues, or databases (or use Durable Functions, 3.4).
- **Execution time limits.** A function has a maximum duration that depends on the plan (for example 5 minutes by default and 10 at most on Consumption). HTTP-triggered functions must respond within about **230 seconds** on every plan, because of the front-end load balancer timeout. Long work belongs in a queue-triggered function or an orchestration.
- **At-least-once delivery for most non-HTTP triggers.** A message can be processed twice after a crash or timeout, so make handlers **idempotent**.
- **Cold starts.** When a serverless app scales from zero, the first request waits for an instance to start (3.4 covers mitigations).
- **Billing.** On serverless plans you pay for executions plus resource consumption (GB-seconds), and idle time is free.

**Example: an event-driven function and the equivalent "always-on" alternative**

```python
# function_app.py: Python v2 programming model
import json, logging
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp()

# Runs once per message; the platform scales instances with queue length
@app.queue_trigger(arg_name="msg", queue_name="orders", connection="AzureWebJobsStorage")
def process_order(msg: func.QueueMessage) -> None:
    order = json.loads(msg.get_body())
    logging.info("Processing order %s (dequeue count %d)", order["id"], msg.dequeue_count)
    # ... charge, reserve stock, ... (must be idempotent: the message may be delivered again)
```

```python
# The same job without serverless: a worker you host, size, and keep running yourself
while True:
    for m in queue_client.receive_messages(max_messages=16, visibility_timeout=60):
        handle(m)                         # you own retries, poison handling, scaling, restarts
        queue_client.delete_message(m)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Functions run code in response to triggers. The platform scales instances with the event load and, on serverless plans, down to zero.
- The function app is the unit of deployment, configuration, and scaling.
- Design for statelessness, time limits (HTTP responses within about 230 s), at-least-once delivery, and cold starts.
- Serverless billing rewards bursty, event-driven work. Constant high load may be cheaper on dedicated compute.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For each workload, say whether Functions fits and why: nightly report e-mail, a WebSocket chat server, thumbnail generation on upload, a 2-hour video transcode.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** A queue-triggered function charges a credit card. Describe how a duplicate delivery could happen and how you would make the handler idempotent.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Serverless means no servers, so we don't need to think about capacity, right?" *Hint:* downstream limits (database connections, API rate limits), instance limits per plan, concurrency per instance, cold starts, and cost at sustained load.

#### Hosting Plans (Consumption, Flex, Premium, Dedicated)

The same function code can run on very different infrastructure, and the **hosting plan** decides how it scales, how fast it starts, whether it can reach private networks, how long it may run, and how you are billed. Choosing a plan is the most consequential Functions decision you make, and changing it later can require recreating the app.

| | Consumption | Flex Consumption | Premium (Elastic Premium) | Dedicated (App Service plan) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scale to zero | Yes | Yes | No (min 1 always-ready instance) | No |
| Scaling | Event-driven, per app | Event-driven, **per function group**, fast | Event-driven, pre-warmed instances | Manual or autoscale rules |
| Max instances (typical) | 200 Windows / 100 Linux | Up to 1,000 | 100 Windows / up to 100 Linux, region-dependent | Plan limit (10–30, 100 Isolated) |
| Cold start | Yes | Reduced with always-ready instances | None for warm capacity | None (Always On) |
| VNet integration | No | Yes | Yes | Yes (Basic and above) |
| Default / max timeout | 5 / 10 min | 30 min / unbounded | 30 min / unbounded | 30 min / unbounded |
| Instance memory | 1.5 GB | 512 MB, 2 GB, or 4 GB (you choose) | 3.5–14 GB (EP1–EP3) | Per plan size |
| OS | Windows, Linux (legacy) | Linux | Windows, Linux | Windows, Linux |
| Billing | Executions + GB-s, free grant | Executions + GB-s, plus always-ready baseline | Per vCPU/memory-second of allocated instances | Per plan instance |

Choosing:

- **Flex Consumption** is the default choice for new serverless apps on Linux. It combines scale to zero with VNet integration, fast scaling, configurable memory, and optional always-ready instances. Microsoft has announced the retirement of the older **Linux Consumption** plan, so new Linux apps should use Flex.
- **Consumption** (Windows) remains for simple, low-volume, public-endpoint apps where cold starts are acceptable.
- **Premium** suits apps that need no cold start, long executions, large instances, or Windows with VNet integration.
- **Dedicated** makes sense if you already pay for an App Service plan with spare capacity, or need predictable cost. Enable **Always On** or non-HTTP triggers stop firing when the app idles.
- Functions can also run on **Azure Container Apps** (chapter 4) when you want them alongside other containers.

Every function app also needs a **storage account** for runtime state: triggers' checkpoints and leases, timer locks, keys, and (on some plans) the deployment package.

**Example: create function apps on different plans**

```bash
RG=rg-func; LOC=westeurope
az storage account create -g $RG -n stfuncorders001 -l $LOC --sku Standard_LRS

# Flex Consumption: Python 3.12, 2 GB instances, scale to zero
az functionapp create -g $RG -n func-orders-flex --storage-account stfuncorders001 \
  --flexconsumption-location $LOC --runtime python --runtime-version 3.12 --instance-memory 2048

# Flex: keep 1 instance always ready for HTTP functions, cap scale-out at 50
az functionapp scale config always-ready set -g $RG -n func-orders-flex --settings http=1
az functionapp scale config set -g $RG -n func-orders-flex --maximum-instance-count 50

# Premium: create an Elastic Premium plan, then an app in it
az functionapp plan create -g $RG -n plan-func-ep1 -l $LOC --sku EP1 --is-linux \
  --min-instances 1 --max-burst 20
az functionapp create -g $RG -n func-orders-premium --plan plan-func-ep1 \
  --storage-account stfuncorders001 --runtime python --runtime-version 3.12 --functions-version 4

# Consumption (Windows), e.g. for a .NET isolated app
az functionapp create -g $RG -n func-reports-cons --consumption-plan-location $LOC \
  --storage-account stfuncorders001 --runtime dotnet-isolated --functions-version 4 --os-type Windows
```

**Key takeaways**

- The plan decides scaling behavior, cold starts, networking, timeouts, memory, and billing model.
- Flex Consumption is the recommended serverless plan for new Linux apps: scale to zero plus VNet, per-function scaling, and always-ready options.
- Premium removes cold starts and time limits at a fixed baseline cost. Dedicated uses App Service capacity you already pay for.
- Every function app depends on a storage account for runtime state. Treat it as part of the app.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Pick a plan for each: a webhook receiving 50 calls a day; an API that must call a database through a private endpoint and respond in under 200 ms at all times; a nightly job that runs 45 minutes.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Estimate the monthly cost of 3 million executions averaging 400 ms at 512 MB on a serverless plan (use the current price sheet), and compare it with one always-on instance. At what volume does the comparison flip?
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why might a function app that worked on Consumption break when moved to a Dedicated plan with autoscale?" *Hint:* Always On, scaling now driven by CPU rules instead of event backlog, instance count limits, and shared capacity with web apps.

#### Triggers and Bindings

A large part of typical integration code is plumbing: create a storage client, poll a queue, deserialize a message, open a database connection, write a result, handle retries. **Triggers and bindings** let you declare that plumbing instead of writing it. The runtime's **binding extensions** connect to the services and hand your function ready-to-use data.

Analogy: a mail room. You tell it, "When a parcel arrives for me (trigger), bring me the matching file from the archive (input binding), and put whatever I put in my out-tray into the outgoing post (output binding)." You never deal with the post office yourself.

- A **trigger** starts the function. Every function has exactly one.
- **Input bindings** load data before the function runs (for example a Cosmos DB document by ID).
- **Output bindings** send data after the function returns (for example a queue message or a blob).
- **Binding expressions** use values from the trigger or configuration: `{id}` (from the route or message), `{rand-guid}`, `{datetime}`, and `%SettingName%` (an app setting).

Common triggers and bindings:

| Service | Trigger | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| HTTP | Yes | | Yes (response) |
| Timer (CRON) | Yes | | |
| Storage queues | Yes | | Yes |
| Blob Storage | Yes (polling, or Event Grid-based) | Yes | Yes |
| Service Bus | Yes | | Yes |
| Event Hubs | Yes | | Yes |
| Event Grid | Yes | | Yes |
| Cosmos DB | Yes (change feed) | Yes | Yes |
| Azure SQL | Yes (change tracking) | Yes | Yes |
| Table Storage | | Yes | Yes |
| SignalR Service | | Yes | Yes |

**Connections** are named by app settings, not hardcoded. A binding's `connection="Storage"` means "look for settings that start with `Storage`". Prefer **identity-based connections**, where the settings contain only an endpoint and the function app's managed identity needs the right data-plane role (see 2.5):

| Setting | Value |
|---|---|
| `Storage__queueServiceUri` | `https://stshop.queue.core.windows.net` |
| `Storage__blobServiceUri` | `https://stshop.blob.core.windows.net` |
| `ServiceBus__fullyQualifiedNamespace` | `sb-shop.servicebus.windows.net` |

Non-.NET languages get binding support from **extension bundles** (configured in `host.json`), so no packages need to be installed. .NET isolated apps reference NuGet packages for each extension.

Failure handling depends on the trigger. A Storage queue message that fails 5 times (`maxDequeueCount`) moves to `<queue>-poison`. Service Bus uses its own dead-letter queue. Event Hubs and Cosmos DB triggers move on with the stream, so you need retry policies or your own error handling there.

**Example: HTTP in, queue out; queue in, Cosmos DB in, blob out; and a timer**

```python
# function_app.py
import json, logging
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp(http_auth_level=func.AuthLevel.FUNCTION)   # require a function key by default

# 1) HTTP trigger + queue output binding: accept an order, enqueue it, return 202
@app.route(route="orders", methods=["POST"])
@app.queue_output(arg_name="out", queue_name="orders", connection="Storage")
def submit_order(req: func.HttpRequest, out: func.Out[str]) -> func.HttpResponse:
    order = req.get_json()
    out.set(json.dumps(order))                       # written to the queue after the function returns
    return func.HttpResponse(status_code=202)

# 2) Queue trigger + Cosmos DB input + blob output
@app.queue_trigger(arg_name="msg", queue_name="orders", connection="Storage")
@app.cosmos_db_input(arg_name="customers", database_name="shop", container_name="customers",
                     id="{customerId}", partition_key="{customerId}",   # values taken from the JSON message
                     connection="Cosmos")
@app.blob_output(arg_name="receipt", path="receipts/{id}.json", connection="Storage")
def make_receipt(msg: func.QueueMessage, customers: func.DocumentList, receipt: func.Out[str]) -> None:
    order = msg.get_json()
    customer = customers[0] if customers else None
    receipt.set(json.dumps({"order": order["id"], "email": customer and customer["email"]}))

# 3) Timer trigger: NCRONTAB with seconds -> every day at 06:00 (UTC unless WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE is set)
@app.timer_trigger(arg_name="timer", schedule="0 0 6 * * *", run_on_startup=False)
def daily_report(timer: func.TimerRequest) -> None:
    if timer.past_due:
        logging.warning("Timer is running late")
    logging.info("Generating daily report")
```

```bash
# Identity-based connections: endpoints only, plus data-plane roles for the app's identity
az functionapp config appsettings set -g rg-func -n func-orders-flex --settings \
  Storage__queueServiceUri=https://stshop.queue.core.windows.net \
  Storage__blobServiceUri=https://stshop.blob.core.windows.net \
  Cosmos__accountEndpoint=https://cosmos-shop.documents.azure.com:443/
```

**Key takeaways**

- One trigger per function, with any number of input and output bindings. Bindings replace client boilerplate for common services.
- Binding expressions (`{id}`, `{rand-guid}`, `%Setting%`) parameterize paths, IDs, and names.
- `connection` names a settings prefix. Use identity-based connections (`<name>__serviceUri` and similar) plus RBAC instead of connection strings.
- Know each trigger's failure behavior: poison queues, dead-letter queues, or stream checkpoints.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write an HTTP function that takes `?name=` and writes a greeting to a blob named `greetings/{rand-guid}.txt`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Make a queue-triggered function fail deliberately and find the message in the poison queue. Then change `maxDequeueCount` in `host.json` and repeat.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you avoid output bindings and use the service's SDK client directly?" *Hint:* transactions or batching control, conditional writes, custom retry, setting message properties, and features the binding doesn't expose.

#### Isolated Worker Model

Functions written in .NET historically ran **in-process**: your code was loaded into the same process as the Functions host. That was fast, but it tied your app to the host's .NET version and dependency versions. A conflicting `Newtonsoft.Json` or a newer .NET release could break you, and you could not control startup the way an ASP.NET Core app does. The **isolated worker model** runs your .NET code in a **separate worker process** that talks to the host over gRPC, the same way Python, Node.js, Java, and PowerShell workers always have.

```text
  In-process (legacy, .NET only)          Isolated worker (current for all languages)
  +--------------------------------+      +------------------+   gRPC   +---------------------+
  | Functions host process         |      | Functions host   | <------> | Worker process      |
  |  host code + YOUR code         |      | (triggers,       |          |  YOUR code          |
  |  same .NET version, same deps  |      |  bindings,       |          |  any supported .NET |
  +--------------------------------+      |  scaling)        |          |  your own deps, DI, |
                                          +------------------+          |  middleware         |
                                                                        +---------------------+
```

The in-process model reaches **end of support on 10 November 2026**. All new .NET function apps should use the isolated model, and existing in-process apps need to be migrated.

| | In-process | Isolated worker |
|---|---|---|
| .NET versions | Only the LTS version the host runs | .NET 8, 9, 10, and .NET Framework 4.8 |
| Startup control | Limited `FunctionsStartup` | Full `Program.cs`: DI, configuration, logging, middleware |
| Dependency conflicts | Possible with host assemblies | None: separate process |
| Binding packages | `Microsoft.Azure.WebJobs.Extensions.*` | `Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.Extensions.*` |
| HTTP model | `HttpRequest`/`IActionResult` | ASP.NET Core integration (`HttpRequest`/`IActionResult`) or `HttpRequestData` |
| `FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME` | `dotnet` | `dotnet-isolated` |
| Support | Ends 10 November 2026 | Current |

Migration mostly involves updating packages and attributes (`[FunctionName]` becomes `[Function]`, and `ILogger` parameters move to constructor injection), adding a `Program.cs`, changing `FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME`, and replacing multi-output patterns. Bindings that returned several outputs through parameters now return a class whose properties carry the binding attributes.

**Example: an isolated .NET function app**

```csharp
// Program.cs: you own the host builder, just like in ASP.NET Core
using Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker.Builder;
using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection;
using Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting;

var builder = FunctionsApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.ConfigureFunctionsWebApplication();               // ASP.NET Core integration for HTTP triggers
builder.UseMiddleware<CorrelationIdMiddleware>();         // custom middleware around every invocation

builder.Services
    .AddApplicationInsightsTelemetryWorkerService()
    .ConfigureFunctionsApplicationInsights();
```
