| `WORKDIR` | Set (and create) the working directory | Metadata (and an empty dir) |
| `COPY` | Copy files from the build context into the image | Yes |
| `ADD` | Like `COPY`, plus URL download and archive extraction. Prefer `COPY` | Yes |
| `RUN` | Execute a command at build time (install packages, compile) | Yes |
| `ENV` | Environment variable available at build and run time | Metadata |
| `ARG` | Build-time variable only (`--build-arg`), not present at run time | No |
| `EXPOSE` | Document the port the app listens on (does not publish it) | Metadata |
| `USER` | User (and group) subsequent instructions and the container run as | Metadata |
| `ENTRYPOINT` | The executable the container runs | Metadata |
| `CMD` | Default arguments to `ENTRYPOINT`, or the default command | Metadata |
| `HEALTHCHECK` | Command Docker uses to test container health | Metadata |

**How the build cache works.** For each instruction, the builder checks whether it already has a layer produced by the *same instruction on the same parent layer* (and, for `COPY`/`ADD`, the same file contents). If so, it reuses the cached layer. The first instruction whose inputs changed invalidates the cache for **itself and every instruction after it**.

The practical rule follows directly: **order instructions from least to most frequently changing.** Dependencies change rarely; source code changes on every commit. Copy the dependency manifest, install dependencies, and *only then* copy the source.

```text
  Bad order                          Good order
  ---------                          ----------
  COPY . .            <- changes     COPY requirements.txt .
  RUN pip install ...    every       RUN pip install ...     <- cached until deps change
                         commit,     COPY . .                <- only this layer rebuilds
                         so pip
                         reruns
                         every build
```

**Other best practices**

- **Use a `.dockerignore`.** Everything in the build context is sent to the builder. Exclude `.git`, `node_modules`, `bin/obj`, local `.env` files, and test data to speed up builds and avoid leaking secrets into the image.
- **Pin base images** to a specific version (`python:3.12.7-slim`), not `latest`, so builds are reproducible.
- **Choose small bases**: `-slim`, `-alpine`, distroless, or Microsoft's "chiseled" Ubuntu images for .NET. Fewer packages means a smaller attack surface and fewer CVEs to patch.
- **Combine related `RUN` steps** and clean up in the same instruction. Deleting files in a later layer does not shrink the image, because the earlier layer still contains them.
- **Run as a non-root user** (`USER`). If the app is compromised, the attacker does not get root inside the container.
- **Use the exec form** for `ENTRYPOINT`/`CMD` (`["dotnet", "app.dll"]`), not the shell form (`dotnet app.dll`). In the exec form your app is PID 1 and receives `SIGTERM` directly, so it can shut down gracefully when Azure stops the container.
- **Never put secrets in the image**: not in `ENV`, not in `ARG`, not in copied files. Anyone who can pull the image can read every layer. Inject secrets at run time (see 4.3 and 4.4), or use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials.

**`ENTRYPOINT` vs `CMD`**

| Dockerfile | `docker run img` runs | `docker run img --debug` runs |
|---|---|---|
| `CMD ["python", "app.py"]` | `python app.py` | `--debug` (replaces CMD, fails) |
| `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]` | `python app.py` | `python app.py --debug` |
| `ENTRYPOINT ["python", "app.py"]` + `CMD ["--port", "8000"]` | `python app.py --port 8000` | `python app.py --debug` |

**Example: a production-grade Dockerfile for a Python API**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM python:3.12.7-slim

# Python runtime settings: no .pyc files, unbuffered stdout so logs appear immediately
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

WORKDIR /app

# Create an unprivileged user early (rarely changes, so it stays cached)
RUN groupadd --system app && useradd --system --gid app --no-create-home app

# 1) Dependencies first: this layer is reused until requirements.txt changes
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt   # --no-cache-dir keeps pip's cache out of the layer

# 2) Source code last: only this layer rebuilds on a typical commit
COPY --chown=app:app src/ ./src/

USER app
EXPOSE 8000

# Container-level health check (used by Docker and ACI; Container Apps and AKS use their own probes)
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health')"

# Exec form: gunicorn is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
ENTRYPOINT ["gunicorn", "src.main:app", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "2"]
```

```text
# .dockerignore
.git
.venv
__pycache__/
*.pyc
.env
tests/
Dockerfile
```

```bash
# Build with BuildKit, tag it, and check the result
docker build -t orders-api:dev .
docker image ls orders-api              # check size
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 orders-api:dev

# Build-time secret (for example a private package index token) without baking it into a layer
docker build --secret id=pip_token,src=./pip_token.txt -t orders-api:dev .
# ...and in the Dockerfile:
# RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token PIP_INDEX_URL="https://$(cat /run/secrets/pip_token)@pkgs.example.com/simple" pip install -r requirements.txt
```

**Key takeaways**

- Each instruction is a cached step. A change invalidates that step and everything after it, so order instructions from stable to volatile.
- Use `.dockerignore`, pinned and minimal base images, and cleanup within the same `RUN`.
- Run as a non-root user and use the exec form so the app receives shutdown signals.
- Secrets never go into an image. Inject them at run time or use BuildKit secret mounts at build time.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Take a Dockerfile that does `COPY . .` before installing dependencies. Time two builds after changing one source file, then reorder the instructions and time them again.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add `ENV API_KEY=abc123` to a Dockerfile, build and push the image, then recover the key using only `docker image inspect` and `docker history --no-trunc`. Rewrite the Dockerfile so the key is supplied at run time instead.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your containers take 30 seconds to stop on every deployment and in-flight requests fail. What could be wrong in the Dockerfile?" *Hint:* shell form versus exec form, which process is PID 1, and who receives `SIGTERM`.

#### Multi-Stage Builds

Compiling an application needs far more than running it. A .NET API needs the SDK (around 800 MB) to build, but only the ASP.NET runtime (around 200 MB, or less with chiseled images) to run. A React front end needs Node.js and hundreds of megabytes of `node_modules` to build, but only a few static files and a web server to serve. If you build and run in the same image, compilers, package caches, and source code ship to production: the image is larger, pulls are slower, and every extra tool is something an attacker can use.

**Multi-stage builds** solve this inside a single Dockerfile. You declare several `FROM` stages. Early stages build the app with all the tooling they need. The final stage starts from a minimal base and copies in *only the build output* with `COPY --from=<stage>`. Everything else is discarded.

Analogy: a restaurant kitchen and the dining room. All the knives, pans, and flour stay in the kitchen (the build stage). Only the finished plate is carried to the table (the runtime stage).

```text
   Stage "build"  (mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:8.0, ~800 MB)
   +-------------------------------------------+
   | dotnet restore  ->  dotnet publish -o /out |
   +-----------------------------+-------------+
                                 |  COPY --from=build /out .
                                 v
   Stage "final"  (mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0-jammy-chiseled, ~110 MB)
   +-------------------------------------------+
   | /app/Orders.Api.dll + dependencies         |   <- only this stage becomes the image
   +-------------------------------------------+
```

Additional benefits:

- **Build stages are cached independently**, and BuildKit runs independent stages in parallel.
- **`--target`** builds a specific stage, for example a `test` stage in CI or a `dev` stage with debugging tools for local work, all from one Dockerfile.
- **Reproducible builds**: the build environment is defined in code, so CI agents need only Docker, not the SDK.

**Example: .NET API with a test stage and a chiseled runtime**

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
ARG DOTNET_VERSION=8.0

# ---------- Stage 1: restore and build ----------
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:${DOTNET_VERSION} AS build
WORKDIR /src
# Copy only project files first so 'restore' is cached until dependencies change
COPY src/Orders.Api/Orders.Api.csproj src/Orders.Api/
COPY tests/Orders.Tests/Orders.Tests.csproj tests/Orders.Tests/
RUN dotnet restore src/Orders.Api/Orders.Api.csproj && \
    dotnet restore tests/Orders.Tests/Orders.Tests.csproj
COPY . .
RUN dotnet build src/Orders.Api/Orders.Api.csproj -c Release --no-restore

# ---------- Stage 2: tests (only built when targeted: --target test) ----------
FROM build AS test
RUN dotnet test tests/Orders.Tests/Orders.Tests.csproj -c Release --no-restore

# ---------- Stage 3: publish ----------
FROM build AS publish
RUN dotnet publish src/Orders.Api/Orders.Api.csproj -c Release --no-build -o /out

# ---------- Stage 4: final runtime image ----------
# Chiseled images: no shell, no package manager, non-root user by default
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:${DOTNET_VERSION}-jammy-chiseled AS final
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=publish /out .
ENV ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS=8080
EXPOSE 8080
# Non-root UID provided by the .NET base images
USER $APP_UID
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "Orders.Api.dll"]
```

**Example: React single-page app served by NGINX**

```dockerfile
# ---------- Build with Node ----------
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci                               # reproducible install from the lock file
COPY . .
RUN npm run build                        # produces /app/dist

# ---------- Serve static files only ----------
# Unprivileged NGINX listens on 8080 as non-root
FROM nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27-alpine AS final
# SPA fallback in nginx.conf: try_files $uri /index.html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 8080
```

```bash
docker build --target test -t orders-api:test .    # CI: run unit tests inside the build
docker build -t orders-api:1.4.2 .                  # default: last stage ("final")
docker image ls orders-api                          # compare sizes of the two tags
```

| Image | Base | Typical size |
|---|---|---|
| Single-stage (.NET SDK) | `dotnet/sdk:8.0` | ~850 MB |
| Multi-stage, standard runtime | `dotnet/aspnet:8.0` | ~220 MB |
| Multi-stage, chiseled runtime | `dotnet/aspnet:8.0-jammy-chiseled` | ~115 MB |
| Single-stage React (Node) | `node:22` | ~1.2 GB |
| Multi-stage React (NGINX) | `nginx-unprivileged:alpine` | ~50 MB |

**Key takeaways**

- Multi-stage builds separate *building* from *running*. Only the final stage becomes the image.
- `COPY --from=<stage>` moves artifacts between stages. `--target` builds a specific stage (tests, dev tooling).
- Small runtime bases (alpine, distroless, chiseled) shrink images by an order of magnitude and remove tools attackers could use.
- Smaller images pull faster, which directly improves cold starts and scale-out speed on ACI, Container Apps, and AKS.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Convert a single-stage Node.js or .NET Dockerfile to a multi-stage build and record the image size before and after.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a `test` stage to your Dockerfile and change your CI pipeline to run `docker build --target test` before building the final image. Make a test fail and confirm the pipeline stops.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A chiseled or distroless image has no shell. How do you debug a running container built from it?" *Hint:* ephemeral debug containers (`kubectl debug`), sidecar debug images sharing the process namespace, a separate `debug` build target, and good logging.

#### Image Tagging Strategies

"Which version is running in production?" should have an instant, unambiguous answer. "Deploy the same thing to production that we tested in staging" should be guaranteed, not hoped for. Both depend on how you **tag** images.

A tag is a *mutable pointer* to an image manifest. Pushing `orders-api:1.4` again moves the pointer to a new image; the old image becomes **untagged** (sometimes called "dangling") but still exists, identified only by its digest. This mutability is convenient for humans and dangerous for deployments.

**The problem with `latest`**

`latest` is just the default tag name when you don't specify one. It does not mean "newest". It means "whatever was last pushed without a tag". Deploying `:latest` causes:

- **Non-reproducible deployments.** Two nodes pulling at different times can run different code.
- **No rollback target.** "Roll back to the previous `latest`" is meaningless.
- **Silent no-ops.** Many platforms see an unchanged image reference and do not redeploy, or reuse the cached image on the node.

**Stable tags vs unique tags**

| Type | Examples | Points to | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stable (moving) | `1`, `1.4`, `latest`, `stable` | Changes as new builds are pushed | Base images you consume, so you get patches; human convenience |
| Unique (immutable by convention) | `1.4.2`, `1.4.2-a1b2c3d`, `20261021.3`, build ID | One build, forever | **Deployments** |
| Digest | `@sha256:9f86d0...` | Exact bytes, guaranteed | Strictest pinning, signing, supply-chain policies |

A common, effective scheme is to give every build several tags at once: one unique, one or more stable.

```text
  Build #318 of commit a1b2c3d for release 1.4.2 is pushed once, tagged four ways:

    crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2-a1b2c3d   <- unique: what deployments reference
    crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2           <- unique per release
    crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4             <- stable: newest patch of 1.4
    crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1               <- stable: newest 1.x

  All four tags -> same manifest  sha256:9f86d0...
```

**Recommended practices**

- **Deploy unique tags or digests**, never `latest` or other stable tags.
- **Include the source commit** (short SHA) in the tag, or as an OCI label (`org.opencontainers.image.revision`), so any running container traces back to its code.
- **Build once, promote everywhere.** The image tested in staging is the exact image deployed to production. Promote by re-tagging or importing between registries (`az acr import`), not by rebuilding.
- **Lock release tags** in ACR so they cannot be overwritten or deleted (`az acr repository update --write-enabled false`).
- **Clean up** untagged manifests and old dev tags with retention policies or `acr purge` (see 4.2) to control storage costs.
- **Multi-architecture images**: a single tag can point to a *manifest list* (OCI image index) containing `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` variants. The runtime pulls the right one automatically.

**Example: tagging in a CI pipeline**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

REGISTRY=crshop.azurecr.io
REPO=orders-api
VERSION=1.4.2                                 # from your release process or a version file
SHA=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)             # e.g. a1b2c3d

UNIQUE_TAG="${VERSION}-${SHA}"

# Build once, apply several tags, and record provenance as OCI labels
docker build \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.revision="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.version="$VERSION" \
  -t "$REGISTRY/$REPO:$UNIQUE_TAG" \
  -t "$REGISTRY/$REPO:$VERSION" \
  -t "$REGISTRY/$REPO:${VERSION%.*}" \
  .                                           # ${VERSION%.*} strips the patch -> 1.4

docker push --all-tags "$REGISTRY/$REPO"

# Resolve the digest and deploy by digest for maximum certainty
DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$REGISTRY/$REPO:$UNIQUE_TAG")
echo "Deploying $DIGEST"                      # crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api@sha256:9f86...

# Lock the release tag so it can never be overwritten or deleted
az acr repository update --name crshop --image "$REPO:$VERSION" \
  --write-enabled false --delete-enabled false

# Multi-arch: build and push amd64 + arm64 under one tag
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t "$REGISTRY/$REPO:$UNIQUE_TAG" --push .
```

**Key takeaways**

- Tags are mutable pointers; digests are immutable. `latest` is a name, not a version.
- Deploy with unique tags (version + commit SHA) or digests. Use stable tags only for convenience and base-image consumption.
- Build once and promote the same image through environments.
- Lock release tags in ACR and purge untagged images regularly.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Push an image as `demo:latest`, change the code, push again, and use `az acr manifest list-metadata` to find the now-untagged manifest from the first push.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a CI script that tags each build with `<semver>-<shortsha>`, pushes it, and writes the resulting digest to a build artifact used by the deployment stage.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A bug appeared in production but not staging, even though both run `orders-api:1.4`. How could that happen and how do you prevent it?" *Hint:* moving tags, pull timing and node image caches, and deploying by unique tag or digest.

<a id="42-azure-container-registry"></a>
### 4.2 Azure Container Registry

Azure Container Registry (ACR) is a managed, private OCI registry that lives next to your Azure workloads. This section covers choosing a tier, moving images in and out, building images in the cloud, replicating across regions, and authenticating without passwords.

#### Registry Tiers

Docker Hub is public, rate-limited for anonymous pulls, and far from your Azure regions. Production images need a private registry that sits on the Azure network, integrates with Entra ID and RBAC, and stays fast under load when hundreds of nodes pull at once. ACR provides this as a managed service. You never patch or scale registry servers yourself; you pick a **service tier** (SKU) that sets storage, throughput, and which features are available.

All tiers share the same API, the same login server format (`<name>.azurecr.io`), and the same core features: Entra ID authentication, RBAC, ACR Tasks, OCI artifacts (Helm charts, signatures, SBOMs), and encryption at rest. The differences are capacity and enterprise features:

| Capability | Basic | Standard | Premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intended use | Learning, dev/test, low volume | Most production workloads | High-scale, multi-region, locked-down networks |
| Included storage | 10 GiB | 100 GiB | 500 GiB |
| Throughput (read/write operations and bandwidth) | Lowest | Medium | Highest |
| Webhooks | 2 | 10 | 500 |
| Geo-replication | No | No | Yes |
| Private endpoints (Private Link) and disabling public access | No | No | Yes |
| Customer-managed encryption keys | No | No | Yes |
| Retention policy for untagged manifests | No | No | Yes |
| Connected registry (on-premises/edge replica) | No | No | Yes |
| Anonymous (unauthenticated) pull | No | Yes | Yes |

Storage beyond the included amount is billed per GiB per day. Throughput limits matter more than people expect: when a large AKS cluster scales out and every node pulls the same image at once, a Basic registry can throttle requests (HTTP 429), which shows up as slow or failed pod starts.

**Choosing a tier**

```text
  Is the registry only for experiments or a personal project?
      yes -> Basic
      no  -> Do you need any of: private endpoints / no public access,
             geo-replication, customer-managed keys, untagged-manifest retention,
             very high concurrent pull volume?
                 yes -> Premium
                 no  -> Standard
```

You can change tiers at any time with no downtime and no data migration. Downgrading is blocked if the registry uses a feature the lower tier lacks (for example, you must remove geo-replicas before moving from Premium to Standard).

**Example: create a registry and change its tier**

```bash
RG=rg-containers
ACR=crshop$RANDOM                # registry names: 5-50 alphanumeric chars, globally unique

az group create -n $RG -l westeurope

# Start on Standard for a typical production app
az acr create -g $RG -n $ACR --sku Standard

# Inspect what you got
az acr show -n $ACR --query "{login:loginServer, sku:sku.name, admin:adminUserEnabled}" -o table
az acr show-usage -n $ACR -o table      # storage used vs included, webhooks used vs limit

# Upgrade in place when you need Private Link or geo-replication
az acr update -n $ACR --sku Premium
```

```bicep
resource acr 'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries@2023-07-01' = {
  name: acrName
  location: location
  sku: { name: 'Premium' }
  properties: {
    adminUserEnabled: false              // use Entra ID, not the shared admin account
    publicNetworkAccess: 'Disabled'      // Premium only: reachable via private endpoint
    policies: {
      retentionPolicy: { days: 7, status: 'enabled' }   // delete untagged manifests after 7 days
    }
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- ACR is a managed private OCI registry. All tiers share the same API and core features.
- Basic suits dev/test, Standard suits most production, and Premium adds geo-replication, Private Link, customer-managed keys, retention policies, and the highest throughput.
- Throughput limits affect large-scale pulls. Throttling looks like slow or failed container starts.
- Tiers can be changed in place without downtime.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a Basic registry, run `az acr show-usage`, and identify the included storage and webhook limits. Upgrade it to Standard and run the command again.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Your security team requires that the registry is reachable only from your virtual network. Determine the minimum tier, and write the Bicep that enforces it.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Pods in a 200-node AKS cluster sometimes fail with `ImagePullBackOff` during scale-out, but only at peak times. What would you check on the registry side?" *Hint:* tier throughput limits and throttling, image size, registry region versus cluster region, and artifact caching or geo-replication.

#### Pushing and Pulling Images

A registry is useful only if images move in and out of it reliably. With ACR, three things are different from Docker Hub: you authenticate with Entra ID instead of a Docker account, the image name must include the registry's **login server**, and you can move images *server-side* without them ever passing through your machine.

**Naming.** To push to ACR, the image reference must start with the login server. Repositories can use namespaces (path segments) to organize images by team or product:

```text
  crshop.azurecr.io / payments/orders-api : 1.4.2-a1b2c3d
  \_______________/   \_________________/   \___________/
    login server       repository           tag
                       (namespace/name)
```

**The basic workflow**

```text
  Developer machine / CI agent                         ACR (crshop.azurecr.io)
  ----------------------------                         ----------------------
  az acr login -n crshop  -------- Entra ID token ---> issues registry refresh token
  docker build -t crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2 .
  docker push  crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2 ---> uploads only layers ACR lacks
                                                       stores manifest, updates tag
  Azure service (ACI/ACA/AKS) <---- pull by tag/digest  (authenticated by managed identity)
```

`az acr login` uses your Azure CLI identity to obtain an ACR token and writes it into Docker's credential store. It requires a local Docker daemon. When no Docker daemon is available (for example with Podman, Helm, or ORAS), use `az acr login --expose-token` and pass the token as a password.

**Server-side operations** avoid downloading and re-uploading gigabytes:

| Need | Command | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Copy a public image into your registry | `az acr import --source docker.io/library/nginx:1.27 --image nginx:1.27` | Avoid Docker Hub rate limits; control what production depends on |
| Promote an image between registries | `az acr import --source crdev.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2 ...` | Build once, promote everywhere |
| Cache an upstream registry on demand | `az acr cache create ...` (artifact cache rule) | First pull fetches from upstream, later pulls are served from ACR |
| Build without local Docker | `az acr build` | See ACR Tasks below |

**Housekeeping.** Every push of a moving tag leaves an untagged manifest behind. Without cleanup, storage grows indefinitely. Use `az acr repository delete` for individual images, the **`acr purge`** command (run as an ACR task) to delete by age and pattern, or a retention policy (Premium) for untagged manifests.

**Example: push, pull, inspect, import, and clean up**

```bash
ACR=crshop
LOGIN=$(az acr show -n $ACR --query loginServer -o tsv)      # crshop.azurecr.io

# 1) Authenticate Docker with your Entra ID identity (token valid for about 3 hours)
az acr login -n $ACR

# 2) Tag a local image with the full registry path and push it
docker tag orders-api:dev $LOGIN/payments/orders-api:1.4.2
docker push $LOGIN/payments/orders-api:1.4.2

# 3) Browse the registry
az acr repository list -n $ACR -o table
az acr repository show-tags -n $ACR --repository payments/orders-api \
  --orderby time_desc --top 5 -o table
az acr manifest list-metadata -r $ACR -n payments/orders-api \
  --query "[].{digest:digest, tags:tags, created:createdTime}" -o table

# 4) Pull it elsewhere (another machine after az acr login)
docker pull $LOGIN/payments/orders-api:1.4.2

# 5) Import a public base image server-side, without Docker
az acr import -n $ACR --source docker.io/library/redis:7.4 --image base/redis:7.4

# 6) No Docker daemon? Use the exposed token with another client (ORAS, Helm, Podman)
TOKEN=$(az acr login -n $ACR --expose-token --query accessToken -o tsv)
podman login $LOGIN -u 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000 -p "$TOKEN"   # fixed GUID username

# 7) Clean up: delete untagged manifests and dev tags older than 30 days
az acr run -r $ACR --cmd \
  "acr purge --filter 'payments/orders-api:dev-.*' --ago 30d --untagged" /dev/null
```

`/dev/null` at the end of `az acr run` means "no source context needed": the purge command runs entirely inside ACR.

**Key takeaways**

- Image references must include the login server (`<name>.azurecr.io`). Use namespaces to organize repositories.
- `az acr login` exchanges your Entra ID identity for a short-lived registry token. Use `--expose-token` when there is no Docker daemon.
- Prefer server-side `az acr import` and artifact cache rules for third-party images and for promotion between registries.
- Plan cleanup from day one with `acr purge` or retention policies, or storage costs grow silently.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build a small image, push it to ACR under a `samples/` namespace, delete it locally, and pull it back from ACR.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Import `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0` into your registry, change your Dockerfile to use the imported copy, and schedule a weekly `acr purge` task that removes untagged manifests older than 14 days.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why would a company import public base images into its own registry instead of pulling them from Docker Hub or MCR during builds?" *Hint:* rate limits and availability, supply-chain control and vulnerability scanning, and reproducibility if the upstream tag moves or disappears.

#### ACR Tasks and Automated Builds

Building images on developer laptops or CI agents has drawbacks: each agent needs Docker (and often privileged mode), builds happen far from the registry so every push crosses the internet, and nobody rebuilds images when the *base image* gets a security patch. **ACR Tasks** moves image building into Azure, next to the registry, and adds triggers for automatic rebuilds.

Analogy: instead of baking bread at home and driving it to the shop, the shop gets its own oven, plus a rule that it re-bakes automatically whenever the flour supplier delivers a new batch.

ACR Tasks comes in three forms:

| Task type | What it does | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Quick task** (`az acr build`) | One-off cloud build of a Dockerfile from a local folder or Git URL, then push | Developers without local Docker, simple CI steps |
| **Triggered task** (`az acr task create`) | Saved build definition that runs on triggers | Automated builds |
| **Multi-step task** (YAML file) | Sequence of build, push, and cmd steps (run containers as steps) | Build, test, then push only if tests pass |

**Triggers** for saved tasks:

- **Source code update**: a commit or pull request in a GitHub or Azure Repos repository.
- **Base image update**: when the base image referenced in `FROM` is updated (in the same ACR, another ACR, or a public registry such as Docker Hub or MCR), ACR rebuilds every dependent image. This is the main reason to use ACR Tasks: OS and runtime patches flow into your images automatically.
- **Timer (schedule)**: cron expression, for example a nightly rebuild.

```text
  Base image updated in MCR (security patch)
            |
            v
  ACR Tasks detects the change in FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:8.0
            |
            v
  Rebuilds orders-api  -->  pushes crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:{{.Run.ID}}
            |
            v
  Webhook / Event Grid event "image pushed"  -->  pipeline redeploys after tests
```

Task runs execute on Azure-managed build agents (Linux by default; Windows and `linux/arm64` are also supported). Each run gets a unique **Run ID** (for example `ca12`) that you can use in tags through the `{{.Run.ID}}` template. Run logs are stored and viewable with `az acr task logs`.

**Example: quick build, triggered task, and a multi-step task**

```bash
ACR=crshop

# Quick task: upload the current folder as build context, build in Azure, push to ACR
az acr build -r $ACR -t orders-api:{{.Run.ID}} -t orders-api:dev .
az acr build -r $ACR --platform linux/arm64 -t orders-api:arm-{{.Run.ID}} .   # Arm build, no local emulation

# Triggered task: build on every commit to main AND whenever the base image changes
az acr task create -r $ACR -n build-orders-api \
  --context https://github.com/contoso/orders-api.git#main \
  --file Dockerfile \
  --image "orders-api:{{.Run.ID}}" \
  --git-access-token "$GITHUB_PAT" \
  --base-image-trigger-enabled true \
  --base-image-trigger-type Runtime        # rebuild when the runtime stage's base image updates

# Add a nightly timer trigger (UTC cron)
az acr task timer add -r $ACR -n build-orders-api --timer-name nightly --schedule "0 2 * * *"

# Run it manually and watch the log
az acr task run -r $ACR -n build-orders-api
az acr task list-runs -r $ACR -n build-orders-api -o table
az acr task logs -r $ACR --run-id ca12
```

```yaml
# acr-task.yaml -- multi-step task: build, run tests in the built image, push only on success
version: v1.1.0
steps:
  - id: build
    build: -t $Registry/orders-api:$ID -f Dockerfile .      # $Registry and $ID are built-in variables

  - id: unit-tests
    cmd: $Registry/orders-api:$ID pytest -q                  # run a container from the image as a step
    when: ["build"]

  - id: push
    push:
      - $Registry/orders-api:$ID
    when: ["unit-tests"]                                     # skipped if tests fail
```

```bash
# Run the multi-step file once against the local folder, or save it as a triggered task
az acr run -r crshop -f acr-task.yaml .
az acr task create -r crshop -n orders-pipeline \
  --context https://github.com/contoso/orders-api.git#main \
  --file acr-task.yaml --git-access-token "$GITHUB_PAT"
```

Tasks can also run with a **managed identity** (`--assign-identity`), which lets steps pull from other registries or read secrets from Key Vault without credentials in the task definition.

**Key takeaways**

- `az acr build` builds in Azure next to the registry. No local Docker daemon is needed.
- Saved tasks trigger on commits, on base-image updates, or on a schedule. Base-image triggers keep images patched automatically.
- Multi-step YAML tasks can build, test, and conditionally push.
- `{{.Run.ID}}` (CLI) and `$ID` (YAML) give each build a unique tag.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use `az acr build` to build and push an image from a folder on a machine that does not have Docker installed (for example Azure Cloud Shell).
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create a base image `base/python-runtime` in your registry and an app image that uses it in `FROM`. Configure a base-image trigger on the app task, push a new version of the base image, and verify the app image rebuilds automatically.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you ensure that a critical OpenSSL fix in your base image reaches all 40 of your services within a day?" *Hint:* base-image update triggers, a central curated base image, automated tests and redeployment after rebuilds, and vulnerability scanning to verify.

#### Geo-Replication

If your application runs in West Europe and East US, pulling images from a single registry in West Europe means every East US node pulls across the Atlantic: slower deployments and scale-outs, cross-region data transfer charges, and a single point of failure. You could create one registry per region, but then every pipeline must push to several registries and every deployment must reference a different registry name per region.

**Geo-replication** (Premium) solves this with *one* registry that has **replicas** in multiple regions. You keep a single login server name (`crshop.azurecr.io`). Pushes and pulls are routed to the closest replica, and ACR replicates content between replicas automatically.

Analogy: a chain of libraries sharing one catalog. You return a book (push) at your local branch, and it soon becomes available at every branch. Readers always borrow from the branch nearest them, using the same library card (registry name).

```text
                     crshop.azurecr.io   (single name, DNS routes to closest replica)
                               |
         +---------------------+----------------------+
         |                     |                      |
   West Europe (home)     East US replica       Southeast Asia replica
   AKS / ACA in WEU       AKS / ACA in EUS      AKS / ACA in SEA
   pull locally           pull locally          pull locally
         ^                     ^                      ^
         +------ asynchronous replication of manifests and layers ------+
```

What to know:

- **Network-close, single name**: deployments use the same image reference in every region.
- **Eventually consistent**: a push lands in the closest replica first and replicates asynchronously. A deployment in another region right after the push may briefly see "manifest unknown". Use per-region webhooks (which fire when the image arrives in *that* replica) to trigger regional deployments.
- **Resilience**: if a region has an outage, other replicas continue serving their regions. You can temporarily stop routing to a replica with `--region-endpoint-enabled false` during maintenance or troubleshooting.
- **Zone redundancy** can be enabled per replica so a replica survives a datacenter (zone) failure within its region.
- **Cost**: each replica is billed as an additional Premium registry for each day it exists, plus storage.
- **Not a backup**: deletes and overwrites also replicate. Protect important tags with locks.

**Example: add replicas and regional webhooks**

```bash
ACR=crshop        # must be Premium

az acr replication create -r $ACR -l eastus --zone-redundancy Enabled
az acr replication create -r $ACR -l southeastasia

az acr replication list -r $ACR \
  --query "[].{region:location, status:provisioningState, zr:zoneRedundancy}" -o table

# Fire a webhook only when the image is available in the East US replica
az acr webhook create -r $ACR -n eusDeploy --location eastus \
  --uri "https://deploy.contoso.com/hooks/eus" --actions push \
  --scope "orders-api:*"

# Take a replica out of routing temporarily (clients are served by other replicas)
az acr replication update -r $ACR -n eastus --region-endpoint-enabled false
```

```bicep
resource replica 'Microsoft.ContainerRegistry/registries/replications@2023-07-01' = {
  parent: acr                              // the Premium registry resource
  name: 'eastus'
  location: 'eastus'
  properties: {
    zoneRedundancy: 'Enabled'
    regionEndpointEnabled: true
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Geo-replication (Premium) gives one registry name with replicas in several regions. Clients pull from the closest one.
- Replication is asynchronous. Use per-region webhooks to deploy only when an image has arrived in that region.
- Replicas improve performance and regional resilience, but every replica is billed and deletes replicate too.
- Combine with zone redundancy for in-region resilience.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add a replica to a Premium registry, push an image, and use `az acr replication list` and the portal to confirm it is available in both regions.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Design a deployment flow for an app running in three regions so that each region deploys only after the new image has replicated there. Describe which webhooks or events you would use.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Should you use geo-replication or separate registries per region?" *Hint:* single name versus per-region configuration, cost, independent failure domains, regulatory data residency, and promotion workflows.

#### Registry Authentication

Every pull and push must be authenticated, and the identity used determines what the caller can do. The challenge is to give each caller (developers, CI pipelines, ACI, Container Apps, AKS nodes) exactly the access it needs, **without passwords that can leak**.

ACR supports several authentication methods:

| Method | Who uses it | Credential | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Individual Entra ID login (`az acr login`) | Developers | User's Entra token, exchanged for a ~3-hour ACR token | Yes, for people |
| Managed identity | ACI, Container Apps, App Service, ACR Tasks, VMs | No secret; Azure-managed token | **Preferred for Azure services** |
| AKS integration (`--attach-acr`) | AKS nodes (kubelet identity) | Managed identity with `AcrPull` | Yes, for AKS |
| Workload identity federation | GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, other clouds | OIDC token exchange (see 2.4) | **Preferred for CI/CD** |
| Service principal with secret | Legacy CI, external tools | Client secret | Only when federation is impossible |
| Repository-scoped tokens | IoT devices, external partners, tools without Entra support | Token name and password, scoped to repositories | Niche cases |
| Admin user | Quick tests | One shared username and two passwords with full push/pull rights | **Avoid**; disabled by default |
| Anonymous pull (Standard/Premium) | Public distribution | None | Only for intentionally public content |

**RBAC roles for ACR.** Data access is controlled by Azure RBAC on the registry (see 2.5):

| Role | Pull | Push | Delete | Sign |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AcrPull` | Yes | | | |
| `AcrPush` | Yes | Yes | | |
| `AcrDelete` | | | Yes | |
| `AcrImageSigner` | | | | Yes (legacy content trust) |
| `Contributor` / `Owner` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Manage registry too |

Registries can also be configured to use **repository-level** permissions with Entra ABAC conditions (role assignments that apply only to repositories matching a prefix, such as `payments/`). This lets several teams share one registry while each can push only to its own namespace.

**How a managed identity pull works**

```text
  Container Apps / ACI / AKS node
     | 1. requests Entra token for its managed identity (IMDS / platform)
     v
  Microsoft Entra ID  -- 2. access token -->  platform
     | 3. exchanges Entra token at https://crshop.azurecr.io/oauth2/exchange
     v
  ACR: checks RBAC (AcrPull?)  -- 4. ACR refresh/access token --> platform pulls layers
```

You never write this code: the platform does it once you configure which identity to use for the registry.

**Example: grant pull access the right way for each consumer**

```bash
ACR=crshop
ACR_ID=$(az acr show -n $ACR --query id -o tsv)

# Disable the admin user (the default for new registries, but verify)
az acr update -n $ACR --admin-enabled false

# 1) A user-assigned identity for container workloads, with pull-only rights
az identity create -g rg-containers -n id-orders
PRINCIPAL=$(az identity show -g rg-containers -n id-orders --query principalId -o tsv)
az role assignment create --assignee-object-id $PRINCIPAL \
  --assignee-principal-type ServicePrincipal --role AcrPull --scope $ACR_ID

# 2) AKS: grant the cluster's kubelet identity AcrPull in one step
az aks update -g rg-aks -n aks-shop --attach-acr $ACR

# 3) CI pipeline with workload identity federation (GitHub Actions app registration)
az role assignment create --assignee "$GITHUB_APP_ID" --role AcrPush --scope $ACR_ID

# 4) A partner device that may only read one repository, for 30 days
az acr token create -r $ACR -n partner-reader \
  --repository samples/edge-agent content/read metadata/read \
  --expiration-in-days 30
```

```yaml
# GitHub Actions: push to ACR with OIDC, no stored registry password
permissions:
  id-token: write          # allow the job to request an OIDC token
  contents: read
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
  - uses: azure/login@v2
    with:
      client-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_CLIENT_ID }}
      tenant-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_TENANT_ID }}
      subscription-id: ${{ vars.AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID }}
  - run: |
      az acr login -n crshop
      docker build -t crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:${{ github.sha }} .
      docker push crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:${{ github.sha }}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Use Entra ID everywhere: `az acr login` for people, managed identities for Azure services, workload identity federation for CI/CD.
- Grant the narrowest role: `AcrPull` for runtimes, `AcrPush` for build pipelines. Use repository-scoped permissions when teams share a registry.
- Keep the admin user disabled. It is a shared, full-access credential with no per-user audit trail.
- Repository-scoped tokens are for clients that cannot use Entra ID.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Assign yourself only `AcrPull` on a registry (remove any broader roles) and confirm that `docker push` fails with an authorization error while `docker pull` succeeds.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Replace a GitHub Actions workflow that uses `docker login` with the admin password by one that uses OIDC federation and `AcrPush`. Then disable the admin user.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An ACR admin password was committed to a public repository. What do you do immediately, and how do you prevent it from happening again?" *Hint:* regenerate both passwords, review registry logs for unexpected pushes, check image integrity, then disable the admin user and move to managed identities and federation.

<a id="43-azure-container-instances"></a>
### 4.3 Azure Container Instances

Azure Container Instances (ACI) is the simplest way to run a container in Azure: give it an image, CPU, and memory, and it runs within seconds, billed per second, with no cluster or VM to manage. This section covers how ACI groups containers, controls their lifecycle, injects configuration and secrets, and persists data.

#### Container Groups

Sometimes you just need to *run a container*: a nightly data export, a one-off migration script, a short-lived test environment, a build agent. Provisioning a VM or a Kubernetes cluster for that is overkill. ACI offers "containers as a service" with no infrastructure to manage. The unit of deployment in ACI is not a single container but a **container group**.

A container group is a collection of containers that are **scheduled on the same host and share a lifecycle, network, and storage**. It is the same idea as a Kubernetes *pod*. Containers in a group:

- Start and stop together, and are billed together.
- Share **one IP address** and port namespace, so they reach each other on `localhost` and must not listen on the same port.
- Can mount the **same volumes**, so one container can write files another reads.
- Have individual CPU and memory **requests**. The group's size is the sum of its containers' requests.

Analogy: a container group is a shared apartment. Each roommate (container) has their own room (process and filesystem), but they share one street address (IP), one front door with numbered mailboxes (ports), and the kitchen (volumes). When the lease ends, everybody moves out together.

```text
  Container group "cg-orders"   public IP 20.x.x.x, DNS: orders-demo.westeurope.azurecontainer.io
  +------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  +----------------------+               +----------------------+ |
  |  | api                  |   localhost   | log-shipper (sidecar)| |
  |  | 1 vCPU / 1.5 GB      |<------------->| 0.5 vCPU / 0.5 GB    | |
  |  | listens on :8080     |               | reads /var/log/app   | |
  |  +----------+-----------+               +-----------+----------+ |
  |             |                                       |            |
  |             +------ shared volume (emptyDir) -------+            |
  |                      mounted at /var/log/app                     |
  |  exposed ports: 8080/tcp                                         |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Common patterns:** a main app with a sidecar (log shipping, TLS-terminating proxy, metrics exporter), or an init container that prepares data before the main containers start.

**Key properties and limits**

| Aspect | Details |
|---|---|
| OS | Linux groups can have multiple containers. Windows groups support a single container |
| Networking | Public IP with optional DNS name label, or private IP inside a virtual network subnet. No built-in load balancer across groups |
| Sizing | Per-container CPU/memory requests (optional limits). Maximums per group depend on region and SKU |
| Scaling | None. One group is one set of instances. For more capacity, create more groups or use Container Apps |
| Pricing | Per second, for the vCPU and memory requested, while the group runs |
| Deployment | `az container create` flags (single container), YAML file, ARM/Bicep (multi-container) |

**When to use ACI**

| Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|
| Batch and scheduled jobs, task automation | Long-running, autoscaling HTTP APIs (use Container Apps) |
| CI/CD build agents, test environments | Microservices needing service discovery, traffic splitting |
| Burst capacity for AKS (virtual nodes) | Complex orchestration (use AKS) |
| Simple, isolated apps with fixed load | Apps needing zero-downtime rolling updates |

**Example: single container from the CLI**

```bash
RG=rg-aci
az group create -n $RG -l westeurope

az container create -g $RG -n aci-hello \
  --image mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aci-helloworld \
  --os-type Linux \
  --cpu 1 --memory 1.5 \
  --ports 80 \
  --ip-address Public \
  --dns-name-label hello-$RANDOM            # FQDN: <label>.<region>.azurecontainer.io

az container show -g $RG -n aci-hello --query "{fqdn:ipAddress.fqdn, state:instanceView.state}" -o table
az container logs -g $RG -n aci-hello
az container exec -g $RG -n aci-hello --exec-command "/bin/sh"   # interactive shell for debugging
```

**Example: multi-container group with a sidecar, pulled from ACR with a managed identity**

```yaml
# cg-orders.yaml -- deploy with: az container create -g rg-aci --file cg-orders.yaml
apiVersion: '2023-05-01'
location: westeurope
name: cg-orders
type: Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups
identity:
  type: UserAssigned
  userAssignedIdentities:
    /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-containers/providers/Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/id-orders: {}
properties:
  osType: Linux
  imageRegistryCredentials:
    - server: crshop.azurecr.io
      identity: /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-containers/providers/Microsoft.ManagedIdentity/userAssignedIdentities/id-orders   # needs AcrPull
  containers:
    - name: api
      properties:
        image: crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2-a1b2c3d
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 1, memoryInGB: 1.5 }
        ports:
          - port: 8080
        volumeMounts:
          - name: logs
            mountPath: /var/log/app
    - name: log-shipper
      properties:
        image: crshop.azurecr.io/tools/log-shipper:2.1.0
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 0.5, memoryInGB: 0.5 }   # group total: 1.5 vCPU, 2 GB
        volumeMounts:
          - name: logs
            mountPath: /var/log/app
            readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: logs
      emptyDir: {}                                    # lives as long as the group
  ipAddress:
    type: Public
    dnsNameLabel: orders-demo
    ports:
      - protocol: TCP
        port: 8080                                    # only ports listed here are reachable
  restartPolicy: Always
```

**Key takeaways**

- The unit of deployment in ACI is the container group: containers co-scheduled on one host, sharing IP, ports, lifecycle, and volumes.
- Containers in a group talk over `localhost`. Use groups for sidecar and helper patterns.
- ACI has no autoscaling or load balancing. It fits jobs, agents, and simple fixed-size apps.
- Use a managed identity with `AcrPull` to pull private images, and YAML or Bicep for multi-container groups.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Deploy `mcr.microsoft.com/azuredocs/aci-helloworld` with a DNS name label, open it in a browser, and view its logs with `az container logs`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy a two-container group in which an NGINX container proxies requests on port 80 to an app container on port 8080 via `localhost`. Expose only port 80.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A team runs its public API on three separate ACI container groups behind DNS round robin. What problems do you foresee, and what would you suggest instead?" *Hint:* no health-aware load balancing, no autoscaling, deployments causing downtime, and what Container Apps or App Service provide out of the box.

#### Restart Policies

Not every container is meant to run forever. A web server should be restarted if it crashes. A database migration should run once and stop. A nightly report job should be retried if it fails, but not rerun if it succeeds. The **restart policy** tells ACI what to do when the containers in a group exit, and it directly affects your bill: you pay only while containers run.

The policy is set on the **container group** and applies to all its containers:

| Policy | Behavior when a container exits | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `Always` (default) | Restart it, regardless of exit code | Long-running services: web servers, workers, agents |
| `OnFailure` | Restart only if it exited with a non-zero code. Stop when it exits with 0 | Batch jobs that should retry on error |
| `Never` | Never restart. The container ends in `Terminated` state | One-shot tasks; you inspect the result yourself |

```text
  Container process exits with code ...
                 |
       +---------+----------+
       | 0 (success)        | non-zero (failure)
       v                    v
  Always    -> restart     Always    -> restart
  OnFailure -> stop        OnFailure -> restart
  Never     -> stop        Never     -> stop
                                  (stopped group: billing for compute stops)
```

Important details:

- **Exit codes matter.** Your job must exit with a non-zero code on failure, otherwise `OnFailure` cannot detect it. Catch exceptions only to log them, then exit with an error code.
- **Restart count** is visible in the instance view (`restartCount`). A container stuck in a crash loop with `Always` keeps restarting, and keeps costing money.
- **Terminated groups remain** as resources (so you can read logs and exit codes) until you delete them. They incur no compute charges. `az container start` runs a stopped group again from the beginning.
- **Overriding the command**: `--command-line` (or `command` in YAML) lets one image serve several jobs with different arguments.
- **`Always` with a job that finishes** creates an endless loop of successful runs. This is a common, costly mistake.

**Example: a batch job that retries on failure**

```python
# export_orders.py -- exit codes drive the restart policy
import sys, logging
from datetime import date

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)

def main(day: str) -> None:
    logging.info("Exporting orders for %s", day)
    # ... query the database and upload a CSV to Blob Storage ...

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else date.today().isoformat())
    except Exception:
        logging.exception("Export failed")
        sys.exit(1)          # non-zero -> OnFailure restarts the container
    sys.exit(0)              # zero -> container stops; billing ends
```

```bash
# Run the export once for a given day; retry automatically if it fails
az container create -g rg-aci -n job-export-20261020 \
  --image crshop.azurecr.io/jobs/export-orders:3.0.1 \
  --acr-identity $ID_ORDERS --assign-identity $ID_ORDERS \
  --restart-policy OnFailure \
  --command-line "python export_orders.py 2026-10-20" \
  --cpu 1 --memory 2

# Watch the outcome
az container show -g rg-aci -n job-export-20261020 \
  --query "containers[0].instanceView.{state:currentState.state, exit:currentState.exitCode, restarts:restartCount}" -o table
az container logs -g rg-aci -n job-export-20261020

# Re-run the same group later, then clean up
az container start -g rg-aci -n job-export-20261020
az container delete -g rg-aci -n job-export-20261020 --yes
```

For recurring jobs, trigger ACI from a scheduler (Logic Apps, Azure Functions timer, a pipeline), or use **Container Apps jobs** (see 4.4), which add built-in schedules, retries, timeouts, and execution history.

**Key takeaways**

- `Always` for services, `OnFailure` for retrying batch jobs, `Never` for one-shot tasks.
- The policy relies on exit codes. Make jobs exit non-zero on failure.
- Stopped groups stop billing for compute but remain until deleted, so you can inspect logs and exit codes.
- Using `Always` for a job that completes causes an endless, billed restart loop.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run a container with the command `sh -c "echo done; exit 0"` under each restart policy and compare `restartCount` and the final state after a few minutes.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a job that fails randomly half the time. Run it with `OnFailure` and record how many restarts occur before it succeeds. Then design how you would cap the number of retries.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A team's monthly ACI bill tripled although the job runs only five minutes a night. What would you look at first?" *Hint:* restart policy versus exit behavior, groups left running, and requested CPU/memory versus actual usage.

#### Environment Variables and Secrets

Twelve-factor apps read configuration from the environment: connection endpoints, feature flags, log levels. The same image then runs unchanged in dev, test, and production with different settings. Some of that configuration is sensitive (database passwords, API keys), and it must not be readable by everyone who can view the resource in the portal or read deployment logs.

ACI offers three mechanisms:

| Mechanism | How it is exposed | Visible in `az container show` / portal? | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Environment variables (`--environment-variables`, `value`) | Process environment | **Yes**, in plain text | Non-sensitive configuration |
| Secure environment variables (`--secure-environment-variables`, `secureValue`) | Process environment | **No** (hidden in resource properties) | Small secrets when nothing better is available |
| Secret volume (`secret`) | Files in a memory-backed (tmpfs) mount | No | Certificates, multi-line secrets, file-based config |
| Managed identity + Key Vault | Your code fetches at startup | Nothing stored in ACI | **Preferred** for real secrets |

Things to keep in mind:

- Secure values are hidden from the Azure control plane, but **inside the container they are ordinary environment variables**. Anyone who can `az container exec` into the container, or any library that dumps the environment in a crash report, can see them.
- Container group properties, including secure values, **cannot be updated in place**. Changing a secret means redeploying the group.
- Secrets passed on the command line can end up in shell history and CI logs. Pass them from a secure pipeline variable or a Key Vault reference in a Bicep parameter file.
- The best option avoids stored secrets entirely: give the group a **managed identity**, and either use passwordless (Entra ID) connections to services such as Storage, SQL, and Service Bus, or read the remaining secrets from Key Vault at startup.

**Example: environment variables, secure values, and a secret volume**

```bash
az container create -g rg-aci -n aci-orders \
  --image crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2-a1b2c3d \
  --acr-identity $ID_ORDERS --assign-identity $ID_ORDERS \
  --environment-variables \
      ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production \
      KEYVAULT_URI=https://kv-orders.vault.azure.net/ \
      AZURE_CLIENT_ID=$ID_ORDERS_CLIENT_ID \
  --secure-environment-variables \
      PAYMENT_API_KEY="$PAYMENT_API_KEY" \
  --ports 8080 --ip-address Public

# Plain values are visible, secure ones are not
az container show -g rg-aci -n aci-orders \
  --query "containers[0].environmentVariables" -o json
# [ { "name": "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT", "value": "Production", "secureValue": null },
#   { "name": "PAYMENT_API_KEY", "value": null, "secureValue": null }, ... ]
```

```yaml
# Excerpt of a container group YAML: secure env var and a secret volume
properties:
  containers:
    - name: api
      properties:
        image: crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2-a1b2c3d
        environmentVariables:
          - name: LOG_LEVEL
            value: Information
          - name: PAYMENT_API_KEY
            secureValue: '<injected by the pipeline, never committed>'
        volumeMounts:
          - name: tls
            mountPath: /mnt/tls            # files appear as /mnt/tls/cert.pem, /mnt/tls/key.pem
            readOnly: true
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 1, memoryInGB: 1.5 }
  volumes:
    - name: tls
      secret:
        cert.pem: <base64-encoded content>  # values in a secret volume must be base64
        key.pem: <base64-encoded content>
```

**Example: preferred approach, managed identity reading Key Vault at startup**

```python
import os
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential     # resolves to the group's managed identity in ACI
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient

credential = DefaultAzureCredential()                 # AZURE_CLIENT_ID selects the user-assigned identity
secrets = SecretClient(vault_url=os.environ["KEYVAULT_URI"], credential=credential)

payment_api_key = secrets.get_secret("payment-api-key").value   # needs 'Key Vault Secrets User' role
```

**Key takeaways**

- Use plain environment variables for non-sensitive config, and `secureValue` or secret volumes when a secret must be injected.
- Secure values are hidden from the control plane, not from processes inside the container.
- Changing variables or secrets requires redeploying the container group.
- Prefer a managed identity with passwordless connections or Key Vault, so no secret is stored in ACI at all.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Deploy a container with one normal and one secure environment variable. Compare what `az container show` returns for each, then `exec` into the container and run `env`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Mount a TLS certificate and key through a secret volume and configure NGINX in the container to serve HTTPS using those files.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Is `--secure-environment-variables` enough to protect a database password in ACI?" *Hint:* who can exec into the container, crash dumps and diagnostic logs, rotation requiring redeployment, and passwordless alternatives with managed identity.

#### Mounting Azure Files Volumes

Containers are disposable: when an ACI container group is deleted, restarted on a different host, or redeployed, everything written to its filesystem is gone. Many workloads need data that outlives the container: uploaded files, reports produced by a batch job, shared configuration read by several groups, or the working directory of a build agent. ACI can mount an **Azure Files** share (a managed SMB file share, covered in 5.4) into a container as a directory.

Analogy: the container is a hotel room that is cleaned completely after every stay. An Azure Files share is a storage locker in the lobby: you can put things in it, check out, and find them there the next time, from any room.

```text
   Container group A (job)            Container group B (report viewer)
   +--------------------------+       +--------------------------+
   | /mnt/reports  (rw)       |       | /usr/share/nginx/html (ro)|
   +-------------+------------+       +-------------+------------+
                 |  SMB 3 (port 445)                |
                 +-----------------+----------------+
                                   v
                 Storage account "stordersdata" -> file share "reports"
                 (persists independently of either container group)
```

What to know:

- **Linux containers only.** Windows container groups cannot mount Azure Files.
- **Authentication uses the storage account key.** You must pass the account name and key; managed identity is not supported for ACI file share mounts. Treat the key as a secret (secure parameter, Key Vault reference in Bicep).
- **The container must run as root** for the mount to work, which conflicts with the "non-root user" practice. Weigh this when choosing between a mounted share and accessing Blob Storage through the SDK with a managed identity.
- **Network access**: SMB uses TCP port 445. If the storage account has its firewall enabled, deploy the container group into a virtual network that can reach the share (service endpoint or private endpoint).
- **Performance**: SMB adds latency compared with local disk. A share works well for files, reports, and shared assets, not for running a database engine.
- A group can mount **multiple shares**, and a share can be mounted **read-only**. Multiple groups can mount the same share at once.
- Other ACI volume types are `emptyDir` (scratch space shared between containers in a group, lost with the group), `secret` (see the previous topic), and the deprecated `gitRepo`.

**Example: mount a share from the CLI**

```bash
RG=rg-aci
SA=stordersdata$RANDOM
SHARE=reports

# 1) Create the storage account and file share
az storage account create -g $RG -n $SA -l westeurope --sku Standard_LRS
az storage share-rm create -g $RG --storage-account $SA -n $SHARE --quota 100     # 100 GiB

KEY=$(az storage account keys list -g $RG -n $SA --query "[0].value" -o tsv)

# 2) Run a job that writes its output to the share
az container create -g $RG -n job-reports \
  --image crshop.azurecr.io/jobs/report-generator:2.3.0 \
  --acr-identity $ID_ORDERS --assign-identity $ID_ORDERS \
  --restart-policy OnFailure \
  --azure-file-volume-account-name $SA \
  --azure-file-volume-account-key "$KEY" \
  --azure-file-volume-share-name $SHARE \
  --azure-file-volume-mount-path /mnt/reports

# 3) Files remain after the container is deleted
az container delete -g $RG -n job-reports --yes
az storage file list --account-name $SA --account-key "$KEY" -s $SHARE -o table
```

**Example: multiple shares in Bicep, one read-only**

```bicep
param storageAccountName string
@secure()
param storageAccountKey string                  // supplied from Key Vault in the parameter file

resource cg 'Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups@2023-05-01' = {
  name: 'cg-report-viewer'
  location: resourceGroup().location
  properties: {
    osType: 'Linux'
    restartPolicy: 'Always'
    containers: [
      {
        name: 'web'
        properties: {
          image: 'nginx:1.27-alpine'
          resources: { requests: { cpu: 1, memoryInGB: 1 } }
          ports: [ { port: 80 } ]
          volumeMounts: [
            { name: 'reports', mountPath: '/usr/share/nginx/html', readOnly: true }
            { name: 'config', mountPath: '/etc/app' }
          ]
        }
      }
    ]
    volumes: [
      {
        name: 'reports'
        azureFile: {
          shareName: 'reports'
          storageAccountName: storageAccountName
          storageAccountKey: storageAccountKey
          readOnly: true
        }
      }
      {
        name: 'config'
        azureFile: {
          shareName: 'config'
          storageAccountName: storageAccountName
          storageAccountKey: storageAccountKey
        }
      }
    ]
    ipAddress: { type: 'Public', ports: [ { port: 80, protocol: 'TCP' } ] }
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Azure Files gives ACI containers persistent, shareable storage that outlives the container group.
- Mounts are Linux-only, require the storage account key, and require the container to run as root.
- Shares can be mounted read-only and by several groups at once. Watch the storage firewall and port 445.
- For application data, accessing Blob Storage through the SDK with a managed identity is often the more secure choice.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Mount a file share into a container that appends a timestamp to `/mnt/data/log.txt` and exits. Run it three times (recreating the group each time) and confirm the file has three lines.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy a writer group (read-write mount) and a reader group running NGINX (read-only mount of the same share) so that files written by the job are served over HTTP.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your batch job needs to persist output files. Would you mount Azure Files or write to Blob Storage with the SDK?" *Hint:* key-based versus identity-based access, root requirement, how downstream consumers read the data, cost, and whether the app expects a POSIX-like filesystem.

<a id="44-azure-container-apps"></a>
### 4.4 Azure Container Apps

Azure Container Apps (ACA) runs containerized microservices and jobs on a serverless platform built on Kubernetes, KEDA, Envoy, and Dapr, without exposing the Kubernetes API. This section covers how apps are organized and versioned, how traffic reaches them, how they scale (to zero and back), how Dapr simplifies service-to-service communication, how to run jobs, and how to handle secrets and identity.

#### Environments and Revisions

Kubernetes gives you autoscaling, rolling updates, service discovery, and traffic splitting, but running a cluster means managing node pools, upgrades, networking add-ons, and YAML for dozens of object types. Many teams only need those *capabilities*, not the cluster. Container Apps provides them as a managed service, built around two concepts: the **environment** (where apps live) and the **revision** (which version of an app runs).

**Environments.** A Container Apps environment is a secure boundary around a group of apps and jobs. Apps in the same environment:

- Share a **virtual network** (either Azure-managed or your own subnet) and can call each other by app name.
- Write logs to the same **Log Analytics workspace** (or another configured destination).
- Share **Dapr components** and environment-level storage definitions.

Put apps that belong to one system (and one environment stage, such as `prod`) in one environment. Use separate environments to isolate systems or stages.

Environments use **workload profiles** that define the compute apps run on:

| Profile | Billing | Characteristics | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consumption | Per second of vCPU/memory used, with a monthly free grant; scale to zero | Serverless; up to 4 vCPU / 8 GiB per replica | Most APIs, workers, event-driven apps |
| Dedicated (D/E series, GPU) | Per node instance in the profile | Reserved VMs; larger replicas; predictable performance; network isolation | Steady heavy loads, memory-hungry or GPU workloads |

**Revisions.** A revision is an **immutable snapshot** of an app's container template: image, environment variables, resources, scale rules, volumes. Every change to the template creates a new revision. Changes to app-level configuration do not.

| Change | Scope | Creates a new revision? |
|---|---|---|
| Container image, command, env vars, CPU/memory, probes, volumes | Revision (`properties.template`) | Yes |
| Scale rules, min/max replicas, revision suffix | Revision (`properties.template`) | Yes |
| Secrets values, ingress settings, registry credentials, Dapr settings | Application (`properties.configuration`) | No (applies to all revisions) |
| Revision mode, traffic weights | Application | No |

Revision names follow `<app>--<suffix>` (the suffix is random unless you set `--revision-suffix`).

**Revision modes**

| Mode | Behavior | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Single (default) | A new revision receives 100% of traffic as soon as it is ready; the old one is deactivated | Simple rolling-style deployments |
| Multiple | Several revisions stay active; you control traffic weights and labels | Blue-green, canary, A/B testing |

**Labels** attach a stable name to a revision and give it its own URL (`<app>---<label>.<env-domain>`), so testers can reach the "green" version directly before it receives production traffic.

```text
  Environment "cae-shop-prod"   (shared VNet, Log Analytics, Dapr components)
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  |  App "orders-api"  (revision mode: multiple)                            |
  |    orders-api--v14  image 1.4.2  label: blue   <-- 90% of traffic       |
  |    orders-api--v15  image 1.5.0  label: green  <-- 10% of traffic       |
  |                                                                         |
  |  App "orders-worker"   (single mode)   orders-worker--k3x9 (100%)       |
  |  Job "nightly-export"                                                   |
  +------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Example: create an environment and an app, then do a canary release**

```bash
RG=rg-aca
ENV=cae-shop-prod
APP=orders-api

az extension add --name containerapp --upgrade
az provider register --namespace Microsoft.App

# Environment with the Consumption workload profile, logs to Log Analytics
az containerapp env create -g $RG -n $ENV -l westeurope \
  --enable-workload-profiles \
  --logs-workspace-id "$LAW_ID" --logs-workspace-key "$LAW_KEY"

# First revision, with a predictable name: orders-api--v14
az containerapp create -g $RG -n $APP --environment $ENV \
  --image crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.4.2-a1b2c3d \
  --registry-server crshop.azurecr.io --registry-identity "$ID_ORDERS" \
  --user-assigned "$ID_ORDERS" \
  --target-port 8080 --ingress external \
  --cpu 0.5 --memory 1Gi \
  --revision-suffix v14

# Switch to multiple revisions and deploy the new version without traffic
az containerapp revision set-mode -g $RG -n $APP --mode multiple
az containerapp update -g $RG -n $APP \
  --image crshop.azurecr.io/orders-api:1.5.0-d4e5f6a --revision-suffix v15
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g $RG -n $APP \
  --revision-weight $APP--v14=100 $APP--v15=0

# Label the new revision so testers can reach it at orders-api---green.<env-domain>
az containerapp revision label add -g $RG -n $APP --label green --revision $APP--v15
az containerapp revision label add -g $RG -n $APP --label blue  --revision $APP--v14

# Canary: 10% to green, then 100% once metrics look good
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g $RG -n $APP --label-weight blue=90 green=10
az containerapp ingress traffic set -g $RG -n $APP --label-weight blue=0 green=100

# Retire the old revision (rollback = shift traffic back before deactivating)
az containerapp revision list -g $RG -n $APP \
  --query "[].{name:name, active:properties.active, traffic:properties.trafficWeight, image:properties.template.containers[0].image}" -o table
az containerapp revision deactivate -g $RG -n $APP --revision $APP--v14
```

**Key takeaways**

- An environment is the boundary for networking, logging, and Dapr. Apps in it reach each other by name.
- Workload profiles choose between serverless Consumption compute and dedicated VM-backed compute.
- A revision is an immutable snapshot of the template. Template changes create revisions; configuration changes (secrets, ingress) do not.
- Single mode replaces revisions automatically. Multiple mode with traffic weights and labels enables blue-green and canary releases.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Deploy a public sample image to Container Apps, change one environment variable, and list revisions to confirm a new one was created. Then change an ingress setting and confirm no revision was created.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement a blue-green deployment with labels: deploy v2 at 0% traffic, test it via its label URL, switch 100% of traffic to it, and roll back to v1 with a single command.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you choose Container Apps over AKS, and what would make you move from Container Apps to AKS later?" *Hint:* operational overhead, access to the Kubernetes API and custom controllers, networking and node-level control, cost at steady high load, and team skills.

#### Ingress Configuration

A container listening on port 8080 is useless until requests can reach it. In Container Apps, you don't configure load balancers, TLS certificates, or reverse proxies yourself. You enable **ingress** on the app, and the platform's Envoy-based edge proxy handles routing, TLS termination, and traffic splitting between revisions.

The first decision is **who should be able to call the app**:

| Ingress setting | Reachable from | URL form | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disabled | Nobody (no inbound HTTP) | none | Background workers, queue processors |
| Internal | Other apps in the same environment (and the VNet, for VNet environments) | `https://<app>.internal.<env-domain>` or simply `http://<app>` | Backend services behind an API or gateway |
| External | The internet (or the VNet only, if the environment itself is internal) | `https://<app>.<env-domain>` | Public APIs, web front ends |

```text
  Internet
     |  https://orders-api.<unique>.westeurope.azurecontainerapps.io
     v
  +--------------------- Environment ---------------------------------+
  |  Envoy edge proxy: TLS termination, IP rules, CORS, traffic split |
  |      | 90%                         | 10%                          |
  |      v                             v                              |
  |  orders-api--v14 (:8080)      orders-api--v15 (:8080)             |
  |      |                                                            |
  |      |  http://inventory-api   (internal ingress, by app name)    |
  |      v                                                            |
  |  inventory-api (:8080)        orders-worker (ingress disabled)    |
  +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

**Main ingress settings**

| Setting | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `targetPort` | Port your container listens on |
| `transport` | `auto` (HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2), `http`, `http2` (gRPC), or `tcp` |
| `allowInsecure` | Default `false`: HTTP requests are redirected to HTTPS |
| `exposedPort` | For TCP ingress: port exposed by the environment |
| `traffic` | Revision/label weights (see previous topic) |
| `ipSecurityRestrictions` | Allow or deny rules by CIDR range |
| `corsPolicy` | Allowed origins, methods, headers for browser clients |
| `stickySessions.affinity` | `sticky` routes a client to the same replica (cookie based); only in single revision mode |
| `clientCertificateMode` | `ignore`, `accept`, or `require` for mutual TLS |
| `customDomains` | Your own hostnames with uploaded or free managed certificates |

Other behaviors to know:

- The proxy enforces a **request timeout** (a few minutes) on HTTP requests. Long-running work belongs in a queue processed by a worker or a job, not in an open HTTP request.
- Within the environment, apps can call each other by **app name** (`http://inventory-api`). The platform resolves the name and load-balances across replicas.
- An **internal environment** (deployed into your VNet with `--internal-only`) has no public endpoint at all. Even "external" apps are reachable only from the VNet, typically behind Application Gateway or Front Door.
- Your app should read the client's original details from the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` headers set by the proxy.

**Example: configure ingress on existing apps**

```bash
RG=rg-aca

# Public API: external, HTTPS only, restricted to the office range plus Front Door
az containerapp ingress enable -g $RG -n orders-api \
  --type external --target-port 8080 --transport auto
az containerapp ingress access-restriction set -g $RG -n orders-api \
  --rule-name office --ip-address 203.0.113.0/24 --action Allow \
  --description "Head office"
az containerapp ingress cors enable -g $RG -n orders-api \
  --allowed-origins https://shop.contoso.com --allowed-methods GET POST \
  --allowed-headers "*" --max-age 3600

# Backend: internal only, gRPC over HTTP/2
az containerapp ingress enable -g $RG -n inventory-api \
  --type internal --target-port 50051 --transport http2

# Custom domain with a free managed certificate (CNAME api.contoso.com -> app FQDN first)
az containerapp hostname add  -g $RG -n orders-api --hostname api.contoso.com
az containerapp hostname bind -g $RG -n orders-api --hostname api.contoso.com \
  --environment cae-shop-prod --validation-method CNAME

az containerapp show -g $RG -n orders-api --query properties.configuration.ingress.fqdn -o tsv
```

```yaml
# Same configuration as part of an app YAML (az containerapp update --yaml app.yaml)
properties:
  configuration:
    ingress:
      external: true
      targetPort: 8080
      transport: auto
      allowInsecure: false
      ipSecurityRestrictions:
        - name: office
          ipAddressRange: 203.0.113.0/24
          action: Allow
      corsPolicy:
        allowedOrigins: [ "https://shop.contoso.com" ]
        allowedMethods: [ "GET", "POST" ]
      traffic:
        - label: blue
          revisionName: orders-api--v14
          weight: 90
        - label: green
          revisionName: orders-api--v15
          weight: 10
```

**Key takeaways**

- Ingress is disabled, internal (environment only), or external (internet or VNet). Choose the narrowest one that works.
- The managed Envoy proxy handles TLS, HTTPS redirection, IP restrictions, CORS, sticky sessions, mTLS, and revision traffic splitting.
- Apps in the same environment call each other by name.
- Ingress settings are application-scoped and do not create new revisions.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Deploy two apps in one environment: a public front end and an internal back end. Verify the front end can call `http://<backend-name>` and that the back end's URL is not reachable from your browser.
