- Use the free tier for learning and reserved capacity for long-lived production workloads.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create one container with manual 400 RU/s and one with autoscale `Tmax` = 1,000. Use `az cosmosdb sql container throughput show` to compare the settings.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** A workload needs 10,000 RU/s for 6 hours per day and 1,000 RU/s otherwise. Estimate the daily RU/s-hours billed for manual (provisioned at peak) vs autoscale (`Tmax` 10,000), accounting for the 1.5x autoscale rate. Which is cheaper?
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you choose serverless Cosmos DB for a production workload, and what would make you move off it?" *Hint:* single region, no throughput SLA, cost at sustained high volume, need for multi-region or predictable latency.

#### Global Distribution

Users in Sydney querying a database in West Europe wait for light to cross the planet twice per request, about 250 to 300 ms round trip before any work is done. And if West Europe has an outage, every user worldwide is down. **Global distribution** solves both problems by keeping full replicas of your data in multiple Azure regions, each one serving local reads (and optionally writes), with automatic failover.

The analogy is a franchise restaurant chain with one recipe book. Every branch has a full copy, customers go to the nearest branch, and if one branch closes, the next nearest takes over. The hard part is keeping the copies in sync when the recipe changes, which is where consistency levels and conflict resolution come in.

**How it works**

- You add or remove regions on the account at any time, with no downtime and no code change. Data is replicated to every region.
- Each region holds at least four replicas within it (and across availability zones if zone redundancy is enabled).
- **Single-region write** (default): one region accepts writes, the others serve reads. Writes are replicated asynchronously (or synchronously for Strong consistency).
- **Multi-region writes**: every region accepts writes. Concurrent writes to the same item in different regions create **conflicts**, which are resolved by policy.
- **Failover**: with **service-managed failover** enabled, Cosmos DB promotes the next region in your priority list if the write region becomes unavailable. You can also trigger a manual failover (for example for DR drills).

```text
                      Single write region
   West Europe (write, priority 0)  ---- async ---->  North Europe (read, priority 1)
             |                                          |
             +------------------ async --------------->  East US (read, priority 2)

   App in Europe: writes -> West Europe, reads -> West Europe
   App in US:     writes -> West Europe, reads -> East US (local, ~ms)

                      Multi-region writes
   West Europe (read/write)  <==== bidirectional ====>  East US (read/write)
   Conflicts on the same item are resolved by Last Writer Wins (/_ts) or a custom policy
```

**Availability SLAs**

| Configuration | Read availability | Write availability |
|---|---|---|
| Single region, no zones | 99.99% | 99.99% |
| Single region with availability zones | 99.995% | 99.995% |
| Multi-region, single write region | 99.999% | 99.99% |
| Multi-region writes | 99.999% | 99.999% |

**Conflict resolution (multi-region writes)**

| Policy | How it works |
|---|---|
| Last Writer Wins (default) | The version with the highest value of a numeric path wins. Default path is `/_ts`; you can choose a custom numeric property such as `/version` |
| Custom | A merge stored procedure you write runs on conflict. If it is not registered or fails, conflicts go to the **conflicts feed** for your application to resolve |

Multi-region writes cannot be combined with Strong consistency, and they cost more (writes are billed in every write region). Choose them when you need write availability through a regional outage or low write latency on several continents, not by default.

**Example: a multi-region account and a region-aware client**

```bash
# Two regions, zone redundancy in the primary, automatic failover on
az cosmosdb create -n cosmos-shop-prod -g rg-data \
  --locations regionName=westeurope failoverPriority=0 isZoneRedundant=true \
  --locations regionName=northeurope failoverPriority=1 isZoneRedundant=true \
  --enable-automatic-failover true \
  --default-consistency-level Session

# Add a third region later (no downtime)
az cosmosdb update -n cosmos-shop-prod -g rg-data \
  --locations regionName=westeurope failoverPriority=0 isZoneRedundant=true \
  --locations regionName=northeurope failoverPriority=1 isZoneRedundant=true \
  --locations regionName=eastus failoverPriority=2 isZoneRedundant=false

# DR drill: make North Europe the write region
az cosmosdb failover-priority-change -n cosmos-shop-prod -g rg-data \
  --failover-policies northeurope=0 westeurope=1 eastus=2
```

```python
import os
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# Each deployment lists its nearest regions first; the SDK routes reads there
# and transparently moves to the next region if one becomes unavailable.
preferred = os.environ.get("COSMOS_PREFERRED_REGIONS", "West Europe,North Europe").split(",")

client = CosmosClient(
    "https://cosmos-shop-prod.documents.azure.com:443/",
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),
    preferred_locations=preferred,
    multiple_write_locations=True,   # only has an effect on multi-region-write accounts
)
```

Without `preferred_locations`, the SDK sends every request to the write region, so remote replicas would be paid for but never used for reads.

**Key takeaways**

- Regions can be added or removed at any time; every region holds a full replica.
- Single-region write is the default; multi-region writes give 99.999% write availability at higher cost and with conflict resolution.
- Service-managed failover promotes the next-priority region automatically if the write region fails.
- Configure preferred regions in the SDK so reads go to the nearest replica.
- Multi-region writes are incompatible with Strong consistency; conflicts are resolved by Last Writer Wins or a custom merge procedure.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a two-region account and use `az cosmosdb show --query "{write:writeLocations[].locationName, read:readLocations[].locationName}"` to see which region accepts writes.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run the Python client with `preferred_locations` set first to one region and then the other. Enable `logging_enable=True` on the client to log request URLs and confirm which regional endpoint served the reads, then trigger a failover priority change and observe the client's behavior.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Design a Cosmos DB deployment for a shopping cart used on three continents where users must never lose the ability to add items." *Hint:* multi-region writes, conflict policy for carts (merge vs last writer wins), consistency per region, partition key by user.

<a id="62-cosmos-db-data-modeling-and-development"></a>
### 6.2 Cosmos DB Data Modeling and Development

Cosmos DB rewards designs that match how the data is accessed and penalizes designs carried over unchanged from relational schemas. This section covers the decisions that set cost and performance for the life of a container (partition key, consistency, indexing, TTL) and the day-to-day code for reading, writing, and querying items.

#### Partition Key Design

The partition key is the most important decision you make for a Cosmos DB container. It decides how data and traffic spread across machines, which operations are cheap, and which are expensive. It is also permanent: you cannot change a container's partition key in place. Changing it means creating a new container and copying the data.

Picture a supermarket with many checkout lanes. If customers are assigned to lanes by the first letter of their surname, the lanes stay roughly balanced. If they are assigned by "what city do you live in", nearly everyone in a local store ends up in a single lane while the others sit idle. A good partition key is the surname rule: many distinct values, spread evenly, so every lane (physical partition) shares the work.

**What makes a good partition key**

1. **High cardinality**: many distinct values (thousands or more), so data can spread across many physical partitions.
2. **Even distribution of storage**: no single value accumulates close to the 20 GB logical partition limit.
3. **Even distribution of requests**: no single value receives a disproportionate share of reads or writes (a "hot partition").
4. **Present in your most frequent queries**: queries that filter on the partition key go to one partition. Queries without it fan out to all partitions, costing more RUs and latency as the container grows.
5. **Transaction scope**: stored procedures, triggers, and transactional batches work only within one logical partition. Items that must change together atomically need the same key.

**Good and bad choices**

| Scenario | Candidate key | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Orders, mostly read per customer | `/customerId` | Good: high cardinality, matches "my orders" queries |
| Orders | `/status` | Bad: a handful of values, "pending" becomes a hot partition |
| IoT readings, millions per day | `/deviceId` | Good for reads per device, but a chatty device can exceed 20 GB over time |
| IoT readings | `/deviceId` + `/yyyyMM` (hierarchical) | Better: bounded logical partitions, still efficient per-device queries |
| Multi-tenant SaaS | `/tenantId` | Risky: a single large tenant can exceed limits or be hot |
| Multi-tenant SaaS | `/tenantId`, `/userId` (hierarchical) | Good: tenant queries target a subset of partitions, large tenants spread out |
| Write-heavy log, no natural key | `/id` | Good for writes and point reads; every non-ID query fans out |
| Orders | `/orderDate` (day) | Bad: all writes for today land in one partition |

**Synthetic keys.** When no single property is good enough, combine properties into one value, or add a random suffix to spread writes:

```python
# Concatenate properties to raise cardinality
order["pk"] = f"{order['tenantId']}-{order['customerId']}"

# Suffix to spread a write-hot key over 10 values; readers must query all 10
order["pk"] = f"{order['date']}-{random.randint(0, 9)}"
```

**Hierarchical partition keys** (NoSQL API) let you specify up to three levels, such as `/tenantId`, `/userId`, `/sessionId`. Data is distributed using the full path, so a large tenant can span many physical partitions, while queries that supply only `tenantId` (a prefix) are still routed to just the partitions that hold that tenant instead of all of them.

```text
Single key /tenantId:               Hierarchical /tenantId -> /userId:
  tenant "contoso" (huge) -> P1       contoso/u1, contoso/u2 -> P1
  everyone else          -> P2..Pn    contoso/u3, contoso/u4 -> P2
  P1 throttled, limited to 20 GB      contoso/u5 ...         -> P3
                                       query WHERE tenantId='contoso' -> P1..P3 only
```

**Model for your access patterns.** Relational design normalizes first and writes queries later. Cosmos DB design starts from the list of queries and their frequency. Common techniques:

- **Embed** data that is read together and bounded in size (order lines inside the order).
- **Reference** data that is unbounded or changes independently (product details referenced by `productId`).
- **Denormalize** frequently read values (copy the customer name into the order) and keep copies in sync with the change feed (see 6.3).
- **Co-locate** different item types in one container with the same partition key (a customer and their orders both keyed on `customerId`), distinguished by a `type` property.

**Example: a container with a hierarchical partition key**

```bicep
resource sessions 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/sqlDatabases/containers@2024-05-15' = {
  parent: shopDb
  name: 'sessions'
  properties: {
    resource: {
      id: 'sessions'
      partitionKey: {
        paths: [ '/tenantId', '/userId' ]   // up to three levels
        kind: 'MultiHash'                   // hierarchical partition key
        version: 2
      }
    }
    options: { autoscaleSettings: { maxThroughput: 4000 } }
  }
}
```

```python
container = db.get_container_client("sessions")

container.upsert_item({
    "id": "s-9001",
    "tenantId": "contoso",
    "userId": "u-17",
    "startedAt": "2026-10-21T09:00:00Z",
})

# Point read needs the FULL hierarchical key, as a list
item = container.read_item(item="s-9001", partition_key=["contoso", "u-17"])

# Prefix query: targets only the partitions holding "contoso"
for s in container.query_items(
    "SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.tenantId = @t",
    parameters=[{"name": "@t", "value": "contoso"}],
    partition_key=["contoso"],                # prefix of the hierarchical key
):
    print(s["id"])
```

**Detecting a bad key.** In Azure Monitor, the **Normalized RU Consumption** metric split by `PartitionKeyRangeId` shows whether one physical partition sits at 100% while others are low. The Insights blade also lists the top logical partition keys by storage.

**Key takeaways**

- The partition key controls distribution, query cost, and transaction scope, and it cannot be changed in place.
- Choose high cardinality, even storage, even request distribution, and a property used in most queries.
- Avoid low-cardinality or time-based keys that concentrate writes.
- Use synthetic or hierarchical keys when no single property works; hierarchical keys allow efficient prefix queries.
- Model from access patterns: embed what is read together, reference what grows without bound.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For a blog platform with posts, comments, and likes, propose a partition key for each entity and justify it against the five criteria.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Load 100,000 synthetic orders into two containers, one keyed on `/status` and one on `/customerId`. Run the same per-customer query against both and compare RU charge and latency, then view the per-partition RU metric.
> 3. **(Interview)** "You chose `/tenantId` for a SaaS product and one customer has grown to 18 GB. What are your options?" *Hint:* hierarchical partition keys, migration to a new container with the change feed or container copy jobs, dedicated containers for large tenants.

#### Consistency Levels

When data is replicated, a read may land on a replica that has not received the latest write yet. Distributed databases traditionally offered only two options: **strong** consistency (every read sees the latest write, but writes are slow and availability suffers during network partitions) or **eventual** consistency (fast and available, but reads may be stale or out of order). Most applications need something in between, so Cosmos DB offers **five well-defined levels**, each a precise trade-off between consistency, latency, availability, and throughput.

An analogy is a live sports score. Strong is watching the match in the stadium. Bounded staleness is a TV broadcast with a guaranteed maximum delay. Session is your own phone app, which always shows the goals you yourself reported. Consistent prefix is a newspaper that may be late but never reports the final score before the first goal. Eventual is gossip: you will hear the result eventually, but possibly in the wrong order.

**The five levels, strongest to weakest**

```text
 Stronger consistency                                         Higher availability,
 higher latency, 2x read RU                                   lower latency, throughput
 <------------------------------------------------------------------------------------>
   Strong   |  Bounded staleness  |   Session   |  Consistent prefix  |   Eventual
```

| Level | Guarantee | Read cost | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strong** | Linearizable: every read returns the latest committed write | 2x | Financial balances, inventory counts that must never oversell (single write region only) |
| **Bounded staleness** | Reads lag writes by at most K versions or T time, whichever comes first; order is preserved | 2x | Near-strong reads across regions with a known maximum lag |
| **Session** (default) | Within a client session: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes. Others see consistent prefix | 1x | Most user-facing apps: a user always sees their own changes |
| **Consistent prefix** | Reads never see writes out of order, but may lag | 1x | Activity feeds, scores where order matters more than freshness |
| **Eventual** | No ordering guarantee; replicas converge eventually | 1x | Counts of likes, non-critical telemetry, analytics |

**How Session consistency works.** Each write response includes a **session token** describing the version the writer has seen. The SDK attaches that token to subsequent reads, and a replica that is behind it waits or forwards the request until it catches up. The SDK manages tokens automatically **within one client instance**. If a user's write is handled by one app instance and the next read by another (load-balanced web farm), pass the token yourself, for example in a cookie or header, or the read may not see the write.

**Bounded staleness limits.** For single-region accounts the minimum is K = 10 writes and T = 5 seconds. For multi-region accounts the minimum is K = 100,000 writes and T = 300 seconds.

**Account default vs request override.** The default is set on the account. Clients may **relax** consistency per client or per request (for example, read at Eventual from a Session account to save latency), but they can never request a **stronger** level than the account default.

**Constraints to remember**

- Strong consistency is not available with multi-region writes, and with regions far apart it increases write latency because writes must commit in every region.
- Strong and Bounded staleness reads cost twice the RUs of the other levels.
- Most applications (more than three-quarters of Cosmos DB accounts) use Session.

**Example: setting the default and relaxing per client**

```bash
az cosmosdb update -n cosmos-shop-prod -g rg-data --default-consistency-level Session

# Bounded staleness with explicit bounds (multi-region minimums)
az cosmosdb update -n cosmos-shop-prod -g rg-data \
  --default-consistency-level BoundedStaleness \
  --max-staleness-prefix 100000 --max-interval 300
```

```python
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient

# A reporting service that tolerates stale data: relax to Eventual for this client
reporting_client = CosmosClient(ENDPOINT, credential=cred, consistency_level="Eventual")

# Session token hand-off between two app instances (web farm)
orders = client.get_database_client("shop").get_container_client("orders")
orders.upsert_item({"id": "o-7", "customerId": "c-42", "status": "paid"})
token = orders.client_connection.last_response_headers["x-ms-session-token"]
# ... return token to the browser (cookie/header), receive it on the next request ...
order = orders.read_item(item="o-7", partition_key="c-42", session_token=token)
```

Per-request override in .NET:

```csharp
ItemResponse<Order> response = await container.ReadItemAsync<Order>(
    "o-7", new PartitionKey("c-42"),
    new ItemRequestOptions { ConsistencyLevel = ConsistencyLevel.Eventual }); // weaker only
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cosmos DB offers five levels: Strong, Bounded staleness, Session, Consistent prefix, Eventual.
- Session is the default and the right choice for most apps: users read their own writes.
- Strong and Bounded staleness double read RU cost; Strong is incompatible with multi-region writes.
- Clients can relax consistency per client or per request but never strengthen it beyond the account default.
- Session guarantees are tied to session tokens; pass them explicitly when requests hop between instances.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Match each level to a scenario: bank transfer, social media like counter, user profile edit, chat message history, stock ticker with a 5-second tolerance.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Read the same item 100 times at Session and then with a client configured for Eventual, logging RU charge and latency. Then switch the account to Strong and repeat. Tabulate the results.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A user updates their profile and immediately reloads the page, but sees the old data, even though the account uses Session consistency. Why?" *Hint:* which client instance served each request, and where the session token lives.

#### CRUD Operations with SDK

Every application ultimately creates, reads, updates, and deletes items. The Cosmos DB SDKs make this look simple, but each call has cost and correctness implications: point reads are far cheaper than queries, updates can silently overwrite another user's change, and creating a new client per request destroys performance. This topic covers the operations and the patterns that make them production-ready.

**The client.** `CosmosClient` holds connection pools, region metadata, and partition maps. It is thread-safe and expensive to create. **Create one per application process and reuse it** (singleton, dependency injection, or module-level variable). Creating a client per request causes high latency and socket exhaustion.

**Operation overview (Python `azure-cosmos` v4)**

| Operation | Method | Behavior | Typical cost (1 KB) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Create | `create_item(body)` | Fails with 409 Conflict if `id` + partition key already exists | ~6 RU |
| Read | `read_item(item, partition_key)` | Point read; 404 if missing | ~1 RU |
| Replace | `replace_item(item, body)` | Fails with 404 if missing | ~10 RU |
| Upsert | `upsert_item(body)` | Create or replace | ~6 to 10 RU |
| Patch | `patch_item(item, partition_key, patch_operations)` | Partial update, up to 10 operations, server-side | ~10 RU, less network |
| Delete | `delete_item(item, partition_key)` | 404 if missing | ~5 RU |

**Optimistic concurrency with ETags.** Two users load the same item, both edit it, both save. Without protection, the second save silently erases the first ("lost update"). Every item has an `_etag` that changes on every write. Send it with your replace, and Cosmos DB rejects the write with **412 Precondition Failed** if someone else changed the item in the meantime.

```text
User A: read (etag=1) ---------- replace(if etag=1) -> OK, etag=2
User B:    read (etag=1) ------------------------- replace(if etag=1) -> 412, reload and retry
```

**Example: a complete repository**

```python
import uuid
from azure.core import MatchConditions
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient, exceptions
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

# Module-level singleton: created once per process
_client = CosmosClient(
    "https://cosmos-shop-dev.documents.azure.com:443/",
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),
)
orders = _client.get_database_client("shop").get_container_client("orders")


def create_order(customer_id: str, lines: list[dict]) -> dict:
    order = {
        "id": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "customerId": customer_id,                  # partition key
        "type": "order",
        "status": "new",
        "lines": lines,                              # embedded: always read with the order
        "total": sum(l["qty"] * l["price"] for l in lines),
    }
    return orders.create_item(body=order)           # returns the item incl. _etag, _ts


def get_order(customer_id: str, order_id: str) -> dict | None:
    try:
        return orders.read_item(item=order_id, partition_key=customer_id)
    except exceptions.CosmosResourceNotFoundError:   # 404
        return None


def update_status(customer_id: str, order_id: str, new_status: str) -> dict:
    while True:
        order = orders.read_item(item=order_id, partition_key=customer_id)
        order["status"] = new_status
        try:
            return orders.replace_item(
                item=order_id,
                body=order,
                etag=order["_etag"],                          # only if unchanged since read
                match_condition=MatchConditions.IfNotModified,
            )
        except exceptions.CosmosAccessConditionFailedError:  # 412: someone else won; retry
            continue


def add_loyalty_points(customer_id: str, order_id: str, points: int) -> dict:
    # Patch: atomic server-side change, no read-modify-write round trip
    return orders.patch_item(
        item=order_id,
        partition_key=customer_id,
        patch_operations=[
            {"op": "incr", "path": "/loyaltyPoints", "value": points},
            {"op": "set", "path": "/updatedBy", "value": "loyalty-service"},
        ],
    )


def delete_order(customer_id: str, order_id: str) -> None:
    orders.delete_item(item=order_id, partition_key=customer_id)
```

Patch operations are `add`, `set`, `replace`, `remove`, `incr`, and `move`. A patch can include a **filter predicate** (`filter_predicate="FROM c WHERE c.status = 'new'"`) so it applies only if a condition holds, which is a lightweight alternative to an ETag check.

**Common exceptions**

| Status | Python exception | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 404 | `CosmosResourceNotFoundError` | Item (or container) does not exist |
| 409 | `CosmosResourceExistsError` | `create_item` with an existing `id` in that partition |
| 412 | `CosmosAccessConditionFailedError` | ETag mismatch |
| 413 | `CosmosHttpResponseError` | Item larger than 2 MB |
| 429 | `CosmosHttpResponseError` | Throttled after SDK retries were exhausted |

**Bulk operations.** For large imports, the .NET SDK has `AllowBulkExecution = true`, which groups concurrent operations by partition into batches. In Python, run operations concurrently with the async client (`azure.cosmos.aio`) and a bounded semaphore, or use transactional batches per partition (see 6.3).

**Key takeaways**

- Use one `CosmosClient` per process; it is thread-safe and expensive to create.
- Prefer point reads (`id` + partition key) over queries; they are the cheapest operation.
- Use ETags with `IfNotModified` to prevent lost updates, and retry on 412.
- Use patch for partial, atomic, server-side updates such as counters.
- Handle 404, 409, 412, and 429 explicitly in application code.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Implement the repository above, create an order, read it, patch it, and delete it. Print the RU charge after each operation.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Simulate a lost update: start two threads that read the same order and each replace the status. Show that without an ETag one change is lost, and with an ETag the loser receives 412 and retries correctly.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why is `SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = 'x'` worse than `read_item('x', pk)` even though it returns the same document?" *Hint:* query engine overhead, RU charge, fan-out when the partition key is unknown.

#### SQL Query Syntax

Point reads cover lookups by key, but applications also need "all open orders for this customer, newest first" or "the top ten products in a category". The NoSQL API uses a **SQL dialect designed for JSON**. It looks familiar to anyone who knows SQL, but it operates on hierarchical documents rather than flat tables, so a few concepts (aliases, `VALUE`, intra-document `JOIN`, array functions) work differently.

**Basic structure**

```sql
SELECT [TOP n] [DISTINCT] [VALUE] <projection>
FROM <container alias> [JOIN <alias> IN <alias.array>]
[WHERE <filter>]
[GROUP BY <expression>]
[ORDER BY <expression> [ASC|DESC]]
[OFFSET n LIMIT m]
```

`FROM c` names the container's documents with an alias (`c` is just a convention). There are no joins between containers or between documents: each query runs over one container, and `JOIN` only expands arrays **inside** a single document.

Assume order documents like this:

```json
{
  "id": "o-1001",
  "customerId": "c-42",
  "status": "shipped",
  "orderDate": "2026-10-01T10:15:00Z",
  "total": 149.90,
  "shipping": { "country": "IT", "city": "Milan" },
  "lines": [
    { "sku": "KB-01", "qty": 1, "price": 99.90, "tags": ["keyboard", "wireless"] },
    { "sku": "MS-02", "qty": 2, "price": 25.00, "tags": ["mouse"] }
  ]
}
```

**Example queries**

```sql
-- Projection with nested properties and renaming
SELECT c.id, c.total, c.shipping.city AS city
FROM c
WHERE c.customerId = 'c-42' AND c.status = 'shipped'
ORDER BY c.orderDate DESC

-- VALUE returns bare values instead of objects: ["o-1001", "o-1002"]
SELECT VALUE c.id FROM c WHERE c.total > 100

-- Intra-document JOIN: one result row per order line
SELECT c.id AS orderId, l.sku, l.qty * l.price AS lineTotal
FROM c
JOIN l IN c.lines
WHERE l.qty > 1

-- Array helpers: orders containing a given SKU
SELECT c.id FROM c
WHERE ARRAY_CONTAINS(c.lines, { "sku": "KB-01" }, true)   -- true = partial match

-- Correlated subquery with EXISTS: orders with any wireless item
SELECT c.id FROM c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT VALUE t FROM l IN c.lines JOIN t IN l.tags WHERE t = 'wireless')

-- Aggregates and grouping
SELECT c.shipping.country AS country, COUNT(1) AS orders, SUM(c.total) AS revenue
FROM c
GROUP BY c.shipping.country

-- Missing vs null: IS_DEFINED distinguishes "no property" from "property = null"
SELECT * FROM c WHERE NOT IS_DEFINED(c.discountCode)

-- String and date functions
SELECT * FROM c
WHERE STARTSWITH(c.shipping.city, 'Mil', true)              -- true = case-insensitive
  AND c.orderDate >= DateTimeAdd('dd', -30, GetCurrentDateTime())

-- Paging (simple but expensive for deep pages)
SELECT * FROM c ORDER BY c.orderDate DESC OFFSET 40 LIMIT 20
```

**Differences from relational SQL**

| Relational SQL | Cosmos DB NoSQL |
|---|---|
| `SELECT *` returns columns | `SELECT *` returns whole JSON documents, including system properties |
| `JOIN` across tables | `JOIN` only expands arrays within one document |
| `NULL` | Both `null` and *undefined* (property absent) exist; comparisons with undefined drop the item |
| Schema enforces types | Values may have different types across documents; comparisons use type ordering |
| `ORDER BY` on any column | `ORDER BY` needs an index; multi-property `ORDER BY` needs a composite index |

**Query execution and cost.** A query that includes an equality filter on the partition key runs on **one partition**. Without it, the SDK fans out to every physical partition and merges the results. Results are returned in **pages**, each with a **continuation token**. For APIs that show "page 3 of results", use continuation tokens rather than `OFFSET`, because `OFFSET` still reads and discards all skipped items (and pays for them).

**Example: parameterized, paged queries in Python**

```python
def list_orders(customer_id: str, page_size: int = 20, continuation: str | None = None):
    query = (
        "SELECT c.id, c.status, c.total, c.orderDate FROM c "
        "WHERE c.customerId = @cid AND c.type = 'order' "
        "ORDER BY c.orderDate DESC"
    )
    pager = orders.query_items(
        query=query,
        parameters=[{"name": "@cid", "value": customer_id}],  # never build SQL by concatenation
        partition_key=customer_id,                              # single-partition query
        max_item_count=page_size,                               # page size
    ).by_page(continuation)                                     # resume from token (or None)

    page = next(pager)                     # one round trip
    items = list(page)
    next_token = pager.continuation_token  # None when there are no more pages
    return items, next_token


items, token = list_orders("c-42")
more, token = list_orders("c-42", continuation=token)   # the client sends the token back
```

**Key takeaways**

- The NoSQL API uses SQL over JSON: `FROM c` aliases documents, `VALUE` returns raw values, `JOIN` expands arrays inside one document.
- There are no cross-document or cross-container joins; model data to avoid needing them.
- Include the partition key in filters to keep queries single-partition and cheap.
- Use parameterized queries for safety and plan reuse.
- Page with continuation tokens rather than `OFFSET` for large result sets.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write queries that return (a) the IDs of all orders over 100, (b) the city of each shipped order, and (c) the number of orders per status.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write a query that returns every SKU sold to customer `c-42` with the total quantity per SKU. Compare the RU charge with and without the partition key filter.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you implement 'show orders with their customer's name' in Cosmos DB, since there are no joins across documents?" *Hint:* denormalization, co-locating customer and orders in one partition, change-feed-driven updates of copies.

#### Indexing Policies

Relational databases index nothing by default, and you add indexes as queries get slow. Cosmos DB takes the opposite approach: **every property of every item is indexed automatically**. That makes ad hoc queries fast from day one, which is essential when documents have no fixed schema. The cost is paid on writes: every indexed property adds RUs to inserts and updates. An **indexing policy** lets you tune that trade-off per container.

Think of a book's index. An index entry for every word in the book makes any lookup fast, but the index becomes enormous and every edit to the text requires updating it. A good index lists only the terms readers actually look up.

**Default policy**

```json
{
  "indexingMode": "consistent",
  "automatic": true,
  "includedPaths": [ { "path": "/*" } ],
  "excludedPaths": [ { "path": "/\"_etag\"/?" } ]
}
```

**Policy elements**

| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `indexingMode` | `consistent` (index updated synchronously with writes) or `none` (no index; point reads only, useful for pure key-value or during bulk loads) |
| `includedPaths` / `excludedPaths` | Which JSON paths are indexed. The more specific path wins |
| `compositeIndexes` | Multi-property indexes for `ORDER BY` on several properties and for filters combined with sorts |
| `spatialIndexes` | Geospatial queries (`ST_DISTANCE`, `ST_WITHIN`) on GeoJSON |
| `vectorIndexes` | Vector similarity search (`VectorDistance`) with `flat`, `quantizedFlat`, or `diskANN` |
| Full-text indexes | `FullTextContains` and BM25 ranking on text properties |

**Path syntax**

| Path | Matches |
|---|---|
| `/*` | Every property in the document |
| `/status/?` | The scalar value at `status` |
| `/shipping/*` | Everything under `shipping` |
| `/lines/[]/sku/?` | `sku` in every element of the `lines` array |

**Two strategies**

- **Opt-out** (default): include `/*`, exclude large or never-queried paths (long descriptions, blobs of JSON, embeddings you search with a vector index). Safe for evolving schemas.
- **Opt-in**: exclude `/*`, include only the paths you query. Cheapest writes, but new query patterns are slow until you add the path.

**Composite indexes.** A query like `ORDER BY c.status ASC, c.orderDate DESC` fails without a composite index on exactly those properties and directions (or their exact reverse). Composite indexes also cut the cost of queries that filter on one property and sort on another.

**Example: a tuned policy for the orders container**

```json
{
  "indexingMode": "consistent",
  "includedPaths": [
    { "path": "/customerId/?" },
    { "path": "/status/?" },
    { "path": "/orderDate/?" },
    { "path": "/total/?" },
    { "path": "/lines/[]/sku/?" }
  ],
  "excludedPaths": [
    { "path": "/*" },
    { "path": "/\"_etag\"/?" }
  ],
  "compositeIndexes": [
    [
      { "path": "/status",    "order": "ascending" },
      { "path": "/orderDate", "order": "descending" }
    ],
    [
      { "path": "/customerId", "order": "ascending" },
      { "path": "/orderDate",  "order": "descending" }
    ]
  ]
}
```

```bash
# Apply it; the index is rebuilt online in the background using spare RUs
az cosmosdb sql container update -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data -d shop -n orders \
  --idx @orders-index-policy.json

# Inspect the policy now in effect
az cosmosdb sql container show -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data -d shop -n orders \
  --query "resource.indexingPolicy"
```

Transformation progress is reported as a percentage in the `x-ms-documentdb-collection-index-transformation-progress` header when you read the container with quota info. While a transformation is running, queries may return incomplete results for newly included paths until it finishes. Plan policy changes outside peak hours.

**Measuring the impact.** Ask the service which indexes a query used and which would have helped:

```python
results = list(orders.query_items(
    "SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.status = 'shipped' ORDER BY c.orderDate DESC",
    enable_cross_partition_query=True,
    populate_index_metrics=True,         # adds the x-ms-cosmos-index-utilization header
))
print(orders.client_connection.last_response_headers.get("x-ms-cosmos-index-utilization"))
# JSON (base64-encoded in some SDK versions) listing utilized single/composite
# indexes and "potential" indexes worth adding
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cosmos DB indexes every path by default; this favors reads and flexible schemas at the expense of write RUs.
- Exclude paths you never query (opt-out) or include only queried paths (opt-in) to cut write cost.
- Multi-property `ORDER BY` requires a composite index; composite indexes also speed filter-plus-sort queries.
- Policy changes are applied online in the background; results for new paths may be incomplete until done.
- Use index metrics to find missing or unused indexes.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Insert an item with 50 properties into a container with the default policy, note the write RU charge, then switch to an opt-in policy with three paths and insert again. Compare.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run `SELECT * FROM c ORDER BY c.status, c.orderDate DESC`. Read the error, add the composite index, rerun, and compare RU charges with index metrics enabled.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you set `indexingMode` to `none`?" *Hint:* pure key-value access by ID, temporary bulk loads, and what happens to queries in that mode.

#### Time-To-Live

Much data has a natural shelf life: shopping carts abandoned after 30 days, sessions after an hour of inactivity, telemetry after 90 days, one-time verification codes after ten minutes. Deleting it yourself means scheduled jobs that query for old items and delete them, which costs RUs, code, and monitoring. **Time-to-live (TTL)** makes Cosmos DB delete expired items automatically in the background.

It works like the "best before" date on groceries, with a fridge that throws out expired items by itself.

**How TTL is configured**

TTL is set at two levels, in **seconds**, measured from the item's last modification time (`_ts`):

| Container `defaultTtl` | Item `ttl` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Not set (off) | Any value | Items never expire; item `ttl` is ignored |
| `-1` (on, no default) | Not set | Item never expires |
| `-1` | `3600` | Item expires 1 hour after its last write |
| `86400` | Not set | Item expires 1 day after its last write |
| `86400` | `-1` | Item never expires (override) |
| `86400` | `600` | Item expires 10 minutes after its last write (override) |

Every write to an item resets its clock, because expiry is relative to `_ts`. That makes "sliding expiration" free: touching a session item extends its life.

**Deletion behavior**

- Expired items **disappear from reads and queries immediately**, even if the physical delete has not happened yet.
- Physical deletion runs in the background using **leftover provisioned RUs**, so it never competes with your requests. On a container at 100% utilization, deletes are delayed (but expired items are still invisible).
- TTL deletes do not appear in the change feed in latest-version mode. If downstream systems must learn about deletions, use the **soft-delete pattern**: mark the item as deleted (which appears in the change feed), and set a short `ttl` on it at the same time.

```text
t=0     write item (ttl=60)        _ts = 0
t=30    patch item                 _ts = 30  -> clock restarts
t=89    read item                  returned
t=91    read item                  404 (expired, invisible)
t=95    background purge           physically removed when spare RUs are available
```

**Example: carts that expire 30 days after last activity, verification codes after 10 minutes**

```bash
# Turn TTL on with a 30-day default for the carts container
az cosmosdb sql container update -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data -d shop -n carts --ttl 2592000

# Turn TTL on without a default (only items with a ttl property expire)
az cosmosdb sql container update -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data -d shop -n codes --ttl -1
```

```python
carts = db.get_container_client("carts")
codes = db.get_container_client("codes")

# Inherits the 30-day default; each update restarts the clock (sliding expiration)
carts.upsert_item({"id": "cart-u17", "userId": "u-17", "items": [{"sku": "KB-01", "qty": 1}]})

# A VIP cart that should never expire
carts.upsert_item({"id": "cart-u99", "userId": "u-99", "items": [], "ttl": -1})

# A one-time code that expires after 10 minutes
codes.create_item({"id": "123456", "email": "ana@example.com", "ttl": 600})

# Soft delete: downstream change-feed consumers see the "deleted" flag,
# then the item vanishes 60 seconds later on its own
def soft_delete_cart(user_id: str) -> None:
    carts.patch_item(
        item=f"cart-{user_id}",
        partition_key=user_id,
        patch_operations=[
            {"op": "set", "path": "/isDeleted", "value": True},
            {"op": "set", "path": "/ttl", "value": 60},
        ],
    )
```

**Key takeaways**

- TTL deletes items automatically a set number of seconds after their last write.
- The container `defaultTtl` must be set (to `-1` or a positive value) for item-level `ttl` to take effect.
- Item `ttl` overrides the default; `-1` means never expire.
- Expired items are invisible immediately; physical deletion uses spare RUs in the background.
- TTL deletes are not in the latest-version change feed; use a soft-delete flag plus a short TTL when consumers need to know.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Enable TTL with `--ttl -1` on a container, insert one item with `"ttl": 30` and one without. Read both after 40 seconds and explain the results.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement a session store where each request patches `lastSeen` so sessions expire after 20 minutes of inactivity. Verify that an active session survives longer than 20 minutes.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An analytics pipeline built on the change feed never learns that old orders were purged by TTL. How do you fix it?" *Hint:* soft delete with a short TTL, or all versions and deletes change feed mode.

<a id="63-cosmos-db-server-side-and-change-processing"></a>
### 6.3 Cosmos DB Server-Side and Change Processing

Most Cosmos DB logic runs in your application, but two problems need more: changing several items atomically, and reacting to changes as they happen. This section covers the server-side JavaScript programming model (stored procedures, triggers, UDFs), the SDK-based transactional batch, and the change feed, which is the basis for event-driven architectures on Cosmos DB.

#### Stored Procedures

In a distributed database, multi-item transactions are expensive because the items may live on different machines. Cosmos DB makes a deliberate compromise: transactions are fully ACID, but only **within a single logical partition**, since all its items live on the same physical replica set. **Stored procedures** are one way to run such a transaction: JavaScript functions registered on a container and executed inside the database engine, next to the data.

The analogy is a bank teller working behind the counter. Instead of you shuttling back and forth with slips (one network round trip per operation), you hand over a single instruction ("move 50 from savings to checking") and the teller does all the steps in the vault. Either all of it happens or none of it does.

**Execution model**

- Written in JavaScript (ECMAScript 2015), registered per container, NoSQL API only.
- Every execution is scoped to **one partition key value**, supplied by the caller.
- The whole procedure is one **ACID transaction** with snapshot isolation. If the script throws, every write it made is rolled back.
- Execution is **bounded**: a procedure has a limited time and RU budget (about 5 seconds). Each operation such as `createDocument` returns `false` when the procedure is close to its limit and the request was not accepted. Well-written procedures check that value and return a **continuation** so the client can call them again for the rest of the work.
- Operations are **asynchronous with callbacks**: you get the collection object with `getContext().getCollection()` and pass callbacks to its methods.

```text
Client                       Cosmos DB (partition "c-42")
  | execute sproc(pk=c-42, params)  |
  |-------------------------------->| begin transaction
  |                                 |  createDocument(...)  ok
  |                                 |  replaceDocument(...) ok
  |                                 |  throw new Error(...)  -> rollback all
  |<--------------------------------| response body or error
```

**When to use them (and when not)**

| Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|
| Atomic multi-item update in one partition with conditional logic | Simple single-item operations (use the SDK) |
| Bulk inserts into one partition with fewer round trips | Cross-partition work (not supported) |
| Logic that must read and decide inside the same transaction | Heavy computation (bounded execution, and harder to test and version) |

For many atomic multi-item writes, **transactional batch** (later in this section) is simpler, because it is expressed in your application language. Choose a stored procedure when the transaction needs logic that depends on data read during the transaction.

**Example: an atomic "place order and reserve stock" procedure**

The customer document and their order live in the same partition (`/customerId`), so one procedure can update both atomically.

```javascript
// placeOrder.js: registered on container "customers" (partition key /customerId)
function placeOrder(customerId, order) {
    var collection = getContext().getCollection();
    var response = getContext().getResponse();
    var link = collection.getSelfLink();

    // 1) Read the customer document in this partition
    var query = {
        query: "SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.id = @id AND c.type = 'customer'",
        parameters: [{ name: "@id", value: customerId }]
    };
    var accepted = collection.queryDocuments(link, query, {}, function (err, docs) {
        if (err) throw err;
        if (docs.length !== 1) throw new Error("Customer not found");

        var customer = docs[0];
        if (customer.creditLimit < customer.openBalance + order.total) {
            throw new Error("Credit limit exceeded");     // throwing rolls back everything
        }

        // 2) Update the balance with an ETag check inside the transaction
        customer.openBalance += order.total;
        collection.replaceDocument(customer._self, customer, { etag: customer._etag },
            function (err) {
                if (err) throw err;

                // 3) Create the order in the same partition
                order.type = "order";
                order.customerId = customerId;
                collection.createDocument(link, order, function (err, created) {
                    if (err) throw err;
                    response.setBody({ orderId: created.id, newBalance: customer.openBalance });
                });
            });
    });

    if (!accepted) throw new Error("Query not accepted; retry");
}
```

**Example: a bounded bulk import with continuation**

```javascript
// bulkImport.js: inserts as many items as the time budget allows, returns how many
function bulkImport(items) {
    var collection = getContext().getCollection();
    var link = collection.getSelfLink();
    var count = 0;

    if (!items || items.length === 0) { getContext().getResponse().setBody(0); return; }
    tryCreate(items[count], callback);

    function tryCreate(item, cb) {
        var accepted = collection.createDocument(link, item, cb);
        // false = budget nearly exhausted; stop and tell the client how far we got
        if (!accepted) getContext().getResponse().setBody(count);
    }

    function callback(err) {
        if (err) throw err;
        count++;
        if (count >= items.length) getContext().getResponse().setBody(count);
        else tryCreate(items[count], callback);
    }
}
```

**Registering and calling from Python**

```python
from pathlib import Path

customers = db.get_container_client("customers")

customers.scripts.create_stored_procedure(body={
    "id": "bulkImport",
    "body": Path("bulkImport.js").read_text(),
})

batch = [{"id": f"n-{i}", "customerId": "c-42", "type": "note", "text": "..."} for i in range(500)]
done = 0
while done < len(batch):
    # params is the list of arguments; the sproc receives one array argument
    inserted = customers.scripts.execute_stored_procedure(
        sproc="bulkImport",
        partition_key="c-42",          # every item must belong to this partition
        params=[batch[done:]],
    )
    done += inserted                   # call again with the remainder (continuation)
```

Stored procedures are versioned as code: keep the `.js` files in source control and deploy them with your pipeline (`replace_stored_procedure` for updates), because the portal-edited copy is easy to lose track of.

**Key takeaways**

- Stored procedures are JavaScript functions executed inside Cosmos DB as an ACID transaction.
- Transactions are scoped to a single logical partition; the caller supplies the partition key.
- Throwing an exception rolls back every write in the procedure.
- Execution is time- and RU-bounded; check the boolean returned by each operation and implement continuation.
- Prefer transactional batch for simple multi-item atomic writes; use stored procedures when the logic depends on reads inside the transaction.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Register a "hello" stored procedure that returns `"Hello, " + name` and execute it from Python with a partition key.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy `bulkImport` and import 10,000 small items into one partition. Log how many items each call inserted and how many calls were needed.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why can't a Cosmos DB stored procedure update documents in two different partitions?" *Hint:* where logical partitions live physically, and the cost of distributed transactions.

#### Triggers and User-Defined Functions

Sometimes you want logic to run around a write: validate a document before it is stored, stamp a timestamp, or maintain a summary document after an insert. In relational databases, triggers fire automatically. Cosmos DB has **pre-triggers** and **post-triggers** written in JavaScript, with one important difference: **they never fire automatically**. The caller must name the trigger on each request. Cosmos DB also supports **user-defined functions (UDFs)**, which extend the query language with custom read-only logic.

**Triggers**

| | Pre-trigger | Post-trigger |
|---|---|---|
| Runs | Before the item is written | After the item is written |
| Typical use | Validate fields, add defaults (`createdAt`), normalize values | Update a metadata/summary item in the same partition |
| Can modify the request item | Yes (`getRequest().setBody(...)`) | No (reads the result with `getResponse().getBody()`) |
| Transaction | Same transaction as the write | Same transaction: a failure rolls back the original write too |
| Parameters | None | None |

Each trigger is registered with a **type** (`Pre` or `Post`) and an **operation** (`Create`, `Replace`, `Delete`, `All`). Only one pre-trigger and one post-trigger can be named per operation.

Because triggers are opt-in per request, every code path that writes must remember to include them. That is easy to forget, which is why many teams prefer validation in the application or in a change-feed consumer.

**User-defined functions**

UDFs are pure JavaScript functions you call from queries with the `udf.` prefix. They are useful for logic the built-in functions cannot express (custom tax rules, a scoring formula), but they **cannot use the index**: a `WHERE` filter on a UDF result evaluates the function for every candidate item. Always combine a UDF with an indexed filter that narrows the candidate set first.

**Example: a validating pre-trigger, a summary post-trigger, and a UDF**

```javascript
// validateOrder.js (Pre, Create): reject invalid orders, stamp createdAt
function validateOrder() {
    var request = getContext().getRequest();
    var item = request.getBody();

    if (!item.lines || item.lines.length === 0) {
        throw new Error("Order must contain at least one line");
    }
    item.createdAt = new Date().toISOString();
    request.setBody(item);                         // the modified item is what gets stored
}
```

```javascript
// updateCustomerStats.js (Post, Create): keep an order counter on the customer item
function updateCustomerStats() {
    var context = getContext();
    var collection = context.getCollection();
    var created = context.getResponse().getBody();

    var query = {
        query: "SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.type = 'customer' AND c.id = @id",
        parameters: [{ name: "@id", value: created.customerId }]
    };
    var accepted = collection.queryDocuments(collection.getSelfLink(), query, {},
        function (err, docs) {
            if (err) throw err;
            if (docs.length !== 1) throw new Error("Customer missing"); // rolls back the order too
            var customer = docs[0];
            customer.orderCount = (customer.orderCount || 0) + 1;
            collection.replaceDocument(customer._self, customer, function (err) {
                if (err) throw err;
            });
        });
    if (!accepted) throw new Error("Post-trigger not accepted");
}
```

```javascript
// vat.js (UDF): VAT by country
function vat(total, country) {
    var rates = { IT: 0.22, DE: 0.19, FR: 0.20 };
    return total * (rates[country] || 0);
}
```

```python
from pathlib import Path

scripts = customers.scripts

scripts.create_trigger(body={
    "id": "validateOrder",
    "body": Path("validateOrder.js").read_text(),
    "triggerType": "Pre",
    "triggerOperation": "Create",
})
scripts.create_trigger(body={
    "id": "updateCustomerStats",
    "body": Path("updateCustomerStats.js").read_text(),
    "triggerType": "Post",
    "triggerOperation": "Create",
})
scripts.create_user_defined_function(body={
    "id": "vat",
    "body": Path("vat.js").read_text(),
})

# Triggers run only when named on the request
customers.create_item(
    body={"id": "o-2001", "customerId": "c-42", "type": "order",
          "lines": [{"sku": "KB-01", "qty": 1, "price": 99.9}], "total": 99.9,
          "shipping": {"country": "IT"}},
    pre_trigger_include="validateOrder",
    post_trigger_include="updateCustomerStats",
)

# UDF in a query: the partition key and type filters use the index first
query = """
SELECT c.id, c.total, udf.vat(c.total, c.shipping.country) AS vat
FROM c
WHERE c.customerId = 'c-42' AND c.type = 'order'
"""
for row in customers.query_items(query, partition_key="c-42"):
    print(row)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Pre-triggers run before a write and can modify the item; post-triggers run after and share its transaction.
- Triggers never fire automatically; each request must name them.
- A failing post-trigger rolls back the original write.
- UDFs extend queries with custom read-only logic but cannot use indexes; narrow results with indexed filters first.
- Keep trigger and UDF code in source control and deploy it with your pipeline.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Register the `validateOrder` pre-trigger and show that creating an order without lines fails only when the trigger is included in the request.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Make the post-trigger throw for a specific customer ID and verify that the order item was not created. Then compare the RU charge of a query with and without the `udf.vat` projection.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your team wants every write to the orders container to be validated. Are Cosmos DB triggers the right tool?" *Hint:* opt-in per request, multiple writers and SDKs, alternatives such as an API layer or change-feed validation.

#### Transactional Batch

Stored procedures give atomicity, but they force you to write JavaScript, deploy scripts, and handle callbacks. Most of the time you just want to say "create this order and update that customer, all or nothing" from your own code. **Transactional batch** does exactly that: you build a list of operations in the SDK, all against the **same partition key**, and Cosmos DB executes them as one ACID transaction.

It is like a shopping basket at checkout: you add several items, and the payment either covers everything or nothing is purchased.

**Rules and limits**

- All operations must target the **same logical partition** (same partition key value).
- Up to **100 operations** per batch and **2 MB** total request payload.
- Operation types: create, read, replace, upsert, patch, delete.
- If **any** operation fails, the whole batch is rolled back and no changes are visible. The response contains a status code per operation: the failing one carries the real error, the others report `424 Failed Dependency`.
- Operations run in the order you add them. Reads inside a batch see the effects of earlier operations in the same batch.
- ETag conditions can be set per operation for optimistic concurrency.

**Stored procedure vs transactional batch**

| | Stored procedure | Transactional batch |
|---|---|---|
| Language | JavaScript inside the database | Your app language via SDK |
| Logic during the transaction | Yes (read, then decide) | No (operations are fixed when sent; use ETag conditions) |
| Deployment | Register and version scripts | Nothing to deploy |
| Limits | Time/RU bounded | 100 operations, 2 MB |
| Typical use | Conditional business logic in one partition | Atomic multi-item writes |

**Example: create an order and update the customer atomically (Python)**

```python
from azure.cosmos import exceptions

customers = db.get_container_client("customers")    # partition key /customerId

def place_order(customer_id: str, order: dict) -> None:
    customer = customers.read_item(item=customer_id, partition_key=customer_id)
    customer["openBalance"] += order["total"]

    operations = [
        # (operation type, positional args, optional kwargs)
        ("create", (order,)),
        ("replace", (customer_id, customer), {"if_match_etag": customer["_etag"]}),
        ("patch", (f"stats-{customer_id}",
                   [{"op": "incr", "path": "/orderCount", "value": 1}])),
    ]

    try:
        results = customers.execute_item_batch(
            batch_operations=operations,
            partition_key=customer_id,     # one partition for the whole batch
        )
        for r in results:
            print(r["statusCode"], r.get("requestCharge"))
    except exceptions.CosmosBatchOperationError as e:
        # Nothing was committed. e.error_index points at the operation that failed.
        failed = e.operation_responses[e.error_index]
        print("batch rolled back; failing op:", e.error_index, failed["statusCode"])
        raise
```

**The same in C#**, where the fluent builder is the most common style:

```csharp
TransactionalBatchResponse response = await container
    .CreateTransactionalBatch(new PartitionKey(customerId))
    .CreateItem(order)
    .ReplaceItem(customer.Id, customer,
        new TransactionalBatchItemRequestOptions { IfMatchEtag = customer.ETag })
    .PatchItem($"stats-{customerId}",
        new[] { PatchOperation.Increment("/orderCount", 1) })
    .ExecuteAsync();

if (!response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
{
    // Transactional batch does not throw on business failures: check the status
    // Each operation result shows which one failed; the rest report 424
    for (int i = 0; i < response.Count; i++)
        Console.WriteLine($"{i}: {response[i].StatusCode}");
}
```

Note that the C# SDK returns a response with `IsSuccessStatusCode = false` instead of throwing, so forgetting to check it silently ignores a rolled-back batch.

**Key takeaways**

- Transactional batch executes up to 100 operations against one partition key as an ACID transaction.
- If one operation fails, all are rolled back; per-operation results identify the failure.
- It needs no server-side code, which makes it simpler than stored procedures for atomic writes.
- Combine it with ETag conditions to protect against concurrent modification.
- In .NET, always check `IsSuccessStatusCode`; a failed batch does not throw.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Execute a batch that creates three items in the same partition. Read them back and print the RU charge of each operation in the batch.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a batch where the third operation creates an item whose `id` already exists. Confirm that the first two operations were rolled back and inspect the status codes of all operations.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you transfer money between two accounts stored in Cosmos DB if they have different partition keys?" *Hint:* no cross-partition transactions; consider a saga or ledger pattern with idempotent steps, or remodeling so that both entries share a partition.

#### Change Feed Processor

Many systems need to react when data changes: update a search index, refresh a cache, project data into a reporting store, send a notification, or keep a denormalized copy in sync. Polling for "rows modified since last time" is wasteful and misses deletes. Cosmos DB provides the **change feed**, a persistent, ordered log of changes to a container, and the **change feed processor**, a library that reads that log reliably at scale.

The change feed is like a building's visitor logbook. Every entry is appended in order, nobody erases it, and different readers (security, reception, cleaning staff) each keep their own bookmark showing how far they have read.

**What the change feed contains**

| Mode | Contains | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| **Latest version** (default) | Creates and updates, latest version of each changed item only. No deletes | Always available |
| **All versions and deletes** | Every intermediate change, plus deletes (including TTL expirations) with metadata | Continuous backup enabled; changes only within the backup retention window |

Order is guaranteed **within a partition key value**, not across the whole container. Intermediate updates can be collapsed in latest-version mode: if an item is updated five times between reads, you may see only the last version.

**How the processor works**

The change feed processor has four parts:

1. **Monitored container**: the container whose changes you read.
2. **Lease container**: stores one lease document per partition range, holding the continuation (bookmark) and the owner. Its partition key must be `/id`.
3. **Compute instances**: one or more processes running the processor with the same processor name.
4. **Delegate**: your code that handles each batch of changes.

```text
Monitored container "orders"         Lease container "leases" (pk /id)
  range 0 --------------------+       { range 0, continuation: "...", owner: "vm-a" }
  range 1 ----------------+   |       { range 1, continuation: "...", owner: "vm-b" }
  range 2 -----------+    |   |       { range 2, continuation: "...", owner: "vm-a" }
                     |    |   |
                     v    v   v
               [vm-a: ranges 0, 2]   [vm-b: range 1]   <- leases balanced across instances
                     |                    |
                     +------> delegate HandleChangesAsync(changes)
                               -> checkpoint (lease updated) after delegate succeeds
```

- Instances with the same processor name **share the work**: leases are distributed and rebalanced automatically when instances start or stop.
- Processors with **different names** each get their own independent copy of the stream (fan-out to several consumers).
- After your delegate returns successfully, the processor **checkpoints** the lease. If it throws, the batch is retried, so delivery is **at least once** and handlers must be **idempotent**.
- By default, a new processor starts from "now". You can start from the beginning or from a point in time on first run only (once leases exist, they win).

**Example: projecting orders into a read model (C#)**

The change feed processor library ships in the .NET and Java SDKs. Python offers the lower-level pull model (shown afterwards).

```csharp
using Microsoft.Azure.Cosmos;

CosmosClient client = new(endpoint, new DefaultAzureCredential());
Container orders = client.GetContainer("shop", "orders");
Container leases = client.GetContainer("shop", "leases");          // partition key /id
Container byStatus = client.GetContainer("shop", "ordersByStatus"); // read model

ChangeFeedProcessor processor = orders
    .GetChangeFeedProcessorBuilder<Order>(
        processorName: "ordersByStatusProjection",   // logical consumer name
        onChangesDelegate: HandleChangesAsync)
    .WithInstanceName(Environment.MachineName)     // unique per compute instance
    .WithLeaseContainer(leases)
    .WithStartTime(DateTime.MinValue.ToUniversalTime()) // first run only: from the beginning
    .WithMaxItems(100)                             // max items per delegate call
    .WithErrorNotification((leaseToken, ex) =>
    {
        Console.Error.WriteLine($"Lease {leaseToken} failed: {ex.Message}");
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    })
    .Build();

await processor.StartAsync();
// ... keep the host running; call StopAsync() on shutdown to release leases cleanly

async Task HandleChangesAsync(
    ChangeFeedProcessorContext context,
    IReadOnlyCollection<Order> changes,
    CancellationToken ct)
{
    foreach (Order o in changes)
    {
        // Upsert keyed by order id: running twice gives the same result (idempotent)
        await byStatus.UpsertItemAsync(
            new { id = o.Id, status = o.Status, customerId = o.CustomerId, total = o.Total },
            new PartitionKey(o.Status),
            cancellationToken: ct);
    }
    // Returning without throwing -> checkpoint; throwing -> batch is redelivered
}
```

**Monitoring lag with the estimator**

```csharp
ChangeFeedProcessor estimator = orders
    .GetChangeFeedEstimatorBuilder("ordersByStatusProjection",
        (long pending, CancellationToken ct) =>
        {
            Console.WriteLine($"Pending changes: {pending}");  // emit as a metric
            return Task.CompletedTask;
        }, TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30))
    .WithLeaseContainer(leases)
    .Build();
await estimator.StartAsync();
```

**The pull model in Python**

When you want full control (or your SDK has no processor), read the change feed yourself and store the continuation token.

```python
orders = db.get_container_client("orders")

def read_changes(continuation: str | None):
    if continuation is None:
        feed = orders.query_items_change_feed(start_time="Beginning")
    else:
        feed = orders.query_items_change_feed(continuation=continuation)

    for item in feed:
        project(item)                              # your idempotent handler

    # The ETag of the last response is the bookmark for the next read
    return orders.client_connection.last_response_headers["etag"]

token = load_token()            # e.g. from Blob Storage or a lease item
token = read_changes(token)
save_token(token)               # persist only after processing succeeded
```

With the pull model you handle scaling and lease distribution yourself, which is why the processor (or Azure Functions, next topic) is usually preferable.

**Key takeaways**

- The change feed is a persistent, ordered (per partition key) log of creates and updates; all-versions mode adds deletes and intermediate versions.
- The change feed processor uses a lease container (partition key `/id`) to distribute partition ranges across instances and checkpoint progress.
- Instances with the same processor name share the work; different processor names consume independently.
- Delivery is at least once; handlers must be idempotent.
- Use the estimator to monitor lag, and the pull model when you need full manual control.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the Python pull-model reader against a container, insert three items, and confirm they appear on the next read. Update one item twice and observe what the feed returns.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run two instances of the C# processor with the same processor name, inspect the lease documents to see which instance owns which range, then stop one instance and watch its leases move.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Design a pipeline that keeps an Azure AI Search index in sync with a Cosmos DB container, including deletes." *Hint:* change feed processor or Functions trigger, idempotent upserts, soft deletes or all-versions mode, lag monitoring.

#### Change Feed with Azure Functions

Running the change feed processor yourself means hosting a long-running process, scaling it, and handling restarts. **Azure Functions** offers a **Cosmos DB trigger** that wraps the change feed processor: you write only the delegate, and the Functions runtime hosts the processor, manages the lease container, and scales instances with the volume of changes.

**How the trigger maps to the processor**

| Change feed processor concept | Cosmos DB trigger setting |
|---|---|
| Monitored container | `database_name` / `container_name` |
| Lease container | `lease_container_name` (default `leases`), `lease_database_name` |
| Processor name | Function name (plus optional `lease_container_prefix`) |
| Start point (first run only) | `start_from_beginning`, `start_from_time` |
| Max items per batch | `max_items_per_invocation` |
| Polling interval | `feed_poll_delay` (ms, default 5,000) |
| Delegate | The function body |

**Things to know**

- **Multiple functions on one container**: each function gets its own leases. If they share a lease container, set a distinct `lease_container_prefix` per function, or they will steal each other's leases.
- **Scaling**: Functions scales out up to one instance per leased partition range. A container with few physical partitions cannot be processed by more instances than it has ranges.
- **Identity-based connections**: configure `<Connection>__accountEndpoint` instead of a connection string. Data-plane RBAC cannot create containers, so create the lease container ahead of time and leave `create_lease_container_if_not_exists` off.
- **Errors**: if the function throws, the runtime may retry according to its retry policy, but the checkpoint then advances; the batch is **not** redelivered forever. Catch per-item failures and send them to a dead-letter store (a queue or container) yourself.
- **Lease container RUs**: leases consume RUs on every checkpoint. Shared database throughput or a small autoscale setting is usually enough.

```text
orders container --change feed--> [Functions host: CFP + leases] --batch--> your function
                                                                             |
                     +-------------------+-------------------+---------------+
                     v                   v                   v
              Cosmos output        Service Bus queue      Azure AI Search
              (read model)         (notifications)        (index update)
```

**Example: Python v2 programming model**

```python
# function_app.py
import json
import logging
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp()

@app.cosmos_db_trigger(
    arg_name="changes",
    connection="CosmosDB",                    # app settings: CosmosDB__accountEndpoint
    database_name="shop",
    container_name="orders",
    lease_container_name="leases",
    lease_container_prefix="notify-",         # unique per function sharing the lease container
    create_lease_container_if_not_exists=False,
    max_items_per_invocation=100,
)
@app.queue_output(arg_name="outbox", queue_name="order-events", connection="Storage")
def on_order_changed(changes: func.DocumentList, outbox: func.Out[list[str]]) -> None:
    messages = []
    for doc in changes:
        order = doc.to_dict()
        if order.get("type") != "order":
            continue                          # co-located item types: filter early
        try:
            messages.append(json.dumps({
                "orderId": order["id"],
                "status": order["status"],
                "version": order["_ts"],      # lets consumers ignore older duplicates
            }))
        except KeyError:
            logging.exception("Malformed order %s", order.get("id"))   # do not fail the batch
    outbox.set(messages)
```

The local settings use identity-based connections, so no keys appear anywhere:

```json
{
  "IsEncrypted": false,
  "Values": {
    "FUNCTIONS_WORKER_RUNTIME": "python",
    "AzureWebJobsStorage": "UseDevelopmentStorage=true",
    "CosmosDB__accountEndpoint": "https://cosmos-shop-dev.documents.azure.com:443/",
    "Storage__queueServiceUri": "https://stshopdevweu001.queue.core.windows.net"
  }
}
```

The function app's managed identity needs the **Cosmos DB Built-in Data Contributor** role on the account (it writes lease documents, so a reader role is not enough):

```bash
principal=$(az functionapp identity show -n func-orders -g rg-app --query principalId -o tsv)

az cosmosdb sql role assignment create -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data \
  --scope "/" \
  --principal-id "$principal" \
  --role-definition-id 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000002   # Built-in Data Contributor

# Lease container created up front (partition key must be /id)
az cosmosdb sql container create -a cosmos-shop-dev -g rg-data -d shop \
  -n leases --partition-key-path /id --throughput 400
```

**The same trigger in C# (isolated worker)**

```csharp
public class OrderProjection(ILogger<OrderProjection> logger)
{
    [Function(nameof(OrderProjection))]
    [CosmosDBOutput("shop", "ordersByStatus", Connection = "CosmosDB")]
    public IEnumerable<OrderSummary> Run(
        [CosmosDBTrigger("shop", "orders",
            Connection = "CosmosDB",
            LeaseContainerName = "leases",
            LeaseContainerPrefix = "projection-")] IReadOnlyList<Order> changes)
    {
        logger.LogInformation("Projecting {Count} changes", changes.Count);
        return changes.Select(o => new OrderSummary(o.Id, o.Status, o.CustomerId, o.Total));
    }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- The Functions Cosmos DB trigger hosts the change feed processor for you; you write only the handler.
- Each function needs its own leases; use `lease_container_prefix` when functions share a lease container.
- With managed identity, pre-create the lease container (partition key `/id`) and grant the Data Contributor role.
- Failed batches are not retried indefinitely; handle per-item errors and dead-letter them yourself.
- Scale-out is limited by the number of partition ranges in the monitored container.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a Python function with a Cosmos DB trigger that logs the `id` of each changed item. Run it locally against your account and insert a few items.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a second function on the same container that writes to a queue. First run both without prefixes on a shared lease container and observe the behavior, then add distinct `lease_container_prefix` values and compare.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your Cosmos DB-triggered function occasionally fails on a malformed document and the team discovers that some changes were never processed. Explain why and propose a design." *Hint:* checkpoint advancement after retries, per-item error handling, dead-letter container, idempotent replay from a point in time.

<a id="64-relational-databases"></a>
### 6.4 Relational Databases

Not every workload fits a document model. Data with strong relationships, complex reporting queries, and multi-row transactions across entities is still best served by a relational database. This section covers Azure's three managed relational engines and the patterns every developer needs when using them from cloud applications: pooling, transient-fault handling, passwordless authentication, and cost-efficient compute models.

#### Azure SQL Database

Running SQL Server yourself means patching the OS and engine, configuring backups, setting up high availability, and planning capacity. **Azure SQL Database** is SQL Server's engine delivered as a fully managed PaaS database: Microsoft handles patching, backups, high availability, and much of the tuning, and you get a database endpoint and T-SQL compatibility.

**The Azure SQL family**

| Offering | What you get | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Azure SQL Database** | A managed database (single or in an elastic pool) on a logical server | New cloud applications; the default choice |
| **Azure SQL Managed Instance** | A managed SQL Server instance with near-100% compatibility (SQL Agent, cross-database queries, CLR, Service Broker) | Migrating existing SQL Server apps that depend on instance-level features |
| **SQL Server on Azure VMs** | Full SQL Server on an IaaS VM; you manage everything | You need OS access, a specific version, or unsupported features |

**Logical server.** Every Azure SQL Database lives on a **logical server**, which is not a VM but a management container providing the endpoint `<server>.database.windows.net`, firewall rules, the Microsoft Entra admin, and auditing settings. Databases on the same server are independent: they do not share compute or storage unless placed in an elastic pool.

**Purchasing models and service tiers**

| Model | Tier | Storage / architecture | Use for |
|---|---|---|---|
| DTU | Basic, Standard, Premium | Bundled compute, memory, and IO measured in DTUs | Simple, small workloads with predictable needs |
| vCore | **General Purpose** | Compute separated from remote premium storage | Most business workloads; budget-friendly |
| vCore | **Business Critical** | Local SSD, Always On availability group with 3 secondaries, a free readable secondary | Low-latency OLTP, high resilience |
| vCore | **Hyperscale** | Distributed storage up to 128 TB, fast scaling, up to 4 HA replicas and named replicas | Large or fast-growing databases, fast restores |

The **vCore model** is recommended for new workloads: you choose hardware, vCores, and storage independently, and you can apply Azure Hybrid Benefit and reservations. Within vCore, the compute can be **provisioned** (always on) or **serverless** (auto-scaling and auto-pausing, see Elastic Pools and Serverless Tier).

**Built-in capabilities developers should know**

| Area | Feature |
|---|---|
| Backups | Automatic full, differential, and log backups. Point-in-time restore for 1 to 35 days (7 by default); long-term retention up to 10 years |
| High availability | Built in per tier; zone redundancy as an option |
| Disaster recovery | **Active geo-replication** (readable secondaries in other regions) and **failover groups** (a stable listener endpoint that follows the primary) |
| Performance | Query Store, automatic tuning (index create/drop, plan regression correction), Intelligent Insights |
| Security | TDE (encryption at rest, on by default), Always Encrypted, dynamic data masking, row-level security, auditing, ledger tables, Microsoft Entra-only authentication |
