- If nothing matches, the **unmatched rule action** (default action) applies. Once you add any Allow rule, the default is typically Deny.
- The main site and the **SCM site** (Kudu, deployment endpoint `*.scm.azurewebsites.net`) have separate rule sets. You can make SCM use the main site's rules or define its own. Lock down SCM too, since it can deploy code.
- Up to 512 rules per site. Blocked requests receive **HTTP 403**.

```text
 Request from 198.51.100.7 to app-shop-prod.azurewebsites.net
   priority 100  Allow  service tag AzureFrontDoor.Backend + X-Azure-FDID = <my profile id>   -> no match
   priority 200  Allow  203.0.113.0/24 (office)                                              -> no match
   priority 300  Allow  subnet snet-jumpbox                                                  -> no match
   default       Deny                                                                        -> 403 Forbidden
```

**Example: accept traffic only from your Front Door, plus the office for SCM**

```bash
RG=rg-shop-prod; APP=app-shop-prod
FDID=$(az afd profile show -g rg-edge --profile-name afd-shop --query frontDoorId -o tsv)

# Main site: only our Front Door profile (service tag alone would allow every customer's Front Door)
az webapp config access-restriction add -g $RG -n $APP --rule-name AllowOurFrontDoor \
  --action Allow --priority 100 --service-tag AzureFrontDoor.Backend --http-header x-azure-fdid=$FDID
az webapp config access-restriction set -g $RG -n $APP --default-action Deny

# SCM site: separate rules, only the office range
az webapp config access-restriction set -g $RG -n $APP --use-same-restrictions-for-scm-site false
az webapp config access-restriction add -g $RG -n $APP --rule-name AllowOffice --scm-site true \
  --action Allow --priority 100 --ip-address 203.0.113.0/24
az webapp config access-restriction set -g $RG -n $APP --scm-default-action Deny

az webapp config access-restriction show -g $RG -n $APP
```

**Firewalls on other services.** The same idea appears across Azure, under different names:

| Service | Control | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Storage | Network rules (IP, VNet, resource instance) | See 5.3 |
| Key Vault | `networkAcls` with IP and VNet rules, trusted services bypass | Default action Deny for production |
| Azure SQL | Server firewall rules (IP), VNet rules, "Allow Azure services" | Avoid "Allow Azure services": it allows every Azure customer's IPs |
| Cosmos DB | IP firewall, VNet rules, private endpoints | Portal access needs its own IPs allowed |
| Container Apps | Ingress IP restrictions (allow or deny list) | Per container app |
| Functions | Same as App Service | Applies to HTTP triggers |

**Application-level IP checks: trust the right header.** Sometimes code must make IP-based decisions (rate limits, audit logs). Behind App Service, Front Door, or Application Gateway, the TCP peer address is the proxy, and the client IP is in `X-Forwarded-For`. That header is a list that the **client can pre-populate**, so only trust entries added by proxies you control:

```python
from flask import Flask, request, abort
from werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix import ProxyFix
import ipaddress

app = Flask(__name__)
# Exactly one trusted proxy hop in front of the app (the App Service front end).
# With Front Door in front of App Service, there are two hops: x_for=2.
app.wsgi_app = ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_for=1, x_proto=1)

ADMIN_NETWORK = ipaddress.ip_network("203.0.113.0/24")

@app.before_request
def restrict_admin():
    if request.path.startswith("/admin"):
        client = ipaddress.ip_address(request.remote_addr)   # taken from the right-most trusted X-Forwarded-For entry
        if client not in ADMIN_NETWORK:
            abort(403)
```

Prefer platform rules over code checks when you can: they block traffic before it consumes app resources and cannot be bypassed by a bug in your middleware.

**Key takeaways**

- Access restrictions filter inbound traffic to App Service and Functions by IP, service tag, or subnet, in priority order, with a default action for unmatched requests.
- The SCM (Kudu) site has its own rules. Restrict it as well.
- Use the `AzureFrontDoor.Backend` service tag **plus** the `X-Azure-FDID` header filter so only your Front Door profile can reach the app.
- Most Azure data services have equivalent firewalls. Avoid broad options such as SQL's "Allow Azure services".
- When checking client IPs in code, trust only `X-Forwarded-For` entries added by your own proxies.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add an access restriction allowing only your current public IP, then confirm you get a 403 from a phone on mobile data. Check whether the SCM site is affected.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Put Front Door in front of an app, lock the app with the service tag only, and show that a second Front Door profile in another subscription can still reach it. Add the `X-Azure-FDID` header filter and show that it no longer can.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A developer implemented an admin IP allowlist in code using the first value of `X-Forwarded-For`. What is wrong?" *Hint:* who writes that header, how proxies append to it, and how many trusted hops there are.

#### Network Security Groups

Once workloads live in subnets (VMs, AKS nodes, App Service integration subnets, private endpoints, Container Apps environments), you need a way to control which traffic can move between subnets and to and from the internet. A **Network Security Group (NSG)** is a stateful, layer 3/4 packet filter: a list of allow and deny rules matching source, destination, port, and protocol, attached to a subnet or a network interface.

Picture the security desks between wings of a building. Each wing (subnet) can have its own desk with a rulebook ("people from wing A may enter wing B through door 443"). Individual offices (NICs) can have their own desk too, and a visitor must pass both. Because the desks are **stateful**, someone allowed in can always walk back out the same way without a separate return rule.

**Rule anatomy**

| Field | Values |
|---|---|
| Priority | 100 to 4096, lower number evaluated first, first match wins |
| Direction | Inbound or Outbound |
| Source / destination | IP or CIDR, **service tag** (`Internet`, `VirtualNetwork`, `AzureLoadBalancer`, `Storage.WestEurope`, `AzureMonitor`, ...), or **application security group** |
| Port ranges | Single, range, list, or `*` |
| Protocol | TCP, UDP, ICMP, or Any |
| Action | Allow or Deny |

**Default rules** (cannot be deleted, can be overridden by lower-priority-number rules):

| Direction | Priority | Name | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Inbound | 65000 | AllowVnetInBound | Allow traffic from within the VNet (and peered/connected networks) |
| Inbound | 65001 | AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound | Allow health probes |
| Inbound | 65500 | DenyAllInBound | Deny everything else |
| Outbound | 65000 | AllowVnetOutBound | Allow traffic to the VNet |
| Outbound | 65001 | AllowInternetOutBound | Allow traffic to the internet |
| Outbound | 65500 | DenyAllOutBound | Deny everything else |

**Evaluation order with subnet and NIC NSGs**

```text
 Inbound:   internet -> [ subnet NSG ] -> [ NIC NSG ] -> VM        (both must allow)
 Outbound:  VM -> [ NIC NSG ] -> [ subnet NSG ] -> destination     (both must allow)
```

**Application security groups (ASGs)** let rules refer to roles instead of IP addresses. You tag NICs with `asg-web` or `asg-api`, and a rule says "allow `asg-web` to `asg-api` on 8080". Scaling out or changing IPs does not require rule edits.

**NSGs and PaaS**

- **App Service integration subnet**: an NSG on it filters the app's **outbound** traffic into (and, with Route All, beyond) the VNet. Inbound to the app is controlled by access restrictions, not by this NSG.
- **Private endpoint subnet**: NSG rules apply to private endpoints only if network policies are enabled on the subnet (`privateEndpointNetworkPolicies`).
- **Container Apps and AKS**: platform-required ports must stay open. Check each service's documented requirements before adding deny rules.

**Example: a three-tier layout with ASGs**

```text
 Internet --443--> [snet-web: asg-web] --8080--> [snet-api: asg-api] --1433--> [private endpoint: SQL]
                       ^ no SSH from internet         ^ only from asg-web           ^ only from asg-api
```

```bash
RG=rg-shop-prod; LOC=westeurope

az network asg create -g $RG -n asg-web -l $LOC
az network asg create -g $RG -n asg-api -l $LOC
az network nsg create -g $RG -n nsg-api -l $LOC

# Allow web tier to call the API tier on 8080
az network nsg rule create -g $RG --nsg-name nsg-api -n allow-web-to-api --priority 100 \
  --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-asgs asg-web --destination-asgs asg-api --destination-port-ranges 8080

# Explicitly deny everything else from inside the VNet (overrides AllowVnetInBound at 65000)
az network nsg rule create -g $RG --nsg-name nsg-api -n deny-vnet-other --priority 4000 \
  --direction Inbound --access Deny --protocol '*' \
  --source-address-prefixes VirtualNetwork --destination-address-prefixes '*' --destination-port-ranges '*'

# Attach to the subnet, and put a VM's NIC into the API role
az network vnet subnet update -g $RG --vnet-name vnet-shop -n snet-api --network-security-group nsg-api
az network nic update -g $RG -n nic-api-01 --application-security-groups asg-api
```

The same rule in Bicep:

```bicep
resource nsgApi 'Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups@2023-11-01' = {
  name: 'nsg-api'
  location: location
  properties: {
    securityRules: [
      {
        name: 'allow-web-to-api'
        properties: {
          priority: 100
          direction: 'Inbound'
          access: 'Allow'
          protocol: 'Tcp'
          sourceApplicationSecurityGroups: [ { id: asgWeb.id } ]
          destinationApplicationSecurityGroups: [ { id: asgApi.id } ]
          sourcePortRange: '*'                 // source ports are ephemeral: almost always '*'
          destinationPortRange: '8080'
        }
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Troubleshooting tools**

```bash
# Combined subnet + NIC rules actually applied to a NIC
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g $RG -n nic-api-01

# Would this packet be allowed? Which rule decides?
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g $RG --vm vm-api-01 --direction Inbound \
  --protocol TCP --local 10.0.3.4:8080 --remote 10.0.1.10:50000
```

For traffic history, use **VNet flow logs** (Network Watcher), which record allowed and denied flows to a storage account and Traffic Analytics. They replace NSG flow logs, which can no longer be created and are being retired.

**Key takeaways**

- NSGs are stateful layer 3/4 filters on subnets or NICs, with rules evaluated by priority (100 to 4096) and first match winning.
- Default rules allow VNet-internal traffic and outbound internet, and deny other inbound traffic. Override them with explicit rules when tiers must be isolated from each other.
- Use service tags and application security groups instead of hardcoded IP ranges.
- Inbound traffic passes the subnet NSG then the NIC NSG; outbound passes NIC then subnet. Both must allow.
- For PaaS, an NSG on an App Service integration subnet filters outbound traffic. Use access restrictions for inbound.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create an NSG that allows only HTTPS from the internet to a VM subnet, then use `az network watcher test-ip-flow` to verify that port 22 is blocked and port 443 is allowed.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build the web/API/SQL layout above with ASGs and show that a VM in the web tier can reach the API on 8080 but not on 22, and cannot reach the SQL private endpoint directly.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why does adding an NSG with a deny-all inbound rule to an App Service integration subnet not block users from reaching the web app?" *Hint:* which direction of traffic the integration subnet carries, and which feature controls inbound access to the app.

<a id="74-secure-development-practices"></a>
### 7.4 Secure Development Practices

The services above only help if the code and the pipeline use them correctly. This section covers the habits and tools that close the most common gaps: keeping credentials out of code and repositories, acting on Defender for Cloud's findings, configuring CORS without opening the API to every website, and enforcing encryption for data in transit.

#### Secret Scanning and Avoiding Hardcoded Credentials

Leaked credentials are one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, and the usual leak path is mundane: a connection string pasted into a config file "just for testing", committed, and pushed. Public repositories are scanned by attackers within minutes of a push, and private repositories leak through forks, laptops, CI logs, and former employees. Deleting the line in a later commit does not help, because Git history keeps it forever.

The defense has two halves, like fire safety: **prevention** (design the app so there is no secret to leak) and **detection** (smoke detectors that catch the secrets that slip through anyway).

**Prevention: remove the secret, or move it**

| Instead of | Use | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| Storage, Service Bus, Cosmos DB keys in connection strings | Managed identity with RBAC and identity-based connections | 2.4, 2.5 |
| Service principal client secrets in CI/CD | Workload identity federation (OIDC) from GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps | 2.4 |
| Passwords in `appsettings.json` or `.env` committed to Git | Key Vault references, App Configuration Key Vault references | 7.1, 7.2 |
| Shared developer secrets in chat or wiki | `az login` + `DefaultAzureCredential` locally, per-developer RBAC | 1.5 |
| Local secrets that must exist | .NET user secrets, `local.settings.json` and `.env` in `.gitignore` | This topic |

Then close the back doors, so a leaked key would not work even if it existed. Disable key-based authentication where the service supports it: `allowSharedKeyAccess: false` on Storage, `disableLocalAuth: true` on Service Bus, Event Hubs, Cosmos DB, and App Configuration. Azure Policy can audit or deny resources that keep local auth enabled.

**Example: the same code before and after**

```python
# BEFORE: a key in source code. It will end up in Git history, logs, and every clone.
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

conn = "DefaultEndpointsProtocol=https;AccountName=stshop;AccountKey=Zm9v...==;EndpointSuffix=core.windows.net"
blobs = BlobServiceClient.from_connection_string(conn)
```

```python
# AFTER: no secret anywhere. Locally this uses your `az login`; in Azure, the managed identity.
import os
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

account_url = os.environ["STORAGE_ACCOUNT_URL"]          # e.g. https://stshop.blob.core.windows.net (not secret)
blobs = BlobServiceClient(account_url, credential=DefaultAzureCredential())
```

For values that must remain secrets during local development, keep them outside the repository:

```bash
# .NET: stored in the user profile, never in the project folder
dotnet user-secrets init
dotnet user-secrets set "Payment:ApiKey" "pk_test_example"

# Everything else: ignore local settings files explicitly
cat >> .gitignore <<'EOF'
.env
local.settings.json
*.pfx
*.publishsettings
EOF
```

**Detection: scanning at every stage**

```text
 developer machine        push                       repository                 runtime
 ---------------         ------                      ----------                 -------
 pre-commit hook   -->   push protection       -->   secret scanning alerts --> Defender for Cloud
 (gitleaks,              (GitHub / Azure DevOps      (history, PRs, issues,     (exposed secrets on VMs,
  detect-secrets)         blocks the push)            partner revocation)         DevOps security findings)
```

- **GitHub secret scanning** detects hundreds of token formats (including Azure Storage keys, Entra ID client secrets, and Cosmos DB keys) and, for many providers, notifies the provider so the credential can be revoked automatically. **Push protection** blocks a push that contains a recognized secret before it lands.
- **Azure DevOps** offers the same capability through GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps (secret scanning with push protection).
- **Open-source scanners** such as gitleaks, detect-secrets, and TruffleHog run in pre-commit hooks and CI pipelines, including against full history.

**Example: a pre-commit hook and a CI gate**

```yaml
# .pre-commit-config.yaml   (install once with: pip install pre-commit && pre-commit install)
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.21.2
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks              # scans staged changes and blocks the commit on a finding
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/secret-scan.yml
name: secret-scan
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  gitleaks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0          # full history, so secrets in earlier commits of the PR are found
      - uses: gitleaks/gitleaks-action@v2
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

**When a secret leaks anyway**, the order of operations matters:

1. **Revoke or rotate** the credential immediately (regenerate the storage key, delete the client secret). Assume it is already compromised.
2. **Investigate** usage with the service's logs (Storage logs, Entra ID sign-in logs for service principals, Activity Log).
3. **Remove** the secret from code and replace it with an identity-based approach.
4. Optionally **rewrite history** (`git filter-repo`) to remove it. This is cleanup, not remediation: clones and forks keep the old commits.

**Key takeaways**

- The best secret is one that does not exist: use managed identities, OIDC federation, and identity-based connections.
- Remaining secrets belong in Key Vault, referenced by apps, never in source code, config files in the repo, or pipeline YAML.
- Disable key-based (local) authentication on services so leaked keys are useless, and enforce it with Azure Policy.
- Layer detection: pre-commit hooks, push protection, repository scanning, and CI gates.
- On a leak, rotate first. Rewriting Git history does not un-leak a secret.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Install the gitleaks pre-commit hook in a test repo and try to commit a file containing a fake storage connection string. Read the finding and add an allowlist entry for a known test fixture.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Take an app that uses a Storage connection string and a Service Bus connection string, convert both to `DefaultAzureCredential` with RBAC, then set `allowSharedKeyAccess: false` and `disableLocalAuth: true` and prove the old strings no longer work.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A developer pushed a Cosmos DB primary key to a public GitHub repo an hour ago and immediately force-pushed to remove it. Is the incident over?" *Hint:* scraping speed, forks and caches, key regeneration, and checking diagnostic logs for use of the key.

#### Microsoft Defender for Cloud Recommendations

Even disciplined teams misconfigure things: a storage account left open to public networks, a Key Vault without purge protection, an app still accepting TLS 1.0, a VM with a management port open to the internet. With hundreds of resources across subscriptions, nobody can check every setting by hand. **Microsoft Defender for Cloud** continuously assesses your resources against a security benchmark and tells you what to fix, how important it is, and how to fix it. Its paid plans add threat detection on top.

Think of it as a building inspector who walks through every floor every day, writes up violations against the building code, scores the building, and, for an extra fee, also installs intrusion alarms in the most valuable rooms.

**Two halves of the product**

| Capability | What it does | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Foundational CSPM** (cloud security posture management) | Assesses resources against the **Microsoft cloud security benchmark (MCSB)**, produces recommendations and a **secure score** | Free, on by default |
| **Defender CSPM** | Adds attack path analysis, cloud security explorer, agentless scanning, governance rules, and code-to-cloud mapping for DevOps environments | Paid |
| **Workload protection plans** | Threat detection and alerts per resource type: Defender for App Service, Key Vault, Storage (including malware scanning), Databases, Containers, Resource Manager, APIs, AI services, Servers | Paid per resource |

**Anatomy of a recommendation**

```text
 Recommendation: "Key vaults should have deletion protection enabled"
   Severity:          Medium
   Security control:  Enable data protection          (contributes to secure score)
   Affected:          kv-shop-dev-weu (Unhealthy), kv-shop-prod-weu (Healthy)
   Remediation:       steps + "Fix" button or Azure Policy "deny"/"modify" effect
   Options:           assign owner and due date (governance), exempt with justification
```

**Recommendations developers meet most often**

| Area | Example recommendation | Developer action |
|---|---|---|
| App Service / Functions | "App Service apps should only be accessible over HTTPS", "should use the latest TLS version", "should have remote debugging turned off", "CORS should not allow every resource to access your apps" | Set `httpsOnly`, `minTlsVersion`, remove `*` from CORS, turn off remote debugging |
| App Service identity | "App Service apps should use managed identity" | Replace connection strings with identity-based access |
| Key Vault | "Key vaults should have deletion protection enabled", "Key Vault secrets should have an expiration date", "should use private link" | Purge protection, expiry dates, private endpoints |
| Storage | "Storage accounts should restrict network access", "Storage account public access should be disallowed", "should prevent shared key access" | Network rules, disable anonymous blob access and shared keys |
| Databases | "Azure SQL Database should be running TLS 1.2 or newer", "should have a Microsoft Entra administrator provisioned" | Minimum TLS, Entra authentication |
| Containers | "Container registry images should have vulnerabilities resolved" | Rebuild images on patched bases |
| DevOps | "Code repositories should have secret scanning findings resolved", IaC misconfigurations | Fix findings surfaced from connected GitHub or Azure DevOps |

**Shift left: catch it before deployment.** Most recommendations correspond to template properties. Fixing them in Bicep or Terraform, and scanning templates in CI, is cheaper than remediating running resources. Connecting GitHub or Azure DevOps to Defender for Cloud surfaces code and IaC findings next to runtime findings, and the **Microsoft Security DevOps** action or task runs analyzers such as Checkov, Trivy, Bandit, and Template Analyzer in pipelines.

```yaml
# .github/workflows/msdo.yml: scan IaC and code, upload results to GitHub code scanning
name: msdo
on: [pull_request]
permissions:
  contents: read
  security-events: write          # needed to upload SARIF results
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: microsoft/security-devops-action@v1
        id: msdo
        with:
          tools: checkov,trivy,bandit,templateanalyzer
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: ${{ steps.msdo.outputs.sarifFile }}
```

**Querying recommendations as data.** Assessments are exposed in Azure Resource Graph, which makes them easy to report on, filter per team, or fail a pipeline on:

```kusto
// Unhealthy recommendations for resources tagged with our team, highest severity first
securityresources
| where type == "microsoft.security/assessments"
| extend status   = tostring(properties.status.code),
         severity = tostring(properties.metadata.severity),
         title    = tostring(properties.displayName),
         resource = tostring(properties.resourceDetails.Id)
| where status == "Unhealthy"
| join kind=inner (
    resources | where tags["owner"] == "checkout-team" | project resource = tolower(id)
  ) on $left.resource == $right.resource
| project severity, title, resource
| order by severity asc
```

```bash
# Run the query from the CLI (resource-graph extension) and enable threat detection for Key Vault
az graph query -q "@unhealthy.kql" --first 100 -o table
az security secure-scores list --query "[].{name:displayName, current:score.current, max:score.max}" -o table
az security pricing create -n KeyVaults --tier Standard
```

**Using recommendations well**

- Fix by **template**, not by portal click, so the fix survives the next deployment.
- Use **Azure Policy** with `deny` or `modify` effects for rules that must never be violated (for example, HTTPS only), so the recommendation cannot recur.
- **Exempt** with a written justification when a recommendation does not apply (for example, a deliberately public static website), instead of ignoring it.
- Treat **alerts** from workload protection plans (for example, "access from a suspicious IP to a Key Vault") as incidents with an owner, not as noise.

**Key takeaways**

- Defender for Cloud continuously assesses resources against the Microsoft cloud security benchmark. Foundational CSPM, recommendations, and secure score are free.
- Paid plans add attack path analysis (Defender CSPM) and per-resource threat detection (Defender for App Service, Key Vault, Storage, and others).
- Most recommendations map to IaC properties. Fix them in templates, enforce them with Azure Policy, and scan IaC in CI.
- Assessments are queryable in Azure Resource Graph for team-level reporting and automation.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Open Defender for Cloud in a test subscription, find three unhealthy recommendations for your resources, and map each to the template property that fixes it.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add the Microsoft Security DevOps action to a repository with a Bicep template that has `httpsOnly: false` and a storage account allowing public blob access. Fix the template until the findings disappear.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your secure score dropped by 8 points overnight but nobody changed anything. What could explain it?" *Hint:* new resources, new or updated benchmark recommendations, newly enabled plans or subscriptions, and how controls are weighted.

#### CORS Configuration

Browsers enforce the **same-origin policy**: JavaScript loaded from `https://shop.contoso.com` may not read responses from `https://api.contoso.com`, because they differ in origin (scheme, host, and port). This protects users: without it, any website you visit could use your logged-in cookies to read your email or bank data from another tab. But it also blocks legitimate designs, such as a single-page app on one domain calling its own API on another. **Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)** is the controlled exception: the API tells the browser which other origins may read its responses.

An analogy: the browser is a strict receptionist who will not hand a letter from company B to a visitor from company A, unless company B's letter explicitly says "you may give this to company A".

**How the exchange works.** For "simple" requests (GET, or POST with form content types), the browser sends the request with an `Origin` header and checks the response. For anything else (custom headers like `Authorization`, JSON bodies, PUT/DELETE), the browser first sends a **preflight** `OPTIONS` request:

```text
 Browser (page from https://shop.contoso.com)                          API (https://api.contoso.com)

 OPTIONS /orders                                                -->
   Origin: https://shop.contoso.com
   Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
   Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type
                                                                <--  204 No Content
                                                                       Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.contoso.com
                                                                       Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST
                                                                       Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type
                                                                       Access-Control-Max-Age: 600        (cache preflight 10 min)
 POST /orders                                                   -->
   Origin: https://shop.contoso.com
   Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
                                                                <--  201 Created
                                                                       Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://shop.contoso.com
 Browser lets the JavaScript read the response.
```

**What CORS is and is not**

- CORS is enforced by **browsers** only. `curl`, Postman, server-to-server calls, and attackers' scripts ignore it entirely. It is not authentication or authorization; your API must still validate tokens.
- Allowing `*` lets any website's JavaScript read your API's responses in a visitor's browser. For public, unauthenticated data that may be fine; for anything else it is not.
- `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` cannot be combined with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. If your API relies on cookies, you must list exact origins.
- Origins match exactly: `https://shop.contoso.com` is not `https://www.shop.contoso.com`, and `http` is not `https`.

**Where CORS is configured in Azure**

| Service | Where | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App Service / Functions | Platform CORS setting (`siteConfig.cors`) | Handled by the platform before your code. If set, it **overrides** CORS handled in your code. Use one or the other, not both |
| Blob, Queue, Table, File storage | CORS rules per service on the storage account | Needed for browser uploads with SAS tokens |
| API Management | `cors` policy | Covered in chapter 8 |
| Container Apps | Ingress CORS policy | Per container app |
| Your code (ASP.NET Core, Express, FastAPI) | Middleware | Most flexible (per endpoint, dynamic origins). Clear the platform setting when using it |
| Static Web Apps | Not usually needed | The API is served from the same origin under `/api` |

**Example: App Service platform CORS**

```bash
APP=app-orders-api; RG=rg-shop-prod
az webapp cors add -g $RG -n $APP --allowed-origins https://shop.contoso.com https://admin.contoso.com
az webapp cors show -g $RG -n $APP
```

```bicep
resource api 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'app-orders-api'
  location: location
  properties: {
    serverFarmId: plan.id
    siteConfig: {
      cors: {
        allowedOrigins: [ 'https://shop.contoso.com', 'https://admin.contoso.com' ]   // never '*' for authenticated APIs
        supportCredentials: true                // only if the browser must send cookies
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Example: CORS in code (ASP.NET Core)** for finer control. Leave the platform CORS list empty when you do this:

```csharp
var allowedOrigins = builder.Configuration.GetSection("Cors:AllowedOrigins").Get<string[]>()!;  // from App Configuration

builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
    options.AddPolicy("spa", policy => policy
        .WithOrigins(allowedOrigins)                     // exact origins, no wildcard
        .WithMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT")
        .WithHeaders("Authorization", "Content-Type")
        .SetPreflightMaxAge(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(10)))); // fewer preflight round trips

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseCors("spa");                                      // before auth and endpoints
app.MapControllers().RequireCors("spa");
```

**Example: browser uploads directly to Blob Storage with a SAS**

```bash
az storage cors add --account-name stshopuploads --services b \
  --methods PUT OPTIONS --origins https://shop.contoso.com \
  --allowed-headers "content-type,x-ms-blob-type,x-ms-version" \
  --exposed-headers "etag" --max-age 600
```

**Debugging tips.** CORS errors appear only in the browser console ("No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present"), while the server log may show a successful request or a 404 or 500 on the preflight. Check the preflight response first: a missing `OPTIONS` handler, an authentication middleware that rejects `OPTIONS` requests without a token, or a platform/in-code conflict are the usual causes.

**Key takeaways**

- CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy for specific origins. It protects users' browsers, not your API, and is not an authorization mechanism.
- Non-simple requests trigger a preflight `OPTIONS` request. Both the preflight and the actual response must carry the right headers.
- List exact origins. Never combine `*` with credentials, and avoid `*` for authenticated APIs.
- In App Service and Functions, platform CORS overrides in-code CORS. Pick one place.
- Storage accounts need their own CORS rules for direct browser access.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Host a static HTML page on one origin that calls an API on another with `fetch`. Observe the CORS error, then fix it with `az webapp cors add` and inspect the preflight in the browser's network tab.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Configure CORS both in the App Service platform and in ASP.NET Core with different origin lists, and determine which one wins. Then implement credentialed requests with cookies and explain the configuration changes required.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Our API sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, but it requires a bearer token, so it's safe, right?" *Hint:* what CORS protects, where tokens are stored in the SPA, whether credentials are involved, and what an attacker's script can and cannot do.

#### Data Encryption in Transit

Data travels between browsers and your app, between your app and its database, and between services. On any of those hops, someone positioned on the network (a compromised router, a malicious Wi-Fi hotspot, a misconfigured proxy) could read or modify unencrypted traffic. **Transport Layer Security (TLS)** prevents this by encrypting the connection and, just as importantly, by proving the server's identity through a certificate. Encryption without identity verification is like whispering a secret to a stranger because they claimed to be your bank: private, but useless.

**What TLS gives you**

| Property | Meaning | What breaks it |
|---|---|---|
| Confidentiality | Nobody on the path can read the traffic | Plain HTTP, legacy protocol versions, weak ciphers |
| Integrity | Nobody can modify traffic undetected | Same as above |
| Authentication | You are talking to the real server | Disabled certificate validation, `TrustServerCertificate=true`, `verify=False` |

**Protocol versions.** TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated and Azure has retired them across its services. TLS 1.2 is the minimum, and TLS 1.3 (faster handshake, only modern ciphers) is preferred where supported.

**Where Azure helps by default, and where you must act**

- Traffic between Azure datacenters is encrypted at the data link layer (IEEE 802.1AE MACsec) by the platform. This protects the physical backbone, but is **not** a substitute for TLS between your components.
- Many services are HTTPS-only by design (Key Vault, Cosmos DB, Entra ID). Others accept plain connections unless you configure them not to, and most let you set a minimum TLS version.
- Inside a VNet, traffic between your own components is not encrypted unless you use TLS. Zero-trust practice is to encrypt even "internal" hops.

**Settings to enforce per service**

| Service | Setting | Recommended value |
|---|---|---|
| App Service / Functions | `httpsOnly` (redirect HTTP to HTTPS), `minTlsVersion`, `scmMinTlsVersion`, `ftpsState` | `true`, `1.2` or `1.3`, `1.2`, `Disabled` (or `FtpsOnly`) |
| Storage account | `supportsHttpsTrafficOnly` (secure transfer required), `minimumTlsVersion` | `true`, `TLS1_2` |
| Azure SQL Database | `minimalTlsVersion` on the logical server, client `Encrypt=True` | `1.2`, `True` (or `Strict` for TDS 8.0) |
| Azure Database for PostgreSQL / MySQL | `require_secure_transport`, minimum TLS version parameters | `ON`, TLS 1.2 |
| Azure Cache for Redis | Non-TLS port 6379 disabled, `minimumTlsVersion` | Disabled, `1.2`, connect on 6380 |
| Front Door / Application Gateway | Minimum TLS policy, HTTPS to the origin (end-to-end TLS) | TLS 1.2+, HTTPS backends |

**Example: enforcing transport security with the CLI and Bicep**

```bash
# App Service: HTTPS only, modern TLS, no plain FTP
az webapp update -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-prod --https-only true
az webapp config set -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-prod --min-tls-version 1.2 --ftps-state Disabled

# Storage: secure transfer required, TLS 1.2 minimum
az storage account update -g rg-shop-prod -n stshopprod --https-only true --min-tls-version TLS1_2

# Azure SQL logical server and Redis
az sql server update -g rg-shop-prod -n sql-shop-prod --minimal-tls-version 1.2
az redis update -g rg-shop-prod -n redis-shop-prod --set minimumTlsVersion=1.2 enableNonSslPort=false
```

```bicep
resource app 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2023-12-01' = {
  name: 'app-shop-prod'
  location: location
  properties: {
    serverFarmId: plan.id
    httpsOnly: true                           // 301 redirect from http:// to https://
    siteConfig: {
      minTlsVersion: '1.2'
      scmMinTlsVersion: '1.2'
      ftpsState: 'Disabled'
      http20Enabled: true
    }
  }
}
```

**Client side: keep certificate validation on.** Encryption settings on the server are only half the story. A client that skips certificate validation will happily talk to an attacker's proxy. These are the lines to look for in code review:

```python
import requests, psycopg

# WRONG: encrypts, but trusts any certificate (man-in-the-middle possible)
requests.get("https://api.partner.example/orders", verify=False)

# RIGHT: default validation against the system/certifi trust store
requests.get("https://api.partner.example/orders", timeout=10)

# PostgreSQL: 'require' encrypts but does not verify the server; 'verify-full' checks the CA and hostname
conn = psycopg.connect(
    host="psql-shop-prod.postgres.database.azure.com",
    dbname="shop", user="app-shop-prod",
    password=entra_token,                     # Entra ID access token, see 2.4
    sslmode="verify-full",
    sslrootcert="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt",   # bundle containing the server's root CA
)
```

```csharp
// SQL Server: Encrypt=True validates the certificate unless TrustServerCertificate=True (never in production)
var conn = "Server=tcp:sql-shop-prod.database.windows.net,1433;Database=shop;" +
           "Authentication=Active Directory Default;Encrypt=True;TrustServerCertificate=False;";
```

**HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS).** `httpsOnly` redirects HTTP to HTTPS, but the very first request may still go out in plain text and could be intercepted. The `Strict-Transport-Security` response header tells browsers to use HTTPS for your domain for a period of time, skipping the plain-text attempt entirely. Add it in your app (for example, `app.UseHsts()` in ASP.NET Core) or at Front Door.

**Enforcement at scale.** Azure Policy has built-in definitions such as "App Service apps should only be accessible over HTTPS", "Secure transfer to storage accounts should be enabled", and "Azure SQL Database should be running TLS version 1.2 or newer". Assign them with a `deny` effect in production so non-compliant resources cannot be created, and let Defender for Cloud report on the rest.

**Key takeaways**

- TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication. Without certificate validation, you lose the authentication and the protection with it.
- Use TLS 1.2 as the minimum everywhere and prefer TLS 1.3 where supported. Disable plain-text endpoints (HTTP, FTP, Redis 6379).
- Azure encrypts traffic between its datacenters, but traffic between your components still needs TLS, including inside a VNet.
- Never ship `verify=False`, `TrustServerCertificate=True`, or `sslmode=require` where verification is possible.
- Add HSTS for browser-facing sites, and enforce transport settings with Azure Policy and IaC rather than manual configuration.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Use `curl -v --tlsv1.1 --tls-max 1.1` against an app configured with minimum TLS 1.2 and read the handshake failure. Repeat with `--tlsv1.2`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Audit a subscription with Azure Resource Graph for App Service apps without `httpsOnly`, storage accounts allowing HTTP, and SQL servers below TLS 1.2. Fix them in Bicep and assign the matching built-in policies with a `deny` effect.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Our services all run inside a private VNet with private endpoints, so we disabled TLS between them to save CPU. Is that reasonable?" *Hint:* zero trust, lateral movement after one compromised workload, compliance requirements, and the real cost of modern TLS.

---

<a id="8-api-management-and-integration"></a>
## 8. API Management and Integration

Once an application exposes more than a couple of APIs, the same cross-cutting problems show up for every one of them: who may call it, how often, which version, how failures are seen, and how other systems are wired to it. This chapter covers Azure API Management (APIM), the gateway that solves these problems once for all APIs through configuration and policies, and Azure Logic Apps, the workflow service that connects APIs, SaaS products, and Azure services without writing glue code for each integration. Together they form the "front door" and the "plumbing" of most integration architectures on Azure.

<a id="81-azure-api-management-fundamentals"></a>
### 8.1 Azure API Management Fundamentals

API Management is a managed service that sits between API consumers and your backend services, giving you one place to publish, secure, transform, document, and observe APIs. This section covers its building blocks, how to pick a tier, how access is packaged into products and subscriptions, how APIs are imported, and how they evolve safely through versions and revisions.

#### APIM Components (Gateway, Management Plane, Developer Portal)

Imagine a company with twenty microservices, each built by a different team. Without a shared entry point, every team re-implements authentication, throttling, logging, CORS, and documentation, each slightly differently. Consumers need twenty base URLs and twenty sets of credentials, and moving a service to a new host breaks every client. API Management solves this by putting a **facade** in front of the backends: consumers talk to one stable endpoint, and the facade applies shared rules before forwarding requests.

A useful analogy is a hotel reception desk. Guests (API consumers) never walk into the kitchen or laundry (backends) directly. They go to the desk, which checks their room key (authentication), enforces house rules (policies), routes requests to the right department (routing), and keeps a record of everything (analytics). The hotel's management office (management plane) decides the rules, and the brochure rack in the lobby (developer portal) tells guests what services exist and how to request them.

APIM is made of three components:

| Component | Role | Who uses it | Endpoint (default) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **API gateway** (data plane) | Receives every API call, applies policies, forwards to the backend, returns the response | Client applications | `https://<name>.azure-api.net` |
| **Management plane** | Defines APIs, operations, products, policies, users, and settings. Exposed through Azure Resource Manager | Administrators, CI/CD, IaC tools (portal, CLI, Bicep, Terraform) | `https://management.azure.com/...` |
| **Developer portal** | Auto-generated, customizable website with API docs, an interactive test console, and self-service subscription sign-up | API consumers (internal or external developers) | `https://<name>.developer.azure-api.net` |

```text
                       Developer portal  <-- consumers browse docs, get keys, test calls
                              |
                              | (reads API definitions and products)
                              v
  Admins / CI/CD ---> Management plane (ARM) ---> configuration
                                                     |
                                                     v
  Client apps -----> API gateway ---- policies ----> Backend services
   (HTTPS)       https://apim-shop.azure-api.net     (App Service, Functions,
                    /orders/...                       AKS, Logic Apps, on-prem,
                    /catalog/...                      third-party SaaS)
```

**What the gateway does on every call**

1. Accepts the request and matches the URL to an API and operation (for example `GET /orders/{id}`).
2. Verifies credentials: subscription keys, JWTs, client certificates.
3. Applies rate limits and quotas.
4. Transforms the request (headers, URL, body) and routes it to the configured backend.
5. Transforms the response, caches it if configured, and returns it.
6. Emits logs and metrics to Azure Monitor and Application Insights.

The gateway is **stateless with respect to your data**: it stores configuration, cache entries, and counters, not business data. Backends remain the source of truth.

**Key vocabulary**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **API** | A collection of operations exposed under a path suffix (for example `/orders`) and mapped to a backend URL |
| **Operation** | One method + URL template, such as `GET /orders/{orderId}` |
| **Backend** | The real service the gateway forwards to. Can be a plain URL or a reusable *backend entity* with credentials, circuit breaker, and load-balancing pools |
| **Product** | A bundle of APIs offered to consumers with its own terms, visibility, and subscription rules (see "Products and Subscriptions") |
| **Policy** | XML-defined statements that run on requests and responses (see 8.2) |
| **Named value** | A reusable key-value (optionally a secret, optionally backed by Key Vault) referenced in policies as `{{name}}` |

**Example: creating an instance and calling the gateway**

```bash
RG=rg-shop-api; APIM=apim-shop-dev-weu   # name is global: it becomes <name>.azure-api.net

# Developer tier: full feature set, no SLA, for dev/test only.
# Classic tiers take 30-45 minutes to provision; v2 tiers take minutes.
az apim create -g $RG -n $APIM -l westeurope \
  --publisher-email api-team@contoso.com --publisher-name "Contoso API Team" \
  --sku-name Developer --enable-managed-identity true

# Every new instance ships with a sample "Echo API" that reflects the request back
az apim api list -g $RG -n $APIM -o table

# Gateway URL used by clients
az apim show -g $RG -n $APIM --query gatewayUrl -o tsv
```

**Key takeaways**

- APIM is a facade: consumers see one stable endpoint, and backends can move or change without breaking clients.
- The **gateway** handles runtime traffic, the **management plane** (via ARM) holds configuration, and the **developer portal** serves documentation and self-service onboarding.
- Cross-cutting concerns (auth, throttling, transformation, logging) are configured once in the gateway instead of re-implemented in every service.
- The gateway is a runtime proxy: every call goes through it, so its tier, capacity, and network placement directly affect latency and availability.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a Developer-tier instance (or use the Consumption tier to save time and cost), open the built-in Echo API in the portal's Test tab, and send a request. Identify the gateway URL, the API path suffix, and the backend URL.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Draw the request flow for a mobile app calling `GET /orders/42` through APIM to an App Service backend. Mark which component is involved at design time and which at runtime, and where logs are produced.
> 3. **(Interview)** "We already have an Application Gateway in front of our microservices. Why would we also need API Management?" *Hint:* compare layer-7 load balancing and WAF with API-level concerns such as subscriptions, per-consumer quotas, transformation, versioning, and a developer portal.

#### Service Tiers

APIM is sold in tiers that differ far more than in price: network isolation, scale-out, multi-region deployment, SLAs, the self-hosted gateway, and even which policies are available all depend on the tier. Picking the wrong tier is one of the most common and most expensive mistakes, because classic tiers cannot always be changed in place (moving between classic and v2 tiers requires a migration) and some features, such as virtual network injection, drive the whole network design.

Think of the tiers like office space options. The **Consumption** tier is a coworking desk paid by the hour: no commitment, scales instantly, but shared and with fewer amenities. The **classic** tiers (Developer, Basic, Standard, Premium) are leased offices with fixed monthly rent and more control. The **v2** tiers are a newer building with faster move-in (provisioning in minutes) and modern networking options.

**Tier families**

| Tier | Billing model | SLA | Typical use | Notable characteristics |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Consumption** | Per call (a monthly free grant, then per million calls) | Yes | Serverless apps, low or spiky traffic, Functions/Logic Apps backends | Scales automatically, possible cold starts, no developer portal, no built-in cache (external Redis-compatible cache only), no VNet, some policies unavailable |
| **Developer** (classic) | Per unit per hour | **None** | Dev/test, evaluation | All Premium features except scale-out, multi-region, and SLA. Never use for production |
| **Basic** (classic) | Per unit | Yes | Small production workloads | Few scale units, no VNet |
| **Standard** (classic) | Per unit | Yes | Medium production workloads | More units and larger cache than Basic, no VNet |
| **Premium** (classic) | Per unit, per region | Yes (higher with multi-region) | Enterprise, regulated, global | VNet injection (internal/external), multi-region, availability zones, self-hosted gateway, workspaces |
| **Basic v2** | Per unit | Yes | Production without network isolation | Fast provisioning and scaling |
| **Standard v2** | Per unit | Yes | Production with private backends | Outbound **VNet integration** to reach private backends; inbound private endpoint |
| **Premium v2** | Per unit | Yes | Enterprise with full isolation | VNet injection, availability zones, higher scale |

Unit counts, cache sizes, and prices change over time. Always confirm current limits in the "API Management limits" and pricing pages before committing.

**Choosing a tier**

```text
Is it for dev/test only? ----------------------------- yes --> Developer (classic) or Basic v2
        | no
Is traffic low/spiky and is serverless billing a fit? -- yes --> Consumption
        | no
Must the gateway be deployed INTO a VNet (no public IP),
or run in multiple regions / on-premises? ------------- yes --> Premium (classic) or Premium v2
        | no
Must it reach backends in a private VNet? ------------- yes --> Standard v2
        | no
                                                         -----> Basic v2 / Standard v2
```

**Networking terms that drive the decision**

| Feature | Direction | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **VNet injection** (external mode) | Inbound public, outbound private | Gateway lives in your subnet with a public endpoint; can call private backends |
| **VNet injection** (internal mode) | Inbound and outbound private | Gateway has only a private IP; often fronted by Application Gateway for public exposure |
| **VNet integration** (v2) | Outbound only | Gateway reaches private backends through a delegated subnet, like App Service VNet integration (7.3) |
| **Private endpoint** | Inbound only | Clients reach the gateway over a private IP from a VNet |

**Scaling.** Classic and v2 tiers scale by adding **units**. Each unit adds roughly fixed throughput capacity. Monitor the **Capacity** metric (a composite of CPU, memory, and network queue length) and scale out when it stays above about 60-70% at peak. Autoscale rules can target this metric.

**Example: Bicep for a Standard v2 instance with outbound VNet integration**

```bicep
param location string = resourceGroup().location
param integrationSubnetId string   // subnet delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms

resource apim 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service@2024-05-01' = {
  name: 'apim-shop-prod-weu'
  location: location
  sku: {
    name: 'StandardV2'
    capacity: 1                    // number of scale units
  }
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' } // used later for Key Vault named values and backend auth
  properties: {
    publisherEmail: 'api-team@contoso.com'
    publisherName: 'Contoso API Team'
    virtualNetworkType: 'External'      // with v2 + subnet: outbound integration
    virtualNetworkConfiguration: {
      subnetResourceId: integrationSubnetId
    }
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- Tiers differ in features, not only capacity: VNet support, multi-region, the self-hosted gateway, built-in cache, and the developer portal all depend on the tier.
- **Developer** has no SLA and is never for production. **Consumption** is pay-per-call and serverless, with fewer features.
- Use **Standard v2** to reach private backends, and **Premium** (classic or v2) for full network isolation, availability zones, and (classic) multi-region or self-hosted gateways.
- Scale by adding units and watch the **Capacity** metric. Check current limits and prices because they change.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For each scenario, pick a tier and justify it in one sentence: a hackathon prototype; a public API with 50,000 calls per month; an internal API whose backends are only reachable through private endpoints; a bank API that must run in two regions with zone redundancy.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy a Consumption instance and a Basic v2 instance with Bicep, measure the provisioning time of each, and compare cold-start latency after 30 minutes of inactivity.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your APIM Standard instance shows the Capacity metric at 85% during peak hours, but backend latency is normal. What do you investigate and what are your options?" *Hint:* expensive policies (large body transformations, many `send-request` calls), caching, scale units, autoscale, and whether a tier change is justified.

#### Products and Subscriptions

An API on its own is just a set of endpoints. To offer it to consumers, you need answers to business questions: Is it free or paid? Does a human need to approve access? Which group of developers may even see it? How many calls are they allowed? APIM answers these with **products**, which package one or more APIs, and **subscriptions**, which grant a consumer access to a product (or API) with a pair of keys.

Think of a streaming service. The catalog contains many shows (APIs). The service sells **plans** (products) such as "Basic" and "Premium", each including a set of shows and certain limits (number of screens, quality). When you sign up for a plan, you get an **account** with credentials (a subscription with keys). The same show can appear in several plans, and each plan has its own rules.

**Products**

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| **APIs** | A product contains one or more APIs. An API can belong to several products |
| **Subscription required** | `true` (protected): callers need a valid key. `false` (open): anyone can call, no key, useful for public or token-only APIs |
| **Approval required** | Subscription requests from the developer portal wait for an administrator to approve them |
| **Subscriptions limit** | Max number of simultaneous subscriptions per user (for example 1) |
| **State** | `notPublished` (only admins see it) or `published` (visible in the developer portal to allowed groups) |
| **Groups (visibility)** | Which developer groups see the product in the portal: built-in `Administrators`, `Developers` (signed-in users), `Guests` (anonymous), plus custom or Entra ID groups |
| **Policies** | Product-scope policies, typically rate limits and quotas that define the plan |

Every new instance has two sample products, **Starter** (low rate limit, approval not required) and **Unlimited** (no limit, approval required). Delete or reconfigure them before going to production.

**Subscriptions**

A subscription is a named credential with a **primary** and a **secondary key**. Its **scope** decides what the keys unlock:

| Scope | Unlocks | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| **Product** | All APIs in that product | The normal case: a consumer signs up for a plan |
| **API** | One API, independent of products | Internal callers that need one API only |
| **All APIs** | Every API in the instance | Admin/testing. Treat it like a master key. The built-in all-access subscription should be disabled in production |

Subscriptions can be **owned** by a developer account (self-service via the portal) or be unowned (created by an admin and handed to an app). Their state can be `active`, `suspended`, `cancelled`, `submitted` (waiting approval), `rejected`, or `expired`.

```text
  Product "Partner-Gold"  (subscription required, approval required, quota 1M/month)
     |-- API: Orders v2
     |-- API: Catalog v1
     |
     +-- Subscription "fabrikam-prod"  (owner: dev@fabrikam.com)
     |       primary key:   3b1f...   secondary key: 9c2e...
     +-- Subscription "tailspin-prod"  (owner: api@tailspin.com)

  A call with fabrikam's key to /orders/... -> allowed, counted against fabrikam's quota
  A call with fabrikam's key to /payments/... -> 401, Payments is not in the product
```

**Example: product, API assignment, and subscription with the CLI**

```bash
RG=rg-shop-api; APIM=apim-shop-dev-weu
SUB=$(az account show --query id -o tsv)

# A protected, published product; one subscription per developer
az apim product create -g $RG -n $APIM --product-id partner-gold \
  --product-name "Partner Gold" --description "Orders and Catalog for partners" \
  --subscription-required true --approval-required true \
  --subscriptions-limit 1 --state published

az apim product api add -g $RG -n $APIM --product-id partner-gold --api-id orders-api

# No dedicated az apim command for subscriptions: use ARM directly
BASE="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/$APIM"
az rest --method put --url "$BASE/subscriptions/fabrikam-prod?api-version=2022-08-01" \
  --body '{"properties":{"scope":"/products/partner-gold","displayName":"Fabrikam production","state":"active"}}'

# Read the keys (POST, because they are secrets)
az rest --method post --url "$BASE/subscriptions/fabrikam-prod/listSecrets?api-version=2022-08-01"
```

**Key takeaways**

- **Products** package APIs with business rules: visibility, approval, subscription requirement, and product-level policies such as quotas.
- **Subscriptions** grant access to a product, a single API, or all APIs, with a primary and secondary key for rotation.
- Open products (no subscription required) suit public APIs or APIs protected only by OAuth. Protected products identify each consumer for quotas and analytics.
- Clean up the sample products and disable the built-in all-access subscription before production.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create two products, "Free" and "Pro", containing the same API. Subscribe to each and confirm that both keys work, then remove the API from "Free" and confirm that key now gets a 401.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Configure "Pro" to require approval and be visible only to an Entra ID group. Sign in to the developer portal as a member and as a non-member and compare what each sees and can request.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A partner asks for access to three of our ten APIs with different monthly limits per API. How would you model this with products and subscriptions?" *Hint:* one product versus several, product-scope versus API-scope policies, and `quota-by-key` keyed on subscription and API.

#### Importing APIs from OpenAPI

Defining every operation of an API by hand in the portal is slow and drifts out of sync with the code. Most backend frameworks can generate an **OpenAPI** document (formerly Swagger), a machine-readable description of paths, parameters, schemas, and security. APIM can import that document and create the API facade automatically: one operation per path and method, with request/response schemas, examples, and descriptions that also feed the developer portal.

The analogy is a restaurant menu. Instead of the front desk memorizing every dish, the kitchen publishes a menu (the OpenAPI document) and the front desk prints it for guests. When the kitchen changes the menu, you re-import it.

**What an import creates**

| OpenAPI element | Becomes in APIM |
|---|---|
| `info.title`, `info.description` | API display name and description |
| `servers[0].url` | Backend **service URL** (can be overridden) |
| Each `paths` + method | An **operation**, with URL template and parameters |
| `components.schemas` | Schemas used for documentation and optional validation (`validate-content` policy) |
| `operationId` | Operation ID (keep these stable: policies attach to them) |
| `securitySchemes` | Informational for the portal. APIM does not enforce them; you configure policies for that |

**Other import sources**: WSDL (SOAP pass-through or SOAP-to-REST), WADL, GraphQL schemas (pass-through or synthetic), gRPC, WebSocket, OData, and Azure resources directly: Function Apps, App Service, Container Apps, and Logic Apps (APIM reads their endpoints and creates the operations).

**Example: a minimal OpenAPI document**

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.1
info:
  title: Orders API
  version: "1.0"
servers:
  - url: https://app-orders-prod.azurewebsites.net/api   # becomes the backend service URL
paths:
  /orders/{orderId}:
    get:
      operationId: getOrder              # stable ID; policies reference it
      parameters:
        - name: orderId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema: { type: string }
      responses:
        "200":
          description: The order
          content:
            application/json:
              schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/Order" }
        "404": { description: Not found }
components:
  schemas:
    Order:
      type: object
      properties:
        id: { type: string }
        total: { type: number }
        status: { type: string, enum: [pending, paid, shipped] }
```

**Example: import from the CLI and from Bicep**

```bash
# CLI: import from a URL the backend exposes (ASP.NET, FastAPI, Spring all can generate one)
az apim api import -g $RG -n $APIM \
  --api-id orders-api --path orders --display-name "Orders API" \
  --specification-format OpenApi \
  --specification-url https://app-orders-prod.azurewebsites.net/swagger/v1/swagger.json \
  --service-url https://app-orders-prod.azurewebsites.net/api \
  --protocols https --subscription-required true

# Client URL is now: https://<apim>.azure-api.net/orders/orders/{orderId}
#                                                \____/ \______________/
#                                          API path suffix   operation URL template
```

```bicep
resource ordersApi 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/apis@2022-08-01' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'orders-api'
  properties: {
    displayName: 'Orders API'
    path: 'orders'                        // API URL suffix
    protocols: [ 'https' ]
    serviceUrl: 'https://app-orders-prod.azurewebsites.net/api'
    subscriptionRequired: true
    format: 'openapi+json-link'           // or 'openapi' with inline YAML in 'value'
    value: 'https://app-orders-prod.azurewebsites.net/swagger/v1/swagger.json'
  }
}
```

**Re-importing.** Importing into an existing API ID replaces its operations with the new definition. Operations whose `operationId` changes are treated as new, which drops their operation-level policies. Re-import into a **new revision** (next topic) rather than the live one, so you can review the diff before it reaches clients.

**Key takeaways**

- Import OpenAPI (or WSDL, GraphQL, Azure resources) instead of defining operations by hand. The definition drives both the gateway and the developer portal.
- The API **path suffix** plus the operation URL template forms the client-facing URL. The `servers` URL or `serviceUrl` is the backend.
- Keep `operationId` values stable, because operation-level policies attach to them.
- Security schemes in the document are documentation only. Enforcement comes from policies.
- Automate imports in CI/CD from the backend's generated spec, and import into a revision first.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Generate an OpenAPI document from a small web API (FastAPI, ASP.NET Core, or Express with swagger-jsdoc), import it into APIM, and call one operation through the gateway.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Change an `operationId` in the spec, attach an operation-level policy to the old operation, and re-import. Observe what happens to the policy and design a CI check that would catch this.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Should APIM be the source of truth for API definitions, or should the backend's code be?" *Hint:* drift, code-first versus design-first workflows, and where reviews and breaking-change detection fit.

#### API Versions and Revisions

APIs must change, but clients cannot all change at the same time. A mobile app released last year may still be calling your API from thousands of phones. APIM separates two kinds of change: **revisions** for non-breaking changes to the same API (a new optional field, a policy tweak, a fixed description), and **versions** for breaking changes that must live side by side with the old contract (a renamed field, a removed operation, a new auth model).

The analogy is a book. A **revision** is a corrected reprint: the same edition, typos fixed, readers don't need to do anything. A **version** is a new edition: chapters reorganized, so readers explicitly choose which edition they read, and both stay on the shelf for a while.

**Comparison**

| | Revisions | Versions |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Safe, non-breaking changes and testing them before release | Breaking changes, multiple contracts in parallel |
| Who notices | Clients see nothing until a revision is made **current**, and then nothing breaks | Clients must opt in to the new version explicitly |
| How clients reach it | Current revision at the normal URL; others via `;rev=N` (for testing) | By version identifier in path, query, or header |
| Relationship | Many revisions per API, one is current | Each version is a separate API, grouped by a **version set** |
| Release notes | Change log entries visible in the developer portal | Each version has its own docs |

**Revisions**

```text
https://apim-shop.azure-api.net/orders/orders/42          -> current revision (rev 1)
https://apim-shop.azure-api.net/orders;rev=2/orders/42    -> rev 2, offline to normal traffic,
                                                             reachable only explicitly for testing
After "make current" on rev 2:
https://apim-shop.azure-api.net/orders/orders/42          -> rev 2
```

A revision is a full copy of the API's operations and policies. You edit it, test it with `;rev=2`, then release it with a change log entry. Rolling back is making the previous revision current again.

**Versions and versioning schemes**

| Scheme | Client request | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Path** (segment) | `GET /orders/v2/orders/42` | Most visible and cache-friendly. Most common choice |
| **Query string** | `GET /orders/orders/42?api-version=2026-01-01` | Common in Azure's own APIs |
| **Header** | `GET /orders/orders/42` with `Api-Version: v2` | Clean URLs, but harder to test in a browser and to cache |

A **version set** groups the versions and stores the scheme and parameter name. The original API can be kept as the "Original" version (no identifier) so existing clients keep working.

**Example: creating a version set, a v2 version, and a revision**

```bash
# 1) Version set using path segments: /orders/v1/..., /orders/v2/...
az apim api versionset create -g $RG -n $APIM \
  --version-set-id orders --display-name "Orders" --versioning-scheme Segment

# 2) Import the breaking v2 contract as a new API in that set
az apim api import -g $RG -n $APIM \
  --api-id orders-api-v2 --path orders --display-name "Orders API" \
  --api-version v2 --api-version-set-id orders \
  --specification-format OpenApi --specification-url https://app-orders-v2.azurewebsites.net/swagger/v2/swagger.json

# 3) Non-breaking change to v2: work in a revision, test with ;rev=2, then release
az apim api revision create -g $RG -n $APIM \
  --api-id orders-api-v2 --api-revision 2 --api-revision-description "Add optional 'tags' field"

az apim api release create -g $RG -n $APIM \
  --api-id orders-api-v2 --api-revision 2 --notes "Orders now include optional tags"
```

**A typical lifecycle**

```text
v1 (current rev 3) ---- deprecation notice ---- sunset date ---- removed
v2 rev 1 -- rev 2 -- rev 3 (current) ----------------------------------->
      ^ new optional field   ^ policy fix
```

Communicate deprecations in the developer portal and in a response header (for example `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers added by an outbound policy on v1), and use analytics to find which subscriptions still call v1 before removing it.

**Key takeaways**

- **Revisions** are for non-breaking changes: build and test them offline (`;rev=N`), then make one current. They are also your rollback mechanism.
- **Versions** are for breaking changes: each is a separate API grouped in a version set, selected by path, query string, or header.
- Path versioning is the most visible and easiest to use. Choose one scheme and use it consistently.
- Retire old versions deliberately: announce, add deprecation headers, check analytics for remaining callers, then remove.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create revision 2 of an API, add a `set-header` policy only in that revision, and call both the current URL and the `;rev=2` URL to confirm only the second returns the header. Then make revision 2 current.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Convert an existing unversioned API into a version set with the original kept as the "Original" version and a new `v2` using path versioning. Verify that existing client URLs still work.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A developer wants to rename the `total` field to `amount` and ship it as a revision because 'it is a small change'. What do you tell them?" *Hint:* what counts as a breaking change for clients, and how a version or an additive change with a transition period avoids it.

<a id="82-apim-policies"></a>
### 8.2 APIM Policies

Policies are where APIM's value is realized: small XML statements that run in the gateway on every request and response, changing behavior without touching backend code. This section covers how policies are structured and inherited, the most important built-in policies for throttling, transformation, caching, and token validation, and the C# expressions that make them dynamic.

#### Policy Structure and Scopes

Without a gateway, every service decides on its own how to authenticate, throttle, and shape its responses. A policy is a declarative instruction to the gateway, such as "check this token", "allow 100 calls per minute", or "remove this header", applied at a well-defined point in the request's journey. Because policies are configuration, they can be changed in seconds and applied to one operation or to every API in the instance.

Think of airport security with layered checkpoints. The airport has rules for everyone (global scope), each airline adds its own (product), each flight may add more (API), and a specific gate may have a final check (operation). A passenger passes through all of them in order, and each layer can decide whether to include the rules of the layer above.

**The four sections**

```xml
<policies>
    <inbound>
        <!-- Runs on the request before it is forwarded: auth, limits, request rewriting -->
        <base />
    </inbound>
    <backend>
        <!-- Runs just before/while calling the backend: forward-request, retry, backend selection -->
        <base />
    </backend>
    <outbound>
        <!-- Runs on the response before it reaches the client: response rewriting, caching -->
        <base />
    </outbound>
    <on-error>
        <!-- Runs if any statement above throws, or a policy returns an error -->
        <base />
    </on-error>
</policies>
```

```text
 Client                    APIM gateway                                Backend
   |  request    +---------+    +---------+                              |
   |------------>| inbound |--->| backend |----------------------------->|
   |             +---------+    +---------+                              |
   |                                               response              |
   |  response   +----------+<-------------------------------------------|
   |<------------| outbound |
   |             +----------+
   |   (any error in any section jumps to)  +----------+
   |<---------------------------------------| on-error |
                                            +----------+
```

**Scopes and inheritance**

| Scope | Applies to | Typical content |
|---|---|---|
| **Global** (All APIs) | Every API in the instance | CORS, correlation IDs, removing server headers, IP filters |
| **Workspace** | APIs in a workspace (Premium) | Team-wide rules |
| **Product** | APIs called with a subscription to that product | Rate limits, quotas defining the "plan" |
| **API** | All operations of one API | JWT validation, backend selection, transformations |
| **Operation** | One operation | Caching, operation-specific transformations |

The `<base />` element is the inheritance point: it says "run the parent scope's policies here". The effective policy for a call is built by nesting:

```text
operation inbound:  [ <base/> -> API inbound: [ <base/> -> product inbound: [ <base/> -> global inbound ] ... ] ... ]
```

- Put `<base />` **first** in `inbound` to run broader rules (for example authentication) before narrower ones.
- In `outbound`, putting `<base />` **last** runs the specific transformation first, then global response rules.
- **Removing** `<base />` skips the parent's policies at that point. This is occasionally deliberate (an operation that must not be cached by a global rule) but is a common source of security gaps, such as an operation that silently skips global JWT validation.

The portal's **Calculate effective policy** button (or the `?effective=true` ARM query) shows the final merged XML for an operation. Use it whenever behavior surprises you.

**Policy fragments** are reusable XML snippets stored once and included with `<include-fragment fragment-id="..." />`, for example a standard JWT check used by many APIs.

**Execution control statements** include `choose` (if/else), `return-response` (short-circuit with a custom response), `retry`, `wait`, `set-variable`, and `send-request` (call another service from the gateway).

**Example: an API-scope policy using all four sections**

```xml
<policies>
    <inbound>
        <base />                                              <!-- global + product rules first -->
        <set-header name="X-Correlation-Id" exists-action="skip">
            <value>@(context.RequestId.ToString())</value>    <!-- keep client's ID if present -->
        </set-header>
        <set-backend-service backend-id="orders-backend" />   <!-- reusable backend entity -->
    </inbound>
    <backend>
        <retry condition="@(context.Response.StatusCode == 503)" count="3" interval="2" first-fast-retry="true">
            <forward-request timeout="20" />                  <!-- the actual backend call -->
        </retry>
    </backend>
    <outbound>
        <set-header name="X-Powered-By" exists-action="delete" />  <!-- don't leak backend tech -->
        <base />
    </outbound>
    <on-error>
        <base />
        <return-response>
            <set-status code="500" reason="Internal Server Error" />
            <set-body>@("{\"error\":\"unexpected\",\"requestId\":\"" + context.RequestId + "\"}")</set-body>
        </return-response>
    </on-error>
</policies>
```

**Applying policies as code**

```bicep
resource ordersPolicy 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/apis/policies@2022-08-01' = {
  parent: ordersApi
  name: 'policy'                          // always 'policy'
  properties: {
    format: 'rawxml'                      // 'xml' escapes characters; 'rawxml' is easier to keep in files
    value: loadTextContent('policies/orders-api.xml')
  }
}
```

**Key takeaways**

- A policy document has four sections: `inbound`, `backend`, `outbound`, `on-error`.
- Scopes are global, workspace, product, API, and operation. `<base />` controls where the parent scope's policies run.
- Removing `<base />` skips inherited rules, including security ones. Check the effective policy.
- Keep policies in source control (Bicep/Terraform/APIOps) and reuse common logic with policy fragments and named values.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add a `set-header` to the global, API, and operation scopes, each appending a different value to the same response header. Call the operation and explain the order you see. Then move `<base />` and observe the change.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create a policy fragment that validates a JWT and include it in two APIs. Change the fragment once and verify both APIs pick up the change.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A security review found that one operation is reachable without a token even though JWT validation is configured at the API scope. What are the likely causes?" *Hint:* a missing `<base />` at operation scope, a `return-response` before validation, or a product configured as open.

#### Rate Limiting and Quotas

A public API without limits is an invitation for problems: a buggy client stuck in a retry loop, a scraper, or a single heavy customer can saturate the backend and degrade service for everyone. Limits also turn an API into a product with tiers: free customers get 1,000 calls per day, paying customers get more. APIM provides two kinds of limits, enforced in the gateway before traffic reaches the backend.

The analogy is a water utility. A **rate limit** is the diameter of the pipe: it caps how fast water can flow right now, protecting the network from surges. A **quota** is the monthly allowance on the bill: it caps the total volume over a long period, regardless of how evenly it is used.

**Rate limits vs quotas**

| | Rate limit | Quota |
|---|---|---|
| Protects | Backend capacity against bursts | Business terms (plan allowance) |
| Typical window | Seconds to minutes | Hours to months |
| Exceeded response | **429 Too Many Requests** + `Retry-After` header | **403 Forbidden** |
| Counts | Calls | Calls and/or bandwidth (KB) |
| Precision | Approximate in distributed gateways (best effort, counters synchronized across units) | Approximate as well. Not a billing-grade meter |

**The four policies**

| Policy | Counter is per | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `rate-limit` | Subscription (and optionally API/operation via its child elements) | Simple per-subscriber throttle in a product |
| `rate-limit-by-key` | Any key you compute: IP, user ID, tenant, client app ID | Throttle anonymous traffic, throttle per user even when many share a subscription |
| `quota` | Subscription | Monthly plan allowance per subscriber |
| `quota-by-key` | Any key you compute | Allowance per tenant/user across subscriptions |

**Example: plan definitions at product scope**

```xml
<!-- Product "Free": burst protection + daily allowance -->
<policies>
    <inbound>
        <base />
        <rate-limit calls="10" renewal-period="60"
```
