```xml
                    remaining-calls-header-name="X-RateLimit-Remaining"
                    total-calls-header-name="X-RateLimit-Limit" />
        <quota calls="1000" renewal-period="86400" />          <!-- 86400 s = one day -->
    </inbound>
    <backend><base /></backend>
    <outbound><base /></outbound>
    <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>
```

**Example: keyed limits for an open API and for per-user fairness**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <!-- Anonymous endpoint: 30 calls per minute per client IP -->
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="30" renewal-period="60"
        counter-key="@(context.Request.IpAddress)" />

    <!-- Authenticated endpoint: per-user limit, only successful calls count against it -->
    <rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60"
        counter-key="@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization","").AsJwt()?.Subject ?? context.Request.IpAddress)"
        increment-condition="@(context.Response.StatusCode >= 200 && context.Response.StatusCode < 400)" />

    <!-- Monthly allowance per tenant, from a claim, across all of that tenant's subscriptions -->
    <quota-by-key calls="500000" renewal-period="2629800"
        counter-key="@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization","").AsJwt()?.Claims.GetValueOrDefault("tid", "unknown"))" />
</inbound>
```

**What a throttled client sees**

```http
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 37
Content-Type: application/json

{ "statusCode": 429, "message": "Rate limit is exceeded. Try again in 37 seconds." }
```

Well-behaved clients honor `Retry-After` and back off exponentially. The Azure SDKs and libraries such as Polly (.NET) or `tenacity` (Python) do this for you.

**Design notes**

- Behind a proxy or Front Door, `context.Request.IpAddress` is the proxy's IP. Key on the client IP header the proxy sets (validated), or on an identity.
- Limits are enforced per gateway deployment: a self-hosted gateway or a separate region keeps its own counters unless documented otherwise.
- For AI backends, APIM also has token-based limits (`llm-token-limit`, `azure-openai-token-limit`) that count model tokens instead of calls.
- Limits protect the backend only if the backend cannot be called directly. Lock the backend down to APIM (7.3).

**Key takeaways**

- **Rate limits** (429) protect capacity over short windows. **Quotas** (403) enforce allowances over long windows.
- `rate-limit` and `quota` count per subscription. The `-by-key` variants count per any expression, such as IP, user, or tenant.
- Counters are approximate. Use them for protection and plan enforcement, not exact billing.
- Return `Retry-After`, expose remaining-call headers, and make sure clients back off.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Apply `rate-limit calls="5" renewal-period="30"` to a product and send 10 requests in a loop with `curl`. Record the status codes and the `Retry-After` value.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement a per-user limit with `rate-limit-by-key` keyed on the JWT `sub` claim with a fallback to IP, and an `increment-condition` that ignores 4xx responses. Prove with two different tokens that each user has their own counter.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Our API has a 'Free' and a 'Pro' plan. A customer complains that they were throttled before reaching their documented limit. What could explain it?" *Hint:* overlapping limits at several scopes, a shared subscription across many users, counters per region or gateway, and how renewal windows align.

#### Request and Response Transformation

Backends rarely expose exactly the contract you want to publish. A legacy service may speak XML while clients expect JSON, an internal header may reveal infrastructure details, a backend URL may have a different shape than the public one, or a response may contain fields that external consumers should never see. Transformation policies adapt requests and responses in the gateway so the public contract stays clean while backends evolve independently.

The analogy is an interpreter at a business meeting. Each side speaks its own language and follows its own etiquette, and the interpreter converts in both directions, also deciding what is appropriate to pass along.

**Common transformation policies**

| Policy | What it changes | Example use |
|---|---|---|
| `set-header` | Add, override, append, or delete headers | Add a correlation ID, remove `X-AspNet-Version` |
| `set-query-parameter` | Add, override, or delete query parameters | Add a backend API key, remove a client-only parameter |
| `rewrite-uri` | Rewrite the backend path and query | Public `/orders/{id}` -> backend `/api/v1/order?id={id}` |
| `set-backend-service` | Change the backend base URL or backend entity | Route by header, region, or version |
| `set-body` | Replace the body (literal, C# expression, or Liquid template) | Reshape JSON, remove fields |
| `json-to-xml` / `xml-to-json` | Convert payload formats | Modern clients in front of SOAP/XML services |
| `find-and-replace` | String replacement in the body | Replace internal hostnames in links |
| `set-method`, `set-status` | Change HTTP method or response status | Expose a GET facade for a backend that requires POST |
| `mock-response` | Return a sample from the API definition without calling a backend | Front-end teams work before the backend exists |
| `return-response` | Short-circuit with a custom response | Maintenance mode, early validation errors |

**Example: URL rewrite and backend routing by header**

```xml
<!-- Operation template:  GET /orders/{orderId}       (public)  -->
<!-- Backend expects:     GET /api/v1/order?id=42     (legacy)  -->
<inbound>
    <base />
    <rewrite-uri template="/api/v1/order?id={orderId}" copy-unmatched-params="false" />
    <choose>
        <when condition="@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("X-Region","") == "us")">
            <set-backend-service base-url="https://app-orders-eus.azurewebsites.net" />
        </when>
        <otherwise>
            <set-backend-service base-url="https://app-orders-weu.azurewebsites.net" />
        </otherwise>
    </choose>
</inbound>
```

**Example: reshape and filter a JSON response**

Backend response:

```json
{ "orderId": "42", "customerEmail": "a@contoso.com", "internalCost": 61.5,
  "lines": [ { "sku": "A1", "qty": 2, "price": 40 } ], "status": "PAID" }
```

Policy with a Liquid template (Liquid exposes the parsed body as `body`):

```xml
<outbound>
    <base />
    <set-header name="Content-Type" exists-action="override">
        <value>application/json</value>
    </set-header>
    <set-body template="liquid">
    {
        "id": "{{body.orderId}}",
        "status": "{{body.status | Downcase}}",
        "items": [
        {% JSONArrayFor line in body.lines %}
            { "sku": "{{line.sku}}", "quantity": {{line.qty}} }
        {% endJSONArrayFor %}
        ]
    }
    </set-body>
</outbound>
```

Client receives (email and internal cost never leave the gateway):

```json
{ "id": "42", "status": "paid", "items": [ { "sku": "A1", "quantity": 2 } ] }
```

The same can be done with a C# expression when logic is more complex:

```xml
<set-body>@{
    var o = context.Response.Body.As<JObject>(preserveContent: true);
    o.Remove("internalCost");                  // drop sensitive fields
    o.Remove("customerEmail");
    return o.ToString();
}</set-body>
```

**Example: JSON facade over a SOAP/XML backend**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <json-to-xml apply="content-type-json" consider-accept-header="false" />
</inbound>
<outbound>
    <base />
    <xml-to-json kind="direct" apply="always" consider-accept-header="false" />
</outbound>
```

**Performance and safety notes**

- Body transformations require buffering the whole body in the gateway. Avoid them on large payloads or streaming responses, and watch the Capacity metric.
- Use `preserveContent: true` when reading a body that a later policy or the backend also needs. Without it, the body stream is consumed.
- Filtering sensitive fields in the gateway is a safety net, not a substitute for the backend not returning them.

**Key takeaways**

- Transformation policies decouple the public contract from backend implementation: headers, query, URL, method, backend, and body can all be changed.
- `set-body` supports literal text, C# expressions, and Liquid templates. Liquid is clearer for reshaping JSON.
- `json-to-xml` and `xml-to-json` let modern clients use legacy XML services.
- Body transformations cost CPU and memory. Use them deliberately and keep payloads small.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Remove the `X-Powered-By` and `Server` headers from all responses at global scope and add an `X-Correlation-Id` header to every request.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Use `mock-response` to publish a new operation from its OpenAPI example before the backend exists. Then switch it to the real backend with `rewrite-uri` without changing the public URL.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you do a transformation in APIM, and when would you change the backend instead?" *Hint:* number of consumers, ownership, latency and capacity cost, testability, and whether the transformation is a temporary bridge or permanent logic.

#### Caching Policies

Many API responses change far less often than they are requested: a product catalog, a list of countries, exchange rates refreshed hourly. Every repeated call to the backend costs latency, compute, and possibly money (database RUs, third-party fees). APIM can cache responses in the gateway so repeated requests are answered in milliseconds without reaching the backend, and it can also cache arbitrary values, such as tokens obtained from another service.

Think of a library's reference desk keeping the most-asked-for books on a cart next to the desk instead of walking to the archive every time. The cart has limited space, and books are returned to the archive (expired) after a while so readers don't get outdated editions.

**Two caching styles**

| Style | Policies | Caches | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Response caching** | `cache-lookup` (inbound) + `cache-store` (outbound) | Whole HTTP responses, keyed by URL and chosen variations | Catalogs, reference data, read-heavy GETs |
| **Value caching** | `cache-lookup-value`, `cache-store-value`, `cache-remove-value` | Any value under a key you choose | Tokens, lookups, results of `send-request` |

**Cache stores**

| Store | Availability | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Built-in (internal)** | Classic and v2 tiers, size depends on tier | Per region/unit group, lost on scale or restart events, not shared with self-hosted gateways |
| **External** (Azure Managed Redis or any Redis-compatible cache) | All tiers, required for Consumption | Survives restarts, shared across units, you control size. Configure under **External cache** and choose `caching-type="external"` or `"prefer-external"` |

**How the cache key is built.** Response caching keys on the URL and method by default. You extend the key with `vary-by-*` elements. Get this wrong in one direction and the cache is useless (hit rate near zero); get it wrong in the other direction and you serve one user's data to another.

| Element / attribute | Adds to the key |
|---|---|
| `vary-by-query-parameter` | Named query parameters |
| `vary-by-header` | Named request headers (for example `Accept`, `Accept-Language`) |
| `vary-by-developer="true"` | The subscription's owner, so each developer has separate entries |
| `vary-by-developer-groups="true"` | The developer's groups |
| `vary-by-custom` | Any custom string (from an expression) |

**Example: cache a catalog list for five minutes**

```xml
<!-- Operation: GET /catalog/products?category=...&page=... -->
<policies>
    <inbound>
        <base />
        <cache-lookup vary-by-developer="false" vary-by-developer-groups="false"
                      downstream-caching-type="public" must-revalidate="false"
                      caching-type="prefer-external">
            <vary-by-query-parameter>category</vary-by-query-parameter>
            <vary-by-query-parameter>page</vary-by-query-parameter>
            <vary-by-header>Accept</vary-by-header>
        </cache-lookup>
    </inbound>
    <backend><base /></backend>
    <outbound>
        <cache-store duration="300" />          <!-- seconds; only cacheable responses are stored -->
        <base />
    </outbound>
    <on-error><base /></on-error>
</policies>
```

On a hit, `cache-lookup` returns the cached response immediately and the `backend` section does not run. `downstream-caching-type` controls the `Cache-Control` header sent to clients and intermediate proxies.

**Example: cache a backend access token as a value**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <cache-lookup-value key="partner-token" variable-name="partnerToken" />
    <choose>
        <when condition="@(!context.Variables.ContainsKey("partnerToken"))">
            <!-- Cache miss: get a token from the partner's token endpoint -->
            <send-request mode="new" response-variable-name="tokenResp" timeout="10" ignore-error="false">
                <set-url>https://auth.partner.example/oauth2/token</set-url>
                <set-method>POST</set-method>
                <set-header name="Content-Type" exists-action="override"><value>application/x-www-form-urlencoded</value></set-header>
                <set-body>@("grant_type=client_credentials&client_id={{partner-client-id}}&client_secret={{partner-client-secret}}")</set-body>
            </send-request>
            <set-variable name="partnerToken"
                value="@((string)((IResponse)context.Variables["tokenResp"]).Body.As<JObject>()["access_token"])" />
            <!-- Store slightly shorter than the token's lifetime -->
            <cache-store-value key="partner-token" value="@((string)context.Variables["partnerToken"])" duration="3300" />
        </when>
    </choose>
    <set-header name="Authorization" exists-action="override">
        <value>@("Bearer " + (string)context.Variables["partnerToken"])</value>
    </set-header>
</inbound>
```

`{{partner-client-secret}}` is a **named value**, ideally a Key Vault reference, so the secret never appears in policy XML.

**Pitfalls**

- Never cache personalized responses without varying by the identity that personalizes them (user, developer, tenant). The safest default for per-user data is not to cache it at all.
- The cache is not invalidated when data changes in the backend. Pick durations the business can tolerate, or remove entries explicitly with `cache-remove-value`.
- Cache only safe, idempotent operations (GET). Response caching ignores responses that are not cacheable.

**Key takeaways**

- `cache-lookup` (inbound) and `cache-store` (outbound) cache whole responses. The `*-value` policies cache arbitrary values such as tokens.
- The built-in cache depends on the tier and is not shared or durable. External Redis-compatible caches work in all tiers and are required for Consumption.
- The cache key is the URL plus the `vary-by-*` elements. Under-varying leaks data between users, over-varying kills the hit rate.
- There is no automatic invalidation: choose TTLs deliberately.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add response caching with a 60-second duration to a GET operation. Call it twice and compare `TotalTime` and `BackendTime` for both calls in the gateway logs or the trace.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement the token-caching pattern above against a mock token endpoint and prove with logs that the token endpoint is called once per cache duration, not once per request.
> 3. **(Interview)** "After enabling caching on `GET /me/orders`, a customer reported seeing another customer's orders. What went wrong and how would you fix it?" *Hint:* what the cache key contains for that URL, `vary-by-developer` versus per-user keys, and whether this response should be cached at all.

#### JWT Validation

Most modern APIs authenticate callers with **OAuth 2.0 access tokens** in JSON Web Token (JWT) format, issued by an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID (covered in chapter 2). Validating those tokens in every backend works, but it duplicates code and configuration. APIM can validate the token at the edge and reject invalid calls before they consume backend resources, so backends receive only authenticated, authorized traffic.

The analogy is a concert venue: the security staff at the entrance check that each ticket is genuine (signature), is for this venue (audience), was issued by the official seller (issuer), is for today (expiry), and includes access to the VIP area if needed (claims). Staff inside don't have to check tickets again.

**What a JWT validation checks**

```text
eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsImtpZCI6Ii4uLiJ9 . eyJhdWQiOiIuLi4iLCJpc3MiOiIuLi4iLCJyb2xlcyI6WyIuLi4iXX0 . <signature>
\_______ header ____________________/   \____________ payload (claims) _________________________/
 alg, kid (which signing key)            aud, iss, exp, nbf, sub, tid, scp/roles, appid/azp

1. Signature   -> signed with one of the issuer's public keys (fetched from OpenID config / JWKS)
2. Issuer      -> iss matches the expected tenant/issuer
3. Audience    -> aud matches THIS API (prevents token reuse across APIs)
4. Lifetime    -> now is between nbf and exp (with small clock skew)
5. Claims      -> required scopes (scp) or app roles (roles) are present
```

**Two policies**

| Policy | Works with | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `validate-jwt` | Any OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.0 provider (Entra ID, Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, ...) and symmetric keys | Most flexible: issuers, audiences, signing keys or OpenID config URL, required claims |
| `validate-azure-ad-token` | Microsoft Entra ID tokens | Simpler configuration for Entra: tenant ID, client application IDs, audiences, claims |

**Example: validate an Entra ID token with `validate-jwt`**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" require-scheme="Bearer"
                  failed-validation-httpcode="401"
                  failed-validation-error-message="Unauthorized. Access token is missing or invalid."
                  output-token-variable-name="jwt">              <!-- parsed token for later policies -->
        <!-- Signing keys and issuer metadata are discovered and refreshed automatically -->
        <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{{tenant-id}}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" />
        <audiences>
            <audience>{{orders-api-client-id}}</audience>         <!-- v2 tokens: the API app's client ID -->
            <audience>api://orders-api</audience>                  <!-- v1 tokens: the App ID URI -->
        </audiences>
        <issuers>
            <issuer>https://login.microsoftonline.com/{{tenant-id}}/v2.0</issuer>
        </issuers>
        <required-claims>
            <!-- App-only callers (daemons) carry app roles in 'roles' -->
            <claim name="roles" match="any">
                <value>Orders.Read</value>
                <value>Orders.ReadWrite</value>
            </claim>
        </required-claims>
    </validate-jwt>

    <!-- Pass the caller's identity to the backend as a trusted header -->
    <set-header name="X-Caller-Object-Id" exists-action="override">
        <value>@(((Jwt)context.Variables["jwt"]).Claims.GetValueOrDefault("oid", ""))</value>
    </set-header>
</inbound>
```

**Example: the Entra-specific policy**

```xml
<validate-azure-ad-token tenant-id="{{tenant-id}}" header-name="Authorization"
                         failed-validation-httpcode="401">
    <client-application-ids>
        <application-id>{{mobile-app-client-id}}</application-id>   <!-- only these clients may call -->
    </client-application-ids>
    <audiences>
        <audience>api://orders-api</audience>
    </audiences>
    <required-claims>
        <claim name="scp" match="any" separator=" ">                  <!-- delegated scopes are space-separated -->
            <value>Orders.Read</value>
        </claim>
    </required-claims>
</validate-azure-ad-token>
```

**Per-operation authorization.** Validate the token once at API scope, then check operation-specific claims at operation scope, for example require `Orders.ReadWrite` only on `POST /orders`. A `choose` with `return-response` (403) works for checks the claim matching cannot express.

**Common mistakes**

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| No `audiences` check | Any token from the tenant, issued for any API, is accepted |
| Accepting tokens from `common`/multi-tenant issuers without checking `tid` | Users from any Entra tenant can call |
| Validating in APIM, but the backend is publicly reachable | Attackers bypass APIM entirely. Restrict the backend to APIM (7.3) |
| Confusing `scp` (delegated, user present) and `roles` (app roles, often app-only) | Valid callers rejected, or the wrong callers accepted |
| Returning 403 for an invalid token | 401 means "not authenticated", 403 means "authenticated but not allowed". Clients rely on the difference |

**Key takeaways**

- `validate-jwt` checks signature, issuer, audience, lifetime, and required claims at the edge. `validate-azure-ad-token` is a simpler variant for Entra ID.
- Use the OpenID configuration URL so signing key rotation is handled automatically.
- Always check the **audience**, and check scopes (`scp`) or app roles (`roles`) for authorization.
- Gateway validation is defense in depth, not a replacement for locking backends down to the gateway.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Register an API and a client app in Entra ID, get a token with the client credentials flow, and protect an APIM API with `validate-jwt`. Call it with no token, an expired or tampered token, and a valid token.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Require app role `Orders.ReadWrite` only on `POST` and `DELETE` operations while `GET` accepts `Orders.Read`. Use operation-scope policies and return 403 with a useful message when the role is missing.
> 3. **(Interview)** "If APIM validates the JWT, does the backend still need to validate it?" *Hint:* network paths that bypass the gateway, zero trust, what the backend needs from the token (user identity, tenant), and options such as mTLS or private networking between APIM and the backend.

#### Policy Expressions

Static policy values cover simple cases, but real rules depend on the request: route by a header, limit by a claim, log the subscription name, return a computed error body. **Policy expressions** are snippets of C# that the gateway evaluates per request, giving policies access to a rich `context` object describing the request, response, subscription, user, and more.

If policies are a form with fields, expressions are formulas in a spreadsheet cell: instead of typing a fixed value, you compute it from other values available at that moment.

**Syntax**

| Form | Syntax | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Single statement | `@(expression)` | `@(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("X-Tenant", "default"))` |
| Multi-statement | `@{ ...; return value; }` | Logic with local variables and `return` |
| Named value | `{{name}}` | Substituted before evaluation. Not an expression, but often combined with one |

Expressions use a subset of C# (language version 7) and only an allowlisted set of .NET types: strings, collections, `DateTime`, `Math`, regular expressions, `Newtonsoft.Json` (`JObject`, `JArray`), XML (`XDocument`), `Convert`, encoding and cryptography helpers, and a few others. You cannot do file I/O, open sockets, or reference arbitrary libraries. To call another service, use the `send-request` policy instead.

**The `context` object (most used members)**

| Member | Contains |
|---|---|
| `context.Request` | `Method`, `Url` (with `Path`, `Query`, `Host`), `Headers`, `Body`, `IpAddress`, `Certificate`, `MatchedParameters` |
| `context.Response` | `StatusCode`, `Headers`, `Body` (in outbound) |
| `context.Subscription` | `Id`, `Name`, `Key`, `PrimaryKey`, `SecondaryKey`, `CreatedDate` |
| `context.User` | The subscription owner: `Id`, `Email`, `Groups` |
| `context.Product`, `context.Api`, `context.Operation` | Names, IDs, paths of what was called |
| `context.Variables` | Values set by `set-variable` or output variables of other policies |
| `context.RequestId` | Unique ID per request, useful for correlation |
| `context.Deployment` | `Region`, `ServiceName`, gateway info |
| `context.LastError` | `Source`, `Reason`, `Message` in `on-error` |
| `context.Elapsed` | Time since the request arrived |

Helpers worth knowing: `GetValueOrDefault()` on headers and query, `AsJwt()` and `TryParseJwt()` on strings, `Body.As<JObject>(preserveContent: true)` for JSON bodies.

**Example: routing, enrichment, and safe defaults in one policy**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <!-- Read the tenant from the validated token, fallback to a header, then to "public" -->
    <set-variable name="tenant" value="@{
        var auth = context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization", "");
        Jwt jwt;
        if (auth.StartsWith("Bearer ") && auth.Substring(7).TryParseJwt(out jwt))
        {
            return jwt.Claims.GetValueOrDefault("tid", "public");
        }
        return context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("X-Tenant", "public");
    }" />

    <!-- Premium tenants go to a dedicated backend -->
    <choose>
        <when condition="@(((string)context.Variables["tenant"]).StartsWith("premium-"))">
            <set-backend-service backend-id="orders-premium" />
        </when>
    </choose>

    <!-- Reject very large uploads early -->
    <choose>
        <when condition="@(long.Parse(context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Content-Length", "0")) > 1048576)">
            <return-response>
                <set-status code="413" reason="Payload Too Large" />
            </return-response>
        </when>
    </choose>
</inbound>
<outbound>
    <base />
    <set-header name="X-Served-By" exists-action="override">
        <value>@(context.Deployment.Region)</value>
    </set-header>
</outbound>
<on-error>
    <base />
    <set-body>@{
        return new JObject(
            new JProperty("error", context.LastError.Reason ?? "error"),
            new JProperty("message", context.LastError.Message),
            new JProperty("requestId", context.RequestId.ToString())
        ).ToString();
    }</set-body>
</on-error>
```

**Named values and secrets**

```bash
# Plain value
az apim nv create -g $RG -n $APIM --named-value-id tenant-id --display-name tenant-id \
  --value "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000"

# Secret value (masked in the portal). Better: a Key Vault-backed named value via Bicep/portal,
# resolved by the APIM managed identity and refreshed on rotation.
az apim nv create -g $RG -n $APIM --named-value-id partner-client-secret \
  --display-name partner-client-secret --value "<secret>" --secret true
```

**Debugging expressions.** Use the **Trace** feature in the portal's test console (or the `trace` policy to write custom entries) to see each policy's input and output, including evaluated expressions and errors.

**Key takeaways**

- `@(...)` is a single C# expression, `@{ ... }` a multi-statement block that must `return` a value. `{{name}}` inserts a named value.
- `context` exposes the request, response, subscription, user, API, variables, deployment, and last error.
- Expressions run in a sandbox: allowlisted .NET types only, no I/O. Use `send-request` for external calls.
- Keep expressions small and readable. Move repeated logic into fragments, and secrets into Key Vault-backed named values.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write an outbound policy that adds an `X-Elapsed-Ms` header containing `context.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds`, and an `X-Subscription` header with the subscription name.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Write an `on-error` policy that returns a consistent JSON error body (`error`, `message`, `requestId`) for all APIs at global scope, and use the trace to verify it on a failing call.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A team wants to implement business pricing logic in APIM policy expressions so they don't need to redeploy the backend. Is that a good idea?" *Hint:* testability, versioning, visibility to developers, gateway CPU, and what belongs in a gateway versus a service.

<a id="83-securing-and-monitoring-apis"></a>
### 8.3 Securing and Monitoring APIs

A gateway is only as useful as the trust it can establish and the visibility it provides. This section covers the three main ways APIM identifies callers (subscription keys, OAuth 2.0 tokens, and client certificates), how it observes traffic through analytics, logs, and metrics, and how the self-hosted gateway extends the same controls to on-premises and other clouds.

#### Subscription Keys

The simplest way to know **who** is calling an API is to give each consumer a unique secret and require it on every call. In APIM, that secret is a **subscription key**, issued with every subscription (see 8.1). Keys are easy to use from any language or tool, which makes them the default for partner and public APIs, but they are an identification mechanism more than a strong authentication mechanism, and they should be understood as such.

The analogy is a gym membership card. The card identifies which member is entering, what plan they're on, and how often they come. But anyone holding the card can get in: it proves possession, not identity. For sensitive areas, the gym asks for photo ID as well (OAuth, certificates).

**How keys are sent**

| Method | Default name | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Header | `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` | Preferred. Not stored in URLs, browser history, or most access logs |
| Query string | `subscription-key` | Convenient for quick tests, but keys leak into logs, proxies, and referrer headers. Avoid in production |

Both names can be changed per API (`subscriptionKeyParameterNames`), for example to `X-Api-Key` to match an existing client contract.

```bash
# Header (preferred)
curl -s https://apim-shop.azure-api.net/orders/orders/42 \
  -H "Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key: $KEY"

# Missing or invalid key
# HTTP/1.1 401 Access Denied
# { "statusCode": 401, "message": "Access denied due to missing subscription key..." }
```

**What a key gives you**

- **Identification** for analytics, rate limits, and quotas (per subscription).
- **Product enforcement**: a key only unlocks the APIs in its scope.
- **Revocation**: suspend or cancel one subscription without affecting others.

**What a key does not give you**

- No user identity: everyone in a partner's organization shares the key.
- No expiry by default, so a leaked key works until someone notices.
- No proof of possession beyond the string itself. Keys embedded in mobile or browser apps are effectively public.

**Rotation with two keys**

Each subscription has a primary and secondary key so you can rotate without downtime:

```text
 Day 0:  clients use PRIMARY               secondary unused
 Day 1:  regenerate SECONDARY  ---------->  new secondary distributed to clients
 Day 2:  clients switch to SECONDARY        primary no longer used
 Day 3:  regenerate PRIMARY                 (old primary is now dead)
 Next rotation: same steps, roles swapped
```

```bash
BASE="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/$APIM"

# Regenerate the secondary key of one subscription
az rest --method post \
  --url "$BASE/subscriptions/fabrikam-prod/regenerateSecondaryKey?api-version=2022-08-01"

# Suspend a subscription immediately (e.g. after a leak)
az rest --method patch \
  --url "$BASE/subscriptions/fabrikam-prod?api-version=2022-08-01" \
  --body '{"properties":{"state":"suspended"}}'
```

Keys can also be set to explicit values, which helps when migrating from another gateway, and subscriptions can have an `expirationDate` so temporary access ends automatically.

**When to turn keys off.** For internal APIs called by your own apps with Entra ID tokens, keys add little and create a secret to manage. Set `subscriptionRequired: false` on the API (or use an open product) and rely on JWT validation. Many public APIs combine both: a key to identify the **application** (and apply its plan), and a token to identify the **user**.

**Key takeaways**

- Subscription keys identify the calling subscription for access, analytics, limits, and quotas. Send them in the `Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key` header, not the query string.
- Keys prove possession only: no user identity, no expiry by default, and anything in a client app is public.
- Rotate with the two-key pattern, suspend subscriptions on leaks, and set expiration dates for temporary access.
- Combine keys with OAuth or certificates for sensitive APIs, or disable keys where tokens alone are enough.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Call an API with the key in the header, in the query string, and with no key. Change the header name to `X-Api-Key` on the API and repeat.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Script a zero-downtime rotation for one subscription (regenerate secondary, update a Key Vault secret used by a client app, wait, regenerate primary) and verify the client keeps working throughout.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A product manager wants to put the API subscription key in our single-page app's JavaScript bundle. What are the risks and what would you propose?" *Hint:* the key is public once shipped, what an attacker can do with it, and alternatives such as a backend-for-frontend, OAuth with PKCE, or keyed limits per user.

#### OAuth 2.0 Integration

Subscription keys identify applications, but most APIs also need to know **which user** is calling and **what they are allowed to do**, and they should never handle user passwords. OAuth 2.0 solves this: an authorization server (Microsoft Entra ID, or another provider) issues short-lived access tokens, the client sends them as `Bearer` tokens, and the API validates them. In APIM, OAuth shows up in three distinct places, and it helps to keep them apart.

Think of a hotel again. Guests get a key card at check-in from the front desk (authorization server), which is valid for a few days and only opens certain doors (scopes). The doors (APIM) check the card. Separately, when the hotel's staff call a supplier, they use the hotel's own account with that supplier, not the guest's card (backend credentials).

**The three roles of OAuth in APIM**

| Where | APIM acts as | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **Client -> APIM** | Resource server: validates incoming tokens | `validate-jwt` / `validate-azure-ad-token` (8.2) |
| **Developer portal test console** | OAuth client for the "Try it" console | An **authorization server** configured in APIM and linked to the API |
| **APIM -> backend** | Client that obtains its own tokens | `authentication-managed-identity` (Entra-protected backends) or **credential manager** with `get-authorization-context` (third-party APIs such as GitHub, Salesforce) |

**End-to-end flow**

```text
 1. Client app ---- (auth code + PKCE / client credentials) ---> Entra ID
 2. Client app <--- access token (aud = api://orders-api, roles/scp) ---
 3. Client app ---- GET /orders  Authorization: Bearer <token> ---> APIM gateway
 4.                                     validate-jwt: signature, iss, aud, exp, roles
 5.                                     authentication-managed-identity:
                                         APIM's identity gets a token for api://orders-backend
 6.                                     ---- Bearer <APIM's token> ---> Orders backend
                                                                       (accepts only APIM's identity)
```

**Entra ID setup (summary)**

| App registration | Purpose | Key settings |
|---|---|---|
| **Orders API** | Represents the API | Application ID URI `api://orders-api`, exposed scopes (`Orders.Read`) for delegated access, app roles (`Orders.ReadWrite`) for app-only access |
| **Client app** | Represents the caller | API permissions to the scopes/roles above, redirect URIs, admin consent |
| **Developer portal client** (optional) | Lets the portal's test console get tokens | Redirect URI to the portal's OAuth callback |

**Example: validate the caller and authenticate to the backend with APIM's managed identity**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <!-- 1) Client -> APIM: is the caller's token valid for this API? -->
    <validate-azure-ad-token tenant-id="{{tenant-id}}">
        <audiences><audience>api://orders-api</audience></audiences>
        <required-claims>
            <claim name="roles" match="any"><value>Orders.ReadWrite</value></claim>
        </required-claims>
    </validate-azure-ad-token>

    <!-- 2) APIM -> backend: replace the caller's token with APIM's own token -->
    <authentication-managed-identity resource="api://orders-backend" />
    <!-- With a user-assigned identity: add client-id="{{apim-uami-client-id}}" -->
</inbound>
```

Token exchange (on-behalf-of) is the alternative when the backend needs the **user's** identity rather than APIM's: the backend or APIM exchanges the user token for a downstream token. Forwarding the original token unchanged works only if the backend accepts that audience.

**Example: calling a third-party SaaS API with credential manager**

Credential manager stores OAuth connections to providers (GitHub, Salesforce, Microsoft Graph, generic OAuth 2.0) and refreshes their tokens. Policies retrieve a valid token at runtime:

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <get-authorization-context provider-id="github" authorization-id="org-bot"
                               context-variable-name="ghAuth" identity-type="managed"
                               ignore-error="false" />
    <set-header name="Authorization" exists-action="override">
        <value>@("Bearer " + ((Authorization)context.Variables["ghAuth"]).AccessToken)</value>
    </set-header>
    <set-backend-service base-url="https://api.github.com" />
</inbound>
```

**Choosing the client flow**

| Client type | OAuth flow | Token contains |
|---|---|---|
| Web app with a backend | Authorization code | Delegated scopes (`scp`), user claims |
| SPA / mobile / desktop | Authorization code + **PKCE** | Delegated scopes (`scp`), user claims |
| Daemon, service, job | Client credentials (secret, certificate, or managed identity) | App roles (`roles`), no user |
| Device without browser | Device code | Delegated scopes |

Implicit and password (ROPC) flows are deprecated for new applications.

**Key takeaways**

- OAuth in APIM has three roles: validate client tokens, let the developer portal obtain tokens for testing, and obtain tokens for backends.
- Use `authentication-managed-identity` to call Entra-protected backends without secrets, and credential manager for third-party OAuth APIs.
- Register the API and client separately in Entra ID. Use scopes for delegated access and app roles for app-only access.
- Pick the flow by client type: authorization code with PKCE for user-facing apps, client credentials for services.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Configure an OAuth 2.0 authorization server in APIM for Entra ID, link it to an API, and use the developer portal's "Try it" console to call the API with a token obtained interactively.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Protect an App Service backend with Easy Auth so it accepts only tokens for `api://orders-backend` issued to APIM's managed identity. Add `authentication-managed-identity` and prove that direct calls with a user's token are rejected while calls through APIM succeed.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Should APIM forward the user's access token to the backend, or replace it with its own?" *Hint:* audience of the token, whether the backend needs user identity, on-behalf-of, least privilege, and what the backend's audit logs need to show.

#### Client Certificates

Some callers cannot or will not use OAuth: B2B partners with existing PKI, IoT devices, regulated integrations (banking, healthcare) that mandate mutual TLS, or legacy systems. **Client certificate authentication** (mutual TLS, mTLS) lets a caller prove its identity during the TLS handshake with a certificate and its private key. Unlike a subscription key, the private key never travels over the network, so intercepting traffic does not reveal a reusable secret.

In ordinary TLS, only the server shows a passport (its certificate). In mutual TLS, both sides show passports at the border, and each checks that the other's passport was issued by a country (certificate authority) it trusts and is not expired or revoked.

**Two directions**

| Direction | Purpose | Configuration |
|---|---|---|
| **Client -> APIM** (inbound mTLS) | Authenticate callers by certificate | Enable client certificate negotiation, upload trusted CA certificates (classic tiers), validate with `validate-client-certificate` or expressions |
| **APIM -> backend** (outbound mTLS) | APIM proves its identity to a backend that requires certificates | Store the certificate (ideally from Key Vault) in APIM, use `authentication-certificate` |

**Enabling inbound certificate negotiation**

- **Consumption tier**: enable the "Request client certificate" setting on the instance (`enableClientCertificate`).
- **Dedicated tiers**: enable **Negotiate client certificate** on the gateway hostname (custom domain or default). Check current tier documentation, as support and settings vary between classic and v2 tiers.
- If a TLS-terminating component (Application Gateway, Front Door) sits in front of APIM, the client certificate ends there. That component must handle mTLS and forward the certificate details in a header, and APIM must trust that header only from that component.

**Example: validate the client certificate with the dedicated policy**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <validate-client-certificate
        validate-revocation="true"
        validate-trust="true"
        validate-not-before="true"
        validate-not-after="true"
        ignore-error="false">
        <identities>
            <!-- Pin a specific partner certificate -->
            <identity thumbprint="{{partner-a-cert-thumbprint}}" />
            <!-- Or accept any certificate with this subject issued by this CA -->
            <identity subject="CN=orders-client.fabrikam.com" issuer-subject="CN=Fabrikam Issuing CA 01" />
        </identities>
    </validate-client-certificate>
</inbound>
```

**Example: the same with an expression, plus mapping certificates to tenants**

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <choose>
        <when condition="@(context.Request.Certificate == null
                          || !context.Request.Certificate.Verify()           // chain + revocation
                          || context.Request.Certificate.NotAfter < DateTime.UtcNow)">
            <return-response>
                <set-status code="403" reason="Invalid client certificate" />
            </return-response>
        </when>
    </choose>
    <!-- Tell the backend which partner called, derived from the trusted certificate -->
    <set-header name="X-Partner-Id" exists-action="override">
        <value>@(context.Request.Certificate.Thumbprint == "{{partner-a-cert-thumbprint}}" ? "fabrikam" : "unknown")</value>
    </set-header>
</inbound>
```

**Example: outbound mTLS to a backend**

```bash
# Certificate stored in Key Vault, referenced by APIM through its managed identity
# (created in the portal under Certificates, or with Bicep:
#  Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/certificates with keyVault.secretIdentifier)
```

```xml
<inbound>
    <base />
    <authentication-certificate certificate-id="bank-gateway-client-cert" />
</inbound>
```

**Operational concerns**

| Concern | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Expiry | Certificates expire. Track expiry dates and automate renewal through Key Vault certificate policies |
| Revocation | Keep `validate-revocation="true"` and ensure CRL/OCSP endpoints are reachable from the gateway |
| Thumbprint pinning | Precise but breaks on renewal. Prefer subject + issuer for partners with managed PKI |
| Self-signed certificates | Acceptable only when pinned by thumbprint. Never disable trust validation globally |

**Key takeaways**

- Mutual TLS authenticates callers by certificate during the TLS handshake. The private key never crosses the network.
- Inbound: enable certificate negotiation, then validate with `validate-client-certificate` or `context.Request.Certificate`.
- Outbound: `authentication-certificate` lets APIM present a certificate (from Key Vault) to backends that require mTLS.
- A TLS-terminating proxy in front of APIM changes the design: mTLS must happen at that proxy.
- Plan for expiry, renewal, and revocation from day one.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a self-signed client certificate with `openssl`, pin its thumbprint in `validate-client-certificate`, and call the API with `curl --cert client.pem --key client.key`. Then call without the certificate.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create a small private CA, issue two client certificates, and configure APIM to accept any certificate issued by that CA with a specific subject pattern. Revoke one and test revocation checking.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A bank partner requires mTLS, and our APIM sits behind Azure Front Door. How do you design this?" *Hint:* where TLS terminates, whether the edge supports client certificates, forwarding certificate information, and how APIM can trust that information only from the edge.

#### APIM Analytics

Once APIs are in production, the questions change: Which APIs are used most? Which consumers are hitting their limits? Is latency coming from the gateway or the backend? Which operation started returning 500s after yesterday's release? Because every call passes through the gateway, APIM is the ideal place to answer these questions consistently for all APIs.

The gateway is like a toll booth on a highway. It sees every car, knows which pass (subscription) it used, which exit (API and operation) it took, and how long the trip took. Aggregating that data tells you about traffic patterns without instrumenting every car.

**Observability options**

| Option | What you get | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| **Analytics** (portal blade, Azure Monitor-based dashboards) | Requests, latency, errors, by API, operation, product, subscription, geography | Quick business and operational overview |
| **Azure Monitor metrics** | `Requests` (with dimensions such as `GatewayResponseCodeCategory`, `ApiId`), `Capacity`, `Duration`, `BackendDuration` | Alerts, autoscale, dashboards |
| **Resource logs** (`GatewayLogs` -> `ApiManagementGatewayLogs`) | One row per request with timings, status codes, IDs, errors | KQL investigation, auditing, cost of access |
| **Application Insights** | Request telemetry, dependencies, end-to-end transaction view with backend telemetry, sampling | Distributed tracing across APIM and backends |
| **Event Hubs** (`log-to-eventhub` policy) | Custom events streamed to anything | SIEM, data lake, custom billing |
| **`emit-metric` policy** | Custom metrics with your own dimensions | Business metrics (orders per tenant) |

**Latency decomposition.** `TotalTime` = gateway processing + `BackendTime` + time to send the response to the client. If `TotalTime` is high and `BackendTime` is low, look at policies, gateway capacity, or slow clients. If both are high, look at the backend.

```text
 Client --------------[ TotalTime: 840 ms ]------------------------------> 
         | gateway in | ---[ BackendTime: 790 ms ]---> backend | gateway out |
         |   ~20 ms   |                                        |   ~30 ms    |
 -> the backend is the bottleneck
```

**Example: enable logs and Application Insights**

```bash
APIM_ID=$(az apim show -g $RG -n $APIM --query id -o tsv)
LAW_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show -g $RG -n law-shop --query id -o tsv)

# Resource-specific table ApiManagementGatewayLogs (instead of the generic AzureDiagnostics)
az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name apim-to-law --resource $APIM_ID \
  --workspace $LAW_ID --export-to-resource-specific true \
  --logs '[{"category":"GatewayLogs","enabled":true}]' \
  --metrics '[{"category":"AllMetrics","enabled":true}]'
```

```bicep
// Application Insights logger + diagnostic setting for all APIs
resource aiLogger 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/loggers@2024-05-01' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'appinsights'
  properties: {
    loggerType: 'applicationInsights'
    credentials: {
      connectionString: appInsights.properties.ConnectionString
    }
    resourceId: appInsights.id
  }
}

resource aiDiagnostics 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/diagnostics@2024-05-01' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'applicationinsights'
  properties: {
    loggerId: aiLogger.id
    alwaysLog: 'allErrors'                         // log every error regardless of sampling
    sampling: { samplingType: 'fixed', percentage: 25 }   // high-volume APIs: sample
    verbosity: 'information'
    httpCorrelationProtocol: 'W3C'                  // traceparent header for end-to-end traces
  }
}
```

Logging request or response bodies is possible (up to a configurable number of bytes) but has a real performance and privacy cost. Enable it selectively, and never for APIs carrying credentials or personal data unless masked.

**Example: KQL queries on gateway logs**

```kusto
// Error rate and p95 latency per API in the last hour
ApiManagementGatewayLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize requests = count(),
            serverErrors = countif(ResponseCode >= 500),
            throttled = countif(ResponseCode == 429),
            p95TotalMs = percentile(TotalTime, 95),
            p95BackendMs = percentile(BackendTime, 95)
          by ApiId
| extend errorRatePct = round(100.0 * serverErrors / requests, 2)
| order by requests desc
```

```kusto
// Which subscriptions still call v1 (before retiring it)?
ApiManagementGatewayLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) and ApiId == "orders-api-v1"
| summarize calls = count(), lastCall = max(TimeGenerated) by ApimSubscriptionId
| order by calls desc
```

```kusto
// Failures with the policy error reason
ApiManagementGatewayLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) and IsRequestSuccess == false
| project TimeGenerated, ApiId, OperationId, ResponseCode, LastErrorSource, LastErrorReason, LastErrorMessage, CorrelationId
| take 50
```

**Example: a custom business metric**

```xml
<outbound>
    <base />
    <emit-metric name="orders-created" namespace="shop-api" value="1">
        <dimension name="API ID" />
        <dimension name="Subscription ID" />
        <dimension name="tenant" value="@((string)context.Variables["tenant"])" />
    </emit-metric>
</outbound>
```

**Alerts worth having**: 5xx rate above a threshold per API, `Capacity` above 70% for 15 minutes, a sudden drop in total requests (clients cannot reach you), and 401/403 spikes (misconfigured clients or attacks).

**Key takeaways**

- APIM sees every call, which makes it the natural place for consistent API analytics.
- Use Azure Monitor metrics for alerts and autoscale, `ApiManagementGatewayLogs` for per-request KQL analysis, and Application Insights for end-to-end distributed tracing.
- Compare `TotalTime` with `BackendTime` to locate latency.
- Sample high-volume telemetry, always log errors, and be careful with body logging.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Enable gateway logs to Log Analytics, generate traffic including some 404s and 429s, and write a KQL query that counts requests by `ResponseCode` per operation.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Connect APIM and an App Service backend to the same Application Insights resource with W3C correlation, and find one request in the end-to-end transaction view showing both the gateway and the backend's SQL dependency.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Users report the API is slow, but the backend team says their service responds in 50 ms. How do you find out who is right?" *Hint:* `TotalTime` versus `BackendTime`, gateway capacity, expensive policies, network distance between client, gateway region, and backend, and client-side measurements.

#### Self-Hosted Gateway

Not every backend runs in Azure. Some APIs live in an on-premises datacenter, at a factory, or in another cloud. Routing all those calls through an Azure-hosted gateway adds latency and egress costs, and sometimes regulation requires that traffic never leaves a location. The **self-hosted gateway** is a containerized version of the APIM gateway that you run wherever your APIs are, while configuration, policies, and the developer portal remain managed centrally in Azure.

The analogy is a franchise. Headquarters (the APIM instance in Azure) defines the menu, recipes, and rules. Each franchise location (self-hosted gateway) cooks locally for local customers, regularly receives updated instructions from headquarters, and keeps working with the last instructions it had if the phone line to headquarters goes down.

**Architecture**

```text
                Azure                                      Your datacenter / other cloud / edge
 +---------------------------------------+               +------------------------------------------+
 | APIM instance (Developer / Premium)    |               |  Kubernetes / Docker                      |
 |  - management plane, policies          | <-- HTTPS 443 |  +------------------------------------+   |
 |  - developer portal                    |  outbound only|  | self-hosted gateway (container)    |   |
 |  - configuration endpoint              |  (config pull,|  |  - same policies as managed gateway|   |
 |    <name>.configuration.azure-api.net  |   telemetry)  |  |  - local cache, local rate limits  |   |
 |  - managed gateway (Azure traffic)     |               |  +------------------------------------+   |
 +---------------------------------------+               |        |                    ^              |
                                                          |        v                    | local calls  |
                                                          |   on-prem APIs          local clients      |
                                                          +------------------------------------------+
```

**Characteristics**

| Aspect | Detail |
|---|---|
| Availability | Developer and Premium tiers. Billed per gateway deployment in Premium |
| Image | `mcr.microsoft.com/azure-api-management/gateway:v2` (Linux container) |
| Connectivity | Outbound HTTPS (443) to the configuration endpoint. No inbound port from Azure needed |
| Authentication | A gateway **token** (expires, maximum 30 days) or Entra ID authentication for the gateway |
| Offline behavior | Keeps serving with the last known configuration. Optional local configuration backup survives restarts while disconnected |
| Deployment targets | Docker, Kubernetes (Helm chart or YAML), Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes (cluster extension), Azure Container Apps |
| Scope | You choose which APIs are assigned to each gateway resource |
| Differences | Some policies and features (built-in cache, some integrations) differ from the managed gateway. Check the feature comparison |

**Example: register a gateway and run it with Docker**

```bash
# 1) Create the gateway resource and assign an API (portal: Deployment + infrastructure > Gateways)
BASE="https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/$APIM"
az rest --method put --url "$BASE/gateways/factory-milan?api-version=2022-08-01" \
  --body '{"properties":{"locationData":{"name":"Milan factory"},"description":"On-prem MES APIs"}}'
az rest --method put --url "$BASE/gateways/factory-milan/apis/mes-api?api-version=2022-08-01" \
  --body '{"properties":{"provisioningState":"created"}}'

# 2) Generate an access token for the gateway (max 30 days; automate renewal)
EXPIRY=$(date -u -d "+29 days" +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
TOKEN=$(az rest --method post --url "$BASE/gateways/factory-milan/generateToken?api-version=2022-08-01" \
  --body "{\"keyType\":\"primary\",\"expiry\":\"$EXPIRY\"}" --query value -o tsv)
```

```bash
# env.conf (keep out of source control)
cat > env.conf <<EOF
config.service.endpoint=$APIM.configuration.azure-api.net
config.service.auth=GatewayKey $TOKEN
EOF

# 3) Run the gateway: HTTP on 80, HTTPS on 443 (container listens on 8080/8081)
docker run -d --name apim-gw -p 80:8080 -p 443:8081 \
  --env-file env.conf \
  mcr.microsoft.com/azure-api-management/gateway:v2

# 4) Local clients now call the gateway, which applies the same policies
curl -H "Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key: $KEY" http://localhost/mes/machines/42/status
```

For production, deploy to Kubernetes with at least two replicas, store the token in a Kubernetes secret, configure TLS certificates for the gateway hostname, and ship container logs to your monitoring stack. The gateway also reports heartbeat and basic metrics back to Azure, visible on the gateway resource.

**When to use it**

| Situation | Self-hosted gateway? |
|---|---|
| Backends on-premises, clients also on-premises | Yes: traffic stays local, policies stay central |
| Backends in another cloud, clients there too | Yes |
| Hybrid with strict data residency at a site | Yes |
| All backends in Azure | No: use the managed gateway (with VNet options) |
| You need a gateway in another Azure region | Usually no: Premium multi-region or a second instance is simpler |

**Key takeaways**

- The self-hosted gateway is the APIM gateway as a container, deployed next to your backends. Configuration and the developer portal stay in Azure.
- It needs only outbound HTTPS to Azure, and it keeps working with its last configuration if disconnected.
- It is available in the Developer and Premium tiers, and gateway tokens expire within 30 days, so automate renewal (or use Entra ID authentication).
- Run it on Kubernetes with multiple replicas for production, and remember its cache, rate-limit counters, and some features differ from the managed gateway.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Using a Developer-tier instance, create a gateway resource, assign the Echo API, run the container locally with Docker, and call the API through `localhost`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the gateway to a local Kubernetes cluster (kind or minikube) with the Helm chart and two replicas. Disconnect the cluster from the internet, restart one pod, and observe what happens with and without the configuration backup enabled.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A manufacturer wants central API governance in Azure but their factory APIs must keep working during internet outages. How would you design it?" *Hint:* self-hosted gateway placement, configuration backup, token lifetime and renewal, local identity provider reachability for JWT validation, and telemetry buffering.

<a id="84-workflow-integration"></a>
### 8.4 Workflow Integration

APIs rarely work alone: an order placed through one API must update a CRM, notify a team, write to an ERP, and archive a document. This section covers Azure Logic Apps, a managed workflow service that connects systems through triggers, actions, and hundreds of prebuilt connectors, how to choose between its two hosting models, and how to combine it with Azure Functions when a step needs custom code.

#### Azure Logic Apps Overview

Integration code is often the least interesting and most fragile code in a system: polling an inbox, calling three APIs in order, retrying on failure, transforming JSON, and handling OAuth tokens for each SaaS product. Written by hand, each integration needs hosting, retry logic, logging, secret management, and monitoring. **Azure Logic Apps** lets you build these integrations as **workflows** assembled from triggers and actions, with the platform providing retries, state, run history, and authentication for each connected service.

Think of an assembly line in a factory. A sensor at the start (the **trigger**) detects that a new item arrived. Each station along the belt (an **action**) does one job: inspect, paint, package. Some stations branch (conditions), some repeat for each part (loops), and a log records exactly what happened to every item. You design the line; the factory operates it.

**Core concepts**

| Concept | Description |
|---|---|
| **Workflow** | A series of steps defined in JSON (Workflow Definition Language), usually edited in the visual designer |
| **Trigger** | The first step, which starts a run: an HTTP request, a schedule, a new message in a queue, a new email, a new row in a table |
| **Action** | Every step after the trigger: call an API, send a message, transform data, run a condition or loop |
| **Connector** | A prebuilt wrapper for a service (Service Bus, SQL, Office 365, Salesforce, SAP, ...) that provides triggers and actions |
| **Run** | One execution of a workflow, with inputs and outputs of every step stored in **run history** |
| **Expressions** | Functions in `@{...}` / `@...` syntax to reference data: `triggerBody()`, `body('Step')`, `variables('x')`, `utcNow()`, `concat()` |

**When to use Logic Apps**

| Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|
| Integrating SaaS and enterprise systems (Office 365, Dynamics, SAP, Salesforce) | CPU-heavy computation or complex algorithms |
| Approval and notification workflows | Very low latency, high-throughput request processing |
| Scheduled data movement and file processing | Logic that is easier to express and test in code |
| B2B messaging (EDI, AS2, X12) | Workloads needing fine-grained control of the runtime |
| Orchestrating several APIs with retries and compensation | |

**Example: a workflow definition**

The designer generates JSON like the following. An HTTP request with an order starts the run, the order is validated, sent to a Service Bus queue, and a response is returned.

```json
{
  "definition": {
    "$schema": "https://schema.management.azure.com/providers/Microsoft.Logic/schemas/2016-06-01/workflowdefinition.json#",
    "contentVersion": "1.0.0.0",
    "triggers": {
      "When_an_order_is_received": {
        "type": "Request",
        "kind": "Http",
        "inputs": {
          "method": "POST",
          "schema": {
            "type": "object",
            "properties": {
              "orderId": { "type": "string" },
              "total":   { "type": "number" }
            },
            "required": [ "orderId", "total" ]
          }
        }
      }
    },
    "actions": {
      "Check_total": {
        "type": "If",
        "expression": {
          "and": [ { "greater": [ "@triggerBody()?['total']", 0 ] } ]
        },
        "actions": {
          "Send_to_queue": {
            "type": "ServiceProvider",
            "inputs": {
              "parameters": {
                "entityName": "orders",
                "message": { "contentData": "@triggerBody()" }
              },
              "serviceProviderConfiguration": {
                "connectionName": "serviceBus",
                "operationId": "sendMessage",
                "serviceProviderId": "/serviceProviders/serviceBus"
              }
            }
          },
          "Accepted": {
            "type": "Response",
            "inputs": { "statusCode": 202, "body": { "orderId": "@triggerBody()?['orderId']" } },
            "runAfter": { "Send_to_queue": [ "Succeeded" ] }
          }
        },
        "else": {
          "actions": {
            "Rejected": {
              "type": "Response",
              "inputs": { "statusCode": 400, "body": { "error": "total must be positive" } }
            }
          }
        },
        "runAfter": {}
      }
    },
    "outputs": {}
  }
}
```

(`ServiceProvider` actions are the built-in connectors of Logic Apps Standard. A Consumption workflow would use the managed Service Bus connector, `ApiConnection`, instead. See the next topics.)

**Reliability features built in**

- **Retry policies** per action (default: exponential, a few retries) for transient failures (408, 429, 5xx).
- **`runAfter`** conditions: run a step after the previous one `Succeeded`, `Failed`, `Skipped`, or `TimedOut`. This is how error handling works.
- **Scopes** group actions so you can implement try/catch/finally:

```text
 [Scope: Try]  -- Succeeded --> [Respond 200]
      |
      +--------- Failed/TimedOut --> [Scope: Catch: log error, notify team, respond 500]
```

- **Run history** stores inputs and outputs of every step for troubleshooting and resubmission. Use **secure inputs/outputs** on steps that handle secrets so they are hidden in history.

**Key takeaways**

- Logic Apps runs workflows: one trigger followed by actions, defined in JSON and usually designed visually.
- Connectors provide triggers and actions for hundreds of services, with authentication handled by the platform.
- Retries, `runAfter` error handling, scopes, and run history make integrations reliable and observable without custom plumbing.
- Use it for integration and orchestration. Put heavy or complex logic in code (Functions, containers).

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Build a workflow with an HTTP Request trigger that accepts a JSON body with a schema and returns a `Response` echoing one field. Call it with `curl` and inspect the run history.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Add a Try/Catch pattern with scopes: in the Try scope call an HTTP endpoint that fails half the time, and in the Catch scope (running after `Failed` or `TimedOut`) send the error details to a queue and return a 500.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why might a team choose Logic Apps over writing the same integration as an Azure Function, and when would you advise against it?" *Hint:* connectors and auth, retries and run history, who maintains it, testability, source control, cost per action, and performance.

#### Connectors and Triggers

The real productivity of Logic Apps comes from connectors: instead of reading an API's documentation, handling its OAuth flow, and writing pagination and retry code, you pick "When a new email arrives" or "Insert row" and fill in parameters. Understanding **how** connectors and triggers work underneath (polling versus push, built-in versus managed, connections and their identities) is what separates a demo workflow from a production one.

Think of connectors as universal power adapters for travel. Each country (service) has its own socket shape and voltage (API, protocol, auth). The adapter handles the differences so your device (workflow) just plugs in. Some adapters are built into your device (built-in connectors), others you rent from a shop that maintains them (managed connectors).

**Connector types**

| Type | Where it runs | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Built-in** | Inside the Logic Apps runtime | Request/Response, HTTP, Schedule, Control (condition, loop, scope), Data operations, Inline code, Azure Functions. In Standard also Service Bus, Event Hubs, Blob, SQL, Cosmos DB and more as "service provider" connectors | Lower latency, no per-connection resource, can reach VNet resources in Standard |
| **Managed** | Microsoft-hosted connector infrastructure, called through an **API connection** resource | Office 365 Outlook, SharePoint, Teams, Salesforce, SAP, Dynamics 365, Dropbox, hundreds more | Shared and throttled per connection. Standard tier connectors and Enterprise connectors are billed differently |
| **Custom** | Your API described by OpenAPI or Postman collection | An internal REST API | Reusable inside your organization like any connector |

A managed connector uses an **API connection** (`Microsoft.Web/connections`) that stores the authentication: an OAuth consent for a user, a connection string, or a managed identity. Prefer managed identity where the connector supports it, and use service accounts rather than personal accounts for OAuth connections, because the connection breaks when that person leaves.

**Trigger types**

| Trigger type | How it works | Examples | Cost/latency impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recurrence** | Runs on a schedule | Every day at 06:00, every 15 minutes | One run per interval |
| **Request** (push) | Exposes an HTTPS endpoint, run starts when called | Webhooks from GitHub, calls from APIM or apps | Instant, no polling cost |
| **Polling** | Checks the service on an interval for new data, starts a run only if something changed | "When a blob is added", "When an item is created" (SharePoint) | Each check is an execution (Consumption billing), latency up to the interval |
| **Webhook** (push) | Subscribes to the service, which calls back when an event happens, unsubscribes when disabled | Event Grid trigger, "When an HTTP webhook is called", Teams | Near-instant, efficient |
| **Sliding window** | Recurrence that processes contiguous time windows, catching up after outages | Hourly aggregation jobs | Guarantees no gap between windows |

```text
 Polling trigger:   [check] ---- 3 min ---- [check: 2 new items] ---- 3 min ---- [check] ...
                                                  |
                                                  +--> run(s) start

 Push trigger:      ............ event happens --> service calls workflow --> run starts immediately
```

**Controlling triggers**

| Setting | JSON | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Trigger conditions** | `"conditions": [ { "expression": "..." } ]` | Start a run only if the condition is true. Filters before a run exists, which saves cost and noise |
| **Split on** (debatching) | `"splitOn": "@triggerBody()?['value']"` | One run per array item instead of one run per batch |
| **Concurrency** | `"runtimeConfiguration": { "concurrency": { "runs": 10 } }` | Limit parallel runs, for example to protect a database |
| **Recurrence / polling interval** | `"recurrence": { "frequency": "Minute", "interval": 5 }` | Balance latency against executions |

**Example: Service Bus trigger with condition and concurrency, Outlook action (Consumption, managed connectors)**

```json
"triggers": {
  "When_a_message_is_received": {
    "type": "ApiConnection",
    "inputs": {
      "host": { "connection": { "name": "@parameters('$connections')['servicebus']['connectionId']" } },
      "method": "get",
      "path": "/@{encodeURIComponent('orders')}/messages/head",
      "queries": { "queueType": "Main" }
    },
    "recurrence": { "frequency": "Minute", "interval": 1 },
    "conditions": [
      { "expression": "@greater(json(base64ToString(triggerBody()?['ContentData']))?['total'], 1000)" }
    ],
    "runtimeConfiguration": { "concurrency": { "runs": 5 } }
  }
},
"actions": {
  "Notify_sales": {
    "type": "ApiConnection",
    "inputs": {
      "host": { "connection": { "name": "@parameters('$connections')['office365']['connectionId']" } },
      "method": "post",
      "path": "/v2/Mail",
      "body": {
        "To": "sales@contoso.com",
        "Subject": "Large order received",
        "Body": "<p>Order @{json(base64ToString(triggerBody()?['ContentData']))?['orderId']} exceeds 1000.</p>"
      }
    },
    "retryPolicy": { "type": "exponential", "count": 4, "interval": "PT10S" },
    "runAfter": {}
  }
}
```

**Securing the Request trigger.** A Request trigger's URL contains a **SAS signature** (`sig=...`) that grants the right to start the workflow. Treat the full URL as a secret: store it in Key Vault, rotate the access keys if it leaks, and for production put the workflow behind APIM, restrict inbound IPs, or require Entra ID tokens (OAuth authorization policies on the trigger).

```bash
# Get the callback URL (contains the SAS signature) for a Consumption workflow
az rest --method post \
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/resourceGroups/$RG/providers/Microsoft.Logic/workflows/la-orders/triggers/When_an_order_is_received/listCallbackUrl?api-version=2019-05-01" \
  --query value -o tsv
```

**Key takeaways**

- Built-in connectors run in the Logic Apps runtime. Managed connectors run in Microsoft-hosted infrastructure through API connection resources that store credentials.
- Prefer push triggers (Request, webhook, Event Grid) over polling for latency and cost. Tune polling intervals when polling is the only option.
- Trigger conditions, `splitOn`, and concurrency control what starts a run and how many run at once.
- The Request trigger URL is a secret. Use managed identities and service accounts for connections, never personal accounts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a workflow with a Recurrence trigger every 10 minutes that calls a public HTTP API and stores the result in a blob named after the current timestamp.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a workflow triggered by a Request receiving an array of 100 items. Compare one run with a `For each` loop versus `splitOn` producing 100 runs: look at run history, execution count, and failure isolation.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Our Logic App polls a SharePoint list every 30 seconds and the bill is higher than expected, while the list changes twice a day. What would you change?" *Hint:* how polling executions are billed, trigger conditions, longer intervals, and push-based alternatives such as webhooks or Event Grid.

#### Standard vs Consumption Logic Apps

Logic Apps comes in two hosting models that look similar in the designer but differ in runtime, pricing, networking, deployment, and development workflow. The choice affects cost, security architecture, and how developers work, so it should be made deliberately at the start.

The analogy is taxi versus a leased car. **Consumption** is a taxi: you pay per trip (per action executed), nothing to manage, but you share the road with everyone and have limited control. **Standard** is a leased car: a fixed monthly cost for dedicated capacity, more control (private roads, your own garage), and it pays off when you drive a lot.

**Comparison**

| Aspect | Consumption | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Runtime | Multitenant, shared Logic Apps service | Single-tenant runtime built on the Azure Functions extensibility model |
| Resource model | One workflow per Logic App resource | One Logic App resource hosts **many workflows** (like a Function App hosts many functions) |
| Pricing | Pay per execution (triggers, actions, connector calls) | Pay for the hosting plan (Workflow Standard WS1/WS2/WS3), plus managed connector calls |
| Workflow types | Stateful only | **Stateful** (run history, durable) and **stateless** (in memory, faster, no history by default) |
| Networking | Public endpoints only. Outbound IPs are shared per region | **VNet integration**, **private endpoints**, access restrictions, like App Service (7.3) |
| Built-in connectors | Core built-in set | Many more built-in "service provider" connectors (Service Bus, SQL, Blob, Event Hubs, SAP, ...) running in-process |
| Local development | Portal or Visual Studio Code (limited) | Full local development and debugging in **VS Code** with the Azure Logic Apps (Standard) extension |
| Deployment | ARM/Bicep templates with the definition embedded | Project files (`workflow.json`, `connections.json`, `host.json`) deployed as a zip, like Functions. CI/CD-friendly |
| Custom code | Inline JavaScript (needs an integration account), Azure Functions | Inline JavaScript, **custom .NET code** called from workflows, Azure Functions |
| B2B / EDI | Needs an **integration account** | Built-in maps and schemas in the project. Integration account still used for some B2B features |
| Hosting options | Azure only | Azure, plus a hybrid deployment model on your own infrastructure (Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes) |
| Best for | Low-volume, event-driven integrations, quick automation | Enterprise integration, high volume, private networking, DevOps teams |

The legacy **Integration Service Environment (ISE)**, which provided network isolation for Consumption workflows, has been retired. Standard is the replacement for workloads that need VNet access.

**Cost intuition**

```text
 Consumption cost ~ (trigger checks + actions + connector calls) x price per execution
 Standard cost    ~ plan instances x hours (+ managed connector calls)

  executions/month   Consumption   Standard (one WS1, always on)
  ---------------    -----------   ----------------------------
  low (thousands)      cheap         fixed cost dominates -> Consumption wins
  high (millions)      grows         flat -> Standard often wins
```

A polling trigger every minute is about 43,000 executions per month before any work is done. Estimate with the pricing calculator using real action counts per run.

**Example: Standard project layout and deployment**

```text
la-orders-std/                    # one Logic App (Standard) = many workflows
|-- host.json                     # runtime settings, extension bundle for built-in connectors
|-- connections.json              # built-in and managed connections (references app settings)
|-- parameters.json               # workflow parameters (per environment values via app settings)
|-- local.settings.json           # local only, in .gitignore
|-- ProcessOrder/
|   `-- workflow.json             # { "definition": {...}, "kind": "Stateful" }
`-- EnrichCustomer/
    `-- workflow.json             # { "definition": {...}, "kind": "Stateless" }
```

`connections.json` for a built-in Service Bus connection using managed identity:

```json
{
  "serviceProviderConnections": {
    "serviceBus": {
      "parameterValues": {
        "fullyQualifiedNamespace": "@appsetting('ServiceBus__fullyQualifiedNamespace')",
        "authProvider": { "Type": "ManagedServiceIdentity" }
      },
      "serviceProvider": { "id": "/serviceProviders/serviceBus" },
      "parameterSetName": "ManagedServiceIdentity",
      "displayName": "Orders Service Bus"
    }
  }
}
```

```bash
# Create a Standard Logic App (needs a storage account for state and run history)
az logicapp create -g $RG -n la-orders-std --storage-account stlaordersstd \
  --plan asp-la-ws1                              # a Workflow Standard (WS1) plan

# Deploy the project folder as a zip, exactly like a Function App
cd la-orders-std && zip -r ../la.zip . -x "local.settings.json" && cd ..
az logicapp deployment source config-zip -g $RG -n la-orders-std --src la.zip

# Consumption, for comparison: one resource per workflow, definition inline
az logic workflow create -g $RG -n la-orders-cons -l westeurope --definition workflow.json
```

**Key takeaways**

- **Consumption**: multitenant, one workflow per resource, pay per execution, public networking only. Great for low-volume and quick automations.
- **Standard**: single-tenant runtime on the Functions model, many workflows per resource, plan-based pricing, VNet integration, private endpoints, stateless workflows, and local development in VS Code.
- Standard's built-in connectors run in-process and can reach private resources. Managed connectors still run outside.
- Choose based on volume, network isolation, and DevOps needs. ISE is retired, and Standard replaces it for isolated workloads.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Estimate the monthly cost of a workflow with a 1-minute polling trigger and 5 actions per run, receiving 200 items per day, under Consumption and under Standard WS1, using the pricing calculator.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create a Standard Logic App locally in VS Code with one stateful and one stateless workflow, run both locally, deploy with zip deploy, and compare run history and latency.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An integration must read from a SQL database reachable only through a private endpoint and must be deployed through a pipeline with environment-specific settings. Which Logic Apps model and why?" *Hint:* VNet integration and built-in connectors in Standard, app settings and `parameters.json`, and project-based deployment.

#### Integrating Logic Apps with Functions
