| Log each tool call with inputs and outputs | Debugging, audit, and evaluation |

**Agent frameworks and services**

Writing the loop yourself is fine for one agent with a few tools. Frameworks add state management, memory, multi-agent orchestration, connectors, and observability:

| Option | What it is | Fits when |
|---|---|---|
| Foundry Agent Service | Managed agent runtime in a Foundry project: hosted threads and state, built-in tools (file search, Azure AI Search, Bing grounding, code interpreter, OpenAPI, MCP), tracing, and content safety | You want Azure to host state and tools, with enterprise networking and identity |
| Microsoft Agent Framework | Open-source SDK for .NET and Python, successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen; agents, graph-based workflows, multi-agent patterns | You host the agent in your own app and want Microsoft-supported orchestration |
| Semantic Kernel | Earlier Microsoft SDK with plugins and planners | Existing codebases; new work generally targets Agent Framework |
| LangChain / LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK | Popular open-source alternatives | Teams already invested in those ecosystems |

**Protocols**

- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** standardizes how agents discover and call tools exposed by a server. Expose your internal APIs once as an MCP server (Azure Functions and API Management can host or front MCP servers) and any MCP-capable agent can use them.
- **Agent-to-Agent (A2A)** lets agents built on different frameworks delegate tasks to one another.

**Multi-agent patterns**

| Pattern | Description |
|---|---|
| Sequential | Agents pass work along a pipeline (draft, then review, then format) |
| Concurrent | Several agents work in parallel and results are merged |
| Handoff | A triage agent routes the conversation to a specialist agent |
| Orchestrator (magentic) | A manager agent plans, delegates, and tracks progress across specialists |

Start with a single agent and a few well-designed tools; add agents only when one agent's instructions and tools become too broad to work reliably.

**Key takeaways**

- Tool calling lets a model request function calls; your code executes them and returns results.
- An agent is a model plus instructions, tools, memory, and a bounded loop.
- Treat tool arguments as untrusted, execute with the user's permissions, and require confirmation for side effects.
- Use Foundry Agent Service for managed hosting and built-in tools, or Microsoft Agent Framework to host orchestration in your own app.
- MCP standardizes tool access; multi-agent patterns are for when a single agent becomes too broad.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add a `get_store_hours(city)` tool to the loop above and test questions that need zero, one, and two tool calls.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Change `create_return` so it is only executed after an explicit "yes" from the user in a following turn, and write tests that try to trigger it through a prompt injection inside an order note returned by `get_order_status`.
> 3. **(Interview)** "When would you use a managed agent service instead of writing your own tool-calling loop?" *Hint:* conversation state storage, built-in tools, scaling, tracing, security boundaries, and how much control you need over orchestration logic.

#### Responsible AI Practices

AI systems fail in ways traditional software does not: they can be confidently wrong, treat groups of people unfairly, leak sensitive data, be manipulated through their inputs, or be used for purposes their builders never intended. Because outputs are probabilistic, you cannot unit-test every behavior into correctness. **Responsible AI** is the engineering discipline of identifying those risks, measuring them, mitigating them in layers, and monitoring them in production.

**Microsoft's Responsible AI principles**

| Principle | What it means for a developer |
|---|---|
| Fairness | Measure quality across user groups (languages, regions, demographics); avoid features that encode bias |
| Reliability and safety | Evaluate before release, handle failures gracefully, keep a human fallback |
| Privacy and security | Minimize and redact personal data, enforce permissions, defend against prompt injection |
| Inclusiveness | Support accessibility, multiple languages, and varied abilities |
| Transparency | Tell users they are interacting with AI, show sources, explain limitations |
| Accountability | Assign owners, keep audit logs, review incidents, document decisions |

**A practical lifecycle: map, measure, mitigate, operate**

```text
  MAP        identify harms for THIS use case: wrong answers, data leaks, jailbreaks,
             unfair outcomes, misuse; decide which matter most (impact assessment)
      │
      v
  MEASURE    build evaluation datasets; run quality and safety evaluators;
             red-team with adversarial prompts (manual and automated)
      │
      v
  MITIGATE   layered defenses (below); re-measure after each change
      │
      v
  OPERATE    monitor in production, collect user feedback, review incidents,
             re-evaluate on every model, prompt, or data change ──> back to MAP
```

**Layered mitigations**

```text
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ User experience: AI disclosure, citations, edit/confirm steps,│
  │                  feedback buttons, clear limitations          │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ System message and grounding: scope, rules, RAG,       │  │
  │  │ "say you don't know", data/instruction separation      │  │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │
  │  │  │ Safety system: content filters, Prompt Shields,   │  │  │
  │  │  │ groundedness and protected material detection     │  │  │
  │  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │  │  │
  │  │  │  │ Model: choose a model suited to the task    │  │  │  │
  │  │  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │  │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │  │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

No single layer is sufficient: a content filter does not stop a well-phrased wrong answer, and a good system message does not stop a determined jailbreak.

**Evaluations**

Evaluations turn "it seems to work" into numbers you can track. Foundry provides built-in evaluators, usable from the portal or the `azure-ai-evaluation` SDK:

| Category | Evaluators | Question answered |
|---|---|---|
| RAG quality | Groundedness, Relevance, Retrieval, Response Completeness | Is the answer supported by the sources and on topic? |
| General quality | Coherence, Fluency, Similarity, F1 | Is it well-formed and close to a reference answer? |
| Agent | Intent Resolution, Tool Call Accuracy, Task Adherence | Did the agent pick the right tools and finish the task? |
| Safety | Hate and Unfairness, Sexual, Violence, Self-harm, Protected Material, Indirect Attack | Does the system produce harmful output under adversarial input? |

**Example: score groundedness and relevance for a test set**

```python
# pip install azure-ai-evaluation
import os
from azure.ai.evaluation import GroundednessEvaluator, RelevanceEvaluator, evaluate

model_config = {                                   # the "judge" model that grades responses
    "azure_endpoint": os.environ["AZURE_OPENAI_ENDPOINT"],
    "azure_deployment": "gpt-4.1",
    "api_version": "2024-10-21",
}

groundedness = GroundednessEvaluator(model_config)

# Single check
score = groundedness(
    query="How many weeks of parental leave do I get?",
    context="Employees are entitled to 16 weeks of paid parental leave.",
    response="You get 16 weeks of paid parental leave, plus 2 extra weeks if you ask nicely.",
)
print(score)                                       # low score: the "2 extra weeks" is not in the context

# Batch over a JSONL file with query, context, response per line
results = evaluate(
    data="eval/rag-test-set.jsonl",
    evaluators={"groundedness": groundedness, "relevance": RelevanceEvaluator(model_config)},
    output_path="eval/results.json",
)
print(results["metrics"])                          # aggregate scores to track over time
```

Run the evaluation suite in CI (see chapter 12) and fail the pipeline when scores drop below agreed thresholds, exactly as you would for failing unit tests.

**Red teaming**

Red teaming probes the system as an attacker would: jailbreaks, prompt injection through documents, requests for harmful content, attempts to extract the system prompt or other users' data. Combine manual testing by people who understand the domain with automated tools such as Foundry's **AI Red Teaming Agent**, which builds on the open-source PyRIT toolkit to generate adversarial prompts and score how often attacks succeed.

**Privacy, data handling, and access**

- Prompts and completions sent to Azure OpenAI are **not used to train** models. Azure stores some data temporarily for **abuse monitoring**; approved customers can apply for modified abuse monitoring when they cannot allow any human review.
- Redact PII before logging prompts (13.1, Language PII detection) and apply retention policies to conversation history.
- Enforce authorization in retrieval and tools, never by asking the model to "not reveal" data.
- Some capabilities (face identification, custom neural voice) are **Limited Access** and require an application describing the intended use.
- Read the service's **transparency note**, which documents intended uses, limitations, and evaluation results.

**Operating in production**

| Signal | How to collect it |
|---|---|
| Quality drift | Scheduled evaluations on sampled production traffic |
| Safety events | Content filter and Prompt Shields results logged per request |
| User feedback | Thumbs up/down with optional comment, linked to the trace |
| Cost and latency | Token metrics and traces in Application Insights (chapter 11) |
| Incidents | An owner, a runbook, and a way to switch off a feature quickly (feature flags, chapter 7) |

**Key takeaways**

- Responsible AI is an engineering loop: map harms, measure them, mitigate in layers, operate and re-measure.
- Defense in depth: model choice, safety system, system message and grounding, and user experience together.
- Evaluate quality, safety, and agent behavior with evaluators and adversarial red teaming, and gate releases on the results in CI.
- Protect privacy: data is not used for training, redact PII, enforce permissions in code, and respect Limited Access requirements.
- Be transparent with users: disclose AI, show sources, and make it easy to give feedback or reach a human.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a one-page impact assessment for a RAG HR assistant: intended users, three most serious harms, and one mitigation per harm for each layer of the mitigation diagram.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Create a 25-row JSONL test set for your RAG app, run groundedness and relevance evaluators with `evaluate`, add a GitHub Actions step that fails when average groundedness falls below a threshold, and deliberately break the system prompt to see the gate trip.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your manager wants to ship an AI feature next week and asks what 'responsible AI' work is truly required. What do you say?" *Hint:* a minimum viable set: an impact assessment, an evaluation set with thresholds, content filters and Prompt Shields, AI disclosure and citations, logging and feedback, and an owner with a rollback plan.

<a id="14-cloud-architecture-patterns-and-best-practices"></a>
## 14. Cloud Architecture Patterns and Best Practices

Every earlier chapter introduced Azure services one at a time; this chapter is about combining them into systems that keep working when parts fail, scale without rewrites, and do not surprise anyone with the monthly bill. It covers the proven cloud design patterns for resiliency, data and messaging, and application structure, then the Azure Well-Architected Framework as a way to evaluate trade-offs, and finally the practical cost-management skills a developer needs. Patterns are vocabulary: once you know them, design reviews and interview questions become conversations about which trade-off fits, not guesswork.

<a id="141-resiliency-patterns"></a>
### 14.1 Resiliency Patterns

In the cloud, failure is normal: instances are recycled, networks drop packets, and services throttle you. This section covers the patterns that turn those everyday failures into non-events instead of outages.

#### Retry with Exponential Backoff

**Why it exists**

Many cloud failures are **transient**: a brief network blip, a load balancer moving traffic during a platform update, a database failing over to a replica, or a service returning `429 Too Many Requests` because you briefly exceeded a quota. The same request a second later would succeed. If your code treats every error as permanent, users see failures that never needed to happen.

Retrying naively is dangerous, though. If a thousand clients all retry instantly and in lockstep after a service hiccup, they create a **retry storm** that keeps the service down. The fix is to wait between attempts, wait longer each time (**exponential backoff**), and add randomness (**jitter**) so clients spread out.

An analogy: when a phone line is busy, you do not redial every millisecond. You wait a bit, then a bit longer, and everybody calling the same number waits a slightly different amount of time.

**What to retry and what not to**

| Retry | Do not retry |
|---|---|
| Timeouts, connection resets, DNS hiccups | `400 Bad Request` (the request is wrong) |
| `408`, `429`, `500`, `502`, `503`, `504` | `401` / `403` (credentials will not fix themselves) |
| Service Bus `ServerBusy`, Cosmos DB `429` | `404 Not Found`, `409 Conflict` (unless your logic expects it) |
| SQL transient error codes (e.g. 40613, 40197, 49918) | Validation or business-rule failures |

Two more rules matter:

- **Honor `Retry-After`**. When a service returns `429` or `503` with a `Retry-After` (or `x-ms-retry-after-ms`) header, it is telling you exactly how long to wait. Use that value instead of your own backoff.
- **Only retry idempotent operations**, or make them idempotent. Retrying `GET` is safe. Retrying "charge the card" without an idempotency key can charge twice, because the first attempt may have succeeded and only the response was lost.

**How the delays grow**

The classic formula is `delay = min(cap, base * 2^attempt)`, and **full jitter** picks a random value between zero and that number:

| Attempt | Exponential delay (base 0.5 s, cap 30 s) | Full-jitter delay (random) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.5 s | 0 to 0.5 s |
| 2 | 1 s | 0 to 1 s |
| 3 | 2 s | 0 to 2 s |
| 4 | 4 s | 0 to 4 s |
| 5 | 8 s | 0 to 8 s |
| 8 | 30 s (capped) | 0 to 30 s |

```text
Without jitter: all clients retry at the same instants -> load spikes
  load
   |  #         #               #
   |  #         #               #
   +--+---------+---------------+-------> time
     t+1s      t+2s            t+4s

With full jitter: retries are spread out -> the service can recover
  load
   |  . : . : . : . . : . . . : . . . . .
   +-------------------------------------> time
```

**Example 1: let the Azure SDK do it**

Every Azure SDK client already has a retry policy (see chapter 1). Tune it rather than wrapping SDK calls in your own loops, which would multiply attempts (5 outer retries x 3 inner retries = 15 calls).

```python
# pip install azure-identity azure-storage-blob
from azure.core.pipeline.policies import RetryMode
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

client = BlobServiceClient(
    account_url="https://stshopdev.blob.core.windows.net",
    credential=DefaultAzureCredential(),
    retry_total=5,                     # at most 5 retries after the first attempt
    retry_mode=RetryMode.Exponential,  # 0.8 s, 1.6 s, 3.2 s ... (with built-in jitter)
    retry_backoff_factor=0.8,          # base delay in seconds
    retry_backoff_max=30,              # never wait longer than 30 s between attempts
)
```

```csharp
// .NET: the same knobs live on ClientOptions.Retry for every Azure SDK client
var options = new BlobClientOptions();
options.Retry.Mode = RetryMode.Exponential;
options.Retry.MaxRetries = 5;
options.Retry.Delay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(0.8);      // base delay
options.Retry.MaxDelay = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30);    // cap
options.Retry.NetworkTimeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30); // per-attempt timeout

var client = new BlobServiceClient(
    new Uri("https://stshopdev.blob.core.windows.net"),
    new DefaultAzureCredential(),
    options);
```

**Example 2: your own HTTP dependencies**

For calls to your own services or third-party APIs, use a resilience library instead of hand-written loops. In .NET that is `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience` (built on Polly v8); in Python, `tenacity` is common.

```csharp
// dotnet add package Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<InventoryClient>(c =>
        c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://ca-inventory.internal.example.net"))
    .AddResilienceHandler("inventory", pipeline =>
    {
        pipeline.AddRetry(new HttpRetryStrategyOptions
        {
            MaxRetryAttempts = 4,
            BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
            UseJitter = true,                        // spread retries across clients
            Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(500),  // base delay
            ShouldRetryAfterHeader = true            // honor Retry-After on 429/503
        });
        pipeline.AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2)); // per-attempt timeout
    });
```

```python
# pip install tenacity requests
import requests
from tenacity import retry, retry_if_exception, stop_after_attempt, wait_random_exponential

TRANSIENT = {408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504}

def is_transient(exc: BaseException) -> bool:
    if isinstance(exc, (requests.ConnectionError, requests.Timeout)):
        return True
    if isinstance(exc, requests.HTTPError) and exc.response is not None:
        return exc.response.status_code in TRANSIENT
    return False                                   # 400, 401, 404 ... fail fast

@retry(
    retry=retry_if_exception(is_transient),
    wait=wait_random_exponential(multiplier=0.5, max=30),  # full jitter, capped at 30 s
    stop=stop_after_attempt(5),                            # 1 attempt + 4 retries
    reraise=True,                                          # surface the real error at the end
)
def get_stock(sku: str) -> dict:
    resp = requests.get(f"https://inventory.example.net/stock/{sku}", timeout=2)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()
```

**Where retries belong in a call chain**

If a web front end retries 3 times, calls an API that retries 3 times, which calls a database that retries 3 times, one user action can produce 27 database calls during an outage. Retry at **one layer**, preferably the one closest to the failing dependency, and let outer layers fail fast. Also bound the total time: a retry policy that keeps a user waiting 90 seconds is worse than an immediate, friendly error.

**Key takeaways**

- Retry only transient failures (timeouts, `429`, `5xx`), never client errors such as `400` or `401`.
- Use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum delay; honor `Retry-After` when the service provides it.
- Only retry idempotent operations, or add idempotency keys so duplicates are harmless.
- Azure SDK clients retry by default: configure their policy instead of wrapping them in extra loops.
- Retry at one layer and cap total time, or retries multiply across the call chain.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Write a Python function that prints the full-jitter delays for 8 attempts with base 0.5 s and cap 20 s. Run it three times and compare the outputs.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Build a small Flask endpoint that returns `503` with `Retry-After: 3` for the first two calls and `200` afterward. Call it with the `tenacity` example, then change the code so it sleeps for the `Retry-After` value when present, and log the actual waits.
> 3. **(Interview)** "During a regional incident your service's dependency starts returning 503s, and your retries make the incident worse. Why, and how do you fix it?" *Hint:* think about synchronized retries, retries at several layers multiplying load, missing jitter and caps, and what should happen after retries are exhausted (see the next topic).

#### Circuit Breaker

**Why it exists**

Retries assume the failure is brief. When a dependency is down for minutes, retrying every request wastes threads, connections, and time: each user waits for several timeouts before getting an error, and your own service can run out of resources while waiting on a dead one. That is how one failing service takes down everything that calls it (a **cascading failure**).

A **circuit breaker** watches calls to a dependency. When failures cross a threshold, it "trips" and makes subsequent calls fail immediately without even trying, giving the dependency room to recover and giving your callers a fast answer. After a cooling-off period, it lets a few trial calls through to check whether the dependency is healthy again.

The analogy is the electrical breaker in your house: when a circuit overloads, the breaker cuts it off so the wiring does not catch fire. You fix the problem, then flip it back.

**The three states**

```text
                failures >= threshold
     +--------+ ------------------------> +--------+
     | CLOSED |                            |  OPEN  |  calls fail immediately
     +--------+ <--+                       +--------+  (no network call)
   calls flow      |                           |
   normally,       | trial call succeeds       | break duration elapses
   failures        |                           v
   are counted     |                      +-----------+
                   +--------------------- | HALF-OPEN |  let a few trial calls through
                                          +-----------+
                         trial call fails ----> back to OPEN
```

| State | Behavior | Exits when |
|---|---|---|
| Closed | Requests pass through; failures are counted in a sliding window | Failure ratio or count crosses the threshold |
| Open | Requests fail fast with a "circuit open" error | Break duration elapses |
| Half-open | A limited number of trial requests pass | Trial succeeds (to Closed) or fails (back to Open) |

**What to do while the circuit is open**

Failing fast is only half the value; the other half is a **fallback**:

- Serve cached or stale data ("prices as of 5 minutes ago").
- Degrade gracefully (hide the recommendations panel instead of failing the product page).
- Queue the work for later (accept the order, process payment when the processor recovers).
- Return a clear error quickly (`503` with `Retry-After`) when none of the above is possible.

**Example 1: a minimal implementation to understand the mechanics**

```python
import time

class CircuitOpenError(Exception):
    pass

class CircuitBreaker:
    def __init__(self, failure_threshold=5, reset_timeout=15.0):
        self.failure_threshold = failure_threshold
        self.reset_timeout = reset_timeout
        self.failures = 0
        self.state = "closed"
        self.opened_at = 0.0

    def call(self, fn, *args, **kwargs):
        if self.state == "open":
            if time.monotonic() - self.opened_at < self.reset_timeout:
                raise CircuitOpenError("dependency unavailable")  # fail fast, no network call
            self.state = "half-open"                               # allow one trial call

        try:
            result = fn(*args, **kwargs)
        except Exception:
            self.failures += 1
            if self.state == "half-open" or self.failures >= self.failure_threshold:
                self.state = "open"                                # trip (or re-trip)
                self.opened_at = time.monotonic()
            raise
        else:
            self.failures = 0                                      # success resets the count
            self.state = "closed"
            return result

# Usage with a fallback
breaker = CircuitBreaker()

def product_page(sku):
    try:
        recs = breaker.call(get_recommendations, sku)
    except CircuitOpenError:
        recs = []                         # degrade: page renders without recommendations
    return {"sku": sku, "recommendations": recs}
```

Production implementations add a sliding time window, a failure *ratio* rather than a raw count, thread safety, and metrics. Use a library.

**Example 2: Polly in .NET combined with retry and timeouts**

```csharp
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentsClient>(c =>
        c.BaseAddress = new Uri("https://payments.example.net"))
    .AddResilienceHandler("payments", pipeline =>
    {
        pipeline.AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10));   // outer: total time budget

        pipeline.AddRetry(new HttpRetryStrategyOptions
        {
            MaxRetryAttempts = 2,
            BackoffType = DelayBackoffType.Exponential,
            UseJitter = true
        });

        pipeline.AddCircuitBreaker(new HttpCircuitBreakerStrategyOptions
        {
            FailureRatio = 0.5,                           // trip when 50% of calls fail...
            MinimumThroughput = 10,                       // ...out of at least 10 calls...
            SamplingDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),  // ...within a 30 s window
            BreakDuration = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(15)      // stay open 15 s, then half-open
        });

        pipeline.AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));    // inner: per-attempt timeout
    });

// While open, calls throw BrokenCircuitException immediately
try
{
    await paymentsClient.AuthorizeAsync(order);
}
catch (BrokenCircuitException)
{
    await outbox.EnqueueForLaterAsync(order);  // fallback: accept now, charge later
}
```

The order matters: the retry sits *outside* the breaker, so once the breaker opens, retries fail fast instead of hammering the dependency.

**Example 3: circuit breaking at the gateway**

Azure API Management backends support a built-in circuit breaker, so every API that routes to a backend is protected without code changes:

```bicep
resource ordersBackend 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/backends@2024-05-01' = {
  parent: apim
  name: 'orders-backend'
  properties: {
    url: 'https://ca-orders.internal.example.net'
    protocol: 'http'
    circuitBreaker: {
      rules: [
        {
          name: 'orders-breaker'
          failureCondition: {
            count: 5                                  // 5 failures...
            interval: 'PT1M'                          // ...within 1 minute trips the breaker
            statusCodeRanges: [ { min: 500, max: 599 } ]
            errorReasons: [ 'Server errors' ]
          }
          tripDuration: 'PT1M'                        // stay open for 1 minute
          acceptRetryAfter: true                      // use the backend's Retry-After if sent
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

Combined with backend **pools**, APIM can route around a tripped backend to a healthy one in another region.

**Key takeaways**

- A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly failing, so callers fail fast and the dependency can recover.
- States: Closed (counting), Open (fail fast), Half-open (trial calls).
- Pair it with a fallback: cached data, degraded features, or queued work.
- Place retries outside the breaker and keep per-attempt timeouts short.
- You can implement it in code (Polly, resilience libraries), in a sidecar (Dapr, 14.3), or at the gateway (APIM backends).

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Using the Python `CircuitBreaker` above, call a function that always raises for 10 iterations with a 0.5 s sleep between calls and print the state after each call. Identify where the circuit opens and when it moves to half-open.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Extend the Python implementation to use a failure *ratio* over a sliding window of the last 20 calls with a minimum throughput of 10, and emit a log line on every state transition so you could alert on it.
> 3. **(Interview)** "What is the difference between a retry and a circuit breaker, and why do you usually need both?" *Hint:* one handles brief faults, the other handles sustained ones; think about what happens to thread pools and user latency when only retries exist.

#### Bulkhead

**Why it exists**

Imagine a web API where every request uses the same pool of 100 outbound connections. One downstream dependency (say, a slow reporting service) starts taking 30 seconds per call. Within moments all 100 connections are stuck waiting on it, and requests that never touch the reporting service, such as checkout, also fail because there are no connections left. One slow dependency has consumed a resource that everything shares.

The **bulkhead** pattern partitions resources so that a failure in one partition cannot sink the others. The name comes from ships: the hull is divided into watertight compartments, so a breach floods one compartment instead of the whole ship.

```text
Shared pool (no bulkheads)              Partitioned pools (bulkheads)

 +--------------------------+            +-----------+  +-----------+  +-----------+
 |  100 shared connections  |            | checkout  |  | catalog   |  | reports   |
 |  ######################  |            | 40 conns  |  | 40 conns  |  | 20 conns  |
 |  (all stuck on reports)  |            |  healthy  |  |  healthy  |  | ######### |
 +--------------------------+            +-----------+  +-----------+  +-----------+
  checkout, catalog, reports              slow reports exhausts only its own pool
  all fail                                checkout and catalog keep working
```

**Levels at which you can apply bulkheads**

| Level | Azure example |
|---|---|
| In-process concurrency | Separate `HttpClient` handlers or semaphores per dependency; Polly concurrency limiter |
| Compute | Separate App Service plans or Function apps for critical and non-critical workloads; AKS node pools; Container Apps workload profiles |
| Messaging | Separate Service Bus queues (or topics with subscriptions) per workload, so a backlog in one does not delay another |
| Data | Dedicated Cosmos DB throughput per container instead of shared database throughput for a noisy workload; separate SQL elastic pools |
| Tenancy | Deployment stamps: one copy of the stack per group of tenants, so a noisy tenant affects only its stamp |
| Region and zone | Zone-redundant deployments, multi-region active-active (chapter 1) |

**Example 1: per-dependency concurrency limits in Python**

```python
import asyncio
import httpx

# Each dependency gets its own budget of concurrent calls
LIMITS = {
    "payments": asyncio.Semaphore(40),
    "catalog": asyncio.Semaphore(40),
    "reports": asyncio.Semaphore(10),    # slow, non-critical: small compartment
}

class BulkheadFullError(Exception):
    pass

async def call_dependency(name: str, client: httpx.AsyncClient, url: str):
    sem = LIMITS[name]
    try:
        # Wait at most 100 ms for a slot; do not queue forever behind a slow dependency
        await asyncio.wait_for(sem.acquire(), timeout=0.1)
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        raise BulkheadFullError(f"{name} bulkhead is full")   # reject fast, protect the caller
    try:
        resp = await client.get(url, timeout=5)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        return resp.json()
    finally:
        sem.release()
```

**Example 2: Polly concurrency limiter in .NET**

```csharp
// dotnet add package Polly.RateLimiting
builder.Services.AddHttpClient<ReportsClient>()
    .AddResilienceHandler("reports", pipeline =>
    {
        // At most 10 concurrent calls, 5 more may wait; the rest are rejected immediately
        pipeline.AddConcurrencyLimiter(permitLimit: 10, queueLimit: 5);
        pipeline.AddTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
    });
// Rejected calls throw RateLimiterRejectedException: map it to 503 or a fallback
```

**Example 3: compute isolation with separate plans**

```bash
# Critical, customer-facing API on its own plan
az appservice plan create -g rg-shop-prod -n asp-shop-api --sku P1v3 --is-linux
az webapp create -g rg-shop-prod -p asp-shop-api -n app-shop-api --runtime "DOTNETCORE:8.0"

# Heavy back-office jobs on a different plan: a CPU spike there cannot starve the API
az appservice plan create -g rg-shop-prod -n asp-shop-backoffice --sku P1v3 --is-linux
az webapp create -g rg-shop-prod -p asp-shop-backoffice -n app-shop-backoffice --runtime "DOTNETCORE:8.0"
```

Apps in the same App Service plan share the same VMs, so putting a batch job next to your public API is the opposite of a bulkhead.

**The trade-off**

Bulkheads cost efficiency: partitioned pools mean some capacity sits idle while another partition is busy, and more plans or queues mean more to manage and pay for. Apply them where the blast radius matters: between critical and non-critical paths, and around dependencies with a history of slowness.

**Key takeaways**

- A bulkhead isolates resources so a failing or slow component exhausts only its own compartment.
- Apply it at several levels: concurrency limits in code, separate compute, separate queues, separate data throughput, and deployment stamps.
- Reject quickly when a compartment is full rather than queuing indefinitely.
- Combine with timeouts and circuit breakers: bulkheads limit damage, breakers stop calling a broken dependency.
- The cost is lower utilization and more moving parts; isolate where the blast radius justifies it.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** List the dependencies of an app you know (database, cache, two external APIs, a reporting service) and classify each as critical or non-critical. Propose a concurrency limit for each.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Using the Python example, simulate a "reports" endpoint that sleeps 10 seconds and a "catalog" endpoint that returns instantly. Fire 200 concurrent requests at each through `call_dependency` and show that catalog latency stays low while reports requests are rejected.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A noisy tenant in your multi-tenant SaaS slows everyone down. How would you redesign to contain it?" *Hint:* consider per-tenant rate limits, separate queues or throughput per tier, and deployment stamps that cap the blast radius to a subset of tenants.

#### Health Endpoint Monitoring

**Why it exists**

A load balancer, orchestrator, or monitoring system needs an answer to a simple question: "Should I send traffic to this instance, restart it, or page someone?" A process that is running is not necessarily working: it may have lost its database connection, exhausted its thread pool, or be stuck in a deadlock. The **health endpoint monitoring** pattern exposes dedicated HTTP endpoints that report the application's actual health, so the platform can act on it automatically.

Think of it as a regular check-up: a doctor does not ask "are you alive?" but checks the vital signs that matter.

**Liveness, readiness, and startup**

Not every check should trigger the same action. Mixing them up is the most common mistake:

| Probe | Question it answers | Action on failure | What to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liveness | "Is this process broken beyond repair?" | Restart the instance | Only the process itself (can it respond at all?) |
| Readiness | "Can this instance serve traffic right now?" | Stop routing traffic to it (do not restart) | Critical dependencies: database reachable, cache warmed, config loaded |
| Startup | "Has the app finished starting?" | Wait; liveness/readiness are paused until it passes | Slow initialization (migrations, model loading) |

Why not check the database in the liveness probe? If the database goes down, every instance fails liveness, the orchestrator restarts all of them, and they all fail again: you have turned a database outage into an application restart loop that also delays recovery.

```text
           Front Door / App Service LB / Container Apps ingress
                 |                 |                 |
           GET /healthz/ready  GET /healthz/ready  GET /healthz/ready
                 v                 v                 v
           +-----------+     +-----------+     +-----------+
           | instance1 |     | instance2 |     | instance3 |
           |  200 OK   |     |  503      |     |  200 OK   |
           +-----------+     +-----------+     +-----------+
                              removed from rotation
                              (restarted only if /healthz/live also fails)
```

**Example 1: ASP.NET Core health checks**

```csharp
using Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.HealthChecks;

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks()
    // Liveness: the process can run code and respond
    .AddCheck("self", () => HealthCheckResult.Healthy(), tags: ["live"])
    // Readiness: critical dependencies are reachable
    .AddCheck<SqlReadyCheck>("sql", tags: ["ready"]);

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz/live", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("live")
});
app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz/ready", new HealthCheckOptions
{
    Predicate = check => check.Tags.Contains("ready")
});

public sealed class SqlReadyCheck(SqlConnectionFactory factory) : IHealthCheck
{
    public async Task<HealthCheckResult> CheckHealthAsync(
        HealthCheckContext context, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        try
        {
            await using var conn = await factory.OpenAsync(ct);
            await using var cmd = conn.CreateCommand();
            cmd.CommandText = "SELECT 1";               // cheap query; never a heavy report
            cmd.CommandTimeout = 2;                     // a health check must answer quickly
            await cmd.ExecuteScalarAsync(ct);
            return HealthCheckResult.Healthy();
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            // Return a generic description; log details instead of exposing them
            return HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy("database unreachable", ex);
        }
    }
}
```

**Example 2: wiring the probes into Azure**

App Service has a built-in **Health check** feature: it pings the path on every instance once a minute and, after repeated failures (10 by default, configurable through `WEBSITE_HEALTHCHECK_MAXPINGFAILURES`), removes the instance from the load balancer. An instance that stays unhealthy for an hour is replaced. It only takes action when the app runs on two or more instances.

```bash
az webapp config set -g rg-shop-prod -n app-shop-api \
  --generic-configurations '{"healthCheckPath": "/healthz/ready"}'
```

Container Apps uses Kubernetes-style probes per container:

```bicep
containers: [
  {
    name: 'api'
    image: 'crshop.azurecr.io/shop-api:1.4.2'
    probes: [
      {
        type: 'Startup'
        httpGet: { path: '/healthz/live', port: 8080 }
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 30            // allow up to 150 s to start
      }
      {
        type: 'Liveness'
        httpGet: { path: '/healthz/live', port: 8080 }
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 3             // restart after ~30 s of no response
      }
      {
        type: 'Readiness'
        httpGet: { path: '/healthz/ready', port: 8080 }
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 3             // stop routing after ~15 s of failures
      }
    ]
  }
]
```

**Example 3: watching from the outside**

Internal probes tell the platform about individual instances. An **Application Insights standard availability test** (chapter 11) calls your public endpoint from several Azure regions and alerts when the service as a whole is unreachable, including DNS, TLS, and Front Door problems an internal probe cannot see. Azure Front Door and Traffic Manager also use health probes to fail over between regions.

**Designing good health endpoints**

- Keep them fast and cheap; they are called constantly by every probe.
- Do not expose internal details (connection strings, versions, stack traces) publicly. Return a status code and minimal JSON, or restrict detailed output to authenticated callers.
- Cache dependency checks for a few seconds so probe traffic does not hammer the database.
- Exclude probe requests from your telemetry sampling noise, or filter them in queries.

**Key takeaways**

- Health endpoints let the platform route around, restart, or alert on unhealthy instances automatically.
- Liveness checks only the process (failure means restart); readiness checks critical dependencies (failure means stop routing); startup protects slow-starting apps.
- Never put dependency checks in liveness, or a dependency outage becomes a restart loop.
- Use App Service Health check or Container Apps probes for instance health, and availability tests for end-to-end health from outside.
- Keep health endpoints fast, cheap, and free of sensitive details.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Add `/healthz/live` and `/healthz/ready` endpoints to a small web app (any language). Make readiness return `503` when an environment variable `DB_DOWN=1` is set, and confirm liveness still returns `200`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the app to Container Apps with the three probes above and two replicas. Toggle the readiness failure on one replica, then use `az containerapp logs show` and the revision's replica list to observe that it is removed from traffic but not restarted.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your orchestrator keeps restarting all pods whenever the database has a blip. What is wrong?" *Hint:* look at which probe contains the dependency check and what action that probe's failure triggers.

#### Queue-Based Load Leveling

**Why it exists**

Traffic is rarely smooth. A flash sale, a marketing email, or a batch upload from a partner can send ten times the normal load in a few minutes. If your web tier calls a slow or capacity-limited backend directly (an ERP system, a database with fixed throughput, a third-party API with a rate limit), the spike either overwhelms that backend or forces you to provision it for the peak, paying for capacity that sits idle most of the day.

**Queue-based load leveling** puts a durable queue between the producers of work and the service that does it. Producers enqueue tasks as fast as they arrive; consumers process them at a steady, sustainable rate. The queue absorbs the spike like a reservoir behind a dam absorbs a flood and releases water at a controlled rate.

```text
 requests/s                                      processed/s
   ^    spike                                      ^
   |    /\                                         |
   |   /  \                                        |  _______________
   |__/    \______         +-------------+         | /               \___
   +------------------> -->|  Service Bus|-->      +-------------------------->
                           |    queue    |
   web tier accepts all    | (buffer: 0  |   workers process at a steady rate;
   requests immediately    |  to 50k msgs)|  the backlog drains after the spike
                           +-------------+
```

**What changes for the client**

The work becomes asynchronous, so the API cannot return the final result in the same request. The usual contract is **202 Accepted** with a status location (the asynchronous request-reply pattern):

```text
POST /orders            -> 202 Accepted, Location: /orders/8f3c/status
GET  /orders/8f3c/status -> 200 {"status": "processing"}
GET  /orders/8f3c/status -> 200 {"status": "completed", "orderId": "8f3c"}
```

**Example: Service Bus between an API and a Function**

The producer (any web framework) validates the request and enqueues it:

```python
# pip install azure-servicebus azure-identity
import json, uuid
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage

sb = ServiceBusClient("sb-shop-prod.servicebus.windows.net", DefaultAzureCredential())
sender = sb.get_queue_sender(queue_name="orders")

def submit_order(order: dict) -> str:
    order_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    msg = ServiceBusMessage(
        json.dumps({**order, "orderId": order_id}),
        message_id=order_id,           # enables duplicate detection if enabled on the queue
        content_type="application/json",
    )
    sender.send_messages(msg)          # fast and durable; the slow work happens later
    return order_id                    # return 202 with a status URL built from this ID
```

The consumer is a Function with a Service Bus trigger. Its throughput is controlled, which is the whole point:

```python
# function_app.py (Python v2 programming model)
import json
import logging
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp()

@app.service_bus_queue_trigger(arg_name="msg", queue_name="orders",
                               connection="ServiceBus")   # identity-based connection setting prefix
def process_order(msg: func.ServiceBusMessage):
    order = json.loads(msg.get_body())
    logging.info("Processing order %s", order["orderId"])
    write_to_erp(order)   # the slow, capacity-limited backend; must be idempotent
```

```json
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "extensions": {
    "serviceBus": {
      "maxConcurrentCalls": 8,
      "autoCompleteMessages": true
    }
  }
}
```

Total consumer concurrency is roughly `instances x maxConcurrentCalls`. To protect a backend that can handle 40 concurrent writes, cap both: for example `maxConcurrentCalls: 8` and a maximum instance count of 5 (`maximumInstanceCount` on a Flex Consumption app, or `maxReplicas` on a Container Apps job or app scaled by KEDA).

**Choosing the queue**

| Need | Service |
|---|---|
| Enterprise messaging, dead-lettering, sessions, duplicate detection | Azure Service Bus queue (chapter 10) |
| Very simple, very cheap, large backlogs | Azure Queue Storage (chapter 5) |
| High-volume telemetry streams | Event Hubs (chapter 9); this is streaming rather than task leveling |

**Things to watch**

- **Queue length is your key metric.** Alert on active message count and on the age of the oldest message; a backlog that never drains means consumers are under-provisioned.
- **Consumers must be idempotent**: delivery is at-least-once, so the same message may be processed twice after a crash or lock expiry.
- **Poison messages** that always fail should land in the dead-letter queue after `MaxDeliveryCount` attempts, not block the queue forever.
- **Latency**: load leveling trades immediate completion for stability. It does not fit operations where the user must see the result synchronously.

**Key takeaways**

- A queue decouples the rate at which work arrives from the rate at which it is processed, protecting capacity-limited backends.
- APIs switch to `202 Accepted` with a status endpoint; clients poll or receive a notification.
- Cap consumer concurrency (per-instance concurrency times maximum instances) to match what the backend can handle.
- Monitor queue length and oldest-message age; use dead-lettering for poison messages.
- Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Create a Service Bus namespace and an `orders` queue. Send 1,000 messages with the producer snippet and watch the active message count in the portal or with `az servicebus queue show --query countDetails`.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the Function consumer with `maxConcurrentCalls: 4` and a maximum of 2 instances, make `write_to_erp` sleep for 1 second, and measure how long the 1,000-message backlog takes to drain. Predict the time first, then double the concurrency and compare.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your nightly partner upload causes database timeouts for daytime users in another region who are still online. How would you redesign the ingestion?" *Hint:* consider a queue in front of the writes, a capped consumer, and whether the partner needs a synchronous answer at all.

<a id="142-data-and-messaging-patterns"></a>
### 14.2 Data and Messaging Patterns

Distributed systems cannot rely on a single database transaction spanning everything. This section covers the patterns for shaping data for reads and writes, recording history, coordinating multi-service workflows, and moving messages and large payloads efficiently.

#### CQRS

**Why it exists**

Most applications start with one model for everything: the same `Order` class and the same tables serve both "place an order" and "show me my order history with product names, totals, and shipping status". As the app grows, those two needs pull in opposite directions:

- **Writes** need validation, business rules, and a normalized shape that keeps data consistent.
- **Reads** need denormalized, pre-joined data shaped exactly like the screen, and they usually outnumber writes 10 to 1 or more.

Forcing both through one model leads to either slow reads (many joins) or a messy write model (columns added just for display). **Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS)** separates them: **commands** change state through a write model; **queries** read from a read model designed for them. The two can live in the same database, or in different stores entirely.

An analogy: a restaurant kitchen (write side) is organized for cooking correctly; the menu (read side) is organized for customers to find dishes quickly. Nobody hands customers the kitchen inventory sheet.

```text
                   +------------------+
   Command  -----> | Command handler  | -- validate, apply rules --> +-------------+
 (PlaceOrder)      +------------------+                              | Write store |
                                                                     | (orders,    |
                                                                     | normalized) |
                                                                     +------+------+
                                                                            |
                                                            change feed / events (async)
                                                                            v
                   +------------------+                              +-------------+
   Query    -----> |  Query handler   | <---- simple lookups ------- | Read store  |
 (MyOrders)        +------------------+                              | (per-screen |
                                                                     |  views)     |
                                                                     +-------------+
```

**Levels of CQRS**

| Level | What is separated | Consistency | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Code only | Separate command and query classes over the same tables | Immediate | Low |
| Same database, separate models | Write tables plus read views or denormalized tables | Immediate or near-immediate | Medium |
| Separate stores | Write store (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB) plus read store (Cosmos DB container, Azure AI Search, Redis) | Eventual | High |

Start at the lowest level that solves your problem. Separate stores bring eventual consistency: right after a user places an order, the "My orders" page may not show it for a second or two.

**Example: Cosmos DB write model with a projected read model**

The command side writes orders partitioned by `orderId`, which is efficient for point writes. The "orders by customer" screen needs data partitioned by `customerId`; a change-feed function keeps that view updated (the projection mechanism is covered in Materialized View below).

```python
# Command side: validate and write; returns no query data beyond an ID
from dataclasses import dataclass
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential

cosmos = CosmosClient("https://cosmos-shop.documents.azure.com", DefaultAzureCredential())
db = cosmos.get_database_client("shop")
orders = db.get_container_client("orders")              # partition key: /orderId
orders_by_customer = db.get_container_client("orders-by-customer")  # partition key: /customerId

@dataclass
class PlaceOrder:
    order_id: str
    customer_id: str
    lines: list[dict]   # [{"sku": "...", "qty": 2, "unitPrice": 9.5}]

def handle_place_order(cmd: PlaceOrder) -> str:
    if not cmd.lines:
        raise ValueError("an order needs at least one line")      # business rule on the write side
    total = sum(l["qty"] * l["unitPrice"] for l in cmd.lines)
    orders.create_item({
        "id": cmd.order_id, "orderId": cmd.order_id,
        "customerId": cmd.customer_id, "lines": cmd.lines,
        "total": total, "status": "placed",
    })
    return cmd.order_id

# Query side: a single-partition read shaped for the screen; no joins, no business rules
def query_my_orders(customer_id: str, limit: int = 20) -> list[dict]:
    return list(orders_by_customer.query_items(
        "SELECT TOP @n c.orderId, c.total, c.status, c.placedAt "
        "FROM c ORDER BY c.placedAt DESC",
        parameters=[{"name": "@n", "value": limit}],
        partition_key=customer_id,                  # cheap single-partition query
    ))
```

**Handling eventual consistency in the UI**

- Return the new ID from the command and show an optimistic "Order placed" state locally.
- For the user who made the change, read their own write from the write store once, then switch to the read model.
- Include a version or timestamp in read models so the UI can tell when the projection has caught up.

**When not to use CQRS**

Simple CRUD apps where reads and writes have the same shape gain nothing but complexity. CQRS pays off when read and write workloads differ greatly in shape or scale, when several read shapes are needed, or alongside event sourcing (next topic).

**Key takeaways**

- CQRS separates commands (change state, enforce rules) from queries (read precomputed, screen-shaped data).
- It can be as small as separate classes or as large as separate stores synchronized by events.
- Separate stores mean eventual consistency; design the UI for it.
- Read models scale independently and can use different technology (Cosmos DB, AI Search, Redis).
- Avoid it for simple CRUD; it adds moving parts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Take a simple "blog posts with comments" app and write the list of commands (e.g. `PublishPost`) and queries (e.g. `GetPostWithCommentCount`). Note which queries would benefit from a denormalized read model.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement the `orders` and `orders-by-customer` containers locally with the Cosmos DB emulator, write the command handler above, and populate the read container from a script. Measure the request charge (RU) of the customer query against both containers.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your product owner reports that customers sometimes do not see an order they just placed. You use CQRS with separate stores. What is happening and how do you fix it without removing CQRS?" *Hint:* projection lag; consider read-your-own-writes strategies and UI design.

#### Event Sourcing

**Why it exists**

A typical database stores only the **current state**: the account balance is 120. How did it get there? Which deposits and withdrawals, in what order, by whom? That history is lost unless you build a separate audit log, which then can drift from the real data.

**Event sourcing** inverts this: the source of truth is an append-only log of **events** that describe what happened (`AccountOpened`, `MoneyDeposited`, `MoneyWithdrawn`). Current state is derived by replaying those events. Nothing is updated or deleted; corrections are new events.

The analogy is an accountant's ledger. Accountants never erase a line; they add a correcting entry. The balance is always the sum of the ledger, and the ledger is the audit trail.

```text
Stream: account-42 (append-only)

 v1 AccountOpened    {owner: "ana"}
 v2 MoneyDeposited   {amount: 100}
 v3 MoneyDeposited   {amount: 50}
 v4 MoneyWithdrawn   {amount: 30}
                                       replay (fold) --> current state: balance = 120
 v5 MoneyDeposited   {amount: 10}      next append must claim version 5;
                                       a concurrent writer claiming v5 gets a conflict
```

**Core concepts**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Event | An immutable fact in the past tense, with a type, payload, and version |
| Stream | All events for one entity (one aggregate), ordered by version |
| Fold / replay | Applying events in order to rebuild state |
| Optimistic concurrency | Appending with an expected version; fail if someone else appended first |
| Snapshot | A saved state at version N, so replay starts there instead of from v1 |
| Projection | A read model built by subscribing to events (this is how CQRS read models are fed) |

**Example: an event store on Cosmos DB**

Cosmos DB works well as an event store: partition by stream ID, and use the version number as the document `id`. Because `id` must be unique within a partition, two writers trying to append version 5 to the same stream cannot both succeed; the second gets `409 Conflict`. That is optimistic concurrency for free. The change feed then streams events to projections.

```python
from azure.cosmos import CosmosClient
from azure.cosmos.exceptions import CosmosBatchOperationError
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from datetime import datetime, timezone

cosmos = CosmosClient("https://cosmos-bank.documents.azure.com", DefaultAzureCredential())
events = cosmos.get_database_client("bank").get_container_client("events")  # partition key: /streamId

class ConcurrencyError(Exception):
    pass

def read_stream(stream_id: str) -> list[dict]:
    return list(events.query_items(
        "SELECT * FROM e ORDER BY e.version",
        partition_key=stream_id,
    ))

def append(stream_id: str, expected_version: int, new_events: list[dict]) -> None:
    ops = []
    for i, ev in enumerate(new_events, start=1):
        version = expected_version + i
        ops.append(("create", ({
            "id": str(version),             # unique per stream: duplicates fail with 409
            "streamId": stream_id,
            "version": version,
            "type": ev["type"],
            "data": ev["data"],
            "occurredAt": datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(),
        },)))
    try:
        # Transactional batch: all events are appended atomically, or none are
        events.execute_item_batch(batch_operations=ops, partition_key=stream_id)
    except CosmosBatchOperationError as e:
        raise ConcurrencyError(f"stream {stream_id} changed; reload and retry") from e

def apply(state: dict, ev: dict) -> dict:
    t, d = ev["type"], ev["data"]
    if t == "AccountOpened":
        return {"owner": d["owner"], "balance": 0}
    if t == "MoneyDeposited":
        return {**state, "balance": state["balance"] + d["amount"]}
    if t == "MoneyWithdrawn":
        return {**state, "balance": state["balance"] - d["amount"]}
    return state                                  # unknown events are ignored, not fatal

def load(stream_id: str) -> tuple[dict, int]:
    state, version = {}, 0
    for ev in read_stream(stream_id):
        state, version = apply(state, ev), ev["version"]
    return state, version

# Command: withdraw with business rule and concurrency check
def withdraw(stream_id: str, amount: int) -> None:
    state, version = load(stream_id)
    if state["balance"] < amount:
        raise ValueError("insufficient funds")       # decided against the replayed state
    append(stream_id, version, [{"type": "MoneyWithdrawn", "data": {"amount": amount}}])
```

**Practical concerns**

- **Snapshots**: if a stream has thousands of events, store a snapshot every N events and replay only the events after it.
- **Schema evolution**: events are stored forever, so their shape must evolve carefully. Add optional fields, version event types (`MoneyDeposited.v2`), or "upcast" old events to the new shape when reading.
- **Personal data**: an immutable log conflicts with the right to erasure (GDPR). Common techniques are keeping personal data outside events (store a reference) or **crypto-shredding** (encrypt per-user data with a per-user key and delete the key).
- **Event Hubs and Kafka are not event stores** by default: they retain events for a limited period and do not support per-stream optimistic concurrency. They are great for distributing events, not for being the source of truth.

**When it fits**

| Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|
| Strong audit requirements (finance, healthcare, legal) | Simple CRUD with no interest in history |
| Domains naturally described as events (orders, bookings, ledgers) | Teams new to eventual consistency and with tight deadlines |
| Need to rebuild new read models from historical data | Data that must be physically deleted on request with no workaround |
| Temporal queries ("what was the state on March 1?") | Reports that need ad-hoc querying across all current states (needs projections) |

**Key takeaways**

- Event sourcing stores what happened as an append-only stream; current state is a replay of events.
- It provides a built-in audit trail, temporal queries, and the ability to build new read models later.
- Use optimistic concurrency on append; in Cosmos DB, version-as-ID plus transactional batch does this cleanly.
- Plan for snapshots, event schema evolution, and personal-data deletion from day one.
- It almost always comes with CQRS, because querying event streams directly is impractical.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Model a shopping cart with events (`ItemAdded`, `ItemRemoved`, `CartCheckedOut`) and write an `apply` function that folds them into the current cart.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Using the Cosmos DB code above against the emulator, run two concurrent `withdraw` calls on the same stream from two threads and show that one fails with `ConcurrencyError`. Then add a retry that reloads the stream and re-checks the balance.
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you implement 'delete my account' in an event-sourced system?" *Hint:* think about what must be physically removed, keeping personal data out of events, and crypto-shredding.

#### Saga Pattern

**Why it exists**

In a monolith, placing an order can be one database transaction: reserve stock, charge payment, create the shipment, and commit or roll back everything together. In a microservices architecture, inventory, payments, and shipping each own their data in separate databases. There is no practical distributed transaction across them: two-phase commit is not supported by most cloud services, and it would couple services and hurt availability.

A **saga** replaces one big transaction with a sequence of **local transactions**, one per service. If a step fails, the saga runs **compensating transactions** that semantically undo the steps that already succeeded (release the stock, refund the payment).

An analogy: booking a trip yourself. You book a flight, then a hotel, then a car. If no car is available, you do not "roll back time"; you cancel the hotel and the flight, possibly paying a fee. Compensation is a new action, not an undo button.

```text
Happy path:
  ReserveInventory --> AuthorizePayment --> CreateShipment --> Done

Failure at CreateShipment:
  ReserveInventory --> AuthorizePayment --> CreateShipment (fails)
                                                  |
  ReleaseInventory <-- VoidPayment  <-------------+   compensations run in reverse order
```

**Choreography versus orchestration**

| | Choreography | Orchestration |
|---|---|---|
| How it works | Each service listens for events and publishes the next event | A central orchestrator tells each service what to do and tracks progress |
| Azure building blocks | Service Bus topics or Event Grid, each service subscribes | Durable Functions, Logic Apps, or a workflow service |
| Pros | No central component; services stay very loosely coupled | Workflow visible in one place; easier to reason about, test, and change |
| Cons | Hard to see the overall flow; risk of cyclic dependencies | Orchestrator is an extra component; risk of putting business logic in it |
| Fits | Few steps, simple flows | Many steps, branching, timeouts, human approvals |

```text
Choreography (events on Service Bus topics)

 Orders --OrderPlaced--> Inventory --StockReserved--> Payments --PaymentAuthorized--> Shipping
   ^                         ^                           |
   |                         +------PaymentFailed--------+   (Inventory releases stock)
   +--------------OrderCancelled------------------------+

Orchestration (Durable Functions)

                     +--------------------------+
                     | PlaceOrder orchestrator  |
                     +--------------------------+
                      |  1     |   2     |  3    \ on failure: compensate 2, then 1
                      v        v         v
                 Inventory  Payments  Shipping
```

**Example: an orchestrated saga with Durable Functions**

Durable Functions persists the orchestrator's progress after every `yield`, so if the host crashes halfway through, the saga resumes where it left off. That makes it a natural saga orchestrator.

```python
# function_app.py (Python v2 model) - pip install azure-functions azure-functions-durable
import azure.durable_functions as df
import azure.functions as func

app = df.DFApp(http_auth_level=func.AuthLevel.FUNCTION)

retry = df.RetryOptions(first_retry_interval_in_milliseconds=2000, max_number_of_attempts=3)

@app.orchestration_trigger(context_name="context")
def place_order(context: df.DurableOrchestrationContext):
    order = context.get_input()
    compensations = []                       # stack of undo steps for completed work

    try:
        yield context.call_activity_with_retry("reserve_inventory", retry, order)
        compensations.append("release_inventory")

        yield context.call_activity_with_retry("authorize_payment", retry, order)
        compensations.append("void_payment")

        # Pivot step: once shipped, we no longer compensate; we only move forward
        yield context.call_activity_with_retry("create_shipment", retry, order)
        return {"status": "completed", "orderId": order["orderId"]}

    except Exception as err:
        # Undo in reverse order; compensations must be idempotent and must be retried
        for step in reversed(compensations):
            yield context.call_activity_with_retry(step, retry, order)
        return {"status": "cancelled", "orderId": order["orderId"], "reason": str(err)}

@app.activity_trigger(input_name="order")
def reserve_inventory(order: dict) -> None:
    ...  # local transaction in the inventory service (or call its API with an idempotency key)

@app.activity_trigger(input_name="order")
def release_inventory(order: dict) -> None:
    ...  # must succeed even if nothing was reserved (idempotent)

# authorize_payment, void_payment, create_shipment follow the same shape
```

**Design rules for sagas**

- **Compensations are business actions**, not technical rollbacks. A refund may need an email; a released seat may have been resold.
- **Every step and compensation must be idempotent**: retries and redeliveries will happen.
- **Identify the pivot transaction**: the point of no return after which the saga only retries forward (here, creating the shipment).
- **Isolation is weak**: other requests can see intermediate states (stock reserved but not yet paid). Countermeasures include semantic locks (`status: "pending"`), commutative updates, and re-reading values before acting.
- **Use timeouts** for steps waiting on external parties; Durable Functions timers (`context.create_timer`) let an orchestrator wait for days at no compute cost.

**Key takeaways**

- A saga coordinates a multi-service business transaction as a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions.
- Choreography uses events and suits simple flows; orchestration uses a coordinator such as Durable Functions and suits complex flows.
- Compensations are semantic business actions, executed in reverse order, and must be idempotent.
- Sagas give eventual consistency, not isolation; design for visible intermediate states.
- Durable Functions persists orchestrator progress, so sagas survive restarts.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For a "book a concert ticket" flow (hold seat, charge card, issue ticket, send email), list each step's compensation and mark the pivot transaction.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Implement the Durable Functions saga above with activities that log their action, make `create_shipment` raise an exception, and verify in the orchestration history (Durable Functions Monitor or the `TestHubNameHistory` table) that compensations ran in reverse order.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Why not use a distributed transaction (two-phase commit) across the order, payment, and inventory databases?" *Hint:* think about service support in the cloud, locks held across network calls, availability when one participant is down, and coupling.

#### Competing Consumers

**Why it exists**

A single worker reading from a queue has a fixed throughput. When the queue grows faster than it can drain, you need more workers, and you want to add or remove them without reconfiguring producers or coordinating which worker takes which message. The **competing consumers** pattern lets multiple consumer instances read from the same queue; the broker ensures each message is delivered to only one of them at a time.

Think of a bank with one queue and several tellers: the next customer goes to whichever teller is free. You open more windows when the line is long.

```text
                                  +------------+
                             +--> | consumer 1 |  (lock on msg A)
 producers ---> [ queue ] ---+--> | consumer 2 |  (lock on msg B)
                 C D E F      +--> | consumer 3 |  (lock on msg C)
                                  +------------+
   each message is locked to one consumer; others take the next available message
```

**How Service Bus makes it safe: peek-lock**

With **peek-lock** (the default receive mode), a consumer receives a message and the broker locks it for a duration (the queue's lock duration: 1 minute by default, up to 5 minutes, renewable). The consumer then:

| Action | Effect |
|---|---|
| `complete` | Message is removed from the queue |
| `abandon` | Lock released; message becomes available again (delivery count increments) |
| `dead_letter` | Message moves to the dead-letter subqueue with a reason |
| Lock expires (consumer crashed) | Message becomes available to another consumer |

Because a message can be redelivered after a crash or lock expiry, delivery is **at-least-once**, and consumers must be idempotent.

**Example: a competing consumer in Python**

Run this script in as many containers or processes as you need; they automatically share the work.

```python
import json
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient

client = ServiceBusClient("sb-shop-prod.servicebus.windows.net", DefaultAzureCredential())

class PermanentError(Exception):
    pass

def handle(order: dict) -> None:
    # Idempotency: skip if this order was already processed (e.g. a unique key in the database)
    if already_processed(order["orderId"]):
        return
    process(order)

with client.get_queue_receiver(queue_name="orders", prefetch_count=10) as receiver:
    for msg in receiver:                           # blocks and yields messages as they arrive
        try:
            handle(json.loads(str(msg)))
            receiver.complete_message(msg)         # done: remove from queue
        except PermanentError as e:
            # Bad data will never succeed: park it for investigation
            receiver.dead_letter_message(msg, reason="invalid-order", error_description=str(e))
        except Exception:
            # Transient problem: let another attempt happen later
            receiver.abandon_message(msg)
```

**Scaling consumers**

- **Azure Functions** Service Bus triggers are competing consumers out of the box, and the platform scales instances based on queue length.
- **Container Apps** and AKS use **KEDA** scalers that add replicas based on message count:

```bicep
scale: {
  minReplicas: 0                       // scale to zero when the queue is empty
  maxReplicas: 20
  rules: [
    {
      name: 'orders-queue'
      custom: {
        type: 'azure-servicebus'
        metadata: {
          queueName: 'orders'
          namespace: 'sb-shop-prod'
          messageCount: '50'           // target: about 50 messages per replica
        }
        identity: 'system'             // KEDA authenticates with the app's managed identity
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Ordering**

Competing consumers process messages in parallel, so global ordering is lost. If messages for the same entity must be processed in order (all updates to order 42), use **Service Bus sessions**: messages with the same `session_id` are locked to one consumer at a time, while different sessions are still processed in parallel.

**Competing consumers versus partitioned consumers**

Event Hubs (and Kafka) work differently: within a consumer group, each partition is read by only one consumer, so parallelism is capped by the partition count, and ordering is guaranteed per partition. That is a **partitioned consumer** model, not competing consumers over a single queue.

**Key takeaways**

- Multiple consumers read the same queue; the broker locks each message to one consumer, so throughput scales horizontally.
- Peek-lock gives complete, abandon, and dead-letter outcomes; a crash releases the lock and another consumer retries.
- Delivery is at-least-once: consumers must be idempotent.
- Use sessions when per-entity ordering matters; global ordering and competing consumers do not mix.
- Scale consumers with Functions triggers or KEDA rules based on queue length.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Start two instances of the Python consumer in two terminals, send 20 messages, and observe how they are split between consumers.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Make the consumer crash (exit the process) after receiving but before completing a message. Measure how long until another consumer receives it, then shorten the lock duration on the queue and repeat. Check the `delivery_count` property on the redelivered message.
> 3. **(Interview)** "You scaled consumers from 2 to 20, but throughput barely changed. What might be limiting it?" *Hint:* check the downstream database, sessions or partitions limiting parallelism, prefetch settings, lock renewal overhead, and the messaging tier's throughput units.

#### Claim Check

**Why it exists**

Message brokers are optimized for small messages. Azure Service Bus Standard caps messages at 256 KB, Premium allows up to 100 MB but large messages still slow the broker and cost more; Event Grid events are limited to 1 MB; and Queue Storage messages to 64 KB. Yet applications often need to pass large data: a scanned PDF, a video, a 20 MB JSON export.

The **claim check** pattern stores the large payload in an external store (typically Blob Storage) and sends only a small message containing a reference to it. The consumer uses the reference to fetch the payload.

The name comes from a coat check: you hand over your coat and receive a small ticket. You carry the ticket around, not the coat, and redeem it when you need the coat back.

```text
 Producer                                                    Consumer
    |  1. upload payload (20 MB)                                 |
    +-------------------------> [ Blob Storage ] <---------------+ 3. download payload
    |                           claim-checks/8f3c.json           |    using the reference
    |  2. send small message                                     |
    +--> [ Service Bus ] -- {"blob": "claim-checks/8f3c.json"} -->+
                         (a few hundred bytes)
```

**Example: manual claim check with Service Bus and Blob Storage**

```python
import json, uuid
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.servicebus import ServiceBusClient, ServiceBusMessage
from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient

cred = DefaultAzureCredential()
blobs = BlobServiceClient("https://stshopprod.blob.core.windows.net", credential=cred)
payloads = blobs.get_container_client("claim-checks")
sb = ServiceBusClient("sb-shop-prod.servicebus.windows.net", cred)

THRESHOLD = 192 * 1024     # leave headroom under the 256 KB Standard-tier limit

def send_report(report: dict) -> None:
    body = json.dumps(report).encode()
    with sb.get_queue_sender("reports") as sender:
        if len(body) < THRESHOLD:
            sender.send_messages(ServiceBusMessage(body))   # small: send inline
            return
        blob_name = f"{uuid.uuid4()}.json"
        payloads.upload_blob(blob_name, body)               # 1. store the "coat"
        ticket = {"claimCheck": blob_name, "size": len(body)}
        sender.send_messages(ServiceBusMessage(              # 2. send the "ticket"
            json.dumps(ticket),
            application_properties={"claimCheck": "true"},  # lets subscription filters route tickets
        ))

def receive_report(msg) -> dict:
    body = json.loads(str(msg))
    if "claimCheck" in body:                                         # a ticket, not the payload
        data = payloads.download_blob(body["claimCheck"]).readall()  # 3. redeem the ticket
        return json.loads(data)
    return body
```

Note that the consumer needs only read access (Storage Blob Data Reader) to the container, granted to its managed identity. Do not put SAS tokens in messages that may be logged or dead-lettered and inspected later, unless they are short-lived and scoped to one blob.

**Example: automatic claim check with Event Grid**

When a file lands in Blob Storage, Event Grid emits a `Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated` event whose `data.url` points to the blob. The event *is* the claim check: upload directly from the client (see Valet Key, 14.3), subscribe a Function or a Service Bus queue to the event, and no code ever sends the large payload through a broker.

**Cleaning up**

Payloads must not live forever. Use a lifecycle management policy on the container, or delete the blob after the consumer completes processing:

```json
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "enabled": true,
      "name": "expire-claim-checks",
      "type": "Lifecycle",
      "definition": {
        "filters": { "blobTypes": ["blockBlob"], "prefixMatch": ["claim-checks/"] },
        "actions": { "baseBlob": { "delete": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 7 } } }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

Keep the retention longer than the message time-to-live plus dead-letter investigation time, or a consumer may redeem a ticket for a coat that was already thrown away.

**Key takeaways**

- Store large payloads in Blob Storage and send only a reference through the message broker.
- It keeps messages under broker limits, reduces broker cost and latency, and avoids exposing sensitive payloads to every system that sees messages.
- Event Grid `BlobCreated` events provide a ready-made claim check for uploads.
- Grant consumers access with managed identity and RBAC, not long-lived SAS tokens in messages.
- Clean up payloads with lifecycle policies, keeping them longer than message retention.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Look up the maximum message size for Service Bus Standard and Premium, Event Grid, Event Hubs, and Queue Storage, and record which ones would need a claim check for a 5 MB invoice PDF.
