An estimate predicts; Cost Management tells you what actually happened. **Cost analysis** breaks actual spending down by service, resource, tag, meter, and time, so you can see where the money goes. **Budgets** and **anomaly alerts** notify you when spending approaches a limit or behaves unexpectedly, so problems are found in days rather than at the end of the month.

The analogy is a household: the calculator is the plan for the month, cost analysis is the bank statement, and budgets are the alert your bank sends when you are close to your limit.

**Scopes and views**

Cost Management works at several scopes: management group, subscription, resource group, and billing scopes (billing account, invoice section, and so on). Developers usually look at a resource group or subscription.

| View / concept | Use |
|---|---|
| Accumulated costs | Month-to-date spending with a forecast line to the end of the month |
| Group by service name, resource, meter, or tag | Find the biggest cost drivers |
| Actual cost | What was billed in the period, with reservation purchases appearing as a lump sum |
| Amortized cost | Reservation and savings plan purchases spread across the days they cover; better for chargeback per team |
| Cost by tag | Allocate costs to teams, products, or environments (`costCenter`, `env`) |
| Exports | Daily or monthly CSV/Parquet exports to a storage account for Power BI or custom reports |
| Anomaly alerts | Email when daily spend deviates from the usual pattern (subscription scope) |

Cost data typically appears within 8 to 24 hours, so Cost Management is not a real-time kill switch.

**Example: query costs programmatically**

The Cost Management Query API returns the same data as the portal. This groups month-to-date cost by the `team` tag:

```bash
SUB=$(az account show --query id -o tsv)

az rest --method post \
  --url "https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/$SUB/providers/Microsoft.CostManagement/query?api-version=2023-11-01" \
  --body '{
    "type": "ActualCost",
    "timeframe": "MonthToDate",
    "dataset": {
      "granularity": "None",
      "aggregation": { "totalCost": { "name": "Cost", "function": "Sum" } },
      "grouping": [ { "type": "TagKey", "name": "team" } ]
    }
  }' \
  --query "properties.rows" -o table
# Older account types expose "PreTaxCost" instead of "Cost" as the aggregation column
```

**Budgets**

A budget defines an amount for a scope and period, plus notification thresholds based on **actual** or **forecasted** spending. Notifications go to email addresses and **action groups**, which can call a webhook, a Logic App, a Function, or an Automation runbook.

```bicep
param startDate string = '2026-11-01'     // must be the first day of a month

resource budget 'Microsoft.Consumption/budgets@2023-11-01' = {
  name: 'budget-shop-dev'
  properties: {
    category: 'Cost'
    amount: 500                            // in the billing currency
    timeGrain: 'Monthly'
    timePeriod: { startDate: startDate }
    filter: {
      tags: { name: 'env', operator: 'In', values: [ 'dev' ] }   // only resources tagged env=dev
    }
    notifications: {
      actual80: {
        enabled: true
        operator: 'GreaterThanOrEqualTo'
        threshold: 80                      // percent of the amount
        thresholdType: 'Actual'
        contactEmails: [ 'team-shop@example.com' ]
      }
      forecast100: {
        enabled: true
        operator: 'GreaterThanOrEqualTo'
        threshold: 100
        thresholdType: 'Forecasted'        // warn early: we are on track to exceed the budget
        contactEmails: [ 'team-shop@example.com' ]
        contactGroups: [ actionGroup.id ]  // e.g. a runbook that scales dev resources down
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Budgets do not stop spending.** Azure will not shut down resources when a budget is exceeded (except for spending limits on some free and credit-based subscriptions). If you want automatic action, wire the action group to automation that, for example, stops dev VMs or scales App Service plans down, and design that automation carefully so it never targets production.

**A practical routine for a team**

```text
 Daily  : anomaly alert emails (automatic)
 Weekly : Cost analysis grouped by service and tag for the team's resource groups
 Monthly: review against budget and estimate; act on Advisor cost recommendations
 Every PR touching IaC: check SKU and scale changes (some teams add cost-estimate tools to CI)
```

**Key takeaways**

- Cost analysis shows actual spending by service, resource, meter, tag, and time; use amortized cost for team allocation.
- Tags are what make costs attributable; without them, costs cannot be owned.
- Budgets notify on actual or forecasted thresholds and can trigger action groups, but they never stop resources by themselves.
- Cost data lags by several hours; use anomaly alerts and forecasts for early warning.
- Make cost review a routine, and automate budgets in IaC alongside the resources they cover.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** In Cost analysis, group the last 30 days of a subscription by service name and then by resource. Identify the three most expensive resources.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the Bicep budget to a resource group with a low amount, connect an action group with an email and a webhook to a Function that logs the payload, and inspect the alert content when the threshold is crossed (or use the action group's test feature).
> 3. **(Interview)** "How would you show each product team what they spend each month in a shared subscription?" *Hint:* enforced tags, amortized cost, grouping by tag, scheduled exports, and how to handle shared resources such as a common Log Analytics workspace.

#### Reserved Capacity and Savings Plans

**Why it exists**

Pay-as-you-go pricing gives maximum flexibility, but you pay a premium for it. Most production workloads have a baseline of usage that runs 24/7 for years: the minimum instances of an App Service plan, database vCores, VMs that never stop. Azure offers large discounts if you commit to that baseline in advance.

The analogy is a gym: paying per visit is flexible, but if you go every day, an annual membership is far cheaper. Committing to a membership you rarely use, though, wastes money.

**The two main commitment models**

| | Azure Reservations | Azure Savings Plan for Compute |
|---|---|---|
| What you commit to | A specific resource type, SKU or size family, and region | A fixed amount of compute spend per hour (e.g. 5 per hour) |
| Term | 1 or 3 years | 1 or 3 years |
| Applies to | VMs, Azure SQL / SQL MI vCores, Cosmos DB RU/s, Redis, App Service (some tiers), storage capacity, Synapse, Databricks, and more | Compute across services and regions: VMs, Dedicated Hosts, Container Instances, App Service Premium v3 / Isolated v2, Functions Premium, Container Apps, and others (check eligibility) |
| Flexibility | Low: tied to service, region, and size family (instance size flexibility within a family for VMs) | High: follows usage across regions, sizes, and eligible services |
| Discount | Typically the deepest for the covered service | Typically somewhat lower than reservations |
| Best for | Stable, predictable workloads that will not change region or size | Compute that may move between services, sizes, or regions |

When both exist, reservations are applied first to matching usage, then the savings plan covers eligible remaining compute, and anything left is billed at pay-as-you-go rates.

**How to decide what to commit**

```text
 hourly compute usage over 30 days
  ^
  |        /\        /\        /\           <- peaks: leave on pay-as-you-go (or autoscale)
  |  _____/  \______/  \______/  \_____
  | |                                  |   <- variable middle: savings plan
  | |----------------------------------|
  | |##################################|   <- steady baseline: reservations
  +--------------------------------------> time
```

1. **Measure** the steady baseline over at least 30 to 60 days (Cost analysis, Advisor recommendations).
2. **Right-size first** (next topic): reserving an oversized resource locks in waste for years.
3. **Commit to the baseline only**, not the peaks.
4. **Choose scope**: a single resource group or subscription, a management group, or shared across the billing account. Shared scope maximizes utilization.
5. **Monitor utilization** monthly; unused commitment is money spent for nothing.

**Example: break-even reasoning**

A commitment pays off only if the resource runs enough hours. The numbers below are illustrative:

```python
def breakeven_utilization(payg_hourly: float, reserved_hourly_effective: float) -> float:
    """Fraction of hours a resource must run for a reservation to beat pay-as-you-go."""
    return reserved_hourly_effective / payg_hourly

payg = 0.20            # illustrative pay-as-you-go price per hour
reserved_1y = 0.13     # illustrative effective hourly price with a 1-year reservation
reserved_3y = 0.085    # illustrative effective hourly price with a 3-year reservation

for name, r in [("1-year", reserved_1y), ("3-year", reserved_3y)]:
    be = breakeven_utilization(payg, r)
    print(f"{name}: saves {1 - r / payg:.0%} at 100% usage; "
          f"break-even if the resource runs more than {be:.0%} of hours")
# 1-year: saves 35% at 100% usage; break-even if the resource runs more than 65% of hours
# 3-year: saves 57% at 100% usage; break-even if the resource runs more than 42% of hours
```

A dev VM that runs 40 hours a week (about 24% of hours) should not be reserved; turning it off at night saves more.

```bash
# See what Advisor recommends reserving based on your usage
az advisor recommendation list --category Cost \
  --query "[?contains(shortDescription.problem, 'reserved') || contains(shortDescription.problem, 'savings plan')].{problem:shortDescription.problem, savings:extendedProperties.annualSavingsAmount}" \
  -o table
```

**Other rate-optimization options**

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| Azure Hybrid Benefit | Reuse existing Windows Server and SQL Server licenses with Software Assurance to reduce VM and SQL costs |
| Dev/Test pricing | Discounted rates for non-production subscriptions under eligible agreements and Visual Studio subscriptions |
| Spot VMs | Unused capacity at deep discounts, evictable with short notice; for batch, CI agents, fault-tolerant work |
| Cosmos DB reserved capacity / serverless / autoscale | Commit to RU/s, or pay per request for spiky low-volume workloads |

Reservations can be exchanged or, within limits, refunded, but policies change over time; check the current terms before buying.

**Key takeaways**

- Commitments trade flexibility for discount: reservations are tied to a service and region, savings plans to an hourly compute spend.
- Commit only to the steady baseline after right-sizing; leave peaks on pay-as-you-go and autoscale.
- Reservations apply first, then savings plans, then pay-as-you-go.
- Track utilization; unused commitment is pure waste.
- Combine with Hybrid Benefit, Dev/Test pricing, and Spot VMs where they fit.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Using the Pricing Calculator, compare the monthly cost of a D4s v5 Linux VM in your region on pay-as-you-go, 1-year reservation, 3-year reservation, and savings plan, and compute each discount.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Export 30 days of hourly usage for an App Service plan (instance count metric) and determine the steady baseline. Calculate how many instances you would cover with a commitment and the expected savings.
> 3. **(Interview)** "Your company is migrating workloads to containers over the next 18 months. Would you buy VM reservations or a savings plan?" *Hint:* consider how usage will shift between VMs, AKS nodes, and Container Apps, and which commitment follows that shift.

#### Right-Sizing Resources

**Why it exists**

Resources are usually sized during initial development, often generously ("let's take the bigger one to be safe"), and rarely revisited. Months later, the database runs at 8% CPU, the App Service plan hosts one small app, and three test environments run 24/7 at production size. **Right-sizing** matches resource size and count to actual demand, and removes what is not used at all. It is typically the fastest, lowest-risk way to cut costs.

The analogy: renting a moving truck. You do not rent the 26-foot truck to move one sofa.

**The right-sizing loop**

```text
   +-------------> Measure (CPU, memory, DTU/vCore, RU/s, instance count; p95 over 2-4 weeks)
   |                    |
   |                    v
   |               Identify (underused, idle, orphaned, over-tiered)
   |                    |
   |                    v
   |               Change (smaller SKU, fewer instances, autoscale, schedule, delete)
   |                    |
   |                    v
   +---------------- Verify (performance targets still met? costs went down?)
```

Use percentiles, not averages: a server averaging 15% CPU but peaking at 95% every hour is not oversized; it needs autoscaling, not a smaller SKU.

**Where waste typically hides**

| Category | Examples | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | Dev/test VMs and databases running nights and weekends | Auto-shutdown, schedules, scale to zero, delete ephemeral environments |
| Over-provisioned | VMs at 5% CPU, Cosmos DB with 10,000 RU/s provisioned but 800 used | Smaller SKU, autoscale throughput, serverless tiers |
| Orphaned | Unattached managed disks, unused public IPs, old snapshots, empty App Service plans | Delete after confirming ownership |
| Over-tiered | Premium storage for archives, Premium Service Bus for low volume | Lower tier, storage lifecycle to Cool/Cold/Archive |
| Over-logged | Debug logs in production, 100% telemetry sampling, long retention for all tables | Sampling, log levels, Basic/Auxiliary log tables, shorter retention |

**Example 1: find orphaned resources with Azure Resource Graph**

```kusto
// Unattached managed disks (still billed for their full provisioned size)
Resources
| where type =~ "microsoft.compute/disks"
| where properties.diskState =~ "Unattached"
| project name, resourceGroup, sku = tostring(sku.name),
          sizeGb = toint(properties.diskSizeGB), createdOn = properties.timeCreated
| order by sizeGb desc
```

```kusto
// App Service plans with no apps
Resources
| where type =~ "microsoft.web/serverfarms"
| where toint(properties.numberOfSites) == 0
| project name, resourceGroup, sku = tostring(sku.name), location
```

```bash
az graph query -q "Resources | where type =~ 'microsoft.network/publicipaddresses' \
  | where isnull(properties.ipConfiguration) and isnull(properties.natGateway) \
  | project name, resourceGroup, sku = tostring(sku.name)" -o table
```

**Example 2: find what drives log costs**

Log ingestion is one of the most common "surprise" costs. The `Usage` table in Log Analytics shows billable volume per table (the `Quantity` column is in MB):

```kusto
Usage
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where IsBillable == true
| summarize IngestedGB = round(sum(Quantity) / 1024, 2) by DataType
| order by IngestedGB desc
```

Typical fixes: enable sampling in Application Insights, raise production log levels from Debug to Information or Warning, stop collecting unneeded diagnostic categories, move verbose tables to a cheaper log plan, and set per-table retention.

**Example 3: stop paying for idle time**

```bash
# Shut down a dev VM every evening at 19:00 (UTC by default)
az vm auto-shutdown -g rg-shop-dev -n vm-build-agent --time 1900

# Scale a dev App Service plan down to the smallest tier outside working hours (run from a scheduled pipeline)
az appservice plan update -g rg-shop-dev -n asp-shop-dev --sku B1

# Delete a whole ephemeral environment when the feature branch is merged
az group delete -n rg-shop-pr-1234 --yes --no-wait
```

For Cosmos DB, consider **autoscale throughput** (scales between 10% and 100% of a maximum RU/s) or the **serverless** capacity mode for low or spiky traffic, instead of a fixed, peak-sized provisioned throughput.

**Making it stick**

- Put right-sizing decisions into IaC parameters per environment (`skuName` for dev versus prod), so they are not overwritten on the next deployment.
- Review Azure Advisor's right-size and shutdown recommendations monthly.
- Use Azure Policy to restrict allowed SKUs in non-production subscriptions.

**Key takeaways**

- Right-sizing matches size and count to measured demand; it is usually the quickest cost win.
- Measure with percentiles over weeks; spiky workloads need autoscaling rather than smaller SKUs.
- Hunt for idle, over-provisioned, orphaned, over-tiered, and over-logged resources.
- Resource Graph and the Log Analytics `Usage` table quickly reveal orphaned resources and log costs.
- Encode sizes per environment in IaC and right-size before buying reservations.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** Run the three Resource Graph queries in a subscription you can access (Azure Resource Graph Explorer in the portal works) and list the findings with their estimated monthly cost.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Run the `Usage` query on a Log Analytics workspace, pick the largest table, and reduce its volume (sampling, log level, diagnostic setting change, or table plan). Measure ingestion before and after over a week.
> 3. **(Interview)** "An Azure SQL database runs at 10% average CPU. Should you downsize it?" *Hint:* look at p95 and p99 utilization, peak times, memory and IO limits tied to the tier, storage needs, and whether a serverless tier or elastic pool fits the pattern better.

#### Designing Cost-Efficient Serverless Apps

**Why it exists**

Serverless platforms (Azure Functions, Container Apps, Logic Apps) bill for what you use: executions, execution time multiplied by memory, and requests, and they can scale to zero. That makes them very cheap for spiky or low-traffic workloads. But the same model punishes certain designs: a function that waits 30 seconds on an external call pays for 30 seconds of memory, a function triggered once per message instead of per batch pays the per-execution overhead millions of times, and a runaway scale-out can multiply costs in minutes.

The analogy is a taxi meter: it is cheaper than owning a car if you ride occasionally, but you pay while sitting in traffic too, so you avoid unnecessary waiting and detours.

**Know the billing models**

| Hosting option | Billed for | Scale to zero | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Functions Flex Consumption | Executions plus GB-seconds of instance memory while executing; optional always-ready instances billed at a lower baseline rate | Yes | Recommended serverless plan: VNet integration, configurable instance memory, per-function scaling |
| Functions Consumption (classic) | Executions plus GB-seconds | Yes | Linux Consumption is being retired in favor of Flex Consumption; check the current timeline |
| Functions Premium (Elastic Premium) | Pre-warmed and active instances per hour (vCPU and memory) | No (minimum 1 instance) | No cold start; predictable baseline cost |
| Functions on App Service plan | The plan, regardless of executions | No | Cheap if the plan already exists with spare capacity |
| Container Apps (Consumption) | vCPU-seconds and GiB-seconds while active, lower idle rate, plus requests; monthly free grant | Yes | Good for HTTP APIs and KEDA-scaled workers |

Each consumption-style plan has a monthly free grant of executions and resource time, so small workloads can run almost free.

**Design rules**

| Rule | Why it saves money |
|---|---|
| Do not wait inside a function | Waiting time is billed; use asynchronous patterns, queues, or Durable Functions timers instead |
| Process in batches | Fewer executions and less per-call overhead (Event Hubs, Service Bus, Cosmos DB triggers support batches) |
| Right-size memory | GB-seconds scale with instance memory; choose the smallest instance memory that meets performance |
| Cap scale-out | A maximum instance count limits runaway costs and protects downstream services |
| Reuse connections | Static clients avoid slow, billed connection setup on every execution |
| Control telemetry | Application Insights sampling and log levels; log ingestion can exceed execution costs |
| Keep data close | Same-region storage and databases avoid egress and latency (which is billed time) |

**Example 1: batching instead of one execution per event**

```python
import json
import logging
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp()

# One execution receives up to a batch of events instead of one execution per event
@app.event_hub_message_trigger(arg_name="events",
                               event_hub_name="telemetry",
                               connection="EventHub",
                               cardinality=func.Cardinality.MANY)
def ingest(events: list[func.EventHubEvent]) -> None:
    rows = [json.loads(e.get_body()) for e in events]
    write_rows_in_bulk(rows)                 # one bulk write instead of N single writes
    logging.info("Wrote %d rows", len(rows)) # one log line per batch, not per event
```

```json
{
  "version": "2.0",
  "extensions": {
    "eventHubs": {
      "maxEventBatchSize": 500,
      "minEventBatchSize": 100,
      "maxWaitTime": "00:00:05"
    }
  },
  "logging": {
    "logLevel": { "default": "Warning", "Function": "Information" },
    "applicationInsights": { "samplingSettings": { "isEnabled": true, "maxTelemetryItemsPerSecond": 5 } }
  }
}
```

**Example 2: wait without paying for it**

```python
import azure.durable_functions as df
from datetime import timedelta

app = df.DFApp()

# Anti-pattern: time.sleep(3600) in a regular function bills for an hour of idle memory
# (and hits the execution timeout). A durable timer unloads the orchestrator while waiting.

@app.orchestration_trigger(context_name="context")
def payment_reminder(context: df.DurableOrchestrationContext):
    invoice = context.get_input()
    yield context.call_activity("send_invoice", invoice)

    due = context.current_utc_datetime + timedelta(days=7)
    yield context.create_timer(due)          # no compute is billed while the orchestration sleeps

    paid = yield context.call_activity("is_paid", invoice)
    if not paid:
        yield context.call_activity("send_reminder", invoice)
```

**Example 3: a Flex Consumption app with cost guardrails**

```bicep
resource func 'Microsoft.Web/sites@2024-04-01' = {
  name: 'func-shop-ingest'
  location: location
  kind: 'functionapp,linux'
  identity: { type: 'SystemAssigned' }
  properties: {
    serverFarmId: flexPlan.id                 // plan with sku { name: 'FC1', tier: 'FlexConsumption' }
    functionAppConfig: {
      runtime: { name: 'python', version: '3.12' }
      scaleAndConcurrency: {
        instanceMemoryMB: 2048                // smallest size that meets performance (512, 2048, 4096)
        maximumInstanceCount: 40              // hard cap on scale-out and therefore on cost
        alwaysReady: []                       // no always-ready instances: accept cold starts in exchange for zero idle cost
      }
      deployment: {
        storage: {
          type: 'blobContainer'
          value: '${storage.properties.primaryEndpoints.blob}deployments'
          authentication: { type: 'SystemAssignedIdentity' }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**When serverless stops being cheap**

Serverless is cheapest for spiky, low-to-moderate, or unpredictable load. For a workload that runs at high, steady utilization 24/7, a pre-provisioned option (Premium plan, App Service plan, Container Apps dedicated workload profiles, or AKS with reservations) is often cheaper per unit of work. Re-evaluate with real usage data once a workload stabilizes, using the Pricing Calculator for both options.

```text
 monthly cost
   ^                               serverless (grows linearly with usage)
   |                             /
   |                           /
   |  ______________________ /_________  dedicated (flat, with steps when you add instances)
   |                       /
   |                     /  <- crossover point: measure where your workload sits
   |                   /
   +-----------------------------------------> monthly usage
```

**Key takeaways**

- Serverless bills for executions and resource time, and scales to zero, which is ideal for spiky or low-volume workloads.
- Avoid paying for waiting: use queues, asynchronous calls, and Durable Functions timers instead of sleeping or polling.
- Batch triggers, reuse connections, right-size instance memory, and control telemetry volume.
- Cap maximum instances to bound both cost and downstream load.
- At high, steady utilization, compare against dedicated plans; serverless is not automatically cheapest.

> 🧪 Practice
>
> 1. **(Beginner)** For a function that runs 3 million times a month for 400 ms with 2 GB of instance memory, calculate the GB-seconds consumed, then look up current Flex Consumption prices and free grants to estimate the monthly cost.
> 2. **(Intermediate)** Deploy the Event Hubs function twice: once with `cardinality=ONE` and once with batches of up to 500. Send 100,000 events and compare execution counts and total execution units in Azure Monitor metrics.
> 3. **(Interview)** "A serverless API costs more than the dedicated plan it replaced. How would you diagnose and decide what to do?" *Hint:* look at execution duration (time spent waiting on dependencies), memory size, per-request executions, telemetry volume, and utilization pattern; then compare with the crossover point for dedicated hosting.
